Albert Eugene Boynton
Grand Master, 1925.1926

It is given to few 111en in a half ce11tury of life to occupy so large
a space in the political, bushiess and fraternal history of our State as
does Albert Eugene Boynton, our fifty-ninth Grand Master. He was
born at Oroville, California, October 9, 1875, was graduated fro111 the
Union High School of his native city in 1894, and from the law department of the University of Michigan in 1900. In 1901, at Afton, Glenn
County, he was married to Miss Susie Clark Davis, a wonnn of splendid
attainments of mind and person, who has proved to be a helpmeet indeed
and who is loved by her legion of friends. Four children, Robert.
Katherine, Elizabeth and Jeannette, have blessed this union.
Shortly after returning from college to Oroville to practice law,
our Grand Master was made a trnstee of the city of Oroville, serving
during the years 1906 and 1907. He has resided in San Francisco since
January, 1907, where for over seventeen years he was identified with
some of the largest business concerns of California. On July 1, 1924,
he was chosen as the Managing Director of the Industrial Association
of San Francisco, which position he holds at the present time. In 1907
he was elected State Senator for the Sixth Senatorial District, comprising
the counties of Butte, Sutter, Yolo and Yuba, and served continuously
until 1915. He was President pro tern and Republican floor leader of
the California State Senate from 1911 to 1915. He served as preside11t
of the Commonwealth Club of California in 1918 and 1919; was a
Republican Presidential elector in 1916, and in 1920 attended the Chicago
convention of the Republican party as a delegate.
In 1919 he was appointed by Governor Stephens as chairman of the
California Committee on Efficiency and Economy and in 1920 was
appointed a member of the State Board of Prison Directors for a term
of ten years, but resigned in 1924. He was chairman of the Republican
State Central Committee of California from 1922 to 1924.

Senator Boynton is a member of the University, Olympic, Commonwealth, Commercial and Masonic clubs of San Francisco; is a member
of the American Bar Association, the California Bar Association, and
the San Francisco Bar Association. He is also a director of the San
Francisco Y. M. C. A.

While most of his fraternal activities have been identified with
Masonry, he found time to serve as president of Argonaut Parlor, No. 8,

N. S. G. W. of Oroville, and as Noble Grand of Oroville Lodge, No. 59,
I. 0. 0. F. of Oroville. He is a life member of Chico Lodge of Elks,
No. 423.
Brother Boynton became a Master Mason in Oroville Lodge, No. 103,
F. & A. M., of which he is a life member, on May 25, 1897, and served
as Master of that Lodge in 1903.
He joined Washtenaw Chapter, No. 6, Royal Arch Masons, on
December 15, 1899, at Ann Arbor, Michigan, and is now a life member
of Franklin Chapter, No. 20, R. A. M. at Oroville. He received the
Royal and Select Master degrees on February 22, 1900, and the Super
Excellent degree on March 7, 1900, in Union Lodge, No. 11, R. & S. M.
at Ypsilanti, Michigan, but is now a life member of California Council,
No. 2, R. & S. M. of San Francisco.
He received the Order of the Red Cross in Oroville Commandery,
No. 5, K. T., on March 6, 1901, and the Temple and Malta, on April 3,
1901. He was Eminent Commander of Oroville Commandery in 1904,
and served as Grand Warder in 1916, and regularly through the stations
to Grand Commander of the Grand Commandery K. T. of California in
1923.
He is a member and officer of San Francisco bodies of the Scottish
Rite; a member of Islam Temple A. A. 0. N. M. S.; St. Francis Conclave, No. 15, Order of the Red Cross of Constantine, of which he was
Sovereign in 1922; San Francisco Pyramid, No. 1, A. E. 0. S.; and the
Order of the Eastern Star. He is trustee of the University of California
Masonic Club House, at Berkeley, and is one of the twelve directors of
the George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association which
has in charge the construction at Alexandria, Virginia, of the Washington
Memorial Temple.
Brother Boynton was Orator of the Grand Lodge of California,
F. & A. M., in 1919-20, and was elected Junior Grand Warden of the
Grand Lodge in October, 1922, Senior Grand Warden in 1923, and Deputy
Grand Master in 1924, and Grand Master in 1925.

MESSAGE OF THE GRAND MASTER
The Grand Master then read his Annual Message, which
wus hy the Deputy Grand Master referred to the following
('ommittee for segregation and distribution: Robert B. Gaylord,
William T. Lucas, William A. Clark.
llrrlhren of the Grand Lodge:
Our Constitution expressly provides that it shall be the duty of the
(;rnnd Master "to present, at each annual Communication a written
1111•ssage, therein setting forth all his official acts during the year,
1•xhibiting the general condition of Masonry within the jurisdiction, and
recommending such legislation as he may deem necessary or expedient
for the welfare of the Craft."
My year as the titular head of this great fraternity in the jurisdiction of one of the largest and most influential Grand Lodges has been
one of mixed pride and humility; pride in that my brethren elevated me
to the exalted station of Grand Master and that they have so cordially
amt whole-heartedly co-operated with me and supported me in my
l'lldeavors to keep the ship of Freemasonry on an even keel; pride in
the evident ambition of my brethren to sustain the reputation of our
venerable Institution for the practical application of our avowed virtues
of brotherly love, relief, and truth; pride in the splendid men who have
in the year been added to the rolls of our membership; pride in the
applied Masonry evidenced in your hearty support of our two visible and
noble monuments to Service, the Masonic Homes, one for the care of
the bodies and the solace of the souls of our aged brethren, their wives,
widows and mothers who, through fickle fortune, have been deprived of
home; and the other for the children who have been bereft of their
natural guardians, in which Home the fraternity is engaged in the Godgiven work of building character and good citizenship. More than even
all this, I am proud of the quiet and unostentatious work of relief conducted by our Lodges and our brethren to those who are in need and
concerning whom the public knows naught. This work is necessarily like
a light hidden under a bushel, but it illustrates the finest characteristics
of Freemasonry and constitutes an enduring monument greater than
marble, not visible except through the eyes of the hearts of those whose
sorrows and distresses hqve been assuaged by the helping hand and the
open purse.
With it all, I have felt humble and inadequate to the work of truly
representing the Masonry of California and the Islands of Hawaii.
"He hath showed thee, 0 man, what is good; and what doth the Lord
require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

11

with thy God?"
am keenly sensible of my shortcomings and my
inability to carry on the program of visitations established by some of
my predecessors. I have, however, earnestly tried to do justly, to love
mercy, and to walk humbly before God.

General Condition of Masonry
The condition of Masonry within the jurisdiction, in the main, is
good. "We are prospering probably as never before, both in material
resources and in the character of our novitiates. We are living in an
age of marvelous scientific clevelopment and in a land favored above
most of the earth, and Peace and Plenty are smiling at our doors. The
blessings which have been showered upon us should make us rejoice as
with David of old: "The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want. He
maketh me to lie down in green pastures: He restoreth my soul. Surely
goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life; and I will
dwell in the house of the Lord forever.''
Twenty-three Lodges are now working under dispensations issued by
the Grand Master, three of them by my predecessor. I believe that each ·
of the new Lodges fills a real want. Before granting any dispensation,
I made careful inquiry concerning the reason why the Lodge should be
formed, and every reasonable precaution was taken to know that the
formation would redound to the social and moral benefit, not only of
Masonry but of the community in which it was to work as a Lodge.
For I hold to the belief that no group of :VIasons should be permitted to
organize as a Lodge unless it first be shown that thereby they will be
an asset to the social and moral life of the State and to the community
in which it is to exist.
A list of the new Lodges, with dates of dispensations and the names
of the original members, will be shown in the report of the Grand
Secretary.
Politics and Masonry
There seems to be a tendency on the part of some misguided and
over-zealous members of our fraternity-and happily they are few in
number-to lose sight of the scheme of our ancient Institution by trying
to inject partisan politics into the Lodges. A few days prior to the
State primary election of August 31, a printed slip was given general
circulation among the Craft in the city of San Francisco, reading as
follows: "Dear Brother: Enclosed herewith is a list of the members
of the Craft, to be voted on at the coming primaries, prepared and
checked over by
Lodge. This list is authentic,'' and followed by
the signature of the :\faster and the name of his Lodge. It was un-

fortunate in several respects. In the first place, it was a reflection on
the intelligence of the voters to. whom it was sent. Secondly, the list did
nnt contain the names of all the candidates who are members of the
fraternity and it did contain the names of some who are not members.
T11irdly, the Master should have known that no Lodge is justified in
nllt•mpting to advance the interest of any candidate or group of candi1latcs for public office. The Old Charges of 1722 respecting the behavior
0£ Masons have ever been a safe guide, and the injunction that we are
"resolved against all politics, as what never yet conduced to the welfare
n£ the Lodge, nor ever will," is a doctrine which must not be infringed.·
The duty of a Mason to take an intelligent interest in all affairs
relating to the public weal is, of course, obvious. As a citizen, he should
give careful consideration to the fitness of a candidate for public office,
and this consideration should go to the individual worth and ability of
aspirants for public favor. The circular sent out by the Master of the
Lodge was a plain and unmistakable intimation that none but Masons
should be voted for at the primary election, without regard to the competency or moral worth of any candidate, thus rightly, in the minds of
non-Masons, placing the Masonic fraternity in a most unenviable light
as being supporters of men merely because of their affiliation with our
Craft.
At the time of the issuance of this political propaganda, I was
visiting the Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands, but a copy was forwarded
to the Deputy Grand Master George L. Jones, at Nevada City, and as
Acting Grand Master he promptly telegraphed to the offending Master,
ordering him to discontinue the distribution of the list of candidates
seeking office.
Another instance of a violation of Masonic ethics was brought to
my attention in July. The secretary of a candidate for one of the
highest offices in the gift of the people sent out a circular letter
addressed "To Masonic Bodies and Affiliated Organizations," extolling
the virtues of his candidate because he was a Mason. \Vhen the offending circular was called to my attention, a letter was at once dispatched
to the Master of the Lodge of which the candidate is a member, reading
in part:

"It is extremely unfortunate that a candidate for public
office should permit matter of the sort to be sent out, for it is
highly un-Masonic and generally results in a reaction against
such candidate. No Mason having regard for the tenets of our
Institution should use or attempt to use his memhership in a
Lodge to further his political ambitions. As Master of the
Lodge in which this candidate is a member, I direct that you
call this matter to the attention of the campaign manager and of

12

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the brother himself. I assume that a mere intimation of the
impropriety will be sufficient. A Mason has no right to subordinate Masonry to his business or political interests and you should
make this very clear to the two offending brethren."

condition which ought to be determined as intolerable and without the
pale of legitimate Masonic ethics.

It should be apparent to every thinking man that Freemasonry
cannot be legitimately employed as an aid to secure public favor or to
gain the confidence of others for the furtherance of political ambitions.
Every man of our fraternity, before even his petition is received by
the Lodge, is required to subscribe to a solemn declaration that he is
prompted to solicit the privileges of Masonry because of a sincere wish
to be serviceable to his fellow creatures, and promises, if accepted, to
conform to all the ancient usages and regulations of the fraternity. I
sincerely hope and believe that our brethren generally will resent the
~fforts .of over-zealous members to involve the good name of Masonry
m partisan political activities. It is happily true that Masons are in the
main good citizens, that in every community they are at the forefront in
all social, civic and moral endeavors for the advancement of the interests
of all the people. But we must not lose sight of the fact that there are
good men and true in the world who are not members of our Fraternity
and who, notwithstanding, are eminently fit to hold public office.

Flag Day
The 14th day of June, 1927, will mark the one hundred and fiftieth
anniversary of the official recognition of the flag of the United States
and it has been suggested to me that the Masonic fraternity of California'
as a testimonial to their fealty to the government for which the fla~
stands, should celebrate the sesqui-centennial of this glorious symbol by
appropriate public ceremonies. Assurances have been made by the Grand
Commander of Knights Templar that the Templars would be pleased to
c?-operate and participate in any program which may be initiated by
Grand Lodge. 1 submit the proposition for your careful consideration.

Masonic Insurance
Complaints of the activities of life insurance companies that profess
to confine their business to Masons only, seem to be perennial. By reference to the annual messages of Grand Masters for many years back
my brethren will note that the subject has been one of much concern and
~ di~icult problem to satisfactorily solve. The past year's experience
m this respect has been but a repetition of the complaints which have
heretofore been made and I believe that Grand Lodge should at this
Communication take affirmative and definite action to put a stop to a

13

One particularly aggravating case, which is typical, is noted here in
the following copy of a letter I wrote to the president of a life insurance
company doing business in California :
"Complaints have reached me from time to time that agents of
your Association, in their zeal for business, have approached
petitioners for the degrees of Masonry for the purpose of soliciting insurance in your Association. Many times the petitioner or
the Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft has been advised that
the Masonic fraternity approved of your business and that a
policy in your Association was necessary to advancement in
Masonry.
"A concrete case is that of a present member of a Lodge
in California who received his first degree December 10, 1925;
the second, January 21, 1926, and the third, May 20, 1926. On
or about January 22, 1926, he was approached by an agent who
solicited insurance in your company from this Fellow Craft,
receiving therefor the sum of $16.40 and giving a receipt on
which was written 'Policy to be dated February 16, 1926.' This
Fellow Craft was led to believe that the insurance thus solicited
was authorized by the Masonic fraternity. As soon as he discovered that the company using same was not so connected, he
ordered that the policy be di?continued.
"This is an intolerable situation, and if your Association
persists in soliciting insurance among the Masons of California
with the implied assurance that our members are being thereby
protected by the fraternity, we will take such steps as may be
necessary to protect our brethren from such further imposition."
The reply of the president of the association was long and specious,
stating, among other things, that "Our agents have the most specific
instructions that no implication should be made as to any connection
with Masonry. Our men throughout the United States are instructed
never to mention their business in a Lodge room, ante-room or any
Masonic building, and to limit their solicitations to occasions when they
call upon the prospect at his home or place of business. It is a fact
that all of the officers and agents of this Association are members of
the Fraternity and that we limit our business to ::Vfasons." Nevertheless,
this association does impose upon the brethren rather than go into the
open field of business endeavor and compete with other life insurance
companies along strictly business lines.

Discipline
From time almost immemorial, it has bt:en the custom of the Grand
Master to officiate at the annual installation of officers of the five old
Lodges located at Sacramento, a city distinguished in many ways, but
particularly, in that the convention which eventuated in the formation of
our Grand Lodge was held there. These ceremonies are by custom always
held on the festival day of St. John the Evangelist, December 27, or, if
that festival falls on a Sunday, the Lodges there usually meet on the
evening of the following day for the purpose of receiving the Grand
Master and for the installation of their officers. The several Lodges of
Sacramento fixed Monday, December 28, 1925, for their annual installations and all incoming officers and members were duly notified of the
date and the purpose. It so happened that another organization in that
city had arranged to officially receive the titular head of that organization on the same date and also to hold a ceremonial of initiation, and
for reasons of its own-which may have been good reasons-refused to
change its time of such reception. I wrote to the Masters-elect that this
would be a splendid opportunity for them and the other incoming officers
to determine whether the Sacramento brethren owed their first allegiance
to Ancient Craft Masonry or to another organization which depends for
its very life upon the favor of members of Lodges; that the presence
of every officer-elect and appointed would by me be expected, and that
any officer who absented himself for the purpose of attending the function of the other organization should not be installed at all. Notwithstanding this admonition, one officer-elect appeared to take the view that
the Lodge was secondary in his allegiance and refused to be present at
the installation ceremonies, and did attend the ceremonial of the other
organization. Subsequently, by my request, the resignation of the offending officer was accepted and another was appointed in his place, one
who would not recognize any fraternal call in preference to that of
the Lodge.

Right of Master to Refuse Petition

and effort of Masters to correct. One Lodge organized twelve years
ago suspended eighteen of its members in June of this year. Two were
restored in the same month. The returns for the current year of
twenty-eight Lodges, taken at random, disclosed suspensions of 418
members, with fifty-six restorations. It is possible, but not probable,
that these suspensions were necessary and for the best interests of the
Lodges and the fraternity, but I am inclined to the belief that in tbo
many instances suspensions are ordered without diligent effort on the
part of the Masters, Secretaries and committees to make every reasonable
inquiry concerning the financial condition of the delinquents and their
attitude of mind with relation to a continuation of membership.
There is only one valid reason why any member should be suspended
for non-payment of dues, and that is that the member desires to definitely withdraw from all Masonic work and interest. The Master
should appoint a committee composed of members who have a knack of
reaching the hearts-and purses-of men, and who will, personally or
by letter, interview every delinquent member and impress upon such
member that his Lodge is the best Lodge in the jurisdiction, and this
without disparagement to any other Lodge ; that there should be a pride
in the membership; that, if the brother is ill or out of employment or
otherwi~e in distress, the dues will be remitted and a receipt issued to
him for the amount of the delinquent dues. Or, if it be ascertained that
the brother may be living beyond his means or has developed some had
habit that entails the expenditure of too much money, to encourage him
into a better mode of living. Some of our larger and more prosperous
Lodges work on this plan with satisfactory results.

A question involving the right of the Master of a Lodge to refuse
to permit a petition for the degrees to be read in the Lodge was presented
to me, concerning whieh it is desired that Grand Lodge should definitely
decide. Two instances will be cited:
1. The Master of a Lodge, for particular reasons which were not
disclosed, directed the Secretary of his Lodge to withhold the petition of
one who, in the opinion of the-Master, was not fit material for membership. Tbe Master claimed that his objection was tantamount to a
rejection which would follow if the petition had been received, referred
and gone to ballot.
2. A Lodge received the petition of a notorious prizefighter who
manifestly was not under the tongue of good report. In this instance,
a storm of protest arose but, as reported to me, the officers of the Lodge
insisted that the petitioner was a moral young man and they intended
to see that he was elected to receive the degrees. It was even alleged
that brethren who protested were threatened with reprisals if their objections to the petitioner were not withdrawn. I am firmly of the belief
that the election and conferring of the degrees in this instance would have
brought odium on the Craft, and that I would have been justified, in
that event, in suspending the charter of the Lodge and ordering charges
preferred against the Master. I advised the Master to that effect. At
a subsequent stated meeting, the. investigating committee reported adversely on the petition and the obnoxious petitioner was declared rejected.
Our law distinctly states that "No Lodge
shall receive an
application for the degrees of Masonry unless the applicant be . . .
of moral conduct" and recommended by at least two members of the
Lodge. In the case of this pugilist, I believe the Master should not only
have refused to permit the petition to go before the Lodge, but that it
was his duty to order his Junior \Varden to prefer charges of unMasonic conduct against the two members of his Lodge who so far
forgot their obligations to the fraternity as to sponsor and recommend
a notorious character whose membership would be a stench in the
nostrils of all decent Masons and make a laughing-stock of California
Masonry.

Tuberculosis
Sponsored by the Grand Lodge of New Mexico, the National
Masonic Tuberculosis Association has been incorporated, having for its
object "to disseminate among the Freemasons of America and their
families and others, scientific knowledge and useful information as to
the causes and methods of treatment for -·the prevention, relief and cure
of tuberculosis." The president of the corporation is M:. \V.". Herbert
B. Holt, Grand Master of Masons in New Mexico. This jurisdiction,
by reason of its climate, has become a sort of mecca for hundreds of
people who are suffering from the dreadful "white plague," and interested
brethren are now endeavoring to enlist the co-operation of the Masonic
fraternity throughout the entire country. It goes without argument
that the problem of caring for tubercular people should be our concern.
How best to help in such work is a question not easily answered. Hence,
I appointed a committee of eminent :\1asons who have been making a
survey of conditions in our jurisdiction and who, by reason of experi-

Territorial Jurisdiction of Lodges
Because of the rapid growth of population in California and the
incorporation of many cities abutting the corporate lines of adjacent
municipalities, the question of territorial exclusive jurisdiction of Lodges
is one which now frequently causes friction and suggests whether it
would not be wise to change our time-honored policy in this respect. The
territory comprising Culver City is partly within the municipal lines of
the city of Los Angeles; the Lodge room occupied by Ocean Park Lodge
is in two cities, the Master's station being in one city and the station
of the Senior Warden in another city; Beverly Hills is a municipal
corporation within the corporate limits of Los Angeles; Signal Hill is
really a part of the city of Long Beach, and so on. Yet, under our
present laws, these Lodges cannot, without the cumbersome process of
having petitioners secure waivers of jurisdiction, receive applications for
the degrees from nearby neighbors. Several Lodges located in Los
Angeles County have this year presented petitions for special jurisdictional territory under the provisions of section 92a of our Constitution
which, if granted, will afford only temporary relief. I respectfully
request your thoughtful inquiry into this problem and, if by you deemed
necessary, that appropriate legislation be enacted to relieve what is now
a frequent cause of irritation.

Last spring I received a communication from the Grand Lodge of
the Philippine Islands regarding an ineffectual protest against the holding of a Shrine ceremonial in that jurisdiction. It appeared from the
communication that the Potentate, of Affifi Temple had gone to Manila

was held with the approval of the Imperial Potentate, resulting in much
ill-feeling as between over-zealous Shriners and the leaders of Craft
Masonry in the Islands. The moral support of the Grand Lodge of
California was requested.

21

Many requests for decisions have been received in the year and,
as is usual, most of them could have been answered by the Masters by
referring to the Constitution and Regulations. Many of the answers
were mere reaffirmations of decisions as printed in the Constitution and
I will not burden the record with them. Two may involve new interpretation of law, and are printed herewith.
1. A resolution to amend the by-laws was presented and in due
course was brought to vote and defeated. It was immediately again
introduced with a request that its consideration take the usual course
of going over until the next stated meeting.
I held that the resolution could not again be presented at the meeting at which a similar resolution was considered and voted on; that the
subject as to that meeting was closed; for it is a principle of parliamentary law that no question can be again offered which is substantially
the same as the one upon which the house has already expressed its
judgment. "If a question which has been determined by the Lodge
should again be proposed at the same communication, either in the
same language or in language substantially the same if it has been
negatived, or in language of a directly contrary import if it had been
adopted, it would be the duty of the Master to rule it as out of order,
and refuse to present it for consideration." (Mackey's Jurisprudence.)
2. A member of a T.odge purchased a life membership for his
father, who was a member of the same Lodge. At that time our section
129 of the Constitution providing a plan for life membership, read that
"only the income thereof shall be used by the Lodge, the original amounts
to be forever kept and maintained as and for a permanent life membership fund." At the annual communication of 1923 the section was
amended by adding this proviso: "Provided. nevertheless, that upon the
death of a life member, such sum as he shall have paid into said fund may
be withdrawn therefrom and become a part of the general fund of the
Lodge." The life member (the father) died subsequent to 1923 and
the Lodge, pursuant to the term of section 129 as amended, transferred
the amount paid by the son for the father's life membership to the
general fund. The son appealed to me that his payment constituted an
irrevocable contract and that the money paid for the life membership
should remain forever in the permanent life membership fund as a
memorial to his father.
I held that the Lodge had the right. under the terms of section 129
as amended, to allocate to the general fund any moneys paid into the
life membership fund for account of any deceased life member.

Co-operative Masonic Service Bureaus
At our annual communication of 1924 a resolution was adopted
providing "that the Grand Master appoint a committee of three to
investigate relief and employment matters and report at the next communication their findings and recommendations." Accordingly, a committee was appointed consisting of Brothers Louis Sutter, Brooklyn
Lodge, No. 225; Harry K. Wolff, Pacific Lodge, No. 136, and Leo
Bruck, Jewel Lodge, No. 374. This committee, by letter and otherwise,
consulted with brethren throughout the United States and reported to
Grand Lodge at our last annual communication, finding that there are
Boards of Relief in our jurisdiction whose organizations are unnecessary
and expensive, and recommending that a permanent Board of Control
should be appointed by the Grand Master, to which Board of Control
all applications for the formation of local Boards of Relief should be
referred. The committee presented the following resolution which, after
reference to the Committee on Policy, was adopted:
"Resolved, that the Grand Master appoint a Board of Control for Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus, consisting
of five members, one to serve three years, two to serve two
years and two to serve one year, and each Grand Master shall
appoint the successors to those whose terms expire, said successors to serve for a period of three years."
The Committee on Jurisprudence was directed to prepare the necessary leg is la ti on to carry the report into effect. That committee requested
that the matter of submitting a plan for carrying out the intent of the
resolution be deferred until this annual communication, and I assume
that it will present legislation thereon for your consideration.
It is an important question, and it is engaging the earnest thought
of other Grand Lodges. The matter of helping the unemployed and of
dispensing relief is, in the opinion of many Masons, one in which the
Pacific Coast jurisdiction should co-operate. At the annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Oregon held last June, Grand Master
Percy R. Kelly reported that through the efforts of the manager of
the Masonic Service and Employment Bureau of Oregon, an organization is being effected whereby co-operation may be had between the
jurisdictions of Washington, Idaho, California and Oregon, and he stated
that "When this is accomplished, it will serve to render the work of our
bureau more effective and, 'at the same time, guard and protect us from
the unworthy and dishonest." The Grand Lodge of Oregon thereupon
adopted the following recommendation of the special committee which
had been studying the problem:
"That the Trustees of this Grand Lodge be authorized and
empowered to assist in the formation of a co-operative organi-

!l3

zation among such Masonic Service and Employment Bureaus
and Masonic Boards of Relief as, in their judgment, may be
proper."
In this connection, I have had several letters from Brother Walter
L. Stockwell, President of the Masonic Relief Association of the United
States and Canada, soliciting the membership of the Grand Lodge of
California. This Association issues a monthly circular to all subscribers,
in which is printed a list of imposters and beggars not worthy of
Masonic consideration. The correspondence will be placed with our
Committee on Jurisprudence for consideration in connection with the
subject of a Central Board of Control.

Sunday Picnics
received a communication from the Master of King David's Lodge,
No. 209, in which he desired to know the attitude of Grand Lodge with
respect to picnics by Lodges on Sunday. My interpretation of the
attitude of Grand Lodge and of my own views on this subject are
expressed in the following letter which was sent to the Master:
"This seems to be a perennial question, and probably the
best answer is contained in part of the Address of Grand Master
Sherman (page 461, Proc. 1923) in which he recommended that
Lodges be prevented from advertising and selling tickets for
Sunday outings. He added that 'there can be no objection to
a quiet gathering of Masons and their families for an outing
on Sunday; nevertheless, the promiscuous advertising or sale of
tickets is not in keeping with the dignity of our fraternity.' The
Committee on Jurisprudence, commenting on the address and
recommendations, said that 'It is difficult to define with absolute precision in written law the duty of Masons in this regard,
and in any event we cannot believe that anything beyond bringing this matter to the attention of the membership is essential.
We heartily approve the sentiment expressed by the
Grand Master in this regard.'
"It would be unwise and unfair for a Lodge to hold a
picnic on a Sunday because many members 'Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy,' and could not participate in such an
outing without offense to their religious beliefs; and no Lodge
should sponsor any gatherings which could not be attended by
every member. If, however, it is desired by some of the members to foregather for an outing on Sunday, taking their lunch
baskets and their wives and children to some selected rendezvous
and there indulge in a sociable picnic, I would say that s.uch an

24

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE

outing would not in any wise derogate from the dignity which
should and does attach to membership in our ancient Institution. Invitations to such outings should be personal or by sealed
enTelope and never in a newspaper."

Base Hospital at Palo Alto
In 1924 Grand Master Crites, having in mind the welfare of those
of our brethren who had served their country well, and were, by reason
of infirmities contracted in the service, confined to the United States
Base Hospital at Palo Alto, appointed Past Master Seale of Palo Alto
and the Masters and ·wardens' Association of San Francisco a committee
to look after those afflicted brethren. Much good work and good cheer
resulted. A small sum of money was allocated for the use of the committee from Grand Lodge funds and the recipients-families of patients
as well as the ex-service men-were made glad, not only by the pecuniary
help but by the kindly interest manifested by our brethren. A small
balanoe is still in possession of the Masters and \Vardens' Association,
and I recommend that it be left there to be used in any way suggested
by the Association.
Masonk: History
At our last annual communication there was adopted the recommendation of Grand Master Reese that a committee be appointed to
report at this communication a plan for the preservation of the Masonic
history of California. I was fortunate in enlisting the services of three
splendid and enthusiastic brethren as members of the committee, namely,
Brothers Arthur M. Ellis, Sydney B. Brown and Milton J. Ferguson,
who will doubtless present to you their views on this important subject.
Brother Ellis, in his letter accepting the chairmanship of this committee,
tersely indicated his ideas, to which I heartily subscribe. He said, among
other things, that:
"There are four important matters that must be eonsidercd
by the Grand Lodge with reference to the subject: The first is
that we have been remiss in our observation of the memories of
a great many very worthy men. Active steps should be taken
to acquaint the ordinary Master Mason with the careers and
and deserts of our illustrious early Masons. Secondly, we should
take immediate steps to overcome the great loss in the burning
of the records of the old Masonic Temple. It is becoming increasingly more difficult to get mementos of our early members.
This should be done by interested and wealthy members of the
Craft in donating materials of this sort. I know of one collector ·in San Francisco, who is not a Mason, who has many of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

25

the writings of the first Grand Masters and, likewise, some of
the records of the early Lodges located in the mining regions.
"Thirdly, we should endeavor to put the Craft in the right
light before the public with reference to the services of its early
members. For instance, the explorations of California were
largely directed by Kit Carson. He was a Mason and a Senior
Warden of one of the military Lodges. Some of the first American settlers of California were Masons. A good illustration
of this is George C. Yount, who established a frontier blockhouse and outpost of American civilization in the Sonoma Valley
before Sutter had even come to California. The making of the
original Constitution of 1849 was largely in the hands of
Masons. Robert Semple, long Treasurer of Benicia Lodge, was
President of the Convention. The actual working out of the
details of the Constitution was put in the hands of Myron Norton, a delegate from San Francisco who later moved to Los
Angeles and who took the first steps in that city toward the
organization of a Masonic Lodge.
"Fourth, the investigation of these matters should serve to
render many of the old Lodges of the jurisdiction more active
in restoring their records and in inspiring their members with
interest in their history."
The points made by Brother Ellis are worthy of the serious attention of Grand Lodge, and I cordially commend them to your consideration and action.
Necrology
Grand Lodge and the world have, in the year past, lost two wellknown brethren in the passing of the Very Reverend Dean William
MacCormack, who served as Grand Chaplain in 1918, and Henry D.
French, who for many years was active in Masonry as an Inspector
and Secretary of Evergreen Lodge at Riverside.
These two Brethren reflected in their lives the best principles of
Freemasonry and the cleanest standards of manhood, and we who knew
them and loved them have profited by their exemplification of all that
goes to make fine, helpful men and good citizens. Each of them earned
and reaped an earthly reward by being dearly beloved by a legion of
men and women, and their influence for good will be felt for many,
many years.
Our Committee on Necrology will present a suitable memorial of
their passing.

Masonic Homes
At the beginning of my term as Grand Master, it was my pleasure
to reappoint Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams as a Trustee
of the Masonic Homes, to succeed himself. It was with much gratification to me that this brother, burdened as he is with many interests, would
again accept this appointment.
Few of our brethren know or can
visualize the tremendous amount of thought and work that are involved
in the management of our two visible monuments to applied Masonry.
It has been my pleasure many times to visit both Homes and see with
my eyes the material labor accomplished, and hear with my ears the
stories told by the old men and women and little children of the loving
interest manifested by all the members of the Board of Trustees in
the welfare of our wards. The Board is a splendidly balanced one:
the President, Brother Wollenberg, is a noted sociologist, and by reason
of natural gifts and long experience in welfare work, is an invaluable
member; the Vice President, Brother Gist, is a banker with a reputation
for industry and ability in the world of finance; Past Grand Master
Samuel E. Burke, through his long experience with the Homes and his
professional skill, is well qualified for useful labor; and Past Grand
Master Adams has not only endeared himself to all the residents of
the Homes but renders-without fee-valuable legal service.
These
Brethren, with the Deputy Grand Master and the Senior and Junior
Grand Wardens, comprise a Board to which we may justly point with
pride.

Hospital at the Masonic Home
One of the outstanding events of my year was the formal presentation by the Grand Commandery of Knights Templar of a hospital at
the Covina Home. The project was initiated at the annual conclave
of the Grand Commandery in 1924, at which time I had the honor of
being Grand Commander, by a donation of $10,000 as a nucleus for a
fund to build a hospital for the benefit of the children. At the annual
conclave in 1925 this fund was augmented by a further gift of $40,000,
all of which was devoted to the erection of the hospital. On the 18th
of September, 1926, the Grand Commandery assembled on the Home
grounds, and by appropriate ceremony the building was declared finished.
The Right Eminent Grand Commander, Auguste J. DeLamare, in his
usual graceful manner, introduced Past Grand Commander Dr. William
C. Hassler, who, in fitting speech, formally presented the hospital to
the Masonic fraternity of California. It was accepted by me as titular
head of the Craft, and the keys to the building were by me delivered
to and accepted by the Trustees of the Masonic Homes.
Hundreds of friends of the Homes were present, including all the
officers of Grand Commandery, drill corps of Southern California,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

27

ladies, and others interested in the great work of caring for the children
who are being schooled and trained to become useful citizens.
It afforded me great pleasure, indeed, to accept this magnificent and
useful gift, not only because of its utility and necessity as a part of the
Home equipment, but because it was indicative of the cordial good will
and spirit of co-operation as between Craft Masonry and the Order of
Knights Templar in California. In the name of the whole fraternity,
I here reiterate my sincere thanks to the Fraters of the jurisdiction for
this noble gift.

White Pine Lodge
On the 15th of August fire destroyed the hall in which White Pine
Lodge, No. 555, located at Weed, held its meetings, and there being
no other hall in that community, permission was granted by Acting
Grand Master George L. Jones for the Lodge to meet for six months
at Shasta. It is expected that at the expiration of this period the Lodge
will have arranged for the use of a suitable hall in the town of Weed.

Public Schools Week
Following the plan successfully commenced by Past Grand Master
Adams and what has now become an established policy of Grand Lodge.
I caused a proclamation to be issued (a copy of which is appended hereto)
fixing the week commencing Monday, April 26, 1926, for the seventh
annual observance of Public Schools Week by the fraternity in the
Past Grand Master Adams, notwithstanding his
entire jurisdiction.
numerous other Masonic and business activities, again accepted the chairmanship of the general committee, and with the hearty co-operation of
his fellow members, the week was observed in a fitting manner, redounding not only to the credit of the fraternity but, I believe, to the benefit
of our public school system. Reports from all over the jurisdiction
indicate that the splendid work of the committee and of the many
brethren who assisted in the work of bringing the subject of education
of the youth of the land to the attention of the whole public, entitled
all who in any way participated, to the commendation of the Craft. I
feel that we, as Masons and as citizens, should continue this great
work, to the end that our public schools will become, as of right, the
peers, and more, of all educational institutions. The idea is growing in
favor, and this year's observance was undoubtedly the most successful
that has been held since its inauguration. It has attracted national
attention, both in the fraternity and among educators, and in an article
in a Masonic publication of an eastern city, was referred to as one of
the most outstanding movements that was ever attempted by any Grand
Lodge and as an example that might well be followed in the jurisdiction
in which the paper was published.

and who is not .a Mason, a letter commending the work that was being
done by the Masonic fraternity and expressing his appreciation of it.
I am informed, by the way, that he was of material assistance in assuring the success of the meetings held in his county.

I believe Grand Lodge should be proud that it has placed California
in the vanguard in the matter of this educational program. In the year
1850, when ritualistic work was different in many Lodges, because of
the different jurisdictions from which the members had come, the movement to draft and choose a ritual which would truly represent the
Masonic spirit as we know it, was started. Our present glorious ritual
resulted. It took until 1899 to bring it to its present shape, with the
exception of the minor corrections made in 1924. That was the first
great step in Masonic education in California. \Ve have now entered
upon our second great step, and I am convinced that there has been laid
down. for us, in the plan adopted last year, a program that will mean
that in years to come our members will have a full and deep knowledge
which will tie them even closer to Masonry than now. Our educational
program appeals to me as a forward movement which should have the
unanimous support of every Lodge and member within our jurisdiction.
I earnestly recommend that Grand Lodge, at this session, adopt the report
of the Educational Committee.

Because of my great interest in the undertaking, I carefully read
each of the many reports, before sending it to the chairman of the
committee with a copy of the letter I had written in acknowledgment
of the receipt thereof. As will, I understand, be pointed out in the
report of the committee, there were two particularly pleasing features
disclosed by the reports: One was that there were several Lodges
which for the first time had joined in the observance this year; and
the other that certain Lodges had redeemed failures in the past by
holding extraordinarily successful meetings this year.
I desire now, publicly, as I have already privately through personal
correspondence, to express my sincere thanks for the co-operation and
assistance received from those Masters, Inspectors and other brethren
whose efforts made the seventh annual observance so great a success.

Masonic Education
Our Committee on Masonic Education will present to you its report
of the efforts which have been put forth during the year to further the
problem of educating the members of our fratemity in the history,
achievements, hopes and aims of this ancient Institution. \Ve were fortunate in securing again a committee compose<! of brethren who have
earnestly and intelligently endeavored to bring matter worth while to
the attention of the Lodges and brethren, and I believe that we are
getting splendid results. Of course, we cannot expect to make every
member a Masonic student, nor can we hope to entirely agree as to
the best method of imparting instruction.
In conformity with the authorization at the 1925 session of Grand
Lodge, I appointed an Educational Committee of twelve members. Upon
the committee reorganizing, the members thereof recommended to me
the appointment of Brother Reynold E. Blight, of Los Angeles. as
the executive director. My investigation proved the accuracy of the committee's recommendation and I, therefore, appointed Brother Blight to
that position. He has pursued his work energetically and capably, and
I believe the accomplishments of our Educational Committee and its
executive director write a bright page in the history of our Grand Lodge
for this year. Tl1ey have issued twenty printed bulletins on timely and
appropriate subjects and sent them to 1,105 officers and committeemen
in the subordinate Lodges. Each bulletin was accompanied by an instruc-

Visit to the Hawaiian Islands
One outstanding and pleasant experience in my year was a visit to
the Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands, aptly and well named "the Paradise
of the Pacific." Accompanied by Mrs. Boynton and my son Robert (a
Mason), I sailed on the 14th of August for Honolulu, at which port we
arrived in the early morning of the 21st, where we were joined by our
daughters Katharine and Elizabeth who had preceded us. W. ·. Charles C.
Pittam, Junior Grand Steward and the Inspector of the 95th District, had
arranged a carefully-planned ititierary and he, with the Masters and other
brethren, met us with a welcome so warm and cordial that we were at
once made to feel and know that our hosts were imbued with a generous
hospitality peculiar to the people of the islands of the Pacific, a hospitality which seems to be a blend of all the loving impulses of the heart
and mind. And we were glad to know that now we were permitted to
"View them near at home, where all their worth and pride is plac'd;
And where their hospitable fires burn clear."

Each day of our visit was but a repetition of the hospitality distilaycd on every hand. By Brother Pittam's genius for organization and
trum-work, the Lodges of the entire group of islands joined in making
our stay memorable.
The genial Governor of the Islands, Brother Wallace A. Farrington,
wns present on numerous occasions, as were all the old-time wheel-horses
of Masonry, and the Masters of the several Lodges with their officers
uml brethren were in evidence with kindly attention at each meeting.
I was privileged to visit every one of the eight Lodges: Hawaiian,
No. 21, le Progress de l'Oceanie, No. 371, Honolulu, No. 409, Schofield,
No. 443, and Pearl Harbor, No. 598, on the island of Oahu; Kilauea,
No. 330, at Hilo, island of Hawaii; Maui, No. 472, at Kahului, and
Kauai Lodge, No. 589, at Lihue. And each island could in truth be
rnlled "the isle of golden dreams." These Lodges are composed of men
who stand in the forefront of the social, moral and political life of the
islands and are a credit to the fraternity. Tbey are growing in membership slowly, as compared with Lodges in our more populous centers, yet
their accessions are, as a rule, not merely names on the roster but are
men apparently fully imbued with the seriousness and significance of their
duties as members of our ancient Craft.
Some of the side-lights of my visit were a flight in a sea-plane from
Pearl Harbor· a dinner which I gave to the Governor, Inspectors,
Masters and 'wardens as partial return for the lavish hospitality
bestowed upon me and my family, and a reception at the Moana Hotel
on the eve of our return home, attended by the brethren generally and
their ladies. The reception was preceded by a concert by the Shrine
Band which was highly appreciated.

Emergency Relief
The newspapers of Sunday, September 19, chronicled the informa·
tion that the west coast of Florida had been visited by a hurricane which
killed and injured many people, destroyed much property and left many
homeless and in dire need. Realizing that in calamities affecting a
considerable population, the old adage that "He gives twice who gives
promptly" is true, after conference with Deputy Grand Master Jones
and Junior Grand Warden Hutaff, I directed the Grand Secretary to
dispatch an authorization to assist the stricken people, which was done
by wire, as follows:
"San Francisco, September 20, 1926.
"Wilbur P. Webster, Grand Secretary,
Jacksonville, Florida.
"The Grand Master and all your Brethren of California
express sincere sympathy in distresses of the people of Florida.

32

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Please draw on me by wire if necessary for twenty-five hundred
dollars. More will be forthcoming if you indicate such need.
"]oHN \\THJCHER, Grand Secretary."
The reply of the Grand Secretary was that "So far we have been
able to handle the situation. Our Lodges that were not affected have
been fine in offering assistance and that, together with what our Grand
Lodge can do, has so far taken care of it. If we find we will need
outside assistance, you may be sure we will feel at liberty to call upon
you and greatly appreciate your offer at this time."
Under date of September 27 I telegraphed to Grand Master Cary
B. Fish, at Sarasota, Florida, renewing our authorization for him to
draw on us by wire. To date no draft has been received against our
funds and we conclude that our good brethren of Florida have been able
to handle the situation without outside assistance.

Masonic Clubhouse, University of California
One of the monuments to which all Masons in California may point,
with pardonable pride, is the Masonic clubhouse of the University of
California in Berkeley. The building, made possible by the generous
contributions of our members, is well adapted to the purpose fo~ w~ich
it was intended; and the use that is being made of it completely Justifies
the expense involved in its erection and maintenance.

College life is entered at the most impressionable and vital age;

1rntl the social conditions of our American universities and colleges are
hl'il!g severely arraigned.

Whether or not there is justification for the

~I riclures being made on college students, there can be no doubt that such

institutions as we are fostering and encouraging through the clubhouse
an· of material benefit in counteracting the effects of conditions of which
romplaint is made. Youth is particularly susceptible to environment;
a11<l in the clubhouse at Berkeley there is an environment that will result
111 the development of many a useful life. I make this statement not
mt'rcly because of my knowledge of the situation, but also because it is
the consensus of opinion of many men and women at the University of
I 'alifornia including, among others, President Campbell, Dean Cadman,
I lean Lucy Stebbins and other administrative officers of the University.
It has been my pleasure to visit the clubhouse on many occasions,
and I recall that on one of these I was filled with pride on hearing the
terms of praise with which President and Mrs. Campbell expressed their
appreciation of what the Masons in California had done for the student
ho<ly in the erection of the clubhouse. They referred especially to the
wonderful influence of the "fire-side gatherings" held every Sunday evening
tl11ring the semester, to which are welcomed not only the members, but
likewise their friends and associates.
As is of course known to Grand Lodge, the clubhouse is used in
common by the l\fasonic Club of the University of California, the \\l omen's
Masonic Club, the De Molay Club and the Ashlar Club, composed of sons
of Masons; and to it are welcomed all sons and daughters of Masons even
though not members of any of the particular organizations referred to.
l ncluded in the clubhouse .council also is a representative of Henry Morse
Stephens Lodge, composed of members of the faculty of the University
of California, administrative officers and students. This contact is, of
course, especially valuable.
It is the clubhouse council which directs the activities under the
supervision of the resident hostess, Mrs. Sally Pease, who also acts as
guide and counselor to all the young people; but the building itself, and
the use which may be made of it, is under the control and supervision of
Grand Lodge acting through a Board of Trustees. At the head of this
Board is the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of California, Brother
'William H. Waste, to whom too much praise cannot be given for the
wonderful service he is performing.
It is perhaps too soon to make plans for the erection of a clubhouse
in each of our other great institutions oi learning in California; but
one of the problems we must solve in the future is how to provide for
the students at the University of Southern California, and at Stanford
and the University of California, Southern Branch, if not elsewhere,

Order of De Molay
In 1922 this Grand Lodge placed itself on record regarding the Order
of De Molay, and again reaffirmed its position in 1924. In its inception
the organization was an experiment, but the numerical growth of this
wonderful movement and the results of its efforts among the young men
of our land has justified its existence and warranted the confidence that
we reposed in those who were inspired to found the Order and have
governed it to the present time.
While it is not a Masonic organization, its importance in the future
of the Craft is one that we cannot overlook. I bespeak for the Order of
De Molay a continued interest by the Masons of this jurisdiction along
the lines embodied in the resolutions above referred to. Our future membership must come from the young man of today. If he is thoroughly
conversant with the principles and teachings of the Masonic Fraternity,
even though taught to him in an organization that is not Masonic but
labors under its shadow, just so far will our future strength and efficiency
be multiplied.
·
There is a time in the life of every boy when some man or older boy
is taken as an ideal. That exemplar may be a good one or an evil one,
but in the initial instance that is not considered. Only after-years can
determine whether his mind has been turned in the proper direction.
I believe that every man and Mason should continually carry this idea
and ask himself the question: "Am I the kind of man I would like to see
my own son or the young man of today become?" Individually and
collectively, Masonry owes a duty to the coming generation. An interest
in an organization that has for its object the building of character and
good citizenship is one that will produce splendid dividends.

Suspension Upon Conviction of Felony Involving Moral Turpitude
Section 192 of our Constitution provides that, upon the conviction of
a Mason in the State or ;Federal Courts of a crime involving moral
turpitude, charges shall be preferred against him in any Lodge having
jurisdiction. To preserve our self-respect and to promptly purge our
roll of unworthy members, it would seem that this section should be so
amended that, upon the conviction of a Mason of a felony involving moral
turpitude, he should be automatically suspended from all the rights and
privileges of Masonry from the moment of his conviction. The Grand

It appears that no definite action was taken in 1921. Grand Master
Rodden, however, in his message to Grand Lodge, referring to the plan
presented by Grand Master Adams, reported that, with the idea that the

most gratifying. He concluded by saying, "Wherever the above plan has
been inaugurated more men have been enlisted in service, new ambitions have been stirred, and the ritualistic work has been improved,
by reason of the immediate and ever-present personal supervision."
Grand Master Reese revived the idea by reporting that his travels
through the Masonic districts of California and his contact with Lodges

is desirable, and that it will furnish relief in a great measure to the

that confront each succeeding Grand Master. It is then that we get to

at the right time. That my predecessors have spoken in heartfelt and
eulogistic terms of the many qualities of heart and mind of our Grand
Secretary, John vVhicher, does not preclude me from reiterating and
reaffirming those sentiments, for after a year of intimate and constant
contact with him, I can speak of his faithful and efficient cooperatio;
only in the most glowing terms. California Masons have in the person
of their Grand Secretary one who measures up in every way to the
highest demands of his office. The personal qualities of John Whicher
are equally matched by his astounding familiarity with all things pertaining to Masonry and his courtesy, efficiency, ability, and good judgment have endeared him to every Grand officer. He possesses all of
those qualities which go to make up a successful captain of industry or
a leader in every other form of human activity.
The Craft in this jurisdiction should feel honored in having his
valuable services, and I earnestly recommend to the Finance Committee
and Grand Lodge that the compensation of the Grand Secretary be
increased to a figure commensurate with the great work he is now
doing in his dual capacity as Grand Secretary and Secretary of our
Masonic Homes and will be called upon to clo in the future.

GRAND LODGE, F. & A. M. OF CALIFORNIA
ALBERT E. BOYNTON, Grand Master
SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA

PROCLAMATION
SEVENTH ANNUAL OnsERVANCE PuBLrc ScnooLs \VEEK

To the 1'vfasters, Wardens and Brethren of the
Several Lodges in This Jurisdiction:
The institution of Public Schools Week by the Masons of California
furnished evidence of our belief in, and active championship of, free
public education for all the children of all the people. Its annual observance is now an established policy of Grand Lodge.
The first observance was practically confined to Masons who assembled with their families and friends in meetings held in their Lodge
rooms. The scope gradually broadened; and last year almost everywhere
throughout the entire State, Public Schools \Veek was observed as a
community affair.
As it was last year, the primary objective this year will be to afford
the public in general, and the parents of school children in particular, an
opportunity to become informed with respect to certain phases of our
public school system that are being discussed and criticized. They will
thus be enabled to determine for themselves whether or not the criticism
is warranted; and if it is, how the defects may be remedied.
Kow therefore, I, Albert E. Boynton, Grand Master of Masons in
the Jurisdiction of California, do now designate and appoint the week
commencing Monday, April 26, 1926, for the Seventh Annual Observance
of Public Schools Week in the Masonic Lodges in this Jurisdiction; and
I do now request and direct that during that week there be held in every
community in California in which there exists a Masonic Lodge at least
one public meeting (and more if practicable), through which the people
of that community may have their attention directed to matters that
vitally affect our public schools.
It is likewise my request and direction that wherever practicable,
the meetings be held in the auditoriums of public schools; and that all
local organizations interested in civic work be urged to co-operate with
the idea and purpose of making the meetings public in every sense of
the word.
A Bulletin containing suggestions for arranging and conducting
meetings and with respect to the nature of the program desired will be

GRAND LODGE OF CALIJ)'OHNIA

43

i.~sued by the General Committee.
Every Mason, however, is hereby
directed to immediately fix a date for a meeting to be held during that
week, and to hold no other meeting or entertainment of any sort that
might interfere with the proper observance of Public Schools Week; and
our Inspectors are requested to give to the Lodges in their districts the
fullest co-operation and assistance.
Dated at San Francisco this 12th day of February, 1926.
ALBERT E. BOYNTON, Gratid Afaster;.

JoHN WHJCHER, Grand Secretary.

GRAND LODGE, F. & A. M. OF CALIFORNIA
ALBERT E. BOYNTON, Grand Master
SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA

San Francisco, ~farch 11, 1926.
To Inspectors of the Jurisdiction:
The primary responsibility for the success of Public Schools Week
of course rests on the Masters of the Lodges; but they should have the
active co-operation of the Inspectors. Jt would materially aid the Committee if they could look to the Inspectors for assurance that the necessary arrangements were being made hy all the Masters of Lodges in
their districts.
The Masters will endeavor to secure their own speakers; but if
unable to do so, they will communicate with their Inspector, and he
should make an effort to secure a speaker before making application to
the Committee. There are few communities in which a qualified speaker
cannot be secured from among the school men and women; and in many
communities there will be found men (or perhaps women) who, although
without any special knowledge of the subject, may readily qualify themselves with the Bulletin for Speakers that will he issued by the Committee and which may be had on application to the Secretary, Bro.
Vaughan MacCaughey, No. 930 Phelan Building, San Francisco.
Herewith enclosed you will receive a copy of the Bulletin Containing
Suggestions for Arranging and Conducting Meetings. Please read it
carefully, and assure yourself by inquiry of the Masters of the Lodges
in your district that they are making· their arrangements in consonance
therewith.
I should like to have a report from yon not later than the 1st day
of April, 1926, advising me of what has heen clone in your district for
the proper observance of Public Schools ·week.
Sincerely and fraternally yours,
ALBERT E. BOYNTON, Grand Master.

SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA

To the llllasters of the Several Lodges of This Jurisdiction:
One of the splendid accomplishments at the last Stated Communication of Grand Lodge was the adoption of the report of our Educational
Committee and the authorization of a similar Committee for this year,
together with the necessary appropriation for the carrying on of its work.
Tbat Committee is now well organized and has commenced to function. Its membership is as follows:
Irving Magnes, Chairman, 514 Easton Building, Oakland; ]. Karl
Lobdell, Vice-Chairman, 819 Hellman Bank Building, Los Angeles;
Charles H. Adams, Oakland; James B. Giffen, Sacramento; A. F. Heuer,
San Francisco; Maj. W. S. Overton, Piedmont; Alexander M. Cuthbertson, Redwood City; George B. Morgridge, Sierra Madre; Judge Ira
F. Thompson, Los Angeles; Cyrus Field Willard, San Diego; A. Huber
Winder, Riverside; Walter K. Tulter, Los Angeles.
Perhaps all of these brethren are well known to most of you, at least
in the respective districts in which they reside. Many of them paid
visits to various of the Lodges throughout the State last year in furtherance of the work of the Committee. Suffice it to say that they are deeply
interested in the work at hand and are anxious to lend every assistance
and support in bringing it to a successful fruition.
After a careful canvass, the Committee recommended the appointment of Brother Reynold E. Blight, 706 Stock Exchange Building, Los
Angeles, as the Executive Director for our Educational work. This
recommendation met with my hearty approval. Brother Blight could
hardly have been more highly recommended for this position than he
was. His Masonic experience is complete. He has been engaged in one
form or another of Masonic endeavor practically all his life. Moreover,
he comes to us with a record of both general and Masonic education and
study which well qualifies him for the work. He has been organizing
the program during the past several weeks and is now ready to present
it to you for your use.
I feel that if the program of our Educational Committee under the
direction of Brother Blight is put in operation in all the Lodges of our
jurisdiction, a long step forward will have been taken in California
Masonry.
I therefore urge that yon offer the Committee your whole-souled
co-operation by lending every assistance possible. I suggest that you
immediately select from your membership some brother who you know
is interested in our work and appoint him Chairman of your local Educa-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

45

Ilona! Committee. You and he should then appoint as many other members
us you deem advisable. The Chairman should be held responsible for
I he work in your Lodge and should be the member who will be in contact
with the Grand Lodge Committee. He should preferably be a brother
who can serve for several successive years in order that he may become
more efficient by experience. I further suggest that when your Lodge
t 'ommittee presents material for the use of your Lodge that you use it
am! let the Grand Lodge Committee have the benefit of your observation as to its results. I also suggest that you calt on the Grand Lodge
( :ommittee for all the assistance you may desire in the matter of
speakers, program arrangements, answers to questions and such general
i11 formation as you may not be enabled to acquire yourself, it being the
function of that Committee to fill such demands.
You will shortly receive a letter from Brother Blight outlining the
work and advising you what he has ready for you, and I cordially
request that you take up the subject matter thereof upon its receipt.
I am much interested in the success of the plan. It is laying the
foundation for a generation of Masons who will have more knowledge
to work with than did you or I. If we do not experience the immediate
results from this plan of work it does not mean that it is of no value;
on the contrary we are pioneering in a field of endeavor that has long
appeared necessary; we are now on the threshold of it. Let us extend
t•very effort toward its success.
Dated at San Francisco this 18th day of February, 1926.
Sincerely and fraternally yours,
ALBERT E. BoYNTON, Grand Ii-foster.

wht'cl was used to further the sale of the tickets. I have advised the
Master of the Lodge who called the matter to my attention, that he should
clircct the Masons who thus violated the laws of Masonry and of California. to return to the buyers all moneys paid for such tickets, failing
in which charges of unmasonic conduct should be preferred against them.
( )ur brethren who are members of other organizations are not by reason
of such other relation released from their obligations as Masons, nor are
thl'Y thereby absolved from any violation of the moral or statute law.
Conducting a lottery is gambling, and is forbidden by the penal laws
of our State, and of course is opposed to the law of Masonry. In order
that our brethren may know the State law relating to the selling of
tickets for chance, I here quote Section 319 of the Penal Code of
California:
"A lottery is any scheme for the disposal or distribution of property
hy chance, among persons who have paid or promised to pay any valuable
consideration for the chance of obtaining such property or a portion of
it, or for any share or any interest in such property, upon any agreement,
understanding, or expectation that it is to be distributed or disposed of by
lot or chance, whether called a lottery, raffle, or gift enterprise, or by
whatever name the same may be known."
The punishment prescribed by law for violation of the above provision is imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding six months, or by
a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars, or by both.
Your Grand Master has only the kindest feelings of friendship
toward other organizations made up of members of our Craft. Many it
not all such societies are doing good and assisting to a large degree in
raising the standard of citizenship and ameliorating the distresses of the
poor. But I insist that Masons must observe the laws of the land
and the laws of Masonry, whether operating under the guise of membership in other organizations or not.
The Old Charges of a Freemason say that "A Mason is obliged by
his tenure to obey the moral law," and a resolution adopted by our own
Grand Lodge states clearly and boldly that "the stern morality of
Masonry is practicable."
We make no pretense of controlling or attempting to control any
other organization, but we do have full penal jurisdiction over all Masons
within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California, whether
affiliated here or elsewhere, and in the exercise of such control I now
declare and order that from and after this date, any Master Mason who
conducts a lottery or sells tickets or chances in contravention of Section
319 of the Penal Code of California, or who otherwise violates the laws
of the land or of Masonry, shall be charged with unmasonic conduct by

Sincerely and fraternally yours,
ALBERT EUGENE BOYNTON, Grand Master.

May 28, 1926.
To All Masons in the Jurisdiction Wheresoever Affiliated:
Your Grand Master has received many complaints that members of
o~r . Fraternity engage in the conduct of circuses, carnivals, Sunday
p1c111cs and other forms of amusement, in which games of chance raffles
and kindred diversions are employed for entertainment purposes ~nd for
raising funds.
Protests have also come to the Grand Master from
Masters of Lodges and from brethren, relating to the misuse of the word
"Mason" and "Masonic" for purposes of personal gain. Insurance companies professing to insure "Masons" only and conducted without profitmerely for the purpose of doing good !-have solicitors in our jurisdiction
who make it their particular business to select newly-made Masons for
their specious line of argument concerning the duty of the member to
carry life insurance in a company which insures Masons only· and either
directly or by inference gives the "prospect" to understa~d that the
corporation is established solely on altruistic lines and with the moral if
not financial indorsement of the Fraternity. Some of the more zealous
agents even go so far as to solicit insurance from men who have only
received one degree in Masonry.
All these are in contravention of the spirit and some of them of the
law of Masonry, and should not be countenanced by members of our
Craft.
I have recently been informed that a group of Masons, as members
of an organization which requires membership in a Masonic Lodge as
a prerequisite to membership therein, had entered into an engagement to
sell chance subscriptions on an automobile to procure funds to meet the
expenses of a coming convention of said organization, and that a roulette

COMMITTEE ON TUBERCULOSIS
San Francisco, June 26, 1926.
To Masters of Lodges and Boards of Relief:
Sponsored by the Grand Lodge of New Mexico, the National
Masonic Tuberculosis Sanatoria Association has been incorporated, having for its object ''To disseminate among the Freemasons of America,
and their families and others, scientific knowledge and useful information
as to the causes and methods of treatment for the prevention, relief and
cure of tuberculosis." The co-operation of the Masons of California has
been requested.
In order that we may know with some degree of exactness the
actual conditions relating to the subject in our jurisdiction, and for the
purpose of informing our brethren, I have appointed a Special Committee
to investigate and report what, if anything, should or may be done by
the Masons of California along the lines suggested by the national association. This Committee consists of Past Grand Masters William P.
Filmer and David J. Reese, and the President of the Board of Trustees
of our Masonic Homes, \Vorshipful Brother Charles M. Wollenberg,
who will report their findings and conclusions at the next annual communication of Grand Lodge.
The questionnaires inclosed have been approved by me, and Masters
of Lodges and Boards of Relief are requested to give heed to them
and return their answers to the Committee before August 10.
Fraternally yours,
ArJlERT E. BOYNTON, Grand Master.

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In the providence of God I am permitted to present to you my
nineteenth annual report of the transactions of the Grand Secretary's
office, with an account of all moneys received and a summary of disbursements, together with all unfinished business. A detailed and
itemized statement of the disbursements of Grand Lodge has been
submitted to the Committee on Finance as required by the Constitution. I also append, merely for your information an account of receipts subsequent to the close of the fiscal year, July 31, 1926, to and
including October 5.
Membership
The membership of chartered Lodges as of July 31, 1925, was
114,555; Lodges under dispensation, reporting October 1, 1925, gave 962
additional members, the total membership then being 115,517. Chartered
Lodges this year show a membership of 121,656, and Lodges under dispensation report a membership of 756, the total being 122,412, a net gain
for the year of 6,895.
The total number of Lodges chartered and constituted since the
organization of Grand Lodge is 627. By consolidation and surrender of
charters 98 Lodges have been listed as extinct and our last number is now
529. If the twenty-two Lodges now working under dispensation are
granted charten at this communication, we will have 551 going Lodges
on our registry. The table following may be of interest:

Certificates for Masters and Past Masters
Last year Grand Lodge adopted a resolution directing the Grand
Secretary to "issue to any Master of a Lodge a certificate . . .

54

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

cedfying that such brother is Master of a Lodge, giving its name
and number and the period for which he has been installed; and any
Past Master may have issued to him a similar certificate showing
his period of service as Master of any Lodge in this jurisdiction."
Pursuant to this resolution I prepared forms of certificates and
mailed one to each Master in the jurisdiction, without fee. The Committee on Accounts was of the opinion that the cost of the certificate was so small that Grand Lodge could afford to absorb it. The
certificates for Past Masters were also prepared and issued on requests of Secretaries. The body of the certificate is 8~ by 11;4 inches,
on pure linen paper 14 by 17 inches, leaving ample white margin
for framing. A facsimile of the certificate is herewith shown. By the
close of the fiscal year 1417 Past Master's certificates had been
issued.

Degrees by Courtesy
As usual, and not for the best interests of Masonry, but rather
for the convenience of candidates, degrees have been conferred as a
courtesy to California Lodges by other jurisdictions, and likewise we
have extended such favors to Lodges outside. \Ve have asked other

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

61

jurisdictions to confer 61 degrees on candidates of our Lodges, and
have approved requests from sister jurisdictions to the number of
369 degrees. In a few instances the requests were for the conferring
of the second and third degrees upon candidates who were unavoidably absent from home for an indeterminate time, but who did not
contemplate remaining within our jurisdiction permanently. Requests
as to such candidates were reasonable. Many requests, however,
were in behalf of men who, after receiving one degree at the old
home, removed to California with their families with the avowed
intention of making a permanent home here. In common with the
sentiments e::tpressed by many Grand Masters and GJil.nd Secretaries
of other jurisdictions, I believe we should adopt the policy that
those who make their homes here and earnestlv desire to become
Master Masons, should secure <limits or waivers .of jurisdiction from
the old home Lodges and in due time regularly petition a Lodge
near their new home for the remaining degrees. In no other way ean
they have an opportunity to engage in any active Masonic work. I
submit this for your thoughtful consideration, in the belief that if we
do adopt some such policy, we could not be accused of a lack of
proper courtesy, but on the contrary we would thereby encourage
active interest in matters Masonic by men who under our present
regulations are given the privilege of merely becoming another name
on the roster of a Lodge, concerning whose activities they would
necessarily know nothing.
