ANNUAL ORATION

w:. Ezra VI/. Decoto, Grand Orator, delivered his annual
oration, which was received with every manifestation of
approval· and delight by the representatives present. The
delivery of the Orator seemed to bring his audience into
more intimate touch, and the cold type cannot do full justice
to the brother's effort. At the conclusion of the oration,
llrother Decoto was tendered a rising vote of thanks and
he was requested to furnish a copy to the Grand Secretary
for publication in the Proceedings, and also that copies be
printed for distribution to the several Lodges. The full
text of the oration follows :
My brethren, I am not sufficiently versed in the history of Masonry
to address you upon its origin, its accomplishments of the past, or its
hopes for the future. Neither am I a deep enough scholar or philosophc1·
to expound to you the real or fancied meaning of its symbols and to
n·ad into its ritual a covert meaning. But I have been permitted, through
my profession and my public service for the last twenty years, as permitted few men, to delve into the lives and motives of many men, to peer
into the minds of many people, to weigh what is worth while in life,
to see the failure of those who strive for false things and to measure
lhc happiness of those who, from instinct or reasoning, seek the real
lhings of life, and when found, treasure them as they sho11ld be trcas11rcd.
An older lawyer once said to me; "The friends who will be your
friends in the days of your prosperity. not envious of what you have
already accomplished, wishing further and continued success, rejoicing
in your advancement, and sharing quietly but none the less deeply in
«very bit of good fortune that comes to you; the friends who will seek
you out in adversity to offer you their assistance or their substance; the
friends who will come to you in the hours of bereavement, sit by your
Ni<le, utter words of comfort and lift the burden of suffering from your
troubled heart; the friends who will follow you alike in adversity as

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

72

73

PROCEEDIXG'3 OF THE

well as in prosperity, in sorrow as well as in happiness; the friends who
will cling to you as a mother clings to her child. with that same faith,
that same pride, that same hope, and that same love-those friends can
be numbered upon the fingers of one hand."
In my youth I doubted him, but as I approach maturity I am more
inclined to agree with him.
Next to love of parents and wife and child and home, my experience
has taught me to place the love of frieI'.d. If there were some one who
had the power to fulfill a promise and he should say to each one of you,
"My brother, your greatest desire will be granted, your dream of years
will be made to come true, you will have all for which you have striven,
the goal of your ambition will be reached, but, in payment for these
things you must walk through the days and years of the future bereft
of frien<ls," unless the boon sought meant the reclamation of some life
very near and dear to you, your answer would uniformly be, "Although
you give the things for which I've longed, for which I have devoted my
life, for which I have fancied I would give my all, still the price you
ask is too great. I might as well be alone upon a desert isle, as well be
adrift alone upon the sea, as travel through this life without friends."
There is no better example of the value of friendship than the price
put upon it by large financial institutions. Every big business, in the
last few years particularly, has awakened to the value of friendly relations between its own personnel and the people with whom it does business.
This has brought about the department of "public relations." All large
corporations, banking businesses and public utilities are stressing more
than ever the value of "public relations." In every service club, in all
fraternal Orders, in all public spirit movements you will find some high
official of some large business institution, some man of executive ability,
willing to take the time and give the energy necessary· to the enterprise.
He is not only permitted by the head of his organization to do this, but
he is encouraged to do it. In every golf club of the country you will
find leading men of big business taking the afternoon off in the miclclle
of the week to play golf. While such recreation has a value of its own,
its main value is the friendships that are formed or continued, a closer
personal touch with those upon whose good will big business depends.
It is a recognized principle of business that one of the most valuable men
that can be employed is one that can keep the friendship of those whose
business is essential.
May I quote from the philosopher, Emerson? "Pleasant are these
jets of affection which make a young world for me again. Delicious is
a just and firm encounter of two, in a thought, in a feeling. How
beautiful, on their approach to this beating heart, the steps and forms of
the gifted and the true! The moment we indulge our affections, the
world is metamorphosed : there is no winter and no night : all tragedies,
all enemies vanish-all duties even; nothing fills the preceding eternity

but the forms all radiant. of beloved persons Let the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

night after night listen to the same inspiring words which, in their final
analysis, teach love of our fellow man. As we sit together, bou~d by
the same sacred vows, one to the other, with the same common ideals,
the same code of ethics and the same sound philosophy, there is and can
be no more fruitful opportunity for the approach of friendship. When
the serious work is done and we gather around the festive board, singing
the songs we love, hearing the brothers we honor speaking to us their
words of wisdom, the mind at rest, the cares of the day forgotten, there
can be no greater chance for the consummation of the most sincere and
lasting friendships.
Again, among the officers of each Lodge, as they climb the ladder
step by step from the least important position to the supreme office of
master, there is the same common interest, the same periods of hard work
and the same periods of relaxation, and there slowly but surely grows
up between them a friendship that exists through the hurrying years and
year by year grows deeper and more enduring. There is to be found the
friendship of the princes among men.
In the entertaining of other Lodges, in fraternal visits, in the meeting
of the Masters and \Vardens Association, in our various Masonic clubs,
there is the same friendly opportunity. If it were left to me to point
out to all the Masonic Lodges of this state their greatest opportunity
toward their members and toward the Craft, I would seek to impress
upon them the desire for good fellowship, which, in the ultimate analysis,
is good friendship. I would point out to them the personal pleasure and
the personal gain that comes to them through the time spent in cultivating
the closer association with the good men of their own Lodge, and I would
try to impress upon them the treasure in store for them in the love and
admiration of their friends, and I would also impress upon them that
"the only way to have a friend is to be one."
There can be nothing more open to criticism than the failure of any
man to remember the welfare of his friend. Nothing can be more open
to censure than the failure of any man to speak up and defend his friend
when he is falsely accused.
Turn with me to Hamlet and listen again to the words of Polonius
in that comprehensive admonition he gave to his son, Laertes, as the
young man was leaving for France:
"There, my blessings with thee!
And these few precepts in thy memory
See thou character. Give thy thoughts no tongue.
Nor any unproportioned thought his act
Be thou familiar, but by no means vulgar.
Those friends thou hast and their adoption tried,
Grapple them to thy soul with hoops of steel."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

75

In conclusion, let me leave with you these words:
"Life's story has been often told yet each must solve anew its problems for himself. Our time upon the stage of action is but brief yet
in the drama each must play a part. The character is left for us to
choose, a villain, if we will, or a man of honor holding high above all
things, high as hope's great throbbing star above the darkness of the
dead respect for virtue and love of wife and home and friend."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MESSAGE OF
GRAND MASTER
The executive ability, sound judgment and personal sympathy of the
M:.w:.Grand Master are exemplified in his message to Grand Lodge.
Terse, yet comprehensive, firm where decision is required, broad in its
humanity, and ever upholding the lofty standards of Masonry, it may well
serve as a model for many a Grand Master to come.
Your committee recommends that its subject matter he segregated
and referred as follows:
I.

To the Committee on Jurisprudence:
Lotteries and raffles.
Master's duty in connection with reception of petitions.
Decisions.

Penalty for conviction of a felony, involving moral turpitude.

To the Committee on Necrology:
Necrology.
111e message of the Grand Master primarily stresses three great
aspects of Masonic obligation: humanitarian, civic and moral.
It may well serve as a chart not only for the present Communication
and the activities of Grand Lodge during the coming year, but it equally
deserves careful perusal and intelligent application by the individual
members ol our Order.
At the outset emphasis is fittingly laid upon the unostentatious relief
work conducted by the Lodges and the brethren, and which the Grand
Master appropriately designates as "an enduring monument greater than
marble." Attention is also directed to the more public benefactions for
brethren suffering from tuberculosis, and the emergency created by the
recent disaster in Florida. Such needs as these, and the continuing
fraternal service of the care for youth and old age extended by our
Masonic homes, deserve unremitting attention on the part of the Craft.
Civic obligation is well emphasized by early reference in the message
to the solemn preliminary declaration of every Mason that he is prompted
by a sincere desire to be serviceable to his fellowmen, and to the fact
that while all Masons owe a primary duty of good citizenship, nevertheless the good name of Mas01iry as an organization must not become

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

77

involved in partisan politics, and that in the absence of personal qualification. no man deserves political support merely because of his fraternal
affiliations. In this same connection, the Grand :\faster most fittingly
reminds Grand Lodge, as he has had occasion to previously admonish us,
that as Masonry pre-supposes good citizenship, and good citizenship presupposes obedience to constituted authority, so should the fair name of
our Order be carefully preserved from connection with lotteries, raffles
and other violations of the law of the land. The emphasis laid upon
the observance of Public Schools \N eek illustrates another aspect of
civic duty, and the fact that our hope for the future rests in the proper
education of American youth.
The moral attitude of Masonry, and the broad spirit of toleration
which must exist among men of many minds who meet upon the level,
is illustrated by the Grand Master's treatment of the ever-recurring
questions regarding the conduct of Sunday amusements. He reminds us
that organized Masonry should not be officially connected with promiscuous Sunday amusement, and, on the other hand, that toleration on both
sides should exist between those who desire private recreation on the
first day of the week, and those who strictly "remember the Sabbath day
to keep it holy." The need and the obligation for greater enlightenment
on the part of the Craft regarding our history, our aims, our opportunities and our accomp1ishments is mentioned in connection with the work
of the Committee on l\fasonic Education; an enterprise which deserves
the sympathetic cooperation of Grand Lodge, Blue Lodge and individual
Mason. As the civic welfare of the nation rests with the youth of today.
equally is the moral welfare of generations to come determined by the
early acquirement of such virtues as those which Masonry inculcates.
The Order of De Molay is strongly commended by the Grand Master as
a titting object for Masonic solicitude; its present conditions are promising, and it is recommended as an appropriate instrument for developing
a proper moral foundation for the lives of young men of Masonic
affiliation. Many of the leaders in the next generation will be found
among those who are now attending institutions for higher education,
and your committee joins with the Grand Master in commending the work
conducted by the Masonic Club House at Berkeley. and in recommending
the extension of that activity to other institutions in California.
It is regrettable that so many Grand Masters have found it necessary
to admonish the brethren against improper use of the name of our Order.
The man whose fraternal affiliations are animated by mercenary motives
has no proper place in Masonry, and we hope that the recommendations
of the Grand Master will lead to such legislation, and to the development
of such an attitude upon the part of members of the Craft as will preclude
the necessity for future rebuke in this connection.
The references in the message to the large number of suspensions for
non-payment of dues deserves fitting emphasis. It is a crying evil; and

78

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the recommendation that greater care be exercised in the reception of
members, and that greater attention be devoted to the existence of the
necessity for suspension, deserves most thoughtful consideration.
The preservation of outstanding features of Masonic history, both
physical and intangible, has been too lightly regarded and too long
neglected; the work of the special committee having charge of that
activity, and the recommendations of the Grand Master in connection
with it, are timely.
The presentation to Grand Lodge by the Grand Commandery of
Knights Templar of a hospital for the children at Covina, is an outstanding feature in the history of the past year. · The presentation was appropriately dignified by the ceremonies which attended it, and by the men
who participated in those ceremonies. It is to be hoped that other bodies
will further demonstrate the cooperation and good will which exist
between Ancient Craft Masonry and the organizations coordinating with
it, and thus exemplify the virtue of Masonic charity.
One of the most important recommendations in the message concerns
the appointment of Deputy Grand Lecturers and District Deputy Grand
Masters; it is to be hoped that these recommendations will inspire legislation solving this oft-recurring and vital problem of recent years.
The message is a worthy valedictory of a Worthy Grand Master.
Throughout his term of office, and during the activities of many previous
years, he has endeared himself to the Masons of California. His ability
and integrity, his self-sacrifice and modesty, his loyalty to his friends
and to the brethren of the Craft, his abounding sympathy and humanity,
are too well recognized to require recital. He has worn the mantle of
authority with credit to himself and with honor to the fraternity, and
his message fittingly closes his year of service.

W. T. LUCAS,

w. A. CLARK,
RoBERT

MASONIC HISTORY
\V.". Arthur M. Ellis, chairman of the Committee on
Masonic History, presented an interesting and instructive
talk, illustrated by stereopticon views, on early-day Masons
and Masonry, following which the report of the Committee
on Masonic History was read, as follows :
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Tl1e committee appointed by the Grand Master at the last Stated
Communication to report a plan for the preservation of the Masonic
.history of California, and on the feasibility of the appointment of a
Masonic Historian, respectfully present the following:
We found at the outset that the problems confronting us in this
State are without any parallel. We have been able to gain practically
nothing from considering the practices in other jurisdictions. In order
to get our feet on the ground we, the committeemen, have individually
and separately as private enterprises travelled practically all over the
the State during the past year. We have had three meetings and are in
complete harmony in our views. 1his report is not signed by Committeeman Milton Ferguson for the reason that he has been absent from the
State for some time on official business as State Librarian.
The first thing con fronting us is that a vast amount of historical
material of the utmost value has been lost. The destruction of the
Grand Lodge Temple by fire was an overwhelming calamity. At every
turn we meet some puzzling historical query which could be readily
answered if the old records had not been destroyed. Next, we find that
an unusually large number of lodges became defunct early in the history
of the Grand Lodge. By 1870 thirty lodges had ceased to exist, some
of which had large memberships in their day. comparatively speaking.
For instance, Rough and Ready Lodge and Polar Star (which latter
had been located at the forks of Poor Man's Creek), were among those
that had disappeared. Jn 1856 Rough and Ready had 55 members,
whereas in the same year the Los Angeles Lodge had 42, Oakland 29 and
San Diego 29. Polar Star boasted 26 members. With reference to
most of these lodges, we are in abject ignorance, although we know that
some of them in the mining regions functioned vigorously and effectively.
In 1854, the Nevada City Lodge had 94 members, and was the largest
lodge in the State excepting the lodges in San Francisco and Sacramento.
But the great outstanding fact relative to early Masonry in this
State is that there was an extensive field of Masonic activity independently of the lodges. Many Masons completely lost touch with their home
lodges through the extreme difficulties of transportation and communica-

80

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

tion and were not in good standing. This did not prevent them from
making themselves known as Masons. The Masonic tie was recognized
in places where there were no lodges and Masonic charity had heavy
demands made on it and to which it fully responded, both through individuals and groups. This phase of Masonry we believe should receive
iinniediate attention, as most of the facts rest in the memories of a very
small number of men, which number is being rapidly diminished by death.
This Grand Lodge is fortunately situated in one respect. The Bancroft Library at the Dniversity of California, and the State Library at
Sacramento contain vast collections of first-hand accounts of early
Masons and their activities and at present the curator of each is a member of this Grand Lodge.
It is our recommendation that for the present the activities of the
Grand I.odge in the historical field be directed actively to the collection
and' storing of authentic information in these fields, namely, the early
history of our older lodges. the extra-lodge :Vfasonic activity of California pioneers and the biographies of such early Masons as were important figures in making this State.
Should this suggestion. or a portion of it, meet the approval of the
Grand Lodge and the matter of establishing a mode of procedure to
accomplish this end, then we make the following recommendations:
First, that three depositaries be established in the State-one to be
the Grand Lodge Temple in San Francisco; one in the :\1asonic Library
in Los Angeles; and one in some suitable place in Sacramento. That all
material deemed worthy of preservation be copied in triplicate and that
one copy be placed in each depositary and there made available to any
interested Masonic student.
It is our view that no responsibility in connection with this work
should he placed on any of the regular lodge officers; they have sufficient
duties as matters now stand. A discussion of this phase of the matter
directly brings us to the matter of the appointment of a Masonic Historian which was referred to us. It is our view that a directing head
will be necessary to any successful work in this line. However, this
State is so large and the scope and sources of historical information
are so scattered and various that we see little hope of achievement without a subdivision of the work. vVe, therefore, recommend that a Grand
Historian be appointed and three Deputy Historians, one to represent
the central Bay region and tribufary territory; one the early mining
regions ; and one Southern California. We believe this is desirable ii1
preference to .the constitution of a Historical Committee as we think
little can be done without giving to those who carry on this work both
official standing and power as well as imposing direct respons.ibility on
them. It is our suggestion that the different Inspei.:tor's districts be
divided among the three Deputies and the Inspectors be instructed to aid

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

81

thl'm in finding in each lodge at least one member who will work in
m11formity with instructions from the Historians. Thus far this com111ittee has worked entirely without expense to the Crand Lodge. It is
apparent, however, that clerical and stenographic work will be entailed
f anything is to be accomplished. If this work is once started, too,
it may as well be admitted at the outset, there will be a future printing hill.

!

.
The ma:ter of gaining zealous cooperation from the various lodges
is one on which we are looking for further light. It is somewhat difficult
to obtain men with the training, time and inclination to do work in this
line that will be worthy of permanent recordation. We do not wish t~
ch-cd;e the members of the Grand Lodge with any roseate pictures of
11ronused results. A year of experiment will make us much more certain
as to what can be expected and also give us some definite idea as to how
wt· can proceed. It has suggested itself to us that it might be desirable
to honor the three lodges in each subdivision that do the best work in
this line during the year by placing them on a special roll of honor with
sp~·cial. recognition to the one of each group adjudged best by the Grand
I ltstonan. We do not believe that much time of the Grand Lodge in its
annual communication can be diverted into historical channels. \Ve
think it would be feasible, however, to have au evening session at some
time during the week at which matters of this sort could be presented and
discussed.

Tt will soon be one hundred years since the first immigrant Mason
h«came a Californian. Since that time we have passed through changes
and developments that in earlier eras would have required a thousand
years. We have spread ourselves over an area with the extent and resources
of an empire. In the work of this empire-building Masons and Masoni~
lrnlg~s have had a p~rt that is but faintly. visioned by the members of
the ~raft, and of which the profane world is absolutely ignorant. Duty
n·qm:es ~hat prop~r respect be inculcated to the memory of our patriarchs,
that Justifiable pride be engendered in us and that permanent records be
made for the multitude of Masons not yet born who will constitute this
<:rand ~odge in generations yet to come. The most effective ways to
a~:complish these .ends, in our opinion, can only be found by experiment.
1·01· the present, 1t seems to us that the mode herein outlined will prove
to he effectual.
Respectfully submitted,
ARTHUR

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
To the 111:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
.
It is with a great deal of pleasure that I herewith submit my
nineteenth annual report, most humbly thanking our Heavenly Father
for the many pleasures, comforts and health which we hav: been permitted to enjoy during the past year, and also for the contmued p~os­
perity of our beloved fraternity. I doubt if we really fully apprec1a~e
all these blessings which have been bestowed upon us, but rather ta ~
all this somewhat as a matter of course. I trust, however, th~t sue
is not the case, but that on the contrary, we are deeply conscious of

•

these blessings.
I have visited all the districts in the State, and have. held lodg_es

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

87

I was reading a report from one of our sister jurisdictions regarding the Inspectors, which said, "The Inspector who is to make a success
of his work should have certain outstanding qualifications for his
duties, but no substitute has yet been found that will satisfactorily
take the place of 'good common sense'." Section 56 of our Constitution explains the powers and duties of the Inspector, and he should give
these the most careful study, so that he may preserve a proper balance
hetween his own prerogative and the recognition due to the officers
and members of the lodges. The Inspector who thinks more of his
powers than of his duties, and who "drest with a little brief authority"
loves to make a display of arbitrary power, will soon find himself the
possessor of a fruitless crown and a barren sceptre. And yet there
arise occasions where firmness is the only alternative left, and where
after all other reasonable means have been exhausted, the Inspectors
must show themselves to be "Men who their duties know, but know
their rights, and knowing, dare maintain."
There have been twenty-two new lodges formed this year. :VIost
of these are in the southern part of the State. Our great concern is
not so much in numbers, but in the implanting of the real precepts of
Masonry, the making of Masons and not mere members, the building
into every life the fundamentals of manhood and the principles of our
institution, the development in all men of those cardinal virtues and
correct tenets which will give them the mastery of themselves and the
ability to serve God, our Country and our fellows. The selection of
officers by the "Who best can work and best agree" method, and not to
reward some personal friend, but by selecting those who when they
become ~faster, which means teacher, their attitude may be devout and
humble and their service a masterful one, considering all men as
brethren, and exercising a real influence in the community in which
they live, by teaching the Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of
man. This may be only the ideal, but surely worthy of imitation.
I would recommend that some definite plan be adopted for the
examination of visitors, whereby the Master of the lodge shall appoint
a selected committee to conduct the examination, they to find out if
the brother is a Master Mason, and not try to find out how much he
knows. Too often committees will keep a visitor answering propounded
<Juestions for a half hour or more. Any visitor should be able to convince a committee in not over fifteen minutes if he knows anything
at all. This may be done simply by the visitor telling the story in his
own way and words, and not by any method of interrogation or
catechism. The first thing for the committee to do is to look up his
receipt and his lodge in the list of regular lodges, and if found correct,
then to administer to him the Test Oath. This method would save much
time and trouble, and be far less humiliating for the visitor. I trust

88

PROCEEDINGS l1F

'l'Hl<~

that some action may be taken in this respect which will be of great
benefit to the lodges, and a blessing and comfort to the visitor.
I have accompanied the M:.w:.Grand Master on many of his
visits to lodges, and various ceremonies, which he has performed. All
these meetings have been productive of much interest and benefit to
the lodges and brethren.
I rlesire to thank the v:.w:.Grand Secretary for the useful information and courtesies extenrled to me in his office during the year, all
of which is greatly appreciated.
It is with much regret that I report the death of Brother Henry
Dearborn French, Inspector of the 98th District, comprising Riverside
County. Brother French occupier! the position of Inspector for sixteen
years, having been appointed in 1910, and a more painstaking and
conscientious officer could not be found, one loved and admired by all
who knew him. Brother French loved his Masonry, and practiced out
of the lodge the real precepts he was taught therein. He was a most
devoted husband and father, an honorable citizen and county ofncial.
In his death Masonry has lost a valuable brother, his lodge and the
community in which he lived, an active member and man.
Thanking the Grand Lodge and the brethren for the confidence
reposed in me as your Grand Lecturer.
Respectfully submitted,
THOMAS J. BAKER, Grand Lecturer.

Referred to the following committee: Charles \V. Go(J(lwin, Gilbert C. DeForest, Roy H. Parkinson.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON INVESTIGATION OF
TUBERCULOSIS
Past Grand Master Filmer presented the following report, which was adopted :
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
llrethren:
Your committee, to which was referred the request of the Grand
Lodge of New Mexico to join with that Grand Lodge and others in the
United States in the matter of caring for members of the Fraternity
suffering from tuberculosis, begs leave to report as follows :
In this matter, our first thought was as to what extent California
is involved; that is, the number of cases requiring financial assistance
of Lodges, whether the Lodges are giving all the assistance needed,
whether Lodges can possibly render all the assistance required, as to
whether hospitalization is available in the jurisdiction of California and
as to the number of cases that go out of the State for treatment.
In order to ascertain this information, the committee circularized
the several Lodges of the jurisdiction, asking each to report on the same,
covering a period of three years, to wit: 1923, 1924 and 1925:

1. Total number of cases, alive and dead.
2. Total number of deaths.
3. Number of patients aided.
4. Number of families aided.
5. Number of members now afflicted.
6. Number of members of families now afflicted.
7. Names and addresses of such sufferers.
8. Addresses of family of each.
9. Members of other jurisdictions suffering from 'tubcrclllosis living
in this vicinity.
'
10. Amount, if any, of assistance given in such cases.
11. Did Lodge of which the brother is a member assist, and to what
amount.
l<EMARKS:
, . The committee received reports from live hundred thirty-nine Lodges.
l hese Lodges reported for the three years three hundred thirty-nine
cases of tuberculosis, one hundred forty deaths and that they had spent
$62,830.88 in caring for afflicted members and their families; that nearly
all cases had been cared for in tubercular hospitals within our borders;

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

that during the three years which our investigation covered the number
of members that had left the State for treatment was negligible and that
most of those who had done so returned after a short absence.
Lodges have spent from a minor sum to five thousand dollars on a
single case of tuberculosis, which indicates their desire to do their duty
to these unfortunates. Many Lodges,· however, have reported small
expenditures and, while we have no reason to question any Lodge, we
believe that the appointment of a speci<!-1 committee to carry on the work
in the hope of gathering further data might be of benefit in solving this
important question.
The California Tuberculosis Association, receiving its information
from the National Tuberculosis Association, reports one hundred fiftythree deaths of Masons in California in 1925, and states that there is
an estimate of about thirteen hundred seventy-seven Masons in the State
who are now suffering with the disease.
Tuberculosis is an expensive disease to combat. One of the principal
causes assisting the cure of a patient is relief from worry, but the man
who is obliged to quit the working activities of life is often soon without
means of support to himself and his family and the worry incident thereto
is often fatal in its results. Very few Lodges can bear the expense
necessary in such cases and, in our opinion, these Lodges should be
helped by Grand Lodge.
From various sources of information we learn that those afflicted
were rendered remarkably uneasy in their environment and were prone,
after staying a short time in one location, to try another. This, we are
told, is due to the nature of the disease.
If Grand Lodge wishes to engage in the work of helping the brethren
of this jurisdiction who are affiitted with tuberculosis, through a bureau
or committee caring for said brethren or for a member or members of
his family in the sanatoriums of th~ State and in relieving the families
of said brethren, we believe that either or both could be done less
expensively than if this Grand Lodge should join with the proposed
National Tuberculosis Sanatoria Association. We further believe that
if this plan be followed the patient will, in all probability, be nearer,
and have the consolation of, his family.
The California Tuberculosis Association informs this committee that
there are thirty-eight tubercular sanatoriums in California; twenty are
county institutions, subsidized by the California State Board of Health.
The California Tuberculosis Association is a State institution and works
in cooperation with all hospitals in an educational way. It sends its
nurses into the homes of families affiicted with tuberculosis, to instruct
said families in curative measures, in avoiding contact with and in
preventing the spread of the disease.

We realize that the New Mexico plan contemplates a hospital, or
hoKpitals, the location of which has not yet been presented, and that the
hoKpitalfaation is for the Masons of the United States; but, at this time,
uot thoroughly knowing our own problem, we do not believe it wise to
rlll(age in any national enterprise because the money thus used might be
•tx-nt right here upon the hospitalization and care of our own brethren
1111d their dependents.

106

107

We cannot, however, but sympathize with our brethren of New
M1·xico in their endeavor to alleviate the sufferings of Masons afflicted
wii h tuberculosis and in their present intention to establish sanatoria and
liospitals. But we have the problem ourselves. The whole Southwest is
h1volved as the place where the sufferers are wont to go in order to
rrnch a favorable climatic condition necessary to a cure, if a cure can be
nlfocted, and here in California we have such climatic locations and
clraw the affected from all parts of the United States.
From reports received, we believe the Lodges are caring for afflicted
~lasons in their distress fairly well at an expense, small, as compared
with what is requested of us by the New Mexico organization, and,
•lumld we join with them, we believe the Lodges would still be obliged
to hear the local burden themselves.

P. FILMER,

DAVID

To the 1v1.'.FV.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University of
California, Inc., submits the following brief report :
Since Grand Lodge met one year ago, student activities at the clubhouse at Berkeley have continued along the now well established lines
of conduct, and in harmony with the approved regulations controlling
such functions at the university. A narrative of what has been done,
and a list of the various activities carried on by our students of .Masonic
affiliation would be merely a recapitulation of what has been said on previous occasions concerning the same matters. Suffice it to say that under
the watchful direction of the beloved "Club House Hostess," Mrs. Pease,
and the carefully considered administration of the student "Club House
Council," there has been no letting down from the very high plane on
which these activities have functioned from the very beginning. The
outstanding feature of the whole matter is that it is the unreserved opinion
of students, faculty members, and of the administrative heads at the
university that no one institution of its kind, on, or near the campus. has
a more stabilizing or beneficent influence on the student body than that
reflected by the Masonic Club House and its constituent activities.
During the year, Masons generally throughout the state have shown
an increasing interest in the Club House. The East Bay Masters and
vVardens Association has been a most helpful and encouraging factor in
bringing about this result. The following donations were received:
$1000.00 from the Grand Chapter Order of Eastern Star, donated,
and used, for the purpose of reducing the debt on the club house property.
$500.00 from the Grand Chapter Royal Arch Masons, donated for
furnishings for the club house; $250.00 used in the purchase of a "grandfather's clock"; $250.00 yet to be expended.
$125.00 from Palos Verdes Lodge, Long Beach, for the purchase of
hooks for club house library.
$100.00 from East Bay Masters and vVarclens Association, for the
purchase of books.
Nine copies of the "Blue and Gold" from 1890 to 1898, inclusive,
a rare gift, from Bro. E. C. Bonner of Alturas.

By Constitutional provision, the Grand Treasurer is Treasurer of
the Homes, and the Grand Secretary is Secretary of the Board of
Trustees of the Homes.

History of the Homes
It may be of interest to Grand Lodge to note here that the beginnings
of the Homes date from the annual communication of 1891, at which
time a resolution was adopted "That a committee of nine be appointed
by the Grand Master, whose duty it shall be to organize a Masonic
Widows' and Orphans' Home Association, or corporation." The committee was duly appointed, and in 1892 a plan of operation was reported,
and adopted, in which it was distinctly made clear that the Home should
always be under the supervision of Grand Lodge, and that the organization "should be only the executor of the charitable intentions of the

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Fraternity and in perfect touch with it at all times." The brethr n
throughout the jurisdiction approved of the proposed work initiated or
the purpose of relieving Lodges of the burden of caring for tq ir
dependent members in a central Home and to the expense of which! all
members personally and through their Lodges, would have an opportunity to contribute.
In 1893 a site near the town of Decato, consisting of 267.46 acres,
was purchased at a cost of $33,093, and plans for a building were
approved. Progress on the project was slow, owing to the general
financial conditions of the country, and little headway was made until
1896, when (October 14, 1896) the corner stone of the Widows' and
Orphans' Home was laid by Grand Lodge. The original building was
completed and dedicated October 12, 1898, and it was opened for the
reception of residents March 1, 1899. The intention to limit the privileges
of the Home to widows and orphans was soon changed to include
d~pendent Masons, and later to mothers.
At that time the gross membership in the jurisdiction was less
than 20,000. More than one hundred thousand good men and true have
since been added to our rolls.
An Endowment Fund was created in 1910, and through the persistent
and untiring efforts of Past Grand Master Motley H. Flint, who has
been Chairman of the Committee for many years, this fund has now
grown to the respectable sum of $513,562, the interest only of which
may be used for the maintenance of the Homes.
In September, 1909, the Masonic Home of Southern California
donated to Grand Lodge a large building originally built for a tourist
hotel, located near San Gabriel, and the children of the Home at Decato,
forty-eight in all, were transferred to San Gabriel.
In 1915 the San Gabriel site was disposed of, and a site for a new
home (35.1 acres) near Covina was purchased. Permanent buildings
were at once erected, and on September 8, 1916, they were with appropriate ceremonies solemnly dedicated to the practical ideals of our
Institution-to applied Masonry.

follbwing, indicate the number of residents for the several years:

Responsibility of Lodges
In our report to Grand Lodge last year we adverted to the matter of Lodges accepting members who become immediate subjects
for relief and who apply for admission to the Home within the
time limit-three years-very wisely fixed by Grand Lodge. We
stated in our last report that your Trustees interpreted their duty
to the Lodges with the widest latitude consistent with what we
conceive to be the fair intent of the craft .in the conduct and management of the Homes; and while it is embarrassing to deny the application of any Lodge in behalf of a needy member, yet we must
adhere to the proposition that Lodges should not attempt to shift

I

I
114:

PHOCEEDINGS OF THE

/.

I

to the Homes their proper work of relief. A particularly urgent ~ase
was recently presented by a Lodge having a membership ofi less
than one hundred, who elected to affiliation a Mason who had /been
a member of an Eastern Lodge for some thirty years. He had!been
a resident of the community in which the Lodge is located for
some six years, when he was prevailed upon by the members to
join the local Lodge. He was at that time well over sixty years of
age and an apparent liability. The Lodge was of course within its
rights to admit this good brother to membership. But in a short
time-much less than three years-he became a charge upon the
Lodge, and application was made in regular form for his admission to the Home. The application _was denied. Your Trustees are
of the belief that however difficult it may be for this small lodge
to maintain this brother, it would be unfair to the other Lodges
of the jurisdiction to shift the burden.
Another application filed in January, 1926, was in behalf of the
mother of a member who affiliated with a California Lodge in September, 1924, from another jurisdiction. The mother was at the tim..:
a patient in a psychopathic institution. The application was denied
for three reasons; That the son was able to maintain his mother;
that his membership here was but little over one year; and that the
mother was mentalty ineligible to the privileges of the Home.
Another case: A Lodge in September, 1924, admitted to membership, on affiliation from another jurisdiction, a brother who was
over the age of seventy, and a sufferer from an affliction of the
heart. In January, 1926,-fifteen months after his affiliation-the
Lodge applied for his admission t_o the Home, ac·companying the
application with bank checks aggregating over two thousand dollars. The Board took the view that the responsibility for the care
of this brother was primarily with the Lodge and returned the checks
with its denial of the application.
Yet another instance: A Lodge applied for the admission of a
member who was prominent in the work of another organization
which maintains a good home for its dependent members. The
brother was possessed of some property, and two of his children
were living, but with whom he preferred not to live. Inasmuch
as the applicant had two sources of relief other than the Lodge and
the Masonic Home, the Trustees were of opinion that the entire
fraternity of our jurisdiction should not be charged with this support, and the application was denied.
Recently application was made in behalf of the mother of two
young brethren, both whom were earning good salaries, but who
did not want the bother of maintaining a household by a hired com-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

115

panion or housekeeper. The Trustees are firm in their belief that
these sons, even at some possible sacrifice to their own conveniT.ce. should not expect the fraternity at large to support their
mother. Needless to say, the application was denied.
At the August meeting of the Trustees an application for admission to the Home was presented from a Lodge in behalf of a
hrother who had been restored to membership at a stated meeting
held July 8, 1926, and the application for admission was dated Au~nst 11, 1926. It was evident that the brother was restored to
~tanding for the express purpose of placing him in the Homeif the Trustees would consent. Of course the application was denied.
It L probably true that the brother is in distress, and entitled to the
sympathetic interest of members of the fraternity, but we submit in
;di candor that the Masonic Home should not be made a mere conV('nience, and that an approval of such an application would have
111 en unfair to the other Lodges of the jurisdiction.
Your Trustees of ~he Homes are· the agents of the entire meml>l'rship, and are endeavoring to faithfully and fairly administer the
~plendid trust we have assumed as your agents. It is no little task
hut it is a work which appeals to our hearts and to our best
lhoughts, and we present some of our problems and embarrassments
to you, not in the way of complaint, but rather that you may
lH" advised of some of the prohlems which confront us, and in the
hope that Lodges may realize that the Homes are maintained hy
.von for the purpose of caring for those of our brethren who are
nrtually dependent, their wives, widows, mothers and children, and
11nt for mere convenience.

Finances and . Building Operations
Your Trustees are dosing the year with a considerable indebtedness, due to the building program necessitated by the rapid
growth of population at both Decoto and Covina. The amount of this
indebtedness will be seen in the Secretary's report.
We feel that our income is sufficient to take care of this indebtedness and to provide funds for the further building operations
that are necessary.
The Administration Building at Decoto (the original building)
is in a dilapidated condition and a survey of the plumbing and
wiring installation indicates that it will all have to be repaired at
once. It has been found that .it will cost something like $35,000 to
make these replacements. After expending this money we still have
a brick exterior with wooden floors and partitions, a dangerous situation from both the standpoint of fire and sanitation. We have, therefore, decided to abandon this building as rapidly as possible for
housing purposes and to erect immediately to the south a new building of sufficient size to care for a hundred residents. Plans are now
being prepared for this purpose. It is estimated that this building

119

will cost approximately $200,000. lneluded in this estimate is the
rerr.odeling of the Administration building, by removing the third
story and converting it into a semi-roof garden, using th~ first
floor as at present for administration purposes and the second floor
for the housing of female employes.
Plans are on exhibition in the Grand Secretary's office, showing various studies to effect this change.

Improvement at Covina
The farmer employed at the Covina Home who is one of our
most valued employes, has been living in a rented house several
miles distant from the Home. Your Trustees were of the unanimous
opinion that he could render better service by living on the Home
grounds, and thereby be subject to instant call for the many emergent duties which pertain to his work. Accordingly a small structure
which was buitt several years before as a bachelor quarters for transient help was remodeled by adding a bed room 12x14, a screen
porch 8x16, a laundry porch 6xl2, and a garage 10x16, all with
necessary doors and windows, electrical fixtures and wiring, automatic heater, gas stove, kitchen sink, laundry trays, toilet, and such
other accessories as were necessary to make a comfortable small
home. The brother who holds the position of farmer, George Gradler, has been with the Home for six years, is happily married to
an estimable woman, and the Trustees consider him to be a real
asset to the Home. The entire cost of reconstructing the cottage
was $1,500.
It was necessary to construct cement curbs, gutters and driveway cuts on the Covina Home grounds, and the following work
has been done: 1000 feet of 18 inch curb and 30 inch gutter, 104 feet
of 4 inch curb on north side of the Superintendent's cottage, 200
feet of gutter 10 inches wide along the front of the hospital, and
to make six cuts and apron approaches to the ground from the
Home driveways.

Camp Tucker
Brother Mervyn Newberg, with his usual tireless energy and
love for the children, has again placed the fraternity under obligations by selling, for account of the Homes, all the holdings at Balboa Island on the west side of the canal, and purchased lots in Section 5 of block 7, where all the Camp buildings are now located. The
Camp site now has twenty-three of the twenty-eight lots in the
block. Sixteen wooden structures in all have been erected, and the

The Lodges composing the Los Angeles Board of Relief have
also displayed in a practical manner the live interest of the brethren
by agreeing to finance the building of a much-needed sea-wall on the
canal front of the Camp property. This will cost approximately
two thousand dollars.

Vacation Employment
Some of the children took advantage of vacation time by seeking-and finding-gainful employment rather than to enjoy the
pleasures of camp life. Fourteen girls and seven boys found work,
and many others were offered employment at labor which was not
considered suitable for them by the Superintendent. One ambitious
boy cut lawns; two worked in stores; one washed dishes in a restaurant; two worked as laborers on new buildings; and one expert
swimmer got a job as a life guard. Of the girls who showeJ their

121

\Ve take pleasure and some pride in reporting the vacation work
of the children, not only as tending to show the character and selfreliance of the youngsters, but as well that the Home is teaching
them the dignity of honest toil, even though it may be what is too
frequently termed menial labor.

Knight Templar Hospital
At the last annual communication of Grand Lodge an appropriation was made for the purchase of $40,000 par value of the stock
of the Masonic Temple Association which had been donated by
the Grand Commandcry Knights Templar of California for the purpose of providing a hospital on the grounds of the Home at Covina.
With the money thus provided plus the ten thousand dollars donated
by the Grand Commandery in 1924, the Trustees caused a hospital
building to be erected, and on September 18, 1926, it was duly and
formally presented by the Grand Commander to the Grand Master
as representing the entire fraternity, and 'in turn the Grand Master
delivered the care and custody of the hospital to the Board of Trustees of the Homes. The program of exercises was in charge of the
Grand Commandcry, and was as follows:

Description of Building.
The building is one story and is of fire proof construction. The
exterior of the building is of dark red brick with cream colored
terra cotta trim to match the other buildings of the Home, and has a
red tiled roof. The building covers an area of one hundred seventy
feet by fifty-seven feet, and has a capacity of twenty beds. Each
room opens on to an open terrace or uncovered porch so that the
patient may be wheeled out direct to the porch for sun baths, etc.
The building also contains a large operating room, where major
operations may be performed if necessary, X-ray room, sterilizing
room, Doctor's scrub-up room, office, head nurse's room, dental
room with two chairs, diet kitchen, and an attractive sun parlor and
play room for the children. In the basement is a large room for
laboratory, work shops, etc.
One attractive feature of the hospital is that the corridor side of
all bed rooms is constructed of plate glass, so that the nurse may
keep an eye on the patients without disturbing them by entering
the room. The building is completely equipped with the very latest
type of hospital furniture and equipment, the furniture being of
steel and having a dark mahogany finish, so that the cold appearance
or atmosphere of an institution is missing and the character of the
Home and restful feeling is established.
The architects of this building were Roth and Parker of Hollywood, who had direct supervision of all construction.
Many generous gifts have been made for the furnishing of the
hospital, all which are noted in the comprehensive report of Mrs.
Miller, Superintendent of the Covina Home.

Visit to Decoto Home.
\Vednesday of this week the representatives to Grand Lodge will
have a·n opportunity of visiting and inspecting the Home at Decoto,
where they will have the privilege of personal contact with the work
of the fraternity in caring for those of our brethren, their wives,
widows and mothers who are domiciled there. As we stated last
year, we ask you to bear in mind that each one of you is a partner in
this enterprise, and that criticism of the management of the enterprise, if of a constructive nature, will be welcomed by the Trustees.
We request that the per capita tax for the maintenance of the
Homes for the year ending July 31, 1927, be fixed at fifty cents.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Report of the Superintendent, Decoto Home.

The new laundry is equipped with modern machinery, a water
softener process has been installed in the basement of the men's
new building and a new 220 horse power boiler, water and oil pumps
have been placed in that part of the power plant formerly occupied
hy the old laundry. These improvements enable the Home to handle
the laundry work with greater economy and the service is adequate
for some years to come.

To the Board of Trustees, Mason,ic Homes of California:

I herewith present for your consideration my seventeenth annual report for the year ending August 31, 1926.
There has been the usual routine in the management of the
Home without any special changes during the year.
The gradual increase in the number of residents will, in the near
future, necessitate additional rooms, it having been necessary to use
the fourth floor of the men's new building for women employes and
the rooms at the cottage for men employes.
The members of our large family have cheerfully rendered assistance according to their strength, in the general routine work.
A loyal' effort on the part of each one has created a special spirit in
the Home and has resulted in a greater degree of contentment and
happiness.
The general health in the Home has been remarkably good,
with the exception of those who are feeble and infirm, owing to advancing years.
There arc now at the Home 218 residents, 114 men and 104
women. During the year there have been 37 admissions, 19 men and
13 women.
There are now 35 members being cared for in our hospital department, where they are receiving every care our physician and
nurses can give them.
The number requiring hospital care is gradually increasing. Additional room, when needed, can be provided by the completion of
the interior of the second floor of the two wings of the hospital
building.
A number of the brethren have assisted by their labors in the
carpenter and paint shops, store room, care of the garage, mail,
passenger and express service, office work, attending phones and
messenger service and light duties in a general way.
All minor repairs during the year have been made by the brethren. The boundary fences have been put in order and two buildings
have been built for farm machinery and tools.
The women residents attend to all the making, mending and
marking of household linen and clothing, and have taken charge not
only of their own rooms, but, as well, the ~alls, stairways, wash
room~ hand laundries and other parts of their departments. They
also a~tend to the changing of table linen and assist at times in work
connected with the pantry and kitchen.

135

As heretofore, the greater part of the hill ranch has been leased,
t•ither on shares or cash rental. The farm has supplied plenty of
fruit for the table, the surplus being dried and stored for future use.
The hay crop has given good returns. The garden has supplied
vegetables, berries and plenty of greens. The hog ranch has also
given good returns. The chicken ranch has furnished all eggs for
table use, the surplus being sold and preserved in water glass for
winter use.
Our deep well pump continues to furnish a plentiful supply of
water for household, garden, irrigating and building purposes.

Social Life.
The social life of the Home has been greatly enriched during the
year by literary and musical entertainments by generous volunkcrs from Oakland, San Francisco and nearby towns. The new assembly hall, with our modern stage and moving picture equipment,
has made possible the presentation of dramatic plays given by visiting Lodges and friends, all of which has contributed to the pleasure
of the members of the family. The evening programs often close
with dancing.
Moving picture entertainments are given every Thursday cvc11ing, card parties on Tuesday evenings, chorus practice on Friday
l'vcnings. Every Sunday afternoon finds the residents of the Home,
with their visiting friends and relatives congregated in the Assembly
I !all for Sunday service, after which a selected program is given
hy the Home Orchestra.
All holidays have been observed with appropriate exercises. The
specials were those held on New Years Eve, New Years day, Lincoln's birthday, Washington's birthday, Easter, Memorial Da·y,
Fourth of July, Thanksgiving Day and Christmas.

Library.
The steady growth of our library continues, there being at the
present time, in our main library and bra11ches, 5000 volumes on the
shelves. In addition we are the recipients, through members of the

136

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Fraternity, of daily papers and periodicals, which are placed on the
reading tables in the men's club room and the women's social rooms.
The Alameda County Free Library has opened a branch at the
Home, which enables our family to obtain many of the latest books
and gives us the opportunity to send for special books.
The donations for the year have been generous and are another
evidence of the deep and growing interest taken by the Fraternity
in the welfare of the Home.
Most \Vorshipful Grand Master, Albert E. Boynton and members of the Grand Lodge have made a number of visits to the
Home, also, many of the brethren and friends have spent many
pleasant hours with us.
I wish to extend my appreciation of· the services rendered by
the officers and employes throughout the year, in their respective
departments and express to the members of the Board of Trustees
my sincere gratitude for the counsel and advice given me when
meeting the various problems connected with the management of
the Home.
Fraternally submitted,
FRANK B. HART.MAN,
Superintendent.

Report of Superintendent, Covina
To the Trustees of the lv1 asonic Homes:
At the close of another year I am glad of the opportunity to
hricfly give you a report of the Home and of our family.
Each year brings its anxieties, its problems that are hard to
solve, its joys and sorrows; but after all, at the close of the year
we look back and see that our every effort has been repaid. We can
see some good that we have done, some child we have been able to
help, and we are able to understand each child a little better, help·
ing them to become men and women able to go out into the world,
carrying with them a realization of all the advantages that have been
theirs through the loving kindness and efforts of the Masons of
California.
The routine has changed very little, and we believe we have
kept up to as high a standard as was previously maintained. Each
child has some duty in keeping the Home in order, the smaller ones
in caring for their respective dormitories, and the larger ones have
added duties in the dining room and kitchen, and in keeping and
beautifying the grounds. This not only teaches them how to work
constructively, but contributes to their own mental and physical
growth, and fits them for more efficient service in future years.
The farm, orchard, garden and lawns have been well cared for
under the excellent supervision of M. G. Gradler, who has been in

152

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

charge of this work for a number of years. The larger boys assist
in this work during their leisure hours.
We have now 172 children in the Home. Out of this number
six are under school age and 53 are in High School. During the
past year the school grades, especially those of the High School
children, proved that they were taking more interest in their work
than they had ever done before. Three girls and two boys were
graduated from High School last June. One girl, who has been an
honor student through her High School course, is now to enter
Pomona College, one is taking a nurse's training course in Lane
Hospital, San Francisco, and one is to take a business course. The
two boys are working at present, but are planning to enter the
university later. One other girl from the Home decided she preferred to enter· a hospital and fit h~self for a nurse before completing her High School course. These children are very deserving of
the opportunity to continue their education and they are very appreciative. Many tears are shed when the time comes for them to leave
the Home that has been a home to them for so many years. Some
may think, since we have so many, that we would not miss the few
that leave us each year, but we do. We have grown to love them
as our own, and although they go out from the shelter of the
Home, they are still our children and we are interested in their welfare. We have one girl who is entering her second year at Univerdty at Berkeley, and another one her second year at the Normal
School at San Jose. Many of the boys and girls who were formerly
in the Home are holding good positions in various places. We keep
in touch with them and they come to see us occasionally.
The progress made by the music pupils the past year is very
gratifying indeed. The music room has been a center of much interest
and activity during this year, and is proving indispensable to the
normal development of the children. Realizing to the fullest the refining influence of music, Mrs. Ambos, the music instructor, has
spared no effort in training the children both in voice and instrumental music. A separate report of this work is appended hereto.
We consider the Sunday School a vital factor in the lives of our
children. The truths contained in the lesson each week are made
practical by applying them to the needs of the every day life. We
find it to the advantage of the children of various ages to divide the
Sunday School into four departments. This permits the children to
conduct their own services in their several buildings, thus giving
each child an opportunity to take. active part. By this means we feel
that the spiritual development of the child will grow naturally and
normally and works out the greatest good to the greatest number.

Our first Sunrise Easter Service was a memorable one. As the
sun' rose, the bugle sounded the church call of the United States
army from the distance, and just as the last note was dying away,
the children's voices arose in a Hallelujah Chorus mingled with the
singing of the feathered songsters gathered about. The raising of the
flag by two Boy Scouts during the singing added solemnity to the
occasion long to be remembered. We enjoyed this service, and we
extend to you a cordial invitation to attend our Sunrise Service
next Easter and enjoy it with us.
Another very beautiful and joyful occasion was the first wedding of the Home. Two of our former children-Ferdinand French

Our first Sunrise Easter Service was a memorable one. As the
sun· rose, the bugle sounded the church call of· the United States
army from the distance, and just as the last note was dying away,
the children's voices arose in a Hallelujah Chorus mingled with the
singing of the feathered songsters gathered about. The raising of the
flag by two Boy Scouts during the singing added solemnity to the
occasion long to be remembered. We enjoyed this ·service, and we
extend to you a cordial invitation to attend our Sunrise Service
next Easter and enjoy it with us.
Another very beautiful and joyful occasion was the first wedding of the Home. Two of our former children-Ferdinand French
aad Esther Ferguson-both full orphans, desired to come home to

155

PH.OCEEDINGS OF THE

GH.AND LODGE OF CALIFOH.NIA

be married, and we were very happy to give them a home wedding. As the bridal party descended the stairs, preceded by two little flower girls, our Girls' Junior Sextette sang the "Bridal Chorus"
from the opera of Lohengrin, with a beauty of tone quite unusual in
such young voices a.nd showing evidence of careful training. The
Vice President of our Board of Trustees, J. B. Gist, gave the bride
away. The assembly room was beautifully decorated, and after the
: ceremony a wedding supper was served. We are indebted to many of
the Masons and Eastern Star ladies for their interest and cooperation
in making that a beautiful wedding for their wards.
A greater effort is being made each year to better equip the dormitories. The children are enjoying their large living rooms very
much, where they meet socially, read, or study. The smaller children have a story hour of evenings and are encouraged to read, tell
or write stories. Some of these stories show quite a little originality
and some ability, and a few have been published.
The health of the children has been carefully guarded by the
doctors in charge, with the result that there has been comparatively
little sickness in the Home in the past year. This efficient service is
appreciated by all.
Every child is encouraged to take care of his teeth. The dentists
who have charge of this work have been generous with their services, so that the children's teeth are kept in good condition.
The new hospital, a gift from the Grand Commandery Knights
Templar of California is a beautiful structure, and is now completed.
It has a dental room, surgical room, sterilizing room, the nurse's
room, diet kitchen, linen closet, a solarium, and eleven wards which
. have been furnished by different lodges and individuals whose names
appear on another page in this report. The surgery, dental room, and
diet kitchen, as yet are not furnished. This is a gift that will be
appreciated far more than is possible to express in words, and will
do much toward promoting the health and the happiness of the
children.
We are most grateful to John F. Taylor of Cleveland City
Lodge, No. 15, for his most generous gift to us. It was his desire to
give something that would be of real value in our new hospital, and
he gave us a new Burdick Air and Water Cooled Quartz Lamp with
applicators. It has already proved itself to be of great value.
Another very necessary addition has been made to our laundry.
A new washing machine and another Prim press have been installed,
making a very complete laundry, and enabling us to meet the laundry problem of our fast growing family.

vVe have greatly appreciated the help given us by the ladies of
San Fernando Chapter, 0. E. S., the 0. E. S. Club of Lyra Chapter,
No. 144, Sunshine Club of Burbank Chapter, 0. E. S., and the Social
Club of Lankershim who have visited the Home and kindly aided us
in the sewing and mending for the children.
The Masons have continued to remember the family with entertainments of various kinds throughout the year. We are especially
indebted to Jack Brown of the Covina Theater, who has often
brought to the Home pictures of special interest and also invited the
children to his theater in Covina on numerous occasions.
The vacation at Balboa is always very enjoyable and looked forward to with much anticipation. It not only gives the children a
change, but affords them an opportunity to enjoy healthful sports.
Each year sees a few more comforts added to the already wellcquipped camp. The children are delighted with their double-decked
beds which were contributed by Mr. Wollenberg. Two new cottages
have been built in the last year. These are supplied with all necessary equipment and add much to the comfort and happiness of those
who have supervision of the children. Thanks to M. J. Newberg,
for this added comfort, for it was through his efforts that they were added.
Concrete walks have been added until practically all dormitories are
now connected with one another and with all other buildings. There
is great need of a new sea-wall to protect our camp during the high
tide, and we have bright prospects of having this built soon. The
Lodges comprising the Los Angeles Masonic Board of Relief have
contributed $2000.00 toward it.
To you, our Board of Trustees, I most sincerely appreciate your
labors and interest, and I cannot praise you enough for your kindly
support and untiring patience with me at all times. I wish also,
through this report, to thank the members of the fraternity for their
hearty support given us during this year. We cannot be too grateful
to them for their continued cooperation.
Respectfully submitted,
MAUDE E. MILLER, Siiperintendent.

Music Report for Season Ending June 21, 1926.
In submitting my report of the activities of this department, I
will endeavor to give a summary of the work done by the pupils of
the Home, the results of which have been most satisfactory.
Interest and desire for study has been maintained throughout.
Practice periods, a record of which is kept, show few absences and

156

PROCEEDINGS OF 'l'IIE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

those mostly on account of illness. One pupil shows a perfect record,
not having missed during the entire year.
Class piano instruction has proven of great value and has enabled ·21 boys and girls to study. Three hours a week is devoted to
this branch of the work. This, in conjunction with the private lessons, makes a total of 43 studying this instrument.
Those who play other instruments are encouraged in their work
by giving them an opportunity to play in Sunday School and on
programs. We have two playing the cornet, one the saxophone, and
one the violin. No child showing musical talent in any direction is
neglected.
The vocal pupils show much progress and several children have
manifested marked singing ability. In order to give as many as possible the advantage of vocal instruction, groups of two, four, six
and eight are given the same work as is given to those who have
individual lessons. Ten pupils have two private lessons per week
of thirty minutes each. Class instruction is a factor in this department. These range in groups of 18, 32, and 47, the latter being
junior boys. These meet once a week and a portion of the time is
devoted to vocal technique.
One of our girls sang an important part in an operetta given by the
Covina High School. In Grammar School the singing by the children
of the Home has received favorable mention, a fact of which we feel
jusly proud.
All holidays are appropriately observed. A program was given for
Highland Park Lodge during "Music Week in the Public Schools," and
other programs have been given throughout the year.
Owing to the number of pupils taking part, three recitals were given
in Studio Hall to close our season's work. It proved of great interest
to the children and gave them an opportunity to demonstrate their ability.
That the love for the best in music is being stimulated in the minds
of the children, is perhaps the most gratifying of all, for the "study of
music exalts life."

We are indebted to Highland Park Lodge, No. 382, Mt. Olive Lodge,
No. 506, Jinnistan Grotto and Jinnistan Vale, Glendale Commandery, No.
53, K. T., Guardian Lodge, No. 596, and San Pasqual Lodge, No. 452,
for entertainments given at the Home.
The Masons of Monrovia were hosts to the Masonic Home children
December 17. Members of the Lodge called for the children with automobiles and took them first to the Colonial Theatre, Monrovia, where
"Little Annie Rooney" was shown, after that to the Masonic Temple
where there was a beautiful Christmas tree and Santa Claus with a
gift for each child. Refreshments were then served. Mr. Baudine,
Mr. Foy and others from Warner's Moving Picture Studio were present
and helped with the entertainment at the Temple.
The Masters and Wardens' Association gave the children a Christmas
party at the Home, December 21. All gathered around a beautiful
Christmas tree and joined in singing "Silent Night." Miss Edith E.
Echholz assisted with the short program that followed, and Monte Blue,
of Utopia Lodge, No. 537, gave a very interesting and entertaining talk
and later came in a real, jolly, good Santa Claus, giving out presents
that had ben furnished by the Masters and Wardens' Association.
On December 25 "Billy Lord" and the children of Radio Station
KMTR brought Christmas cheer to the children at the Home. They

gave a musical entertainment, dancing, singing and instrumental numbers, and after the program the orchestra furnished music for all to
dance.
The Covina Masonic bodies took the high school and eighth grade
children of the Home to the football game (Covina and Bakersfield
teams playing) at the Coliseum in Los Angeles.
The Friars Club from the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co. visited
the Home and entertained the children with a minstrel show given by
the members of the club.
Glen Chapter, No. 357, 0. E. S. entertained the children of the
Home, taking them to the theatre at Glendora and after the show treated
them to ice cream cones.
A concert under the auspices of San Pasqual Lodge, No. 452, was
given at the Home June 13. The music was furnished by the Pasadena
Sciots' Band, Pasadena Chapter DeMolay Glee Club, Mrs. Edna Holbrook Bliss, violinist, and Miss Helen Dorothy Bliss, harpist.
