REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
WEEK
San Francisco, October 12, 1926.
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
At the request of the M:. W:. Grand Master this report of the
Committee on Public Schools \Veek is made directly to Grand
Lodge.
It is extremely gratifying to your Committee to be able to begin
their report with the statement that the seventh annual observance
was undoubtedly the most successful that so far has been held; and
this notwithstanding the fact that a very high mark was set last year.
Interest in the movement has evidently become far more widespread; and there seems to be a more general recognition and appreciation of its worth and importance by both members of the Craft, and the
public at large. This was made evident by the notable increase in attendance reported by the Lodges, and also, amt more particularly, by the fact
that there were several communities where the observance this year was
the first that had been attempted. Severnl of the• Masters reported increases in attendance over previous years in terms of percentage varying
from 50% to 300%; and there were many occasions where the auditorium
in which the meeting was held was not large enough to accommodate
all who sought admittance. In some cases, under such circumstances,
overflow meetings were held; while in others hundreds were turned
away. This was the situation even iJl one of our largest cities which
heretofore had been one of the "dark" spots; and this notwithstanding the fact that during the week there were seven meetings held in
that city. In more than one report from a small community it
appeared that at least one-half the entire population attended the
meeting.
The observance this year was apparently made more of a community affair than was even that of last year; and in far more numerous instances the chairman of the meeting was selected because
of his position in the civic life of the community without regard to
his fraternal affiliations. The reports disclosed the fact that where
particularly successful meetings were held, those in charge had
sEcured the cooperation of the local service clubs as well as of the
Parent Teacher Associations and the school people. There were
meetings at which the Presidents of the local service clubs were
guests of honor and were provided with seats on the p)atform. This
was in strict accord with the desire of the Grand Master and carried
out a suggestion emphasized by our Committee. It must be remem-

182

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

bered that our appeal is community wide; and that we are especially
desirous of enlisting the support and active cooperation of not only
the school people and the Parent Teacher Associations, but also of
all civic organizations in the community such as the Chamber of
Commerce and the service clubs. Our purpose in this is two-fold.
In the first place it will, of course, be of material assistance in securing a large attendance at our meetings; and in the second place it
will carry into those organizations a knowledge of the work in which
we are engaged. If we could secure for our movement the active
cooperation of such organizations as the Rotary, Kiwanis, Lions,
Exchange and similar service clubs, we would have gone far in the
effort we are making to arouse in every community an active interest
in our public schools.
The arrangements made by our Committee were substantially
the same as those adopted for the sixth annual observance. \Ve,
therefore, deem it unnecessary, in view of the very comprehensive
and extended report made last year, to detail our proceedings; and
instead, we purpose contenting ourselves with a recital of some of
the outstanding features disclosed by the reports from the Lodges.
In passing, however, it may be said that considerable material was
added to the Speakers Handbook issued by the Committee; and that
tl:erc were incorporated therein such portions of the "Public School
Catechism" prepared by Bro. A. R. Heron as it was believed would
prove of value to the speakers. A sufficiently large edition was
printed to not only meet the demands from speakers, but as well to
provide a supply for more general distribution. Copies may be
obtained on application to the Grand Secretary; and in this copnection it is interesting to note that several Lodges have already
secured a sufficient number for distribution to their members.
Reports were received from 462 Lodges. Of the Lodges reporting, there were only 14 that did not hold a meeting either separately
or jointly with some other Lodge. Of these 14 there were 7 whose
:Masters gave reasons which in the judgment of the Grand Master
and that of your Committee were believed to be good and sufficient;
and there were 3 others who had fairly good excuses. In addition
to the reports received from the Masters on the questionnaire prepared by the Committee, there were communications received from
some of the Inspectors reviewing in general terms the meetings
held in their districts with several containing extremely valuable
suggestions for the future.
We believe that public mention should be made of the fact that
the Grand Master acknowledged the receipt of every report by writing a personal letter to the Master of the Lodge reporting. This was
not merely an exceedingly gracious and thoughtful act which was,

of course, duly appreciated by the Lodges, but one, we believe, that
will result in great good; because the expression of his appreciation
of the splendid work that had been done, and of his gratitude for
the cooperation received from the Lodges, and his kindly words of
encouragement where the results were not all that they might have
been, will certainly be an incentive to further effort in the future.
The reports received by the Grand Master were promptly forwarded
to our Committee with copies of the letters he had written; and if
there was anything in any report that seemed to call for further
word from our Committee it was immediately forthcoming. This
was, generally speaking, in two classes of cases: One where the fact
that a meeting had not been the success that was anticipated was
attributed to local conditions, and it appeared from the report that
those in charge of the meeting had not followed the suggestions
made by our Committee; and the other where there was constructive criticism of either something in connection with the particular
meeting reported, or with respect to the general plan.
It was evidently a matter of great surprise to some of the
Masters with whom we corresponded with respect to their
reports, to learn that it was not a pro forma proceeding, or even
merely to ascertain whether or not a meeting had been held, that a
report was required ; but that each was carefully analyzed not only
with the purpose of securing data with respect to the instant observance, but as well to obtain information on which might be predicated
suggestions for the future. In passing it may be said that many of
the reports will prove of great value; and your Committee is particularly obliged to those Masters who not only fully answered the
questionnaire on which the report was made but who amplified it
with an accompanying letter. Many valuable suggestions were
received and have been noted and tabulated so that they will be available to the Committee in charge of next year's observance. Among
them was one from the chairman of a joint committee appointed by
a Masters and Wardens Association in charge of the observance in
a large city suggesting that in future separate plans be outlined for
communities in which the observance would be handled by a Masters
and Wardens Association, or some similar organization, or by a joint
committee from several Lodges in the same com~unity. By a
curious, coincidence there came to the Committee from another large
city the suggestion of a plan for handling the observance that was
very similar to that which had been pursued in the city first referred
to; including the idea of having no "work" in any Lodge on the
night in which a Public Schools Week meeting was being held in
that community. This was one of the things that had been done
in consonance with the ideas of the joint committee, and

183

184

PROCEEDINGS OF TIJl1J

also in compliance with the express desire of the Grand Master of
which every Lodge in the jurisdiction had been notified. In this connection it may be said, not by way of criticism, but merely as a
matter of information, that there were ideas suggested under the
belief, of course, that they were original, that were identical with
those set forth in the Suggestions for Arranging Meetings issued
by our Committee; and this was not the only indication that we
might cite of the fact that those charged with the arrangements of
a meeting had evidently not made themselves familiar with the suggestions contained in the pamphlet issued by our Committee.
As has been intimated, it is not our purpose to make specific
reference to every suggestion that we believe valuable. There is
however, one other to which we think attention should be herein
called because it was received from several sources, and also
because the advisability of its adoption in the future is made
apparent from facts disclosed by the reports; and that is, that
so-called "neighborhood Lodges" should not be requested to join
with any other Lodge outside of its immediate neighborhood. This
would not preclude arrangements for neighborhood meetings being
made by a Masters and Wardens Association, or similar organization, or by a joint committee acting for all the Lodges; but contemplates only that a separate meeting should be held in the auditorium
of some school in the neighborhood in which a Lodge is located.
So successful were the meetings held this year in the residential districts
of a large city that there is being seriously considered the idea of next
year holding a meeting in every school possessing an auditorium, and
having the necessary facilities, with the purpose of making an especial
appeal to the parents of the children of that school and the public of that
particular district; it being understood that where there is a neighborhood
Lodge, the details of the meeting should be handled by that Lodge.
This would also afford an opportunity to have the particular school
in which the meeting is held opened to the public either before or
after the meeting, with exhibits of work in the manual training,
domestic science and art departments.
In more than one report of the type to which we have referred
as being of great value to your Committee appears criticism of the
program, and in some instances of the speakers, which would appear
to be well founded. Generally speaking, indeed with very few exceptions, the programs were excellent, admirably arranged, and must
have proved exceedingly entertaining as well as instructive. Many
of the Lodges this year, as last, made the meeting itself only an
incident of the observance; including as a part of their program
visits to the schools and a display of school work either on the
evening of the meeting or on some other day or evening during the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

185

week. At more than one meeting there were provided refreshments
which had been prepared and were served by pupils of the domestic
science department, or the "chef's class," in some particular school.
There were, however, some programs which were entirely too
long and badly arranged with respect to the speakers. If a speaker
is placed at the end of a long program not only is he called upon to
address a tired and jaded audience, but perhaps because of the
nature of the program there has been created an "atmosphere" not
conducive to the kind of talk our speakers are expected to make.
Furthermore, it occasionally results in many of the audience leaving
before the speaker's place on the program is reached; some because
it is not the speaker's address that attracts them to the meeting, and
others who really would like to hear the speaker but who are unwilling to remain until a late hour even for that purpose. The very
f.rst consideration that should be uppermost in the minds of those
arranging a program is that it should not be too long; and generally
speaking, the "entertainment," particularly if by school children,
should follow, rather than precede, the speaker's address.
This
would not, of course, in any event, preclude an opening number by
a school choral or glee club.
The principal criticism with respect to the speakers was that
the address was not such as was expected and was inappropriate
to the occasion. While this is to be deplored, we do not see how it
can well be avoided; unless some arrangement could be made to
assemble prospective speakers at three or four meetings held in
different parts of the State some weeks, or perhaps months, before
the date of the observance. If this could be done, we might perhaps
be assured of speakers who would confine their addresses to subjects
we particularly desire discussed, and disseminate the information
promised the public. That, of course, was the primary purpose with
which our Handbook for Speakers was prepared; but although a
copy was furnished every speaker whose name was reported to the
Committee, it developed that unfortunately there were some who
made absolutely no use of it. Not only did they not familiarize themselves with the data therein contained, but their subjects were entirely foreign to the purpose of the observance. Instead of preparing
an address appropriate to Public Schools Week the speaker was
apparently content to repeat one, excellent in itself, but prepared
for a totally different occasion.
While on the subject of speakers, we feel we might here properly
call attention to the opinion expressed by one of the ablest of our
Inspectors who has been of great assistance in the work in which we
are engaged. He believes that wherever practicable the speaker should

186

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

be a man conversant with the local situation with respect to the schools.
\Ve are in accord with the views he entertains, provided of course that
there be kept in mind at all times the fact that at no meeting by any
speaker should there be any discussion with respect to any controversy
between individuals, or groups, in a community; even though it be in
connection with, or grow out of, public school matters. It is undoubtedly
true that the people composing the average audience are more interested
in the discussion of the school problems of their own community than
they are in a general dissertation on the subject of education; and it is
with respect to their own schools that they desire, and should have defi·
nite, authentic information. The speaker need not be necessarily a local
man; but he should be conversant with local conditions.
There were two particularly pleasing features disclosed by the
reports. One was the fact, to which reference has been already made,
that this year meetings were held by Lodges which have heretofore, for
one reason or another, failed to make any effort to join in the observance
of Public Schools Week; the other, that wonderfully successful meet·
ings were reported by Lodges whose officers had become discouraged
and disheartened by failures in the past, but who had persisted in the
face of apathy and even opposition.
As we stated in our report last year, we are not disposed to mention
any Lodge by name with either praise or censure ; because for obvious
reasons we could not name every Lodge entitled to great credit, and no
good purpose would be subserved by calling public attention to the few
whose Masters did not api)arently possess that vision, ability, energy and
courage so essential to leadership when difficulties are to be met and
overcome. We cannot, however, forbear making specific mention of a
few instances illustrative of the two features to which we have referred.
Among those which this year for the first time joined in our annual
observance, was a little Lodge with about 60 members located in a
sparsely settled community away up in the extreme northeastern portion
of the State, practically isolated from even the adjoining county. In past
years, everyone apparently assumed that the condition absolutely precluded
all hope for a meeting; and no one had the temerity to suggest that an
attempt be made. This year, however, perhaps encouraged by what had
been done by that little mountain lodge to which reference was
made in our report last year, it was decided to at least make an effort.
A committee was therefore appointed and the chairman promptly com·
municated with our committee explaining the situation and asking for
advice. In his letter he stated that they could not of course expect us to
send them a speaker but that if we would send them our literature they
would endeavor to obtain some one in the community to prepare an
address. \Ve were of course more than willing to be of such assistance

as we could be, and a program was prepared along lines suggested by us.
With what spirit these brethren engaged in their undertaking is indicated
by the fact that not only did they secure as their speakers the Judge of
the Superior Court and their Superintendent of Schools, but they had
the school children present the play "The Critical Hour" written . last
year for our committee. The meeting was a great success. Indeed, with
the spirit in which it had been undertaken, and the indomitable will,
energy and intelligence with which the arrangements had been made and
carried into effect, it could not have been otherwise.
We have made especial mention of this meeting not to give the praise
so richly deserved (because there are other Lodges no less entitled to
mention on that ground) but because it was typical of what was done
by other Lodges similarly handicapped, if not to the same extent, which
this year for the first time joined in our annual observance. Furthermore,
it furnishes a complete answer to those Masters, fortunately few in
number, who believed that conditions peculiar to their locality precluded
the possibility of a successful observance and were therefore unwilling
to make any attempt. If a Lodge handicapped as is this one can hold a
successful meeting, there would seem to be no reason for failure anywhere. It confirms our belief that the success, or failure, of any meeting is not determined by the size of the community, its geographic
location or the character of the population. Our meetings are public
meetings, with a community-wide appeal. However the people of any
community may differ in their views with respect to other matters, they
are all, generally speaking, interested in their schools; and wherever there
are school children there are parents constituting a prospective audience
for the right sort of meeting.
No less pleasing than the reports from Lodges for the first time
joining in our observance were those from Lodges which had each year
held a meeting, but this year, for the first time, had secured results they
believed anything like commensurate with the effort that had been made.
There were scores of such instances !mt we shall make mention of only
three.
It may be perhaps remembered by some, that in our report last year
we made mention of a comparatively large community having four Lodges
with an aggregate membership of nearly 1,000 in which the meeting was
a total failure for lack of an audience, there being only 15 persons
present. The reason given was "lack of cooperation." This year apparently that cooperation was not lacking, because instead of a failure they
reported one of the most successful meetings held anywhere. Not only ·
did the Masters of the four Lodges work in the utmost harmony, but
thev obtained announcements of their proposed meeting from the Rotary,
Ki~vanis, and Civic Commercial clubs, and secured the assistance and
active cooperation of the County Superintendent of Schools, the City

187

188

PROCEEDINGS OF THE:

Superintendent and the Boards of Education, and also of the Principals
of the High and Grammar Schools. Incidentally it may be stated
that all the meetings held in that county were particularly successful,
and that we believe it was due in great part to the fine cooperation given
by the school people.
There was another community in which a splendid success was
achieved this year where last year "the meeting was a disgrace to
Masonry"; and lest the characterization of last year's meeting may seem
too harsh, and unwarranted under any circumstances, we hasten to add
that the language is not ours, but is quoted verbatim from the report
made to the Grand Master. Fortunately the Master making that report
was able to add, "but this year it was a credit to all of us, and we are
very proud of the result." And well might they be. The attendance last
year was 45. This year it was 1,500; and a particularly gratifying fact
was that the Masons in the community were not "conspicuous by their
absence," 60 per cent of the membership of one Lodge being represented.
In making their arrangements it appears that they followed very closely
the suggestions made by our committee, giving especial attention to
securing the cooperation of the school people and of the civic organizations in the community.
The results achieved this year in the two communities to which reference has just been made indicate that in the last analysis success is largely
a question of the zeal, industry and intelligence with which arrangements
for a meeting are made and carried into effect. If further evidence were
needed, it would seem to be furnished by the last report to which we
purpose calling attention as illustrative of the instances in which successful meetings were held this year in spite of failures in the past.
This was from a Master who with evident, and justifiable pride
reported the success of a meeting which he had arranged in the face of
not only the apathy of the members of his' Lodge, but of even the pronounced opposition of some of them including most of his officers. They
had become disheartened and discouraged by failures in the past, and
because of their belie( that there was such a lack of interest in the
community that it would be impossible to hold a successful meeting
endeavored to dissuade the Master from making any attempt. He, however, in view of the proclamation of the Grand Master, believed it
was his duty to make an effort even though it might not be crowned
with success; and the effort he made was certainly not a half-hearted
one.
Apparently recognizing the fact that he could not depend to any
great extent on the Masons, he devoted almost his entire effort toward
awakening an interest in the remainder of the community, which by the
way was a small one. In the prosecution of his plans he made an

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

189

especial appeal to the parents of the school children. To do this he
first secured the cooperation of the County Superintendent of Schools
and of the principals and teachers of the Grammar School in his town
and also of the consolidated Union High School located in an adjoining
community. Through them he had the children take home to their
parents typewritten, or perhaps mimeographed, notices of the meeting
which was arranged to take the form of practically a school entertainment. It was these parents, with their relatives and friends, that apparently constituted the greater portion of the audience, but many others
of the community were also attracted to the meeting; and best of all
there were many members of the Lodge who although opposed to holding
a meeting nevertheless through loyalty to their Master, and recognizing
the interest that was being aroused, gave it their earnest support. So
successful was the meeting, and so pleased were all who were in attendance that, as he wrote, "Now everyone is delighted and we are all
looking forward to a rousing meeting next year."
Although there continues to be a more or less general complaint of
the failure of the Craft at large to attend our meetings, there was this
year a material improvement in this respect. This was probably the
result of the letter sent out by the Grand Master, and read in all the
Lodges, calling attention to the fact that the only disappointing feature
of last year's observance was that even at particularly well-attended meetings Masons did not constitute the proportion that would be naturally
expected; and perhaps also because of special eFforts made by the Maste~s
with their brethren. Several Lodges reported the percentage of their
members in attendance. It varied from 30 to 87 per cent, with one Lodge,
a comparatively small one it is true, reporting as present all its officers
with the exception of the Junior Warden who was ill and every member
with the exception of three who, as the Master put it, "could not possibly
get there."
The attendance apparently con,tinued to be the measuring stick by
which the success of a meeting is gauged by most of the Masters reporting; and of course this is not at all surprising. We ca.nnot, however, too
often remind our brethren that attendance after all 1s only one factor
to be considered. Keeping in mind the fact that the real purpose of an
annual observance such as ours is to direct attention of all the people in
the State to the same thing at the same time, it should be evident that the
mere fact that a meeting is held in any community in the observance of
Public Schools Week of itself accomplishes something; because the attendant publicity (and we have never heretofore had so much as was gi:en us
this year both through the press and by radio) focuses the attention of
the people of that community, at least for the time being, on their public
schools.

191

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is of course desired that all our meetings shall be well attended;
but if that desire were everywhere achieved it would be extraordinary.
The fact of the matter is that we are prone to expect too much. '!hose
arranging the meetings work hard and earnestly and, not unnaturally,
are disappointed and perhaps discouraged if their efforts do not result
in attracting the attendance for which they hoped. They lose sight of
the fact that they are contending with a condition which of itself militates against the probability of a large attendance. Indeed, paradoxical as
it may seem, there would be no need for holding meetings if they were
as well attended as they should be. The lack of attendance of which
we complain is due primarily to the apathy that brought about the
conditions that gave birth to the idea of Public Schools Week, and it
is to overcome and dispel that apathy that these meetings are being held.
The problem is of course one of education pure and simple. No good
will be accomplished by "scolding," and our brethren will pay little
heed to an appeal to their duty until they are awakened to a realization
of the worth of the movement in which we are engaged. It is the concrete only that appeals to those who have not the vision to sense the
opportunity presented to the Craft in California by the annual observance
of Public Schools Week; and it would be of course extremely difficult
to point out any definite tangible result that is being accomplished. It
would seem, however, that they should recognize the fact that the movement in which we are engaged is certainly well worth while, or it would
not have received the commendation and support of those who because
of their intimate connection with our public schools are best qualified
to form an opinion. In this connection we may say that among many
other letters received by our committee was one from the Acting Commissioner of Education in Washington in which he characterized Public
Schools Week as being "of tremendous value," and expressed the opinion
that no one with a knowledge of the situation would question that statement; and that one of the most influential Masonic publications in the
United States referred in glowing terms to our annual observance and
commended it as an example that might well be followed in the jurisdiction in which the paper is published.
Perhaps as succinct and comprehensive a statement of the idea
underlying our observance as has ever been made was contained in an
article in a newspaper published in a county particularly proud of its
schools. That article appeared in the form of an editorial and was
written by the County Superintendent of Schools. Referring to existing
conditions, and advocating and encouraging a fit and proper observance
of Public Schools Week in that community, it was therein said, "To
combat this destructive criticism, to correct errors which may creep into
an institution dealing as intimately with humanity, and to cement an
abiding friendship, faith and confidence with the public and patron,

there must be close contact between the public and its schools together
with free and open discussion of all questions involved." That, brethren,
is the real aim and purpose of Public Schools Week, and we celebrate
its annual occurrence in the belief that we are thereby doing our part
to assure to every child his rightful heritage to a sane, sound education
fitting the individual for a life of self-respecting, self-supporting, lawabiding citizenship.
All which is respectfully submitted.

REPORT OF EDUCATIONAL COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of the
Jurisdiction of California:
Brethren:
Your Educational Committee, authorized by the last session
of this Grand Lodge and pursuant to such authorization, having
been appointed by the Most Worshipful Albert E. Boynton, Grand
Master, herewith presents this report of its work for the year past.
The membership of the committee is as follows:
Charles H. Adams, Oakland;
Alexander M. Cuthbertson, Redwood City;
James B. Giffen, Sacramento;
A. F. Heuer, San Francisco;
George B. Morgridge, Sierra Madre;
Maj. W. S. Overton, Piedmont;
Judge Ira F. Thompson, Los Angeles;
·waiter K. Tuller, Los Angeles;
Cyrus F. Willard, San Diego;
A. Heber Winder, Riverside;
J. Karl Lobdell, Vice-Chairman, Los Angeles;
Irving Magnes, Chairman, Oakland.
The first item of importance was the appointment of an Executive Director for this Committee. After a careful survey of those
brethren who might be available for such work, The Most Worshipful
Grand Master, on the recommendation of the Committee, appointed
Brother Reynold E. Blight of Los Angeles. Brother Blight came
to us with the highest recommendations as to his qualifications not
only from a Masonic standpoint but generally, and the manner in
which he has proceeded with the work has, in the opinion of your
Committee, justified his appointment. He has given to the Craft
the benefit of his extensive education and wide experience and this
Committee feels that too much cannot be said with respect to the
good results which have been obtained from his energetic attention
to the work.
The Committee calls attention to its report of last year wherein
was set forth the plan of action for its guidance, which plan was
adopted by Grand Lodge. The effort of the Committee has been to
follow such portions of this plan as were deemed advisable and to
put in operation the general features thereof. Pursuant thereto the
following items represent the activities of the Committee during the
past year:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

193

1. Contacts have been formed with every Lodge in the jurisdiction

(a) By correspondence with all Lodges;
(b) By personal visits to many.
The correspondence has included letters of information indicating how the work of this Committee can be advanced within the
Lodges and pursuant to such advice numerous bulletins or pamphlets
hereinafter referred to have been furnished the Lodges.
Personal contact has been made by visits which the members of
the Committee have made to eighty. per cent of the districts in the
State; at such meetings the purpose of the work and the methods
of pursuing it have been outlined.
2. The most important feature of the Committee's work (incidentally one which is entirely new and not used in any other jurisdiction) is the establishment of contact men between the local
Lodges and the Committee. The Masters have been requested to
appoint local Lodge Educational Committees, the Chairman of which
are the representatives from the local Lodges to the Grand Lodge
Committee. This Chairman is the person who is responsible for the
educational work in the Lodge. He arranges for the meetings and
addresses, establishes and supervises the study circle, encourages
the ~oung Masons to read and study, takes care of the Lodge library,
and m every way cooperates with the Master in promoting an int~rest in Masonic affairs. Over three hundred of these representatives have been appointed and additionally many Masters have written to the E~ecutive Director saying that for the time being at
least they desired to handle the educational work in their Lodges
themselves. The Committee feels that as a result of these efforts
during the past year Masonic education is a vital factor in the
affair_s of the vast majority of the Lodges in our State. By the
appomtment of these representatives the Master has been relieved
of the burden of the work, has had an earnest, active worker cooperating with him in this distinctive Lodge activity and a nucleus
of ':orkers ha.s be:n form:d who will continue to function sympathetically and mtelhgently irrespective of changes in the official body
of the Lodge. Your Committee feels and recommends to the local
Lo~ges that s~ch representative should be retained in his position
durmg successive years (unless, of course, it should be found that
he cannot handle the work) in order that, having gained experience
he may utilize such during succeeding years. Of course, new mem~
bers may be added to the Committee and from these additional
members the Chairman of future years. may be chosen.

3. Development of local speakers. The Committee feels that
in the past too much dependence was had upon Masonic speakers.
These speakers were availahle only for Lodges within a close radius
of the centers of population and even in the cities small Lodges
were reluctant to ask busy business and professional men to give
the time necessary to make such speeches. Speakers who were well
versed in Masonic law a11d were qualified to make authoritative
addresses on Masonic themes were few. Other speakers, while interesting and authoritative upon their own special subjects, were
often diffuse and platitudinous when they speak on Masonic topics
and were prone to indulge in "glittering generalities," so that the
result was frequently unsatisfactory from an educational standpoint.
For the benefit of those Lodges that can not have well known Masonic speakers local talent is developed. This is done through the
medium of bulletins prepared by your Committee and which have
had in mind the express idea of being valuable for the use of local
speakers. The bulletins contain specific data of a Masonic character. The local speaker can find at the public library general information on the topic and the advice of the Committee has been
that m!'mbers of the Lodges whose interest has been and can be
aroused should use these bulletins as the basis of a talk, never to
exceed fifteen minutes, furnishing the Lodge thereby with the information contained in the bulletins issued by your Committee. A
very large number of Lodges have followed this plan and the results
appear to have increased interest and attendance at the meetings. As
times goes on these speakers will naturally develop and your Committee feels that they will constitute a large body of members who
can present in an interesting and instructive manner information,
Masonic and otherwise, to their own Lodges as well as to other
Lodges which they may visit.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON REPORT OF THE
GRAND SECRETARY
Perhaps the most important subject matter in the report of the
Grand Secretary is found in the comparative tabulation of the membership of the Craft. The net increase in 1926 was nearly double the
increase in 1918, and during this period of eight years, the membership
has expanded from 63,986 to 122,412 Masons in California. The net
increase for 1926, however, is approximately 1000 less than the net
increase in 1922.
The discouraging feature of the report is found in the heavy
increase in the number of those who have been suspended for nonpayment
of dues. In 1918, 609 were suspended for this cause; the number was
reduced to 467 in 1922, but in 1926 it increased to 982. The suggestions
of both the Grand Secretary and the Grand Master, that serious consideration be given to this loss and the causes which contribute to it,
cannot be too strongly emphasized.
The report contains many statistical features, which are of interest
to the Craft, but which do not require special mention in this report, as
they speak for themselves.
\Ve recommend that the report be segregated and referred as
follows:
1. To the Committee on Policies and General Purposes: Affiliation of
resident Masons, whose membership is in other jurisdictions (considered
under the heading "Degrees by Courtesy").
2. To the Committee on Jurisprudence: (a) Legislation with reference to the control of relief work (unfinished business). (b) Physical
qualifications for Masonry (unfinished business). (c) Amendment of
Sec. 115 on the Constitution (unfinished business).
3. To the Committee on By-Laws: Amendments to By-Laws.
4. To the Committee on Ritual: (a) Jewel for Past Grand Master
and Past Master (unfinished business). (b) Changes in the Ritual
(unfinished business).
5. To the Committee on Finance: Financial Report of the Grand
Secretary.
We join most sincerely with the M.'.W.'.Grand Master, in expressing the appreciation of the Grand Lodge for the manner in which the
office of the Grand Secretary is administered. We are deeply indebted
to the present Grand Secretary for the many evidences of administrative
efficiency and ability. We cherish even more highly his unfailing kindness and courtesy, and the daily manifestations of his ability and his
desire to promote the welfare of the Craft. Words can only feebly

199

express the affection for him which is found in the hearts of the
brethren. We trust that, for many years to come, he will continue to
be the cornerstone of Grand Lodge administration.
Respectfully submitted,

Duty of Junior Warden to Prefer Charges
In collaboration with the Committee on Grievances your Committee
on Jurisprudence has been endeavoring to formulate some legislation
that would make the transfer of a trial from one lodge to another on the
score of the disqualification of the Master less frequent. The added
expense, time, and labor involved in virtue of such transfer are cause for
rather frequent complaint. Of course, if the lodge itself, for some
cause be disqualified, transfer should and may always be had. A disqualification and consequent trans fer arising, however, out of the disqualification of the Master, due to his directing the Junior Warden to
prefer charges may, we think, with propriety be avoided. To that end
therefore we recommend that Section 189 of the Constitution be amended
by adding thereto, at the end thereof as it now reads, the following:
"If facts shall be brought to the attention of the Junior Warden of a
lodge showing any member, of whom his lodge has jurisdiction, to be
guilty of un-Masonic conduct, and if, for the period of thirty days following the bringing of such facts to the attention of the Junior vVarden, no
Master Mason in good standing shall have preferred charges against
such member, then and thereupon it shall become the official duty of
such Junior Warden to prefer such charges, in the manner in this
section provided as for a Master Mason."

Upon the adoption of the foregoing, in our judgment, paragraph 410
of the Regulations will no longer be necessary. vVe, therefore, recommend that it be repealed.

The report was adopted and Section 189 amended by
unanimous vote; and Regulation No. 410 repealed.

Right of Master to Refuse to Receive Petition

It will be noted that the procedure so prescribed is general in its
terms and without exception.· It would seem in the instant case that this
procedure so prescribed was strictly followed. The proposal to amend,
limited as it was, was in the opinion of your committee such notice as is
contemplated by that portion of Article XIII, just quoted.
The Grand Master has apparently confused the proposal with the
consideration of the proposal. It is unquestionably true that the amendment could not be considered or acted upon at the same meeting at which
it was defeated. Nor could it be acted upon at the same meeting at
which it was introduced. But we can find nothing in our law which
prevents a resolution to amend a By-Law being introduced at any meeting irrespective of any action which might have been taken at that meeting upon this or any other subject.
We find ourselves unable to agree with the Grand Master's decision,
and we therefore recommend that the same be not approved.

The Grand Master presents two matters concerning which, he says,
the Grand Lodge should definitely decide :
'( 1) The Master of a lodge "directed the secretary of the lodge to
withhold the petition" of one who, in his opinion was not fit to be
received. This was done by the Master under the belief that his action
"was tantamount to a rejection which would follow if the petition had
been received, referred, and gone to ballot."
In this we think the Master was in error. The action of the Master.
was the equivalent of a refusal on the part of the lodge to "receive" the
petition at all. This may be done only by a majority vote of the lodge,
see Section !01 of the Constitution, and not by the Master acting upon
his own motion. Nor was this the equivalent of a rejection following
reception of petition and unfavorable ballot. In the latter case jurisdiction over the petitioner with respect to his right again to petition for
the Degrees would be retained for a year. In the instant case, the petition
not having been received at all, it was substantially the equivalent of a
withdrawal and no jurisdiction was retained.
(2) The Grand Master recites the tendering to a lodge of a petition
for the Degrees from a person manifestly not under the tongue of good
report and notoriously unfit for membership. It is to the credit of the
lodge, these things being known, that upon consideration by the investigating committee the candidate was declared rejected. This prompt and
efficacious action served to advise the world that such proposed membership would not be tolerated and I think we may safely rely upon our
lodges to guard our interests in similar fashion should an exigency
again occur.

Report adopted.
Proposal to Amend By-Laws May Be Reintroduced Immediately
After Adverse Vote
Your committee has had under consideration the decision of the
Grand Master that a resolution to amend the By-Laws of a lodge could
not be reintroduced at the same meeting at which such an amendment was
defeated. It seems in the case under consideration that while such a
resolution was introduced, it was so introduced with the expressed
stipulation that it should not be considered until the next Stated Meeting.
Article XIII, of the Uniform Code of By-Laws definitely prescribes the
procedure where an amendment is contemplated, as follows :
"These By-Laws may be amended at any Stated Meeting by the
votes of two-thirds of the members present; provided, that written notice
of such amendment shall have been given at the Stated Meeting next
preceding."

Board of Control
In response to the direction of the Grand Lodge at its last Annual
Communication the Committee on Jurisprudence was directed to prepare
legislation to create a Board of Control to supervise and control the
activities of the several Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus
operating under the supervision and direction of the Crand Lodge, State
of California.
Section I. There is hereby created a Board of Control to consist
of five members to be appointed by the Grand Master. The term of office
of the members of the Board of Control shall be three years; provided
that the members of the first Board of Control to be appointed after the
adoption of this resolution shall hold office as follows:
Two members for the term of three years.
Two members for the term of two years, and
One member for the term of one year.
Their successors to be appointed for the full term of three years.
Section 2. The Board of Control shall have control over and
supervise the activities of Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus
now existing or hereafter to be crt'ated under the authority of the
Grand Lodge of California.
Section 3. Immediately upon assuming office the Hoard of Control
hereby created shall cause a survey to be made of all Boards of Relief
and Employment Bureaus now existing. and shall make a report to the
Grand Master as to the efficiency, usefulness, and necessity for each of
said boards; and shall also make such investigation as it deems proper
with reference to the creation of new Boards of Relief and Employment

204

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Bureaus in other localities other than those organizations now existing
and make such recommendations to the Grand Master with reference
thereto as they shall deem advisable.
Acting upon the report and recommendation of the Board of Control
the Grand Ma~ter shall have full power to abolish any Board of Relief
or Employment Bureau now operating and existing and upon a~plication
therefor to create such new and additional boards as in his Judgment
will best serve the interests of the Craft in this State.
Section 4. All applications to organize new and additional Boards
of Relief or Employment Bureaus shall be directed to the Board of
Control. The board shall make such investigation as in its judgment the
situation warrants and report its conclusions and recommendations to
the Grand Master, who shall take such action as in his discretion he
shall deem advisable.
Section 5. All applications from Boards of Relief or Employment
Bureaus or lodges for funds or reimbursement shall be made to the
Board of Control at least thirty days prior to each Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge. The Board of Control shall make thorough
investigation of the merits of such applications and report its findings
and recommendations to the Chairman of the Finance Committee of the
Grand Lodge on or before the opening day of each Annual Communication of said Grand Lodge.
Section 6. The Board of Control shall make such rules and regulations as they shall deem necessary for the effectual operation of the
several Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus within this State,
and shall endeavor so to standardize the work that the operations of the
several Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus may be conducted
economically and efficiently.
Section 7. The members of the board shall be entitled .to their
actual necessary expenses incurred in the performance of their duty;
claims for which shall be itemized and presented to the Grand Master
for his approval and when so approved shall be presented to the Grand
Secretary, who shall draw his warrant in payment of same on the Grand
Treasury.

Your committee to which was referred the decision of the Grand
Master with reference to the allocation of Life Membership Funds to
the General Fund of the Lodge. have had the same under consideration,
and respectfully report as follows:
In his decision the Grand Master says :
"2. A member of a lodge purchased a life membership for
his father, who was a member of the same lodge. At that time

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

205

our Section 129 of the Constitution providing a plan for life
membership, read that 'only the income thereof shall be used
by the lodge, the original amounts to be forever kept and maintained as and for a permanent life membership fund.' At the
Annual Communication of 1923, the section was amended by
adding this proviso: 'Provided, nevertheless, that upon the death
of a life member, such sum as he shall have paid into said fund
may be withdrawn therefrom and become a part of the general
fund of the lodge.' The life member (the father) died subsequent to 1923 and the lodge, pursuant to the term of Section
129 as amended, transferred the amount paid by the son for the
father's life membership to the general fund. The son appealed
to me that his payment constituted an irrevocable contract and
that the money paid for the life membership should remain forever in the permanent life membership fund as a memorial to
his father.
I held that the lodge had the right, under the terms of
Section 129 as amended, to allocate to the general fund any
moneys paid into the life membership fund for account of any
deceased life member."
In presenting its report to the Grand Lodge in 1923, with reference
to the adoption of the proviso to life membership legislation above set
out in the quotation from the Grand Master's decision, this committee
used the following language :
"At the last Annual Communication the Committee on
Policy reported against the proposed change, and this committee
concurred in the view of the Committee on Policy. \Ve still
adhere to the view then expressed by both committees, and
present the proposed amendment without recommendation, for
such action as the Grand Lodge desires to take. In doing so
we think it proper to state that it is necessarily prospective in
effect and applicable only to future resolutions."

It is manifest from this language that in the opinion of the Jurisprudence Committee, this legislation could have no retroactive effect,
and we are firmly convinced that the proviso above referred to, is
ineffectual for the purpose it was intended to accomplish. The relationship between the life member and his lodge is a solemn binding contract
between the parties that cannot be abrogated except by the unanimous
consent of all the parties interested therein. It is our judgment that
before funds paid in by a life member may be diverted to the General
Fund of the lodge, a resolution to that effect must be concurred in by
unanimous vote of the lodge. It follows from the foregoing that the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

conclusion of the Grand Master that the lodge had a right to allo:ate
the funds of the life member to the General Fund of his lodge, can not
be sustained.
In order to present this matter fairly to the Grand Lodge to the end
that there may be a clear understanding as to the status of life membership funds, we recommend that Section 129, appertaining to life membership, be amended as follows :

Manual for Conduct of Trials

206

Section 129, page 125, Constitution and Regulations, Second Edition,
beginning on line 26 and ending on line 30 of said page, so that same
will read as amended as follows:
"Provided nevertheless that upon the death of a life member such
sum as he shall have paid into said fund, may be withdrawn therefrom
by unanimous vote of the members present at a stated meeting of the
lodge, provided notice in writing of such proposed action, shall have
been mailed to all of the members of the lodge at least thirty (30) days
prior thereto; and upon such unanimous vote, said sum shall become
a part of the General Fund of the lodge."
If this legislation is passed, we are satisfied that any lodge desiring
to divert such life membership fund to the General Fund of the lodge
may do so under this iegislation, and the diversion may be accomplished
both retrospectively and prospectively.
It may be suggested that before this amendment shall become
effective, it will be necessary for any lodge intending to divert such life
membership funds to the General Fund, to incorporate the provisions of
this amendment in its life membership resolution, after the same notice
as was required for the adoption of the original resolution.

The report was adopted, and Section 129 of the Constitution was amended by unanimous vote.

Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom was referred. a proposed amendment to Section 202 of the Constitution, recommend the
adoption of the following :
Sec. 202. The Master, or other person designated by the Grand

Affidavits or depositions taken without notice cannot be received. Hearsay evidence is not admissible. Admissions or confessions of the accused
such as would be admissible in the courts of the land, are admissible'.

be exercised. The records and reporters' transcripts of testimony made
in courts of the land, properly authenticated, may be allowed in evi-

Master May Receive Request for Waiver of Jurisdiction
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has proposed an amendment to
Section 96 of the Constitution, and reports thereon as follows:
The amendment is to permit a Master to receive request for waiver
and appoint committee to investigate the required matters, and report
to the lodge at the stated meeting following, which can thereupon take
action, thus saving one month's time in such cases. This amendment is
intended to facilitate action upon requests for waivers, and seems to fill
the requirement.
We, therefore, recommend the adoption of the amendment proposed,
which reads as follows :
Sec. 96. Except that in the case of one who has the qualification
of residence, the lodge within whose jurisdiction he resides may, upon
his request in writing and for good cause shown, authorize another lodge
to receive and act upon his application. The Master shalt receive the
1·equesl and a committee shall be appointed to investigate as to whether
or not the lodge actually possesses jurisdiction, and whether or not the
reasons alleged for the request are good and sufficient, which committee
shall report at the next stated meeting. The request may be granted
by majority vote; and except in the case of a person belonging to the
army or navy of the United States, whose application, though he have
not that qualification of residence, may be received hy dispensation from
the Grand Master, as provided in Section 43.

Report adopted and the section amended by unanimous
vote.

Masonic Insurance
4. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes commends the
utterance of the Grand Master on the subject of Masonic insurance, and is
of the opinion that at times unwarranted advantage is taken of candidates
and young Masons at the period when they are most susceptible to
influence by reason of their enthusiasm for Masonry and their zeal to
conform not only with every requirement but with every expectation with
respect to Freemasonry.
It often happens that the candidate or young Mason is solicited to
buy insurance, books, periodicals, to join clubs, and to do other things
in response to solicitation based upon the representation that it is his
Masonic duty to do so. It can be well said that a candidate has the
right to exercise his business discretion and judgment and that the fact
of his receiving the Masonic Degrees does not deprive him of the right
to contract or refuse to contract in any business matter. While Grand
Lodge does not condemn nor endorse any legitimate business enterprise,
nevertheless, it is true that abuses are practised by reason of the misunderstanding of the initiate or by reason of his zealous effort to conform
at every point with what is represented to him to be his duty. In order
to correct such abuses, and in order to avoid a repetition of such complaints as those concretely stated by the Grand Master, your committee
is of the opinion that instruction on this point should be given to the
candidate at the time he receives the First Degree.
Your committee, therefore, recommends that the Committee on
Education prepare a statement on this subject, for use throughout this
entire jurisdiction, which statement may embrace other matters upon
which a candidate should be informed, and that such statement be given
by the Master in writing to each candidate at the time he receives the
First Degree of Masonry.

Report adopted.

Proper Usage Concerning the Flag

7. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has carefully
considered the resolution presented by Brother ]. G. Sutherland, on the
proper usage concerning the American Flag in the lodge room, and is of
the opinion that no recommendation should be made with reference
thereto.
There are certain definite rules regarding the use and handling of
the American Flag, which through usage by the United States Army
and Navy and by adoption of various patriotic societies, in the course
of time has become an unwritten code for our guidance. We are very
sure that the members of our institution are imbued with patriotic
sentiment and that their good taste and good sense will govern their
use and handling of our Flag, and that no rule or regulation on the
subject is necessary or desirable.

Adopted.

8. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered
the resolution introduced by Brother Leo Bruck, providing for the
amendment of Section 73 of the Constitution by changing the time of
notice of intention to apply for dispensation from forty-five to ninety
days.
Your committee is of the opinion that sixty-five days is ample time
to accomplish the purpose .intended by said Section 73 and, therefore,

216

PROCEEDI:'.'IGS OF THE

recommend that said Section 73 be amended by substituting sixty-five
for forty-five days and that the Committee on Jurisprudence prepare
and submit the form of amendment.

The Committee on Jurisprudence approved the form of
the above, and Section 73 of the Constitution was amended
by striking out forty-five days and inserting the words
sixty-five days in the fourth line of page 93 of the second
edition of the Constitution and Regulations.
Proposal to Defer Ballot on Petitions
9. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes to which was
referred the resolution introduced by Brother William G. Greene
on behalf of South San Francisco Lodge 212, proposing a change in
Section 82 of the Constitution, to provide that no ballot shall be taken by
a lodge on a petition until the second stated meeting after the receipt by
the lodge of said petition.
Your committee is of the opinion that the proposed amendment would
not constitute an improvement of our present law with respect to the
matter of notices among lodges having concurrent jurisdiction. We are
not sure that there is a weakness in the practice as observed by the lodges,
but we do not feel that the proposed amendment would cure such weakness that may exist and, therefore, recommend that it be not adopted.

Report adopted,
Relative to Endowment Committee's Report
10. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has carefully
considered the report of the Endowment Committee of the Ma:.onic
Homes of California, and are gratified that the Endowment Fund raised
by the committee now amounts to in excess of $500,000.00.
The Endowment Committee is of. the opinion that the fund could be
doubled by co-operation and active work and that an "old-fashioned
drive" for such purpose would be timely.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is not disposed
at this time to recommend a drive for funds and submits this matter
to the Grand Lodge without recommendation. It may be that the Grand
Lodge is disposed to enter upon a campaign to increase the Endowment
Fund to $1,000,000, but your committee is not advised of its wishes in
this respect.

On motion, Grand Lodge voted that a "drive" at this
time is inadvisable.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

217

Facilities for Meetings of Grand Lodge
11. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered
the resolution introduced by the Inspectors of San Francisco that a
Special Committee of Three be appointed by the M:.w:.Grand Master
to survey the situation with reference to the facilities for the meeting
of Grand Lodge in its Annual Communication, and to report thereon at
the next Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge.
Your committee is of the opinion that this subject matter is entitled
to careful consideration, and that the convenience of Grand Lodge should
be promoted as far as possible, and that a commodious and appropriate
place of meeting should be secured if possible.
We therefore recommend the adoption of the resolution.

Report and resolution adopted.
Pay of Expenses of Inspectors
12. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has carefully
considered the resolutio~ introduced by the Masters and Wardens Association of Los Angeles providing that each of the elective Grand Officers
and Inspectors shall be entitled to receive payment for the amount of his
necessary expenses in attending Grand Lodge or any of its Communications, which expenses shall be ascertained by the Committee on Finance,
and report to and allowed by Grand Lodge.
Your committee does not think that any change should be made in
the present law respecting the allowance to Officers and Inspectors of the
cost of transportation to and from the sessions of Grand Lodge.
In our opinion it would be impossible during the brief Comm11nication
of the Grand Lodge to ascertain and audit the varying expenses of hundreds of individuals. some coming to the Communication by automobile,
others by train, and still others by boat.
So far as this committee has been able to ascertain the elective
Grand Lodge Officers have received exactly the same payment that has
been allowed to the representatives of subordinate lodges and Inspectors.
Your committee, therefore, recommends that the resolution be not
adopted.

Consideration of the above was made special order for
2 o'clock this afternoon, at which time, by request of the
proponents of the resolution, the matter was laid over for
consideration at the next Annual Communication.

Educational Committee
13. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recognizes the
the excellent work performed during the past year by the Educational
Committee as displayed in its report to Grand Lodge, and your committee
recommends that the . Grand Master appoint an Educational Committee
of twelve members to hold office during the ensuing Masonic year, and
that such committee shall have power to proceed with the educational
program adopted by Grand Lodge at its session of 1925.

Adopted.

has directed our attention to defects and inconsistencies appearing upon
the seal. If Grand Lodge is to have an heraldic seal it should be formed
in accordance with the laws and rules of heraldry.
Your committee therefore recommends that the Grand Master appoint
a committee consisting of three members to make a study of the seal of
the Grand Lodge of California, and to recommend at the next Communication such revision of the seal as to said committee may seem best.

Adopted.
Grand Lodge Not a Political Body

District Deputy Grand Masters
14. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
referred that portion of the Grand Master's address relative to the
appointment of Deputy Grand Lecturers and District Deputy Grand
Masters, are of the opinion that the subject matter is of such far reaching
importance and will require so many changes in our organic law that it
would be wise and expedient to postpone a consideration of the matter
until the next Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge. During the
interim the subject matter may be carefully considered by the Committees
on Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes, and the subject
may be more fully and fairly presented at the next Annual Communication than is possible at the present time.
We, therefore, respectfully recommend that the entire matter be
referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General
Purposes, with the direction that they report thereon at the next
Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.

Report and recommendation adopted.

17. There have been referred to your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes several resolutions which seek to commit this Grand
Lodge to the approval or disapproval of subjects of legislation which will
be acted upon by the California electorate at the forthcoming general election. The Grand Lodge is not a political body, and its policy during all
the years of its existence has been to refrain from any participation in
political controversies, and from this policy it should never depart.
Your committee therefore recommends that Grand Lodge refuse to
indorse or condemn any measure of legislation pending before the people
of California.
WM. RHODES HERVEY,
GEO.

F. RODDEN,

DAVID ]. REESE,
EUGENE E. ELKUS,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
To the lrf:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Necrology presents the following report :
While we realize that life is ours but for a span, and that as God
has given, so shall He take away, none of us is desirous of making the
change ourselves, nor are we ever quite prepared to have our friends
pass from us into that mystic land of life eternal. He who has lived an
honorable, upright life here is assured of admission into that Celestial
Lodge above, for has not the Great Master of love said: "Let not your
heart be troubled; ye believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father's
house are many mansions; if it were not so, I would have told you. T
go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I
will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye
may be also."
During the past year death has removed from our midst many of
our brethren-staunch and true, among them being the Very Reverend
Dean William MacCormack, and Worshipful Bro. Henry D. French.
Brother MacCormack was born in the year 1866, and answered the
final summons Monday, January 4, 1926. His was a lovely life, and a life
of love. During his eighteen years as Dean of St. Paul's Protestant Episcopal Cathedral in Los Angeles, he endeared himself, not only to the members of his congregation and his :\fasonic brethren, but to all who knew
him or knew of him. His going was a distinct loss to all. Dean :\facCormack possessed all those attributes which go to make a man's man, and he

235

was truly' such. He possessed to a marked degree that essential characteristic of the Great Architect of the Universe-love. Love-which serves
without hope of reward and gives without expectation of return. 'vVe
hear much about the influence of love; its kindness, unselfishness, and
its pleasures and delights, but too little do we realize that love is more
than all these-it is power, a force that is mighty. It never fails, and it
alone can endure to the end, and will survive when all else succumbs.
Love is not boastful, nor does it behave itself unseemly. "How rare and
how precious is the jewel of love." Brother Maccormack showed us
what love is; in fact he gave it to us and it will keep him with us, and
will not let him go.
Dean MacCormack served as Grand Chaplain of this Grand Lodge
and, at the time of his death, was orator of the Scottish Right Bodies of
the Valley of Los Angeles. He was an honorary member of the Supreme
Council 33°. He was also a Knight Templar, and a member of the
Shrine, and served both bodies in a number of offices of distinction.
Brother Henry D. French of Riverside, Inspector of the 91st Masonic
District, answered the call on July 19, 1926. He was born in 1863 and,
as he grew to manhood, developed attributes of the highest type. For
nearly twenty-five years he gave much of his time to, and used his
splendid abilities for, the advancement of Freemasonry in the City an<l
County of Riverside, and throughout our California jurisdiction.
"By their works ye shall know them," and by his works was Brother
French best known. Not only did he labor faithfully in the Masonic vineyard, the Blue Lodge, Chapter, Commandcry, Consistory and the Shrine,
but took an active part in city and county civic affairs, as a result of
which he earned, through his untiring efforts, the love and esteem of his
brethren and the confidence of all who knew him.
Many others of our brethren-good men and true-have been taken
from our ranks during the year and, while it is not possible for us at
this time to chronicle their names, or their deeds of love and kindness,
we have no doubt but what they have found an abiding peace in "that
spiritual building; that house not made with hands-eternal in the
Heavens."
Respectfully submitted,
BEN G. \VRIGHT,
MAX A. Pr.UMll,
w ALTER L. RERGE!l,
Committee.

The report was adopted, and Grand Lodge was called
up in silent tribute to those of our brethren who have
passed to the realm "where the rainbow never fades."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS

io the M.".W.".Grand Lodge of California:
This is the report of your Committee on Charters:
, The great fraternity of Freemasons throughout its entire existence,
(and who dare say how many years that represents?-) has always insisted that men should come to its doors entirely of their own free will.
It wanted as new members only those freeborn, worthy, reputable .men
who had formed a favorable judgment about the fraternity, and came to
it for that excellent reason and not from feelings of curiosity. It did
not then, and does not now, acquire members by solicitation.
There is no such rule, however, about acquiring new lodges. Naturally, based on residence and life work, Masons form different family or
lodge groupings, and change these from time to time. In some cases,
our western cities and towns have grown so fast that inevitably the
time came where one lodge would no longer serve, but two or three, or
dozens more, have been added from time to time. The advantage of
many new lodges is great. The membership in each such lodge being
smaller, know each the other brother, and know something of his work,
his family, his general welfare. In these small bodiPs, no doubt there is
more cordiality and good fellowship, more lodge friendships and brotherly handshakes, more conviviality at banquets even though the banquets
are perforce more. frugal, more open and generous and helping hands to
the distressed Mason and to his widow and orphan children. The only
possible advantage a lodge in excess of 300 members has over small
lodges, is in its financial ability to erect, as a credit to the fraternity, the
many superb Masonic temples that have been builrled in the past five
years in this State.
Probably no one has been more insistent in declaiming the advantages
of many lodges (many members are not wanted if they merely become
members and not Masons) than Past Grand Master Samuel Edgerton
Burke. His Grand Master's message and many addresses in the year
1922, emphasized his belief; his own year brought to us 26 new lodges;
that of Brother Grand Master Sherman, his successor, brought 39; of
Brother Grand Master Crites, in 1924, 21 lodges; of Brother Grand
Master Reese last year, 27 lodges. This year, under our Grand Master
Albert Eugene Boynton, your present Committee on Charters, had to
consider the cases of 22 new lodges. The aggregate for the five years
is 135 lodges or an average of 27 new lodges yearly.
It is interesting to observe that these 22 dispensations this year were
issued on petitions for dispensations which were signed by 626 brothers;
and their returns show 125 affiliations and 130 members raised, or a
total membership of 881.

REPORT ON WESTERN STAR LODGE
To the M.'.W:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee appointed to investigate and report to this Grand
Lodge what necessary steps should be taken to restore, preserve and
safeguard the old Masonic Building o_f Western Star Lodge No. 2 at
Shasta, its old records and relics, beg leave to report as follows :
In order to fully advise you .of the conditions surrounding this
matter a brief description of this Masonic Building is necessary.
The Masonic Hall building at Shasta is a two-story and basement
brick building constructed of native brick in 1853. As was customary
in those days the doors and windows are iron shuttered ; in fact the
whole ensemble is remindful of the days of '49. The lodge room is
upstairs and its furniture is likewise of an ancient vintage, the only
modern thing in the1 building being electric lights.
The town of Shasta is situated about seven miles from Redding
on the Weaverville lateral of the State Highway system which forms
the connecting link of the Eureka or Coast to Sacramento Valley Highway terminating. at Redding. More and more travel passes this old
Masonic Building yearly. In his annual report, Past Grand Master
Reese marked the fact that the Tiler's register shows numerous visitors
annually viewing the relics of this old lodge.

240

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Western Star Lodge has acquired a two-story brick building, 3Sx
feet, immediately adjoining the hall which, if the plan herewith subm' ted is carried out, will be used for its meeting place in the future.
It is proposed to leave the old lodge room intact, to be used, h wever, as a Masonic Museum where may be seen the old records, f niture and relics which have accumulated there for the past eighty y ars.
The building will be substantially fireproof, it being proposed to re 10ve
therefrom such inflammable material as can be dispensed with.
I
A competent architect has carefully gone over the buildings and
has estimated the cost of restoring the buildings to approximate seven
thousand dollars. Your committee feels that the expenditure of this
amount of money is justified by the end gained for the fraternity at
large. That the records, building and relics should be preserved there
is no question but they also should be accessible to the travelling Masonic brother when good fortune brings him into this locality and this
can only be accomplished by the plan proposed.
Your committee therefore respectfully suggests that the sum of
seven thousand dollars or any such part thereof be appropriated by this
Grand Lodge for the purp<;>ses aforesaid, said money to be spent under
the direction of a committee of three appointed by the Grand Master.
Respectfully submitted,

G. c. DEFOREST,
TosEPH }ONES,
OTTO

G.

TRAUTZ,

Committee.

'

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was rnferred trial record
No. 513 tried in Stanislaus Lodge No. 206 respectfully reports as
follows:
Accused was charged with un-Masonic conduct as set forth in one
specification: "That on or about the 25th day of Ivfarch, 1924, he was
arrested and convicted of the crime of bootlegging." At the trial the
Master stated that the court record was the testimony of the guilt of
the accused, from which the charge was made. The record then shows :
"No further testimony being offered, the matter was submitted to the
commissioners for decision." It must be obvious that as a matter of
fact no competent evidence was presented. The bare statement of the
Master, which is the rankest sort of hearsay evidence, unaccompanied
by a certified copy of the court records and unsupported by any other
ev!dence cannot justify the action of the trial commission. In addition,
it appears from the record that no vote was taken on the specification,
the vote being only on the charge of un-Masonic conduct. This is not
in accordance with the provisions of Section 205 of the constitution
which requires that a vote be taken on each specification and on the
charge of un-Masonic conduct.
Your committee is of the opinion that the judgment of the trial
commission must be reversed and therefore offers the following resolution and moves its adoption :
Resolved, that the judgment of the trial commission in the case
covered by trial record No. 513 be and the same is hereby reversed
and the case is remanded for a new trial.

Adopted.
