Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred trial record
No. 472 from Torrance Lodge l'\o. 447, begs leave to report as follows:
The accused, a member of Torrance Lodge, was charged by the
Junior Warden of Torrance Lodge, acting under the direction oi the
Worshipful :\faster of Torrance Lodge with un-Masonic conduct as set
forth in two specifications.
Torrance Lodge convened for the purpose of electing trial commissioners and by vote of the lodge determined that the number of
commissioners should be five: The Master named the time and place
of the first meeting of the commissioners and at the time and place so
designated, the trial was had. After all of the testimony had been received, the commissioners proceeded to deliberate upon th~ir verdict and
sentence. The vote on the first specification was "Not Guilty."
No vote was taken on the second specification. The vote on the
charge of un-Masonic conduct was "Guilty."
Your committee is of the opinion that the judgment of the commission must be reversed and the same remanded for a new trial, for
the reason that the trial of the accused was had in a lodge which had
-ro jurisdiction to try the case; the charges having been made by the
Junior Warden of Torrance Lodge acting under the direction of the
Master. Regulation No. 410 at page 334 of the Constitution and Regulations, 2nd edition, 1925, provides that the lodge or Master may be the
accuser and may direct the junior warden to prefer the charges, in
which case the trial cannot be held in that lodge, and the charges shall
be presented to the Grand Master, who will designate the lodge in which
the trial shall be had. It may not be amiss in passing to call attention
to the fact that the number of commissioners elected by the lodge may
not be less than seven-Section 196 of the constitution-and that a vote
for guilty or not guilty shall be taken upon each specification and upon
the charge-Section 205 of the constitution. In the instant case such
vote was taken upon only one specification.
Your committee, therefore, offers the following resolution:
Resolved, that the judgment in the case covered by trial record N'o.
472 be, and the same is hereby reversed and the case remanded for a
new trial in a lodge which shall have jurisdiction of it.

Adopted.
Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred trial record
No. 475, from El Centro Lodge No. 384, begs leave to report as
follows:
The accused, a Fellow Craft, was charged with un-Masonic conduct
as set forth in two specifications. The lodge convened for the purpose
of electing trial commissioners on Dec. 9, 1925, and the Master named

249

December 15, 1925, as the time for the first meeting of the commissioners. The record shows that on December 10, 1925, the secretary
wrote a letter to the accused addressing him at Portland, Oregon, advising him that the commissioners elected by the lodge would meet on
December 15 to try him on a charge of un-Masonic conduct and, that
"Masonic law states that we must give you ninety days in which to
appear but if it is agreeable with you we would like to proceed Dec.
15th." The record fails to disclose the issuance or service of summons
or that the secretary furnished the accused with a copy of the charges.
On December 15, 1925, a telegram from the accused dated at Portland,
Oregon, on December 14, 1925, was received by the secretary acknowledging receipt of the secretary's letter of December 10, stating that it
was impossible for him to be present but that he had wired an attorney to appear for him so that the commissioners might proceed with
the trial on December 15. The accused was not present but was represented by an attorney.
Section 199 of the constitution provides that "if the accused be without the state and his residence i.e known the summons and copy of the
charges shall be issued at least ninety days before the trial and shall be
forwarded to his address by the secretary by mail or other usual mode
of conveyance." The provisions of this section are mandatory and compliance with them is requisite to enable the lodge to secure jurisdiction
of the accused. Waiver of such compliance by the accused will not
serve to cure the jurisdictional defect.
Your committee is therefore of the opinion that the judgment of
the trial commission must be reversed and the same remanded for a
new trial on the ground that jurisdiction was not acquired in the manner provided by the constitution.
Your committee, therefore, offers the following resolution:
Resolved, that the judgment in the case covered by trial record
No. 475 be, and the same is hereby reversed, and the case remanded
for a new trial.

Adopted.

The trial commissioners met on February 8, 1926, and adjourned to meet
again on February 16, 1926. On February 1, 1926 a summons issued
requiring the accused to appear for trial on February 16, 1926. This
summons was personally served on February 4, 1926. On February 16,
1926 the trial was had resulting in the conviction of the accused.
Section 200 of the constitution provides: "The commissioners shall
assemble at the time and place appointed ..." This provision is mandatory and may not be omitted. The failure to meet at the time set
by the Master for the first meeting of the commissioners ipso facto dissolved the commission (Haas' Manual, page 30).
Your committee is of the opinion that the judgment of the trial
commission must be reversed and the same remanded for a new trial.
Your committee, therefore, offers the following resolution:
Resolved, that the judgment in the case covered by trial record No.
483, be, and the same is hereby reversed, and the case remanded for
new trial.

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred trial record
Ko. 502, tried by Dinuba Lodge No. 385, respectfully reports as follows:
The accused was charged with unmasonic conduct, as set forth in
one specification. The record in this case is complete and unusually
well prepared. Unfortunately, it appears from the record that the
charge was made by the Junior Warden of Dinuba Lodge ~o. 385 by
direction of the Master of said lodge and that the case was tried in
Dinuba Lodge. Regulation No. 410 provides that the lodge or Master
may be accuser and may direct the Junior Warden to prefer the charges,
in which case !the trial cannot be held in that lodge, and the charges
shall be presented to the Grand Master, who will designate the lodge
in which the trial shall be had. The reason for the rule thus announced
is obvious. The lodge or its titular head being the accuser, common
fairness precludes the trial of the accused by his accuser. For this reason your committee is of the opinion that the judgment must be reversed,
and, therefore, presents the foilowing resolution, and moves its
adoption:
Resolved, that the judgment in the case covered by trial record No.
502, be, and the same is hereby reversed and the case remanded for
a new trial.

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred trial record
No. 470, from Welcome Lodge :-Jo. 255, on appeal by the accused from
a judgment of expulsion, begs leave to report that an examination of
the record shows that no error in procedure appears and that the
accuser presented evidence which, if believed by the trial commissioners.
would amply support the charge and specification, and the penalty
fixed is only commensurate with the seriousness of the offense. Further,
the long-established rule that a verdict should not be set aside unless
there has been a gross miscarriage of justice, precludes in our opinion
a reversal of the judgment in this ease. We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption :

The trial commission fixed the penalty at reprimand. adding "The
commission was also unanimously of the opinion that the entire fault
in the case did not lie with the accused, but that Delta Lodge, by and
through its Finance Committees and officers in charge of the affairs of
the lodge, had been lax over a period of years in permitting the default
of the accused to continue unnoticed. The commission desires to incorporate in the record the statement that this feeling of remissness on the
part of the lodge influenced their vote and that the Master of the lodge
in reprimanding the accused in open lodge express these views of the
commission."
The commission may also have been influenced in its vote by the
strong plea of the attorney for the lodge, the accuser, on behalf of the
accused. In fact he says "Brother (the accused) has been a very
loyal and devoted worker in Delta Lodge, and whatever the commission
sees fit to do in this case, whether it be a reprimand or a suspension,
or whatever you feel justified in meeting out here, will be satisfactory
to Delta Lodge."
There is ample testimony to justify the trial comm1ss1on in its
observations relative to the remissness of the Finance Committee and
officers in charge of the affairs of the lodge but your committee is
of the opinion that the trial commissioners should neither have allowed
the above fact nor the plea of the attorney for the lodge accuser to
have influenced their vote as to the penalty for the un-Masonic conduct
of the accused. He had used such of the lodge funds as he needed in
his business and deposited the balance to his account as Treasurer of
the lodge. He continued to use this money in his business from 1919
to 1925.
In the opinion of your committee reprimand is not a penalty commensurate with the offense the accused admits he continued to commit
for six years. Your committee offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption.
Resolved, That the finding of guilty by the trial comm1ss1011 in
trial record No. 473 be and the same is hereby affirmed, but that the
penalty be and the same is hereby modified to suscpnsion.

Rcsoh•,,d, That the judgment of the trial commissioners in trial
record No. 470, of \Velcome Lodge No. 255, be and the same is hereby
affirmed.

Adopted.

to the credit of the lodge or in the bank. The accused testifies that it
was because he knew that the Treasurer had once appropriated lodge
funds to his own use, that he adopted the method of turning over to
him the duplicate deposit slips from the bank instead of the money, which
he might do as before, use such part of it as he needed in his own business
and deposit the balance in the bank to his account as Treasurer. This
appears to have justified the action of the accused in this particular and
he should be commended for it rather than found guilty of un-Masonic
conduct.
That the accused concealed the defalcation of the Treasurer from
January 1, 1921, to April 16, 1925, as charged in the ninth specification
there is no evidence at all. It is admitted by accused that he knew .of
the defalcation when he was :\faster, which was prior to January 1,
1921, when he became Secretary, but had been informed that the defalcation had been made good.
The record shows that upon the discovery of the defalcation of
the Treasurer of the Lodge in 1920, the Auditing Committee recommended that such defalcation be kept secret to prevent the possible
disintegration of the lodge, to which recommendation the accused, then
:.\faster, agreed. At most this would only be said to be a mistake in
judgment made in good faith for the benefit of the lodge and not a
Masonic offense.
Neither is the charge in specifications fifth to eighth, inclusive,
borne out by any evidence. His report as Secretary did not and had
no occasion to report cash in bank for it was the Treasurer and not the
Secretary that has or should have cash in bank.
The first four specifications relate to shortages of the accused as
Secretary. According to the audit on which the charges are based, for
some periods of his incumbency as Secretary he was short, for other
periods he was long, but in the aggregate he was short some $690.20.
No one, however, can read the trial record without being astounded
at the lax method of the accused during all his terms of office, in
performing his clerical duties. It is hard to see how anyone could keep
accurate accounts, who attended to his duties as spasmodically as he

The first four specifications charge accused with wilfully, wrongfully and fraudulently appropriating certain amounts of money belonging to Delta Lodge to his own use.
The fifth specification charges that accused as Secretary, wilfully,
knowingly and intentionally on or about November 30, 1921, made a
false and fraudulent annual statement to the lodge in this that he knew
the Treasurer was short $588.55 and notwithstanding this knowledge he
reported to the lodge the said sum of $588.55 as cash on hand in bank,
when in truth and in fact he knew that said bank account was short
to that extent. The sixth, seventh and eighth specifications are the
same as the fifth except as to date of statements, which are for 1922,
. 1923 and 1924.
The ninth specification is that accused was Secretary from January
1, 1921, to April 16, 1925, and did during the entire time knowingly,
wilfully and intentionally conceal the defalcation of the Treasurer.
The eleventh specification is that the accused as Secretary, from
December 1, 1920, to December 1, 1921, failed to pay moneys over to the
Treasurer. The twelfth, thirteenth and fourteenth specifications are the
same as the eleventh but apply to the next three succeeding years.
The trial commission find accused guilty on all of the above specifications. On the tenth specification he was found not guilty.
The trial record in this case covers approximately 600 typewritten
pages. Much of it is complicated accounting. Because of the importance of the question herein involved both to the lodge and to the
brother accused and because of the further fact that a more just conclusion might reasonably be reached by those who have the typewritten
transcript before them than by those who heard the oral testimony from
time to time, and did not have the benefit of having the testimony
reduced to writing for their study, because of these considerations the
members of your committee have separately and collectively given a
great deal of earnest study and consideration of this very lengthy
transcript and to its careful analysis.
The charge contained in the last four specifications, eleventh to
fourteenth inclusive, your committee consider is not sustained by any
evidence in the record. Section 150 of the Constitution relating to
duties of Secretaries provides "4th. To collect and receive all moneys
due to the lodge and pay them over to the Treasurer." The Secretary
is accused of having not paid the moneys over to the Treasurer. The
evidence is that the Secretary deposited the money in the bank to the
account of the Treasurer, took a duplicate deposit slip from the bank
and turned it over to the Treasurer and took his receipt for the money

255

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

256

did. Each Master under whom accused acted as Secretary failed in
his duty when he did not remove the Secretary from office becaU5<! of
his lax methods in performing his duties.
The auditor who made the audit on which these specifications are
based served on the Auditing Committee two separate years, which
committee audited the books of the Secretary and Treasurer. This,
too, is the same auditor who signed a report of an audit November 29,
1924, as follows:
"We, the committee appointed to audit the books of the Secretary
and Treasurer for the year ending December l, 1924, have checked
the same and found them to be correct.
"\Ve wish to commend the Secretary and Treasurer for the efficient
manner in which the records have been kept."
This auditor is now Secretary of the Lodge.
The Senior Warden who participated in the preparation of these
charges was also on the auditing committee in 1923 and 1924 who gave
the Secretary and Treasurer a clearance as above noted.
Had any auditing committees ever performed its duties that acted
during any year accused held office as Secretary, affairs of the lodge
wonld certainly have been better off today. Furthermore the accused
had a right to rely on the reports of these auditing committees and
believe that an audit had been made and that his accounts were correct.
There is a vast difference between moneys lost by embezzlement
and moneys lost by careless or negligent handling. One is a criminal
offense; the other merely civil.
There is no attempt to show, and no showing of any intentional
misbehavior on the part of the accused as to his handling of lodge funds
and diversion of these funds to his own use. On the contrary it is
shown that at all times he had sufficient personal bank balance so that
he had no need of lodge funds for his own use and ample to pay any
deficiency that ever occurred. He was able and did voluntarily pay his
shortages as soon as the amount thereof was ascertained.
There being no •testimony in the record sufficient to sustain a finding
of un-Masonic conduct, your committee is of the opinion that the judgment of the trial commission should be reversed, and therefore offers
the following resolution and moves its adoption :
Resolved, That the judgment in the case covered by trial record No.
466, be and the same is hereby reversed.
Fraternally submitted,

were made with the Forest Lawn Memorial Park to set aside a beautiful

on this account.

of all moneys received on account of the sale of said graves; that all
moneys so received be repaid to this Grand Lodge by said board ; and
that the Grand Secretary be annually apprised of these facts and figures,
so that proper record may be kept."
We recommend that these instructions be strictly adhered to.

Masonic Homes of California
The annual report of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, together with their financial statements, have been carefully
examined by your committee.
Because of the tremendous increase in number of residents of the
Homes, both at Decato and Covina, the Trustees have been forced to
spend large sums of money in the erection of new buildings, and are at
present in debt approximately $140,000.00, which money has been expended entirely in the construction of said new buildings.
Your committee is of the opinion that this indebtedness should be
wiped out at the earliest possible date.
Your committee is of the opinion that this object can be best accomplished by raising the tax on initiates from $20.00 to $25.00 rather than
by an increase in the per capita tax against lodges.
Your committee has, therefore, caused a resolut.ion to be introduced,
amending the Constitution, in order to bring about this objective, which
amendment has been adopted by this Grand Lodge.
Your committee recommends that the $25.00 tax on initiates be
collected on each petition for degrees and application for affiliation received by the subordinate lodges on and after the first day of January,
1927. (This was made effective February 1, 1927.)

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON REPORT OF
GRAND LECTURER
To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee, to whom has been referred for consideration the
report of the V.'.W,".Grand Lecturer, respectfully submits the following:
We congratulate the Grand Lecturer on his nineteenth annual report.
Replete with beauty of expression and words of Masonic wisdom, it
clearly indicates that time has not dimmed his vision, nor lessened his
efforts in behalf of the Craft.
Coming, by the very nature of his activities in close contact with
the lodges through the officers and coaches, he has endeared himself to
the members of the Craft by his ever willingness at all times and with
personal sacrifices, to aid and assist, not only in connection with the
rendition of the work, but with a desire to inculcate the spirit of the
fraternity.
His advice to the Inspectors is timely, for they are in a sense the
instruments provided for the carrying out of his policies, and upon their
actions and accomplishments are reflected in a large measure, the final
analysis of his efforts.
His suggestion as to the consideration of quality; rather than
quantity is highly commendable, as the very essence of our order is
dependent upon those definite fundamentals which are the basis of the
requirements of the initiate.
His comment in relation to the selection of officers is most important,
and Masters of lodges should give due and serious consideration to the
qualifications required of the Brother to be appointed.
His recommendation for the adoption of some definite plan for the
examination of visiting brethren is worthy of serious consideration, and
your committee suggests that some definite method be adopted universally
throughout the jurisdiction, thereby avoiding much confusion to committees and saving unnecessary embarrassment on occasions to visiting
brethren.
Finally your committee expresses its sincere appreciation to the
Grand Lecturer for the service he has rendered, and we ask of Our
Supreme Grand Master who Rules our destinies, to give unto him
continuous Wisdom to direct him, Strength to support him and the Beauty
of Holiness to adorn his labors during his allotted time.
Respectfully submitted,

C. W. GOODWIN,

LEO BRUCK,

c. RUPPEL,

Roy H. PARKINSON,

G. c. DEFOREST,

J. M. ARGARBlTE,
Committee.

against the Grand Lodge, as were received by the Grand Secretary.

CENTENNIAL COMMUNICATION
Representatives of Sacramento Lodges presented the
following, which was adopted:
WHEREAS, this Grand Lodge was conceived and born in th: City
of Sacramento in the year 1850, and thereafter flourished therem for

many years; and,
.
WHEREAS, it is fitting and proper that upon the lOOth anmvers~ry
of the founding of this Grand Lodge its appoinkd place of meetmg
should be at Sacramento; and,
WHEREAS, The Masters & \Vardens Association of Sacra:nento have
extended to this Grand Lodge the invitation of all tl1e Masomc Brethren
of the Capital City to hold its regular annual meeting marking .the lOOth
anniversarv of its founding at Sacramento; now, therefore, be it
Resol~ed, that it is, and it is hereby declared to be, t~e sense of
this Grand Lodge that the lOOth anniversary of the foundmg thereof
be celebrated at said City of Sacramento by holding the regular annual
meeting thereof in the year 1949 in said city.

A resolution was presented in behalf of sundry brethren,
providing that the ballot box should never be placed on
the Bible. Referred to the Committee on Ritual.

MASONRY IN FOREIGN COUNTRIES
Past Grand Master Hervey delivered an interesting talk
on the condition of Masonry in European and South American countries, in which the hope was expressed that Masonry
in foreign countries would ere long be conducted along
lines somewhat akin to English-speaking Lodges and become committed to the doctrine of pure fraternity without
political bias or interference.

REPORT
of the

Committee on Correspondence
October, 1926
By JESSE M. WHITED

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
Herewith my Sheth Report as Chairman of the Committee on
Correspondence. The expressions of opinion under the various subjects as heretofore, are those only of the Chairman.
The Proceedings of the various Grand Lodges show that the
fraternity generally is pursuing "the even tenor of its way," some of
them endeavoring to put into practical operation the great idea of
service in fields of endeavor most useful to their respective communities.
The outstanding question in a large number of jurisdictions
appears to be "What should our Institution do in the affairs of the
world either through the individual or collectively."
As Brother Raymond Daniel of Georgia has said: "It is an
axiom of Holy Writ that no man liveth to himself and no man dieth
to himself. This imperishable statement is true of individuals and
equally true of every profession and business or calling."
He also says that the life of every Mason is divided into three
cycles-ONE, the Age of Awakening; TWO, the Period of Performance; THREE, the Millenium of Achievement."
It would appear that we are passing from the "Age of Awakening" into the "Period of Performance."

The Grand Master of Delaware perhaps best answers the question as to how a Mason individually can serve his community as
follows:
"First of all he can give his moral and financial and physical
support to those institutions in the community which make for its
welfare. He can lend the church a helping hand, whether he likes
the minister's sermons or not. The minister isn't the Church any

2

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE
REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

more than the Master of a Lodge is Masonry. He can get behind
the task of public education and work to see that the boys and girls
of the present generation have the best schooling in books and character building that money and brains can give them.
He can
encourage public playgrounds, libraries, night schools, hospitals,
De Molay Chapters, and Y. M. C. A., and Y. W. C. A. movements.
To him who has the spirit to serve, opportunities are not lacking."
The following from a talk made a few months ago by Dr. J.
Fort Newton, Masonic reader, speaker and scholar, rector of St.
Paul's Church, Philadelphia, outlines what one writer has termed
could be the corporate contribution of American Masonry to the
world's civilization:
"The future of Freemasonry depends on the knowledge that is
imparted to the young men of today, because they will assume our
duties in the future. I have no criticism to offer against the young
people. They are honest and candid in their actions. I believe in
them, and want them to have their own philosophy of life. In this
day and time they are subject to much adverse criticism, but they
are only doing on the front porch what their parents did on the back
porch. I would suggest that a committee of men, thoroughly familiar
with the history of Freemasonry, write a series of lectures to be
given every year for the benefit of young men who wish to know the
principles on which we conduct our association. It would be the
answer to a question that is universally unknown, and it would
enable the next generation to know more about Freemasonry and
use it to better ends. This method already has been adopted in the
state of Massachusetts, and eventually will become universal.
"There are three things which we must do, one of which I have
mentioned as providing for the education of young men in Freemasonry. Another important step is to do our part in healing
America of her racial rancour, which is the mother of war and yet
the undertone of jurisdiction in every American community today.
There is room for everything in this great free country except bitterness and hatred, and this great issue should not come between
us and. the prospects of the greatest civilization ever known.
"The last thing ·we can do is to heal America of her religious
rancour. We want peace and harmony, where religion is based
on religious principles that give religious satisfaction. It was William Penn who said, 'Men who fight about religion have no religion
to fight about,' and he was right. We must work together in this
fellowship of Freemasonry, considering all it has done and all it
can do."

Indiana (1924):
Your attention is directed to the fact that the Grand Lodge does not
assume responsibility for any commercial organizations that may appeal
to Masons on the ground that they are owned and operated by Masons,
and that they only do business with Masons. Nor does it stand sponsor
for any papers or publications not specially authorized by it. The only
paper that has received its approval is the very excellent journal published by our Masonic Home.
Iowa (1926):
Sometimes Masons act more like sheep than like Masons.
And yet there is a touching side to the matter after all, one which
shows a Mason's faith in his institution. Tell him a thing is "Masonic,"
and he is for it right then and there without question or hesitation, so
great is his faith in his beloved institution.
Maine (1925):
The Committee on Jurisprudence emphatically disapproves of the
use of the adjective l\fasonic in connection with private publications,
and calls attention to the General Regulation which prohibits and forbids the use of such designation, or the use of any Masonic emblem, as
part of the business name or concern or to adopt such word for any
such newspaper or like publication as any part of the name thereof.
He (Grand Master, Texas) also warned the brethren against the
alleged "Roberts Texas Masonic Directory." This correspondent is
moved to say that in this leviathan of annual reports of more than
one thousand pages, the entire roster of the Texas membership is printed
in full, so why a directory when 132,774 names and addresses are
given. What a fruitful field for Klan propaganda, on the quiet! What
a bonanza for patent medicine advertisers! Or insurance sharks! Or
anything under the sun that wants to get "a toe-hold" for its wares or
its alleged message and mission. We may be sure that such a field is
being surreptitiously plowed and furrowed and assiduously tilled by all
these designing organizations and commercial enterprises.
Missouri (1925):
Any Freemason using the word "Masonic" or any other term, sign
or symbol of Freemasonry for commercial or other business enterprises,

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

6
shall be deemed guilty of unmasonic conduct; provided, that this section
shall not apply to Masonic books, journals or periodicals, or a legitimate
trade i.n Masonic supplies ; and provided that any Freemason engaged in
the business of publishing any Masonic book, journal or periodical, who
permits the printing of any advertisement in any such publication using
the word "Masonic," or any other term, sign or symbol of Freemasonry
for commercial or other business enterprises, the use of which is prohibited by the Grand Lodge by-laws, shall be deemed guilty of unmasonic
conduct.
Montana (1924):
The following resolution was adopted :
Improper Use of Emblems. Resolved, that this Grand Lodge reprehends the practice indulged in by many Masons of using and wearing
Masonic Emblems and signs for the purpose of attracting attention to
wares or merchandise which they expose for sale. The use of the
Square and Compass for other than Masonic purposes is hereby prohibited.
Pennsylvania (1924):
The Grand Master : During the past year there have been received
in the Grand Master's office many complaints which show a tendency to
commercialize Freemasonry. The complaints cover life insurance, subscriptions principally for Masonic publications and books, mainly exercised against new initiates, and it is alleged that even threats are made
to stop advancement unless the subscription is forthcoming. It has come
to my attention recently that a general advertising company has circularized all the Lodges in this Jurisdiction for information as to officers,
addresses, and phone numbers. I cannot say too strongly that all these
matters are strictly unmasonic, and any specific case where assistance
has been given to these outside life insurance companies or book agencies
and publications enabling them to prey upon new initiates will be summarily dealt with, and the Secretaries of Lodges should be thoroughly
conversant, as also the members, that the furnishing of any information
concerning the Lodge to any publication or any company not authorized
by the Grand Lodge is prohibited.
Pennsylvania (1925):
The Grand Master : Recently I was obliged to call a halt on a
number of Lodges which had formed, in a given district, a Masonic
Bowling League. The use of the word "Masonic" or the name "Freemasonry," it has been repeatedly decided by my predecessors, is not
permitted for outside functions by any social club or association, and
I do not believe from my knowledge of the rivalry which generally pre-

Pennsylvania (1925):
No greater responsibility can be placed upon a member of the
Lodge, than a careful scrutiny of the fitness of those who knock at
our doors for admittance. The recommenders are both to know the
petitioner. This knowledge should be close, personal, intimate. They
should both know, beyond a question of doubt, that he is a man above
reproach; that he is one with whom they are, themselves, glad to associate, and to recommend to the association of their brethren, and whom
they can and do introduce, without hesitation or doubt, into their own
homes. Nor should the second recommender depend on the statements
of the first. His responsibility is as great, and his knowledge ~hould
be as complete and his acquaintance at least as long as that required of
the first. The Ahiman Rezon provides that one of the recommenders
shall have known the petitioner for at least a year, which would seem
to point to the inference that the personal knowledge of the other is of
minor importance.
The investigation of the Committee of Inquiry should be thorough,
searching, all-embracing. It is not enough that they know of nothing
that would seem to render the petitioner unworthy. Their knowledge
should be positive, not negative. They should satisfy themselves, beyond
the possibility of a doubt, that the statements cbntained in the petition
are true, and should vouch for what, if their duty has been well and
truly performed, they have definitely ascertained to be a fact, that the
petitioner is worthy of having the prayer of his petition granted.
Queensland (1925):
The regulations governing admission to membership in a Lodge are
very strict. Candidates must be known personally to those who propose
and those who second their applications, for a specified period of time.
The information obtained by the investigating committee must be submitted to the Grand Lodge Committee on "Permission to Ballot," together
with a definite recommendation accepting or rejecting a candidate.
Texas (1925):
The following 1s lifted in its entirety from the Grand Master's
Address:
Under this heading, can do no better than quote from our former
brother, George C. Connor, who in the Proceedings of 1891, page 791,
laid clown the following suggestive rules as a test of applicants for
admittance into the Fraternity:
I. The applicant should be a gentleman, as Americans interpret th;:it
word. He should be of refined manners and tastes, no matter what his

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

standing in the so-called social world. vVe have known hod-carriers to be
more refined than some Senators of the United States.
2. He should believe in the existence of a Supreme Being, Creator,
and Master of all.
3. He should believe in the Immortality of the Soul. An annihilationist cannot participate in our Mysteries, and would be an atom of
foreign matter in our Ceremonials.
4. He should be able to make himself known to the Craft by the
means of Recognition unknown to the profane. ·The details of that
ability should be entrusted to the individual Lodges.
5. He should be known to be a good citizen, a true friend, a kind
father, or son, or husband, or brother.
6. He should be a man who seeks the general good of his kind,
and is not a greedy or selfish person to the known detriment of others.
7. He should be a temperate man in eating, drinking and in speech;
orderly, forebearing, not contentious, nor inclined to speak evil of others.
Such men are worthy of admission within our portals; aye, such are
capable of "holding the My;tery of the Faith in a pure. conscience."

giving of a book will not insure its reading. "You can lead a horse
to water, but you can't make it drink" will apply as far as this
custom is concerned as it will in any attempts to educate or instruct
one by persuasion, direct or implied.

Utah (1925):
The Committee on Jurisprudence, in line with the decision of the
Grand Master, recommended the adoption of a by-law providing that
no member shall recommend a candidate for the degrees who has not
been known to him personally for at least one year. The proposed by-law
was adopted.
West Australia (1925):
With us, the brethren so "carefully refrain from recommending"
any applicant whose value to the Craft is doubtful, and so close is the
inquisition into the life, character and antecedents of each applicant
before he is proposed to any Lodge, that what is termed a "foul" ballot
is the exception, and rejections would scarcely amount to a percentage.
BIBLES
Whether the presentation of the Holy Bible to a newly raised
Brother produces any lasting effect, other than for the moment of
the ceremony, is a debatable question. Every well regulated household undoubtedly should possess a volume of the Great Light.
Whether it is perused there. or elsewhere will depend entirely upon
the individual. Without an incentive other than possession, the mere

Iowa (1926):
The Grand Master : We are wondering whether the custom of p.resenting Bibles on any occasion has resulted in getting the recipients to
read and study them. If it has, then the custom cannot help but prove
a wholesome one, good not only for the reader of The Great Light but
for every one with whom he comes in contact.
New York (1924):
It would appear that out of 884 Lodges reporting, no less than 563
are now presenting their newly made Master Masons with copies of
the Holy Bible. This is worthy of note.
Ohio (1925):
The Grand Master favors the obligation of each candidate upon
an individual Bible and the presentation of the Bible, suitably inscribed,
to the candidate. His views were apparently approved by the Committee
on Jurisprudence and adopted by the Grand Lodge. Such use and presentation of the Bible will be voluntary on the part of the Lodges, "an act
of love and not of law."
Philippine Islands (1926):
The Grand Master: One of the most impressive little ceremonies
that I have ever witnessed is that of presenting a Bible to a newly
obligated brother, on the occasion of his being raised to the sublime
degree of Master Mason.
This beautiful custom has been adopted by the Lodges of many of
our sister Grand Jurisdictions, the presentation being made in some cases
when the candidate is initiated, and in others when the candidate becomes
a Master Mason.
The Ritual as adopted by our Grand Lodge does not provide for this
ceremony, and there has been no action. of our Crand Lodge that could
be construed to be against such a presentation.
Wyoming (1925):
Therefore, Be It Resolved, That the Cram! Lodge A., F. & A. M.
of Wyoming, in Annual Communication at Sheridan, \Vyoming, recommend that the Lodges of vVyoming adopt the practice of presenting to

BOUQUETS AND BRICKBATS
· Reports of the various Committees on Correspondence, afford
an opportunity for us to see ourselves as others see us.
The following is taken from the Proceedings reviewed as comments on the Annual Communication for the year in question.
The 75th Annual Communication, Arthur J. Crites, Grand Master, October 14, 1924.
Alberta (1925):
The annual address of the Grand Master gives a comprehensive
report of the manifold duties discharged by him during the year.
The brethren of this jurisdiction seem to be unduly burdened
by those of other jurisdictions in the matter of conferring "Courtesy
Degrees."
w:. Bro. Jesse M. Whited presented his fifth repor.t on F~r­
eign Correspondence and his topical summary makes very mterestmg
reading.
Georgia (1925):
Not only was the year a Diamond Jubilee insofar as the observance of the three-quarters of a century milestone, but also on account
of the splendid achievements of the passing twelve months. One
reads with pride of the many educational and benevolent features
of the grand jurisdistion.
The topical review-more of an essay-is presented by Brother
Jesse M. Whited-his fifth. It is introduced with a condensed sy1~op­
sis, and followed by extracts from various Grand Lodge proceedmgs
with regard to many subjects. There are several paragraphs from
Georgia's proceedings.
There will always be differing opinions as to the the value of
"topical" reports.
Idaho (1925):
A special feature is made of the Grand Oration. It is carefully constructed, the theme being the qualifications for Masonry,
its teachings, ideals and practical application.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

13

This is contributed by Brother Jesse M. Whited, who closes
five years' service in this capacity. Attendance at Lodge meetings,
the Use and Misuse of the Ballot, Masonic Trials, Masonic Education and other matters, are editorially reviewed and summarized
in the preface. The report is of the "topical" order; that is, the subjects are taken about as enumerated in the preface, and then what is
said or done in the sister jurisdictions on a particular subject is collated under that head. Thus from the Idaho Proceedings of 1923
are taken Grand Master Scott's observations on Masonic Education, the Masonic Service Association, and other matters. Very
fine statistical tables are forthcoming, and there is a very complete
list of Masonic publications in the United States, amongst which
The Idaho Freemason appears. Another useful tabulation is that
of the various Grand Lodges, with their dates of meeting.

Louisiana (1926):
We only regret that further details of the report cannot be reproduced for the benefit of our brethren.
Brother Jesse M. Whited presents his fifth report on Foreign
Correspondence, which is in topical form. The review is extensive
and highly educational, covering one hundred and fourteen pages of
gripping interest.
Mexico (1925):
The report of Grand Master's report is an exceedingly able
and exhaustive report and touches on every angle of Masonic activity.
Can you wonder what the climate of California does to the
Masonic spirit and inspiration? Let's imitate the example even if
we can't enjoy the climate.
An excellent report was made by the Grand Lecturer * * *
Missouri (1925):
The proceedings of the Grand Lodge of California for 1924 have
been read with unusual interest on account of the fact that they
record the Diamond Jubilee of the Grand Lodge. The volume before us abounds with many outstanding items~ of importance.

South Dakota (1925):

Six pages of decisions are reported-nothing of unusual interest.
Two of them related to two Masons who dimitted long ago and who
wished to be reinstated. One, who withdrew 36 years ago, lives in
another state, and the other, who has dodged responsibility in connection
with the Craft for 25 years, now wishes to be reinstated so he can be
taken care of by the Fraternity! Probably the Grand Master's decision
accords with South Dakota's law-that in each case applications might
be entertained by the Lodge ! Probably the ballot box will take care
of these enthusiastic Masons! The one who wished to regain standing
so that he might give the brethren the privilege of caring for him-what
a hyper-sensitive, unselfish character he must be: so thoroughly and
keenly alive to the real meaning of Masonry. But in another way, that
man in effect says: While it is true that I have spurned Masonry for
25 years, this organization may be good enough for me to permit it to
take care of me in my old age. Really will not reinstatement jeopardize
the morals of that applicant (if he ever had any) ? Surely in such a
case a Lodge should move carefully, otherwise lasting harm might be
done to this man's nervous system, and this is something to be avoided
at all hazards. We are quite overwhelmed by the unmistakable evidence
of that man's bump of unselfishness and the strong desire he manifests
to do-the other fellow, for alt that he can. Really, brethren of South
Dakota, the unrelieved contemplation of such high and lofty ideals is
too much for our own sensibilities. \Ve must cease-knock off-quitturn to other and less harrowing subjects.

Wisconsin (1925):
The Grand Lodge has decided to have a Wisconsin Masonic Foundation, and to that end a committee was appointed in 1924 to draft a
declaration of trust for such foundation. The committee made an extended report incorporating a resolution, which was adopted with the
report, providing "that a board of nine trustees be and hereby is created
for the purposes of encouraging charity, benevolence, education and
philanthropy, and of securing greater uniformity of purposes, powers
and duties of administration in the management and control of property
given, devised or bequeathed for charitable, benevolent, educational or
philanthropic purposes, and that such board of trustees or any corporation organized by them for the purposes herein provided may accept
gifts, devises and bequests of property for the uses and purposes, and
with the powers and duties, hereinafter set forth, which board of trustees
and successor corporation, if any, and the property so held shall con~titute and be known as the Wisconsin Masonic Foundation.

CLUBS
Clubs of various kinds having as a pre-requisite for joining membership in the Masonic Fraternity continue to multiply and thrive.
There must be a demand for them, otherwise they could not succeed.
It comes back to the original proposition that these clubs are trying
to fill a want that is not supplied by a subordinate Lodge.
If the Organizers and Members bear in mind the fact that they
are Masons first last and at all times, there should be little cause
for complaint. Generally they have been conducted satisfactorily,
and the exceptions are undoubtedly due more to misguided enthusiasm than a desire to violate the written or unwritten laws of
Masonry. In such cases the individual should be disciplined rather
than the entire organization.

Louisiana (1925):
The Grand Master: We do not believe it wise for this Grand Lodge
to endorse or approve several Masonic Clubs, at once, without having
made any investigation of same. These organizations are doubtless doing
a good work, but this matter in each individual case rests with the
Grand Master, and the Grand Lodge expresses to these Social Clubs
our good will and hope that they will always remember the cardinal
virtues of this order: Fortitude, Prudence, Temperance and Justice.
As a legal proposition, no social club has the right to use the name
Masonic in connection with its title unless the same shall be authorized
by the Grand Lodge.
Massachusetts (1924):
It was observed that in their functioning these organizations in
varying measure revealed the virtues and the shortcomings that all
purely social groupings possess. Yet bearing the title Masonic they
became representative even in their inevitable shortcomings, of the Craft
in general. There was slowly growing in the public mind a confusion
as to who or what "~epresented Masonry; a confusion that was more
than liable to resolve itself into a conclusion that was false. The consistently public nature of their life may be considered an excuse for the
Past conditions warranted their
clubs being placed in this position.
being falsely regardtd as Masonry's representatives. In consideration

response has been most gratifying. Some have already eliminated the

Utah (1925):
All Masoni~ Clubs, or similar organizations for social purposes in
this Jurisdiction, that shall require as a prerequisite to membership that
the members thereof shall be Masons, shall be subject to the regulatory
supervisions of the Grand Lodge, and all such organizations hereafter
formed shall submit to the Grand Master for his approval their Constitution and By-laws and a statement of the scope of their intended activities.
Such organizations shall not commence their proceedings or activities
without such approval from the Grand Master, and it shall be the duty
of the Grand Master, whenever it comes to his attention that such an
organization is in existence, to require such organization to comp!! with
the terms of this By-law. No such organization shall engage m any
activity which is in conflict with the established customs and practices
of the Craft.

West Australia (1925):
Grand Lodge (Virginia, 1924) amended its law relating to Masonic
Clubs by making it read: "It is a violation of Masonic law for a number
of Masons to form themselves into a club and meet for social purposes
and adopt the name Masonic Club. The organization of any club within
the membership of a Lodge is forbidden by this Grand Lodge." Well,
there are clubs and clubs--especially in the United ·States, where
thousands of organizations which, formed for purposes, social, political,
electioneering, and otherwise, instead of calling themselves committees
or societies, prefer the high-sounding title "club." Exactly what a
Masonic Club would be in America may not be obvious· but in Australia
including our own State, there are Masonic Clubs, formed for sociai
purposes, just the same as there are in some Masonic jurisdictions in the
United States (this writer was made an honorary member of two of
them), and up to the present it has not been felt that their establishment
was "a violation of l\fasonic law." But, of course, there is no Prohibition (Eighteenth Amendment) in Australia.

COORDINATE BODIES
The desire to legislate regarding membership in co-ordinate
Bodies appears to have died out. Some of the Grand Lodges that
passed laws requiring certain length of time to elapse before Master
Masons could petition some of the so-called "higher Bodies" have
acknowledged that this did not produce any material results as far
as attendance at Lodge was concerned, or increase the enthusiasm
of the average member.
Every man fits into a certain place in the Masonic Fraternity,
and if it is provided for him, his interest and activities will be continuous in the brymch that most appeals to him. Regulating the
individual by too many laws will have the same effect in Masonry
as in National and State affairs.
British Columbia (1925):
It is scarcely ~ecessary to remind our readers that in the past few
years new societies, or associations or orders based upon or claiming
connection with Masonry have been established in the republic to the
south of us with a prodigality rivalling France in the eighteenth century.
It is gratifying to note that many Grand Masters, as well as writers
of these Reports, apparently realize that it is time to call a halt, and
more or less practicable suggestions are offered to remedy this state of
things. Just how effective these remedies may be remains to be seen,
but we fear that none of them strikes at the root of the evil.

Manitoba (1925):
There are certain troubles which are common to many Grand Masters
and Grand Lodges; one of the most, if not the most, persistent of these,
being the fact that various organizations would like to make it appear
that they actually form a part of Freemasonry, are branches of it, or
are under its fostering care. Tbe Freemasons of the present day hope
to hand Masonry down to those who come after them as clean as it
was when they received it. In order to do this it is necessary to be conservative, e'ven at the risk of being accused by those who are not
members of the Craft, and even by some who are, of being too much so.
Dangers from without consist largely of the attempted grafting of such
growths which do not properly belong to the Masonic body, on to it,
and can be guarded against. Freemasonry has successfully withstood
attacks of many kinds from without for centuries, and can keep on
doing so.
Massachusetts (1924):
The Grand Master: These bodies have been aptly designated by an
unbiased analyst as "semi-Masonic" or "pseudo-Masonic." To the
existence of these organizations per se we have no objections. It is
possible that our temperament as a people has encouraged these Social
Constructions. They are here regardless of the presence or absence of
any necessity as a basis for their existence. What concerns me is not
that they are, but rather the measure of value which the Masons who
are members thereof place upon them.
It becomes a matter of concern to the administrators of the Craft
when it is observed that Masons, as they sometimes do, substitute in the
seat of sovereign interest a pseudo-Masonic body for one that is recognized as purely Masonic.
As time goes on I trust that the criticisms of Master Masons,
namely, that they care nothing for the Lodge and have no time for its
labors because of their absorption in semi-Masonic organizations, will
lose its validity. We must continually remind ourselves that faithfulness
to the duty imposed upon us by our membership in a Lodge is the first

part of Masonry"?

Michigan (1925):
The Grand Master : During the past week information reached me
as to certain illegal activities of a non-Masonic organization, which
requires as a prerequisite to membership therein some sort of a Masonic
connection. Believing that the situation presented is serious enough for
some decided action and not wishing to move hastily without being in
possession of all the facts, I therefore recommended that a special committee of three be appointed to make an investigation of this and other
organizations which may be organized and operating along similar lines,
and bring the information thus obtained to the attention of the Grand
Master for his action, and to make a report with suitable recommendations for the guidance of Grand Lodge at its next Annual Communication.

The spirit of intolerance is somewhat natural to mankind, but the
Mason, if sincerely conscientious, is tolerant. He is taught to be gen- "
erous in his estimation of others; every human being has a claim upon
his kind offices, but more especially the household of the faithful. It

Pennsylvania (1926):
The Grand Master: \Vithout in any wise reflecting upon organizations of this character now in the field, I am clearly of the opinion
the time has come to halt further development along these lines. It is
my thought that the time is ripe for the enactment of regulatory measures
that will deny to members the right to accept membership in any outside
organizations, predicating its membership on Masonry, except any such
of these organizations as may at this time be in existence, unless permission for creation of such organization shall first have been obtained
of this Grand Lodge. This would put a stop to a growing tendency
which is calculated to weaken the influence of Masonry and leave to the
future the solution of problems that may arise because ofthe existence
of organizations already formed and now in operation.

Virginia (1925):
The Grand Master: It has come to my attention that organizations
making Masonry a basis for membership have been demeaning themselves contrary to the usages and laws of the Grand Lodge of Virginia.
Every Grand Lodge claims and exercises the right to prescribe the
conditions necessary to obtain membership in any Lodge under its Jurisdiction. This is an inherent right exercised from the first foundation
of Masonry. The Grand Lodge also claims and exercises the right to

30

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

pass laws governing the Craft and this right cannot be questioned,
therefore, in consequence of which sovereignity over the Craft the Grand
Lodge has the undoubted right to prescribe the conditions under which
a Mason can retain his membership. Masons as individuals, or in
groups, or in organizations as Masons, are therefore amenable to the
laws and authority of the Grand Lodge. Organizations whose prerequisite
to membership is Masonic affiliation are Masons acting as such just as
much as if they were a group of brethren from a Blue Lodge, no matter
how many degrees may intervene between that organization and the
Blue Lodge. Therefore, as a consequence, they are amenable to Grand
Lodge authority. As a consequence, also, the Grand Lodge by authority
inherent in it can prohibit Masons as such from becoming members of
any organization whose laws do not prevent and whose policies encourage
a violation of a spirit of Ancient Craft Masonry.

CORNER STONES
In some cases in various communities the laying of Corner
Stones under Masonic auspices has produced friction. This should
not be so, if it could be brought home to the general public that the
ceremony is not intended as advertising propaganda, or self aggrandizement. The Correspondent from North Carolina has perhaps
given us a modern idea.
In olden times the ceremony had a significance that does not
exist today, either from an historical or practical standpoint.

North Carolina (1926):
The contents of a "corner stone" would sometimes make a jackass
laugh. One never sees accounts of any two corner stone layings in
• which the list of things deposited within the cavity is given, in which
the same lists are shown as inventory. Somebody will make a great
fuss about presenting a Lincoln penny to be included therein : some other
will put in a lot of old badges; some scribe of great talent will write
a "Letter to a church a hundred years hence" (every generation feels
it to be its duty to utter solemn warning to those succeeding) ; and the
town paper will almost always find its way into the sacred stone. Thereis something fascinating about the idea of leaving a record which future
generations may read; the small boy climbs a little higher up the tree
than any one else has gone, there to carve his initials, picturing to himself these magic letters as they will be seen in the dim future; the great
man who has spent his life in amassing a fortune, as the day of dissolution approaches, gives the millions to the founding of a great institution,
that this may bear his name to his honor after all that is mortal of him
shall have gone to join the immemorial dust; and parents name their sons
with the names of their fathers.

A.t the laying of the corner stone of the Administration Building of
the Masonic Home the vVorthy Grand Matron of the Order of the
Eastern Star had "a hand in spreading the cement." This is the first
time we recall where a woman took part in this form of "operative"
work.

CORRESPONDENCE REPORTS
It is unfortunate tliat the Correspondents Report of the various
jurisdictions are not available to the Craft generally. Published only
in the Proceedings they generally reach but the Lodges, their Officers and those in attendance at the Grand Lodge, where advance
copies are distributed. Some of the Messages of the Grand Masters
favor the idea that a way should be devised whereby the labors of
those who perform this work can be made more generally available.
Let us hope that some method can be found toward this end. The
recommendation of the Committee from New South Wales is one
workable plan.
While we cannot agree entirely with the pessimistic idea expressed by the Correspondent from New Mexico, still there is considerable truth in what he says.

Florida (1926):
We observe that the report for 1923 covered 120 pages of the
printed minutes of the Grand Lodge, or approximately one-seventh
of said minutes and that the reprinting of this report cost the Grand
Lodge approximately $450. In view of this cost we think that it
is advisable in the future for the chairman of said committee to
shorten and make more brief said report if possible.
At the same time over five hundred pages are devoted to the
returns of Lodges, which apparently gives the name of every officer
and member of every Lodge, as well as those suspended and reinstated. While this is of great value to the mail order concern it also •
causes one to wonder if its educational value is equal to the one
hundred and over pages given to an instructive and thoughtful review of what is being done in the great realm of Freemasonry
which is in fraternal relations with the Grand Lodge of Mississippi.
,Idaho (1924):
The report of the correspondent in this state is topical in character, which, for the benefit of those of our rank and file who
are not likely to read this effusion, means that a particular subject
is taken and everything noteworthy under that heading in any
of the Jurisdictions is collated under the said caption. This is a
method which enables anyone to get a very good idea of what has
been done as a whole on any one thing, but for the egotistic it presents the difficulty that it is hard to ascertain exactly what has been
said with regard to a particular Jurisdiction.
Illinois ( 1924) :
A review of the proceedings of the Grand Lodges of the world
furnishes almost a liberal Masonic education, and the reading by
the individual Masons of a review of such proceedings should give a
more comprehensive and accurate view of the trend of Masonic
thought and legislation than can be obtained in any other way. In at
least one Grand Jurisdiction the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge
prepares a synopsis of the Grand Lodge proceedings and this is
read in the various constituent lodges. We were impressed with the
value of such a course, as it affords all the officers as well as the
members of the individual lodges knowledge of what their own
Grand Lodge is doing. Few officers or members will read the entire
proceedings, and indeed much of the published proceedings would
not be of interest, but a properly prepared synopsis could be made
extremely interesting as well as instructive reading.

New South Wales (1924):
Your Committee recommends a circular letter be sent from
Grand Lodge to each Lodge in the Jurisdiction, drawing attention
to the various articles contained in its report, and submitting them

New York (1925):

Occasionally it has been said that our reviews are severely condensed. They are. In no other way would it be possibel to present
in comparatively few pages a record of the trend of Masonic thought
and action the world over. The reviews include decisions rendered
on serious and puzzling questions of Masonic law; memoranda
of changes in membership and administration; reference to improved
methods for making the benevo.lcnces of the Craft accomplish the
greatest amount of good; indications of dangers threatening regular
Masonry from without and within; evidences, in many quarters, of
a renewed determination to uphold the fundamental principles of the
Craft, to resist departures therefrom, reaffirming particularly the
the Fatherhood of God as a necessary condition for the promotion
of the brotherhood of man, and also checking influences which would
persuade the Lodges to occupy themselves with contentious political
questions more or less subtly introduced. All these and other matters
are noted as they appear in the various Proceedings which have
come to us during the year.
North Carolina (1926):
We thank him (Bro. Eggleston, Virginia) for his kindness when he
says, "We call his attention to the adage idiots and fools, only, never
change their minds." Not being quite sure as to just what use he
would think we should best make thereof, we accept it as an admonition we should do well to "change our mind." Well, we venture
to propose a little game that both of us twain may play. Whenever
Brother Eggleston discovers that he has "changed his mind," we
surmise that, if he were to glance at the mental state of this scribe,
he would discover that the North Carolina reviewer will have done
the same equally as often-and very probably more often. That's
fair; is it not?

Utah (1926):
Now and again we come upon a Report on Correspondence that
hasn't enough of real life to it to even suggest the possibility of
stirring our interest. In this connection we place-or they place
themselves-those who wouldn't for the world venture to assume to
express an opinion of their own concerning the doings of Grand
Masters and other representatives of Grand Lodges and Grand Jurisdictions. "The Brethren want to know what is going on in other
jurisdictions-they don't care about our comments," etc. That's
about as poor an alibi as we know anything about-it's about as
thin as a late-fall calf, fed on skimmed milk, and stabled in a fence
corner, on the shady side of a snowdrift, through a Michigan winter, when spring comes. Our Pennsylvania Brother's reports are not
in this class, hence our sincere appreciation of his production, even
while we dissent decidedly from some of his statements and from a
certain air of finality with which he sets forth opinions on subjects
about which there appears to us to be room for debate. For example
his references to the land-marks, more especially to certain propositions which he asserts are among these fundamentals. They may be
so regarded in Pennsylvania and it is entirely within the province
of the Grand Lodge of the Keystone State to declare what shall be
so understood within its own jurisdiction. But it's a cat of a different stripe to assume that therefore any divergence, or departure
from certain propositions is of necessity an "innovation." Whenever we meet with warnings against innovations in the "body of
Masonry" some trick of fancy, or vagrant train of association
brings to mind that story told in the "Golden Ass" of Apuleius,
which relates how a valiant citizen attacked three robbers who
were breaking into his house, and how he ran them through with hi,;
sword and slew them all. When required later by the Magistrate
to uncover the bodies of the supposed robbers they were found to
be no more than three inflated wine-skins pierced in various parts!

in an evening in a profitable way when no degree work is offering.

Texas (1925):
The Grand Master: I received communication from Fraternity
Lodge, El Paso, Texas, in which was stated that "On June 2, 1923,
White Mountain Lodge No. 3 of Globe, Arizona, was requested as
a courtesy to this lodge, to confer the degrees upon Lewis M.
Robinson, a candidate of this lodge. On January 10, 1925, the Arizona lodge conferred the Third Degree upon the brother, and sent
us a bill of $7.75 for a banquet given at the end of the degree.
This is such an unusual thing the lodge instructed me to ask your
advice in the matter. You will understand that courtesy degrees
are constantly being conferred by all lodges and it would seem
to me quite unmasonic to begin the practice of making a charge
for the work."
I replied in a suggestive way that it occurred to me, that too
many Masons and too many lodges were placing everything on a
commercial basis, and the sooner we put a stop to such things the
better off the Masonic Fraternity would be. If through a spirit of
generosity we should pay such charges it would set a precedent for
such requests in the future and we had just as well commence right
now to stop such things.

Kansas (1925):
CRIMES
In a body composed of men drawn from all walks and conditions of life there must necessarily be at times unworthy ones. At
times there is a tendency to favor the individual at the expense of
the Lodge and overlook the "greatest good to the greatest number." One undesirable Brother, if continued on the rolls, will do
more to bring the Fraternity into disrepute than the work of perhaps the entire membership of the Lodge itself.
No human organization is composed of saints, but when we have
offenders among us our duty is clear.

a number of our lodges a reluctance amounting almost to an unwillingness to deal with those who have been accused and convicted
of offences of a serious and criminal nature. In one instance the unwillingness was so pronounced that I finally took the case into my

Montana (1925):
A member of a Lodge in this Jurisdiction who shall have been
convicted of a felony in any State or Federal Court shall be deemed
suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry as of the
date of the entry of the final judgment of his conviction. He shall
not be re-instated to any of the rights and privileges of Masonry
within one year from the date of his release from imprisonment
pursuant to the judgment, and then only after his application for
restoration to membership, reference of the application to, and report by, an investigating committee, and a unanimous ballot in
his favor by the Lodge of which he was a member when suspended,
if the Lodge be then in existence; if the Lodge be defunct, then he
may be restored to the rights and privileges of Masonry only by the
unanimous vote of the Grand Lodge in his favor. This section is
retroactive as well as prospective in operation.
Ontario (1924):
It is found that there is too much leniency extended to Masons
who are guilty of criminal offences. This shows either a spirit of indifference, or a readiness to conceal or forgive crimes which should
not be tolerated. The constitution is clear on the question of crime.
A Masonic trial should be inaugurated and if the Brother is found
guilty, expulsion should follow.
Masons are not perfect men. Among our hundred thousand,
there are sure to be some "black sheep"; but in order to preserve
our order pure and unsullied, it should be purged of all offenders
against the laws of God or man.
Immorality in every form must be banished from our lodges.
Our laws must be enforced. He who violates the laws of God or
State must be expelled from the body of Masonry. See to it that
Masonry means something in your community. Guard well the
outer door. Let no unworthy man be admitted. If you arc in doubt,
give the Lodge, give Masonry the benefit of that doubt. The standard
of Masonry must not be lowered. The institution of which we are
so proud must not suffer from unworthy members. At all hazards,
and under all circumstances, let us purify our lodges, that they
may, with God's blessing, become beacon lights for humanity.

DEMOLAY
The Order of DeMolay is perhaps occupying more attention in
the Masonic World than any other activity at the present time.
In preparing a report of this character, material is ~rranged
according to subjects. The average amount for each sub1ect was
between four and five pages, while that regarding DeMolay covered
32 pages.
Five of the Jurisdictions followed California in holding that as
the Order of DeMolay was not a Masonic body, individual Lodges
could not act as sponsor for Chapters. Even with this ruling, the
highest praise was given the Order for the great good it has accomplished.
Five Grand Lodges, who had existing laws that only a Masonic
Lodge could meet in the Masonic Temple, changed the same so that
DeMolay Chapters were given this privilege. One of the great
English statesmen truly said: "The Youth of today i~ the Trustee
of posterity." Masonry's interest in the boys and girls of today,
whether through the Order of DeMolay, the Daughters of Job or
the Order of the Rainbow, means building for that future,
The Order of DeMolay is not a junior Masonic organization,
and this is firmly impressed upon its members. Neither is it a
Masonic kindergarten or a preparatory school for Masonry. We
kn9 w, however, that a young man who h~s graduated froz;n its ranks
is in a better position to understand the ideals and teachings of the
Masonic Fraternity than one who has not.
The Order now exists in every State in the United States, Canada, Mexico, Porto Rico, Panama, France and Italy. The membership is over 155,000, embraced in over 1500 Chapters.
Arkansas (1925):
Grand Master Whaley: If my year's work is ever recalled in ~ny
man's memory, I would rather he would r~member me as havmg
raised my voice and used my utmost effort m behalf of better educational opportunities for our children.
I therefore, am strongly in favor of the DeMolay. I believe
one ~f Masonry's greatest opportunities is among the near Appren-

43

tices. I fear your apprenticeship and mine began too late to make
of us the finished workmen and conscientious Masters that we
should be. Masonic scholars in all ages have been disappointed in
the small part of Masonry that the average Mason ever grasps
or understands, but the Mason is not to blame. For the first 21
years of his life he has been kept in total ignorance and darkness
regarding its teachings. If he dares to show any boyish interest or
curiosity, he has been met with a wise shake of the head and a
knowing smile and told to wait until he is 21 years of age before
trying to learn anything about Freemasonry.
The truth is if we would turn the average boy of from 14 to
20 years of age loose in a Masonic library, he would absorb more
of its history and teachings than the average Mason learns in four
years of Lodge work. I am proud that my generation has given to
the world the DeMolay. When a DeMolay knocks at the door of
our preparation room, he will come not as one groping in ignorance, but one filled and saturated with the fundamental principles of
Masonry.
·
Delaware (1925):
This organization for young men has shown a very substantial
growth during the past year. Many men prominent in the Craft in
our State have actively taken up the work, and their earnestness
and zeal is commendable.
·
All the aims of this organization are praiseworthy, but surely
that essential which tends to make better boys, better men, better
citizens is a factor in itself. An institution working with such symbols as the Holy Bible, the American Flag and the school-books, is
surely worthy of our interest and support.
Iowa (1926):
So far as we are personally concerned, we arc willing to make
an exception in favor of this order and to exclude it from the rest
of the barnacle organizations which are having such a destructive
effect upon the good work of our institution. 'N c know that in our
own comn11111ity it is doing a great anrl a good work for the youth
of our city, a work of which auy institution might well he proud.
As we sec it, it is hardly fair to class the Order of DeMolay for
boys with these shabby barnacle societie~. This for two reasons:
First, mrmbcrship in the DcMolay is not based on Masonic membership, and, second, it is a boys' and not a men's order.
We believe this Order is doing a great and good work in helping the young men of our day to find themselves. This Order

enters into their lives with its beneficent influence during the period
of adolescence, for, if ever, a guiding and a controlling hand is
needed, it is then. Many a young man who does not get the right

Kentucky (1924):
The Grand Master says: We are convinced that Freemasonry
is today engaged upon a greater field of service, doing more constructive work, exhibiting a larger degree of the true spirit of fraternity, than ever before in its history. To have had a part in this
great work will be, to me, a treasured memory. That our membership in Kentucky may continue to march in the front ranks of accomplishment, with other forces for good, is my fondest hope.

Missouri (1924):
The Grand Master: I do not want this occasion to pass without
formally approving the splendid work that is being done by the
DeMolay organization in this and other states. While this is not a
Masonic organization, yet it is a movement for the improvement
and protection of the youth of the land and, therefore, I am deeply
interested in the movement and heartily approve of all that has been
accomplished by it so far.
Missouri (1925):
The Grand Master: The DeMolay organization which has many
chapters throughout the State, and is being sponsored by the best of
the Masonic Fraternity, should receive the support of all Freemasons. This organization is engaged in the work of associating young
men between the ages of sixteen and twenty, and instructing them
in the great principles of the brotherhood of man, reverence for God,
rectitude of conduct and good citizenship. Its work cannot help but
be a blessing to every young man who has become associated with
it. and its benefits will no doubt be reflected in the future lives of
these young men as citizens. Some have mistakenly termed this
organization "Junior Masonry," which is wrong. It is not a Masonic
organization, although it has the active support of and is sponsored
by Freemasons.

New Hampshire (1925):
In the address the Grand Master (Montana) made a rather
savage attack upon the DeMolay, building, as we read it, a thing
of straw. The Grand Lodge told him, by vote, that he was wrong.
New Mexico (1925):
Masonry is assuming a new attitude toward its purposes, and is
translating its beautiful philosophy into terms of constructive usefulness. Chapters of DeMolay are multiplied; the Order of Rainbow
for girls and the Daughters of Job are spreading over the country.
Vigilance in the perpetuation and improvement of our public schools
characterizes the Fraternity. Boy Scouts and Camp Fire Girls are
being trained in the fundamentals of useful citizenship, obedience to
law, respect for authority and recognition of the rights of others.
In short the rising generation is recognized as our greatest treasurehouse. Drought may wither our crops, financial institutions may
crumble and war may lay us waste, but the youth of our land holds
in its keeping the elements of our future destiny.

North Carolina (1926):
We read something today-at a place in Texas we believe,that a cornerstone-laying procession was formed, in which were the
DeMolays. This proclaims to the world something which is not a
fact. So does their meeting in lodge rooms, we believe. We think
it would be very well that they be given the privilege of using portions of the Temples, but there is some doubt about this matter of
using the lodge rooms-unless in conditions like that in Korth Carolina, where nobody seems to care what or how many organizations
meet in the same hall, if the local members are satisfied. Joint
occupancy is the rule in small places.
Oklahoma Masonry supports the Boy Scout movement; it supports the DeMolay movement; it organized the Rainbow work; it
has done and is proud of, many things that some few other Grand
Lodges regard as anathema-and Oklahoma Masonry is thriving,
as much as, or more than, these other jurisdictions. It is far from
being ruined yet, or in the future.

The Grand Master: About twenty Grand Masters express their
high appreciation and approval of the Boys Order of DeMolay,
which seems to be spreading very rapidly. Two Grand :Vfasters refused to recognize it or permit meetings in Masonic Lodge Halls.

South Dakota (1925):
The Grand Master of Ohio wa.s obliged to decline dispensations
to lodges to act as sponsors for lodges of DeMolay because he construed the Grand Lodge by-laws to prohibit it. He says:
"I wish to be understood in this regard that I am deciding

We hope to see the day when every Grand Lodge will amend
its laws to permit the sponsoring of this splendid Order by the local
lodges.
\Ve feel that with all the noble aspirations of the Fraternity
