DUES
Masonry is a luxury, and as such those who desire to avail
themselves of it should pay the cost. Jurisdictions are beginning to
realize this and establish a minimum fee which will be able to take
care of the expenses of the Lodge and its charities. It is a business
proposition and should be handled as such, without regard to sentiment. The decrease in the purchasing power of the "Almighty Dollar" operates in Masonry the same as in every other walk of life.
Florida (1926):
Much importance is attached to the efficient work of the District Lecturers, which brought out a laxness in the payment of annual dues. It was contended that a Brother "is either able to pay
his dues or he is not," and that in the case of those who are able to
pay, but do not, "the sooner you proceed against such a Brother,
the better it will be for the Lodge and for Masonry."
Georgia (1925):
The statement "that the suspension for non-payment of· dues
does not deprive a Mason of any except lodge privileges," strikes
us as too broad. If a member of a lodge able to pay his dues (and

47

dues are remitted for those unable to pay) does not think enough
of Freemasonry to pay the yearly pittance, then he should not be
entitled to any privileges. This, however, does not make it any more
right for a Freemason to assault a suspended member than to attack
a profane.
Kansas (1926):
Notwithstanding the adoption by the Grand Lodge of a standard form of record books and blanks to be used by all lodges,
which includes a form of warrant for the payment of all claims
against a lodge, it is found that in the payment of Grand Lodge
dues many personal checks of secretaries are used, indicating that
not only the per capita tax but the settlement of all bills against the
lodge is paid in the same manner.
This naturally raises the question whether all money received
by the secretary is paid over to the treasurer and whether the treasurer is paying out moneys of the lodge on the order of the Worshipful Master with the consent of the lodge.
The new warrant is in practically the same form as the drafts
now used by banks, indicating that it is drawn on the treasurer,
and payable at a certain bank in which the funds are kept, thereby
granting to every lodge an up-to-date business system for keeping
and protecting the funds of the lodge.
The practice of paying Grand Lodge clues by personal checks
of the secretaries has grown to an extent where the method of handling the funds of such lodges should receive consideration at the
hands of the Grand Lodge.
Louisiana (1925):
The Grand Master: I find that a great many Lodges have fixed
their dues so low that they have nothing left after paying their
Grand Lodge dues and their per capita tax to the Orphanage, with
whi~h to care for their own afflicted and dependent ones. They are
constantly calling on the Grand Master for relief which they should
be in a position to render themselves. I am of the opinion that if a
man's Masonry is not worth fifty cents per month to him, that he
should not remain a member of the Order, because he is getting
nothing out of it, and giving nothing to it, and is a liability rather
than an asset to his Lodge.
I recommend that no Lodge shall be permitted to hold a Charter that has less than twenty-five active members living within hail.
Too many of our weak Lodges are merely drifting along and instead
of being an assistance to the Fraternity they are a drawback and

North Carolina (1924):
The Grand Master feels that Masonry is cheapened, if it costs
little. He says:
In the first place, there is constant grumbling among large
numbers of the brethrer: at the "high cost of Masonry." I am well
aware of the fact that a great many of our members have a hard
struggle to support themselves and their families. But I do not
believe any man has any business joining a Masonic lodge unless he
is not only able but happy to bear his share of the expenses of the
Order and to take some worthy part in contributions to the great
objects fosterecl by the Grand Lodge. The day when Masonry could
be run as a sort of cheap charity show has passed, and I, for one,
thank God for it. Moreover, it is undeniably true that "where your
treasure is, there will your heart be also."
North Carolina (1926):
There is, to our way of thinking, only one prohable danger in
small gain. It is that in some places, where lodges have been living to large extent on fees, the shortage of revenue will pinch their
programs; that for this reason they will look too long and longingly
at the offered fees of undesirable candidates; and that as a result
those may be received who will be undesirable material, and will
hurt the Craft in years to come. The same condition prevails generally; and the same danger is everywhere apparent. The business
of living on initiation fees has crept on some of the lodges by
stealth; they had more money from fees in boom times than they
had ever had before, and at the same time the purchasing power of
their dues dollars decreased. They paid the difference from balance
"on hand." How we do object to raising those little dues we pay!
And how we do like to have a "feed" at lodge expense some-

like. We wonder if these projects are in all respects necessary to
good Masonry. It is so easy to tax. There are so many ways in
which money can be put to good use. And he who invents a new
form of Masonic Charity wins such honor. But taxes are burdens.
May not the time come when those who are charitable with the
living of their less affluent brethren may be swept from power by
;,h~ rank and file of Masonry which now is only "grumbling" at the
high cost of Masonry?" The per capita tax for the next year
was set at $2.50.

EDUCATION
The safety of our Nation and its institutions can only be perthrough the. development of our Public Schools System.
This is a field where Masonry as an institution can function without
danger to itself and for the greater good of all. At the present time
pet~a~ed

it seems there is a tendency to pass some of the responsibility of
the Home and Church on to the Public Schools. If this continues,
it calls for increased interest, not only on the part of Masonry but
every American citizen to strengthen this bulwark of our liberties.
In some of the previous reports we have given our opinion as
to the George Washington Memorial Temple at Alexandria. We
cannot help but think that if in place of being only a Memorial it
had been made a great National University an untold good would
have been accomplished. Our interest in the Public Schools and
the boys and girls attending them should be active rather than
passive.
This Grand Lodge, with the "Public Schools Week," has Eur
nished one example "worthy of all emulation."
Mississippi (1924):
It would be well if the Masters of our Lodges developed the
practice of acquainting themselves with the subject matter to be
presented by lecturers whom they invite; many a false impression
upon new members would not then be made, the real purpose of our
association would not be clouded; it would be impossible for any
political, sectarian, or religious dogma to invade those portals within
which they could never, in very nature of the case, be anything
but stranger.
Missouri (1924):
Twenty-five centuries ago Diogenes said: "Education is the
basis of the Greek State."
Freemasonry has always stood for the education and enlightenment of the masses with equal opportunity for all children,
and to that end, I urge all Freemasons at all times to support and
develop our public school system, including alike the rural school!>
the city schools, teachers' colleges and the State University. The
public school systems of the several States are the very foundation
stone of our government, and the best means for the education
of the American children and certainly, the only proper means for
the Americanization and amalgamation of the constant stream of
foreigners and their children coming to our shores. Let us make
the public school, non-partisan, non-sectarian and for al! the children of all the people, all the time.

ENTERTAINMENT
The Masonic Lodge should only furnish clean, wholesome entertainment for its members either at strictly Masonic functions 01·
those open to the general public. We cannot help but think that
where there has been cause for criticism, it has been due more to
mistaken judgment rather than a deliberate intent to depart from
our traditions.
The social side of life offers the greatest avenue for education.
Bound by no general set rules it offers such a wide field that abuses
can easily creep in.
Illinois (1925):
The Grand Master: Many of our Masters seem to have a rather
distorted idea of the kind of entertainment the members of their
Lodges desire. Several cases have been brought to my attention during the year of proposed entertainments not in keeping with the
dignity of the fraternity. Ih one instance a Lodge planned to give
a banquet and dance in a well-known cafe, on Sunday night. In
other cases entertainments of a vulgar nature were proposed.

FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
We sympathize with our Brethren in Italy. From press reports
at the present they have bowed to the inevitable. We can only hope
that time and enlightenment will change the present condition of
affairs.
The invasion of the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania by the Grand Orient of France terminated the fraternal
relations existing between practically all of the Grand Lodges of
the United States who had heretofore recognized the Grand Orient
and those Grand Lodges. Perhaps it is only by such a drastic method.
that European Grand Bodies, who are inclined to differ from the
American Masonic idea of exclusive jurisdiction, can be brought to
time.
Arkansas (1925):
Throughout the entire foreign jurisdictions there is a spirit of
umest; the enemies of Freemasonry are very active in their efforts
to suppress Masonry.
This is especially true in the Grand Orient of Italy, where after
the clashes between Masonic Lodges and the enemies of Masonry,

Minnesota (1926):
Whereas, it appears that a clandestine body styled the "Regional Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania" and calling itself "Ancient
Accepted Scottish Rite Universal Freemasonry,'' claiming the right
to confer the first degrees in Freemasonry and to institute new
Lodges in the United States wherever it may deem expedient, has
invaded the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania;
And, whereas, it appears that said clandestine body has been
taken "under the wing" of the Grand Orient of France, by a formal
contract made between them, under which the said clandestine body
shall receive warrants issued by the Grand Orient of France for new
Lodges created and instituted in the State of Pennsylvania and in
any other State or Territory of the United States, except the States
of Alabama, Iowa, Minnesota, Rhode Island and New Jersey, with
whom the Grand Orient of France is in fraternal relations;
And, whereas, the Grand Lodge of Minnesota regards the Grand
Lodges of the several States and Territories of the United States,
which have heretofore been recognized by it, as supreme and sovereign and holding exclusive jurisdiction over the Symbolic Degrees
of Freemasonry within the territorial limits of their respective States
and Territories, and regards any attempt on the part of any other
Masonic Grand body, whether recognized as legitimate or not, to
invade the territorial jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of any State

57

or Territory of the United States, as a violation of that paramount
and fundamental principle of American Freemasonry, which lies
at the foundation of the supreme sovereignty of the Masonic Grand
Lodges of this country;
And, whereas, the Grand Lodge of Minnesota regards the aforesaid action of the· Grand Orient of France as an invasion of the
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania and a violation of
the principle of exclusive territorial jurisdiction;
Resolved, that the Grand Lodge of Minnesota supports the
efforts of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania to sustain and maintain inviolable the American Masonic doctrine and principle of exclusive territorial jurisdiction of Grand Lodges.
That the fraternal relations now existing between the Grand

FUNERALS
It is true that there is a lack of attendance of Brethren at
Masonic funerals. In this day and age the inclination is for a private
ceremony rather than a public function. We believe this is right and
proper.
The remarks of the Correspondent of the Grand Lodge of Utah
are applicable to a large number of Lodge Funerals.
Connecticut (1925):

It is not generally known in American lodges that there is no
~fasonic funeral nor burial service in Great Britain, though there is
m some of the colonies. In England the brethren pass around the
grave and deposit a sprig of evergreen, but there is no national
religion which has the burial service. There is, however, a hard and
fast burial service in every Grand Lodge in the United States, and
ma.ny Masters, probably believing it came down to us like an apostolic succession, stickle for it as vigorously as if it were a landmark
frequently offending an attending clergyman, and at other times be~
ing offended by a sensitive preacher.

One Lodge sent out notices for a funeral, hut only two of
the brethren reported for duty. We think it to be true that there
is a growing dislike to attend a Masonic burial. It does not
seem to be as stylish as it once was. Nevertheless, the duty remains.

Utah (1926):
The Grand Master: My observation is that our Fraternity often
makes a very poor impression upon the public upon practically the
only occasions when it appears in public, namely, at funerals, because of thoughtlessness on the part of the brethren and lack of
familiarity on the part of the officers and brethren with the funeral
ritual. I am of the opinion that Grand Lodge such recommend to
the constituent Lodges that their officers and members at convenient times rehearse the funeral ceremonies contained in the ritual
both for use at the public funeral ceremonies and at the grave, until
both officers and members are thoroughly familiar with the service
and the various signs and movements which are a part of it. I
would not go so far as to suggest that each Lodge designate some
Past Master regularly to officiate on all such occasions, but such a
suggestion might not be amiss. The brethren also ought to be cautioned by their officers to refrain from smoking on such occasions
and from loud conversation or laughter while the members are in
view of the public.
Wisconsin (1925):
To assist in the burial of a deceased brother is one of the most
sacred duties of a Master Mason. Every Mason, even at a sacrifice, or at some inconvenience, to himself, should feel in duty bound
to render this last service to a worthy member of the craft, even
though it may have been asked for an utter stranger.

Connecticut (1925):
The Grand Master: I feel that a marked change has come over this
Grand Jurisdiction in this last year. Every one has loyally upheld the
regulations regarding lotteries passed at our last Annual and the sentiment is overwhelmingly against such practices. Other bodies such as the
Shrine and the Grotto have put their stamp of disapproval upon them.
This being so in regard to this one phase of respect for law let us press
forward to the point where all the citizens of these United States, Masonic or otherwise, shall have that supreme regard for the law of the
land and the constituted authority the lack of which is placing us as a
nation in such poor light.
Illinois ( 1924) :
The Grand Master: It is my firm conviction that the practice of
holding any raffle, circus or any form of chance or gaming for the
use and benefit of any Masonic Lodge, and the use of punch boards
for the distribution of prizes in connection with and under the auspices
of constituent Lodges or members thereof, are detrimental to Masonry
and not in keeping with the principles of our great Fraternity. Individual
Masons who participate in the activities as outlined above are liable to
Masonic discipline under Section No. 235 of the Grand Lodge By-laws,
which is as follows :
"All Lodges and the members thereof are strictly forbidden to
give, or attempt to give, the aid or countenance of Masonry to any
raffle, lottery or gift enterprise."
From and after the date hereof, no Lodge of Masons nor member or
members of any Masonic Lodge shall engage in or have any part in the
conduct of any raffle, circus, or any form of chance or gaming. Furthermore, no Lodge of M'asons nor any member thereof, may use or participate in the use of punch boards, or similar devices, for the distribution
of prizes in connection with any enterprise conducted in the name of
Masonry or directly or indirectly for the pecuniary benefit of Masonry
or any Masonic Lodge, or any organization when membership is com-

Kentucky (1924):
The use of gambling devices of any nature, such as raffles, lotteries,
punch boards, paddle wheels, spinning jenneys, and games of chance of
whatsoever nature, for the raising of funds for charitable or other
purposes, in connection with circuses, carnivals, theatricals, musicals,
fairs, bazaars, games, shows, or entertainments of any description,
whether held or operated under the auspices of any Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons itself, or any of its auxiliary organizations, such as
clubs, band, drill team, drum or bugle corps, orchestra, glee clubs, etc.,
also the giving away of chances on prizes whether attached to admission
tickets for such affairs, or otherwise, shall be strictly prohibited.
This amendment in no way bars legitimate entertainments for the
raising of funds, without gambling features in any form.
Louisiana (1924):
To the \Vorshipful Masters, Wardens, Officers and Members of Constituent Lodges under the Grand Lodge of Louisiana.
Brethren:
The tendency of the Masonry of the State of Louisiana to indulge
in the practice of giving fairs, circuses, and bazaars, the raffling of
automobiles or any other commodity, and the use of punch boards,
paddles, and other devices, for the distribution of prizes, under the
auspices of Lodges, and organizations composed entirely of Masons,
reflects upon the good name of Masonry and is not in keeping with the
tenets and principles of our beloved Fraternity; and, therefore, it now
becomes my duty to issue this Order prohibiting such practice by any
Lodge, Organization of Masons, or Mason.
The things forbidden in this Order are simply forms of gambling
and lottery which are prohibited by the laws of the state.
When any Masonic Lodge or Mason participates in, or carries on,
one of these gambling devices they not only violate the laws of the
State of Louisiana, but violate the law of Masonry.
Every Masonic Lodge, Organization composed of Masons, carrying
on these practices, and every Mason participating in these practices, is
guilty of un-Masonic conduct and subject to discipline.

You are directed to read this Order in your Lodge, and to warn
members against the things mentioned, and to see that charges are preferred against any Mason who violates the terms of this Edict.
Massachusetts (1924):
One of the fundamentals of our profession as Masons is respect
for the law. Now, while, as Masons, each of us may be privately guilty
of some infraction of the law, when as a Lodge or group of Masons
we indulge in a lottery we are making a public proclamation that our
profession is not to be taken seriously. The excuse is given that other
organizations conduct lotteries, why shouldn't we; and it is pointed out
that the law is not enforced upon them. What other organizations do or
do not do does not enter into the case. It is a question of what we
should do. It ill becomes us to engage in any practice, however it might
be excused by the presence of a necessity, which often does not exist,
that will give anyone an opportunity to sneer at our profession. The
position of Masonry is too high to be in any manner endangered; its
contribution to life is too valuable to be impaired in even the slightest
degree by any practice which, while it may be winked at, still remains
and in the last analysis will be regarded as a deliberate violation of the
statutes.
Lotteries. A lottery or raffle is a financial operation forbidden
by the law. The operation of lotteries and the sponsoring of financial methods that partake of the character of gambling by the Masonic Lodges of this jurisdiction will be adjudged a Masonic offense; and for the sake of our continued harmonious association, and
for the sake of the good name and character of our Fraternity,
such practice must cease.
Michigan (1924}:
The Grand Master found that an order issued by him to support an order against gambling devices was disregarded in some
cases. After making full report, he says:
I am satisfied, however, that Masons generally have come to a
realization of the fact that it must not be done, and feel that in the
future there will be no further cause for complaint.
Masonry is too big an institution to be obliged to run a gambling
house or give questionable entertainment for the purpose of raising
money to build Temples which are dedicated to certain holy things,
or to furnish the same, and, as this also was· the sentiment of Grand
Lodge, I have tried to eliminate these things from Masonic activities,
and have endeavored to drive home to Master Masons the idea that

64

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Masonry stands for something worth while, and should be an influence for good in the community, and that certainly it does not
countenance law breaking in any form. This institution of ours was
never intended to be popular in its present-day sense, and, above all
things else, it never was intended to be a playground for "jazz" and
the wearing of red pants.
Every tree is to bear fruit, and every institution must be productive. If the underlying principles of these organizations are not
such as to give them life and maintain a respectable standing in the
community without Masonic connection, then surely there is no good
excuse for their existence. The devising of new titles and jewels
for men to wear, and the desire to don some distinctive or outlandish garb, furnish no just argument to compel Masonry to stand
the criticism for their inexcusable activities.
Masons who live in the memory of their fellows, are those who
serve their fellows. The din and the noise and the display, and those
who cause it, are forgotten when they are gone. What we do or fail
to do to promote the welfare of those about us, is the test of service, not the regrettable parade and blare of trumpets and ribald
songs which cause decent, clean-minded men to hang their heads in
shame.

and the selling or buying of something, with or without value, and
giving or receiving tickets that entitle the holder to a chance to win
something.

Texas (1925):
As the writer sees it the Masonic lodge is no place for the man
who habitually uses vile and filthy profanity, and all such men ought
to be kicked out. About the most disgusting thing we can think of
is for the master of the lodge to open the lodge with prayer, and
close it with another prayer (always taking off his hat when he
mentions the name of God) and then go out on the public streets
and vomit vile and filthy profanity, like Vesuvius in eruption. Such
conduct ought to make a monkey blush with shame.
Virginia (1925):
The Grand Master: It has come to my attention that organizations making Masonry a basis for membership have been demeaning themselves contrary to the usages and laws of the Grand
Lodge of Virginia. Every Grand Lodge claims and exercises the
right to prescribe the conditions necessary to obtain membership in
any Lodge under its jurisdiction. This is an inherent right exercised from the first foundation of Masonry. The Grand Lodge also
claims and exercises the right to pass laws governing the Craft
and this right cannot be questioned, therefore, in consequence of
which sovereignty over the Craft the Grand Lodge has the undoubted right to prescribe the conditions under which a Mason can
retain his membership. Masons as individuals, or in groups, or in
organizations as Masons, are therefore amenable to the laws and
authority of the Grand Lodge. Organizations whose prerequisite to
membership in Masonic affiliation are Masons acting as such just
as much as if they were a group of Brethren from a Blue Lodge,
no matter how many degrees may intervene between that organizatio~ and the Blue Lodge. Therefore, as a consequence, they are
amenable to Grand Lodge authority. As a consequence, also the
Grand Lodge by authority inherent in it can prohibit Masons as
such from becoming members of any organization whose laws do
not prevent and whose policies encourage a violation of a spirit of
Ancient Craft Masonry.

Montana (1925):
Brother Hepner: The purpose of the Grand Lodge is to elect
all the Grand Officers above Grand Tyler. Out of forty-nine Jurisdictions, besides Montana, in the United States, forty-two,-or twenty-eight, to start with, absolutely have the same law as ours: California, Colorado, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, New York, New Mexico, North Dakota, North Carolina, Ohio, Michigan, Pennsylvania,
Rhode Island, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, and so
forth; they elect exactly the same way as we do. There are five who
elect in addition one other officer to those; the other officer that
they so elect is the Grand Lecturer. The reason for making that
provision is because the Grand Lecturer comes in close contact with
the respective officers of the Lodges, and so they feel that he, by
all means, should be one whom they should select. So, there are five
of those. Oklahoma in addition, elects for some reason or other,
the Grand Tyler, and they elect the others the same as we do. In
Alabama, it is the same. The Grand Master, Senior and Junior Grand
Wardens, the Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer, which is the
same as ours, except the Deputy Grand Treasurer is elected in Iowa
and Massachusetts. In Massachusetts they have no Deputy Grand
Master. In Iowa, the Deputy Grand Master is a personal appointee
of the Grand Master. Mississippi elects the six we do, and in addition to that, the Grand Chaplain. They are particular as to their
Grand Chaplain, and they take no chances. In New J erscy and Wisconsin, they elect the same as we do, except they make the office
of Assistant Grand Secretary an elective office. In Washington, they
elect the same officers, except that they have no Grand Treasurer.
In the states of Kentucky and Virginia, they elect the first six officers we elect, an.cl in addition to that, the Senior and Junior Grand
Deacon. In Oklahoma, they elect the Grand Orator and Grand
Lecturer. All the officers are annually elected in the District of Columbia, Michigan and Arkansas, except the Grand Chaplain and the
Grand Tyler. In Georgia, in 1923, they elected the same as we did.
In the last report I have, there is a resume of the election and
installation without any suggestion that there was any change.
In forty-two out of the forty-nine, practically, they are elected
exactly the ~ame as we do.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

A void Excessive Legislation. Masonic Grand Bodies, especially
in the last few years, have found themselves affected by the same
malady or disease which has attacked all public organizations,
namely, an excessive desire to legislate. When an assumed evil is
called to attention, the desire seems to be almost overpowering to
deal with it by legislation, regardless of what the results of such legislation might be. No one is especially to be blamed for this malady
which seems to have affected our entire civic and political life. But
it is time to remind our brethren that Masonry does not depend
upon legislation for its existence. If Masonic bodie.s cannot exist
without the regulation of the minutest details, not only for their own
procedure, but also of the life and conduct of the individual members and those who would seek to unite with the Fraternity, then
the process of decay of the Fraternity has already commenced. We
are usurping the functions of the Master, whose duty it is to set the
Craft to work and give them good and wholesome instructions for
their labors.
New Mexico (1925):
In looking through the various Proceedings, I find that some
jurisdictions, to save the Grand Master and to relieve the steady'
grind of Committee work, have Grand Orators, and they orate.
Many of these efforts are truly eloquent, and so long as the speakers
k~ep in the open waters of Masonic ethics and citizenship, what
they have to say deserves a better fate than interment in the pages
of Annual Proceedings where not one percent of the local membership and only the Committees on Foreign Correspondence ever read
them. Possibly this is well, for when some of these orators leave the
safe waters of ethics and hit the shallows of Risto-Traditional
Masonry, a student is filled with wonder, and a desire to know where
they get the authority for the stuff they deliver themselves of. Of
one thing we may be assured, Masonry will never have an acceptable
and accepted history, so long as these orators are permitted to inflict their imaginings on their "less informed Brethren."
New Zealand (1924):
Whenever a vacancy occurs in the office ·of Grand Secretary,
the Board of General Purposes shall advertise such vacancy in the
official paper of the Craft, and invite applications for the position,
and shall submit all such applications to a special committee of four
Past Grand Masters who have filled the position of Grand Master,
one from each of the four centers, who shall consider all such applications and make recommendation, the Grand Master will appoint,
and at the proper time Grand Lodge will confirm.

North Carolina (1926):
Grand Master David E. Moulton evidently finds the duties
of Grand Master exacting; for he remarks in the exordium, in his
Annual Address, that "it is a source of wonder" how Grand Masters

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

in the past have "contributed so much to the Craft from out their
busy lives." It is a matter of the difference between the outside looking in, and the inside looking out. The average Mason looks on the
Grand Master as a figurehead who puts on a six-quart hat to lay a
corner stone once in a while, or makes a nice speech at a lodge banquet when he feels like going, or at the end of his year dolls up in his
best clothes, reads a paper, opens Grand Lodge, tells a few of them
they are out of order or are recognized, invites them all to say
"aye" or "no" in proper season, and calls it a year of glory. The
Grand Master with a year's experience in office knows better. He
verily is no lounge lizard!
We also agree with this. We simply cannot see how any Grand
Master may say to a lodge, "Your by-laws say you shall meet on
the first Monday at eight p. m., I give you permission to make
Thursday at four a regular meeting." And yet a dozen of them are
doing this very thing, and "getting away with it" under the "prerogative" claim. We do not believe any man or set of men has any
right or prerogative to cause disrespect for law-deliberately-and
yet that is what such a dispensation does. An ordinary man like
themselves can say, "Yes, go on and meet when you wish, tomorrow afternoon, and ballot and transfer business." The fact that they
installed him as Grand Master a while ago make little difference;
he is only a man like themselves. Next time, they will ask for the
dispensation; and, if it is slow in coming, they will say, "Well, it
will be all right. Let's go ahead!" Then next time, they forget to
ask for any dispensation; and the law to them is worth the proverbial tinker's dam.

HIGHER DEGREES
After selecting this title the following, written by Albert Pike,
came to our attention:
"It may be too late to change a common terminology. But,
however we may refer to these ancillary of appendant degrees let
us not make the mistake of pretending that a 33• Maso~ is
'higher' than a Master Mason, much less than the Master of a
Lodge. Let us by our conduct and our speech always acknowledge
the Grand Master of Masons in his own Jurisdiction to be the highest officer the Masonic World has ever known or ever can know."
. It ~s a~ true today as when penned. Education along this line
m!ght m time tend to eliminate the practice with corresponding
good results.
Maryland (1924):
And he;e it must be noted that a grave responsibility rests upon
the Symbolic lodges-the constitutent bodies which form this great
and. noble Grand Lodge. The lodges which are represented here
are the very cement and support of Freemasonry. You are the foundation of Ma.sonic endeavor in whatever form it may choose to assume .. To~ little attention is given to the importance-the over:Vhelmm~ in:portance-of the Blue Lodge so that one of the dangers
m America is t~e fact that too often Symbolic Masonry is regarded
as a me.:e. step~mg-stone to other degrees which in the final analysis
are no higher' than the first three.
. The M~son .who wears the emblem of Commandery, or Scottish
Rite: or Shrme, IS erroneously and too frequently considered to have
received those "arcana" which entitle him to greater Masonic knowledge and standing when, as a matter of fact, it is the practical appli-

cation of those truths we have learned in the Symbolic Lodge which
entitle him to Masonic regard. How seldom do we see the "Square
and Compasses" in comparison with the emblems of other degrees!
Let it not be thought we wish to detract from a due regard for
Chapter, Council, Commandery or Scottish Rite, but here is the
thought intended to be conveyed; all of these are outgrowths of
the Symbolic Lodge and are appendant orders only. All of them are
not only appendant but dependent upon the first three degrees,
not only from the fact that a man must be a Master before he can
join these other bodies, not only because the history of our Order
tells us that all Masonic effort sprang from the "Blue" Lodges, but
also because a man must continue to be a Master Mason if he
wishes to remain in the above-mentioned appendant orders.

North Dakota (1925):
It is not probable that we will ever get rid of the term "Higher
Degrees" or that many within the Craft will ever get to know that
there is no such thing as a higher plane than the level of equality
on which we all stand. The desire to take additional degrees and
to be the holder of sounding titles will always persist and we shall
reach the time when the question will not be under discussion. One
Grand Master suggests making the Lodge so interesting by study,
discussions and research that the members will not need to seek
elsewhere for entertainment and information. In other Grand Jurisdictions an attempt to curb aspirants for advancement is in the form
of restrictive legislation, requiring proficiency in certain lectures or
work, or that a prescribed time must elapse between taking the
Master Mason Degrees and petitioning for the degrees in the Chapter or Scottish Rite. This is largely a moot question. Some men
will become Masons. A whole lot will never be anything but
Joiners.

Oregon (1924):
The Grand Master: The by-laws of the Grand Lodge are under
revision. At our last Communication we passed a by-law which prohibited a Master Mason from applying for any of the so-called degrees until after he had been a Mason one year, and had passed
a satisfactory examination in the candidate's lecture of the third
degree. This provision has worked a great injury upon the Royal
Arch Chapter and the Knights Templar, and I presume on other
organizations dependent upon Blue Lodge Masonry. It has never
been my idea that one could force a man to be a good Mason by prohibiting him from seeking more light in it. The place to determine

77

It has so often been iterated and reiterated that the higher de·
grees are no part of Freemasonry. This statement is no more a tor·
rect one than for the grade school principal to say that there is no
more to education after the student has gotten his eighth grade
diploma or for one to say that arithmetic is all there is to mathematics. Scottish Rite Masonry is just as much Masonry as is that
of the Blue Lodge and it is high time that those who are instructors
in our Order admitted it and endeavored rather to make a distinction
which will be intelligible to the neophyte.
Ancient Craft Masonry comprises the three degrees hut Ancient
Craft Masonry in Scotland and England contemplates more than
three degrees. In the United States it is confined to three and it is
these three that our Grand Lodges guard with justifiable jealousy.
But to say that they are all there is of recognized Masonry is misleading and equivocal, especially when our Grand Lodges at their
Communications received and honor as such, high officials in Chapter, Commandery and Consistory and work in cooperation with them
in charitable and benevolent enterprises, sharing their temples and
in fact often being the same individuals in one or the other of all
these higher bodies. Let us get away from the dissimulation and get
a ground of common understanding and expression and phraseology.
Call ourselves Ancient Craft Masons, or Blue Masons, but let us not
arrogate to ourselves the only right to be called Masons for this is
not correct.

Maine (1925):
An exchange has this to say about the first Grand Master under
the American system:
Prior to the American Revolution all charters for Masonic
Lodges in this country were issued by the authority of a provincial Grand Master, appointed from Great Britain, or the Grand
Lodge of England, Scotland or Ireland granted warrants.
When the Declaration of Independence was issued there was
a movement at once among our Masonic Lodges to declare their
independence. Eventually they elected John Blair, an attorney of
note at Williamsburg, who with his officers, was installed October
30th and the American system was established. The system is now
the same in every State in the Union.
George Washington recognized Blair's ability as a jurist by
making him a member of our first Supreme Court in 1789. This able
lawyer, loyal citizen and Mason died at Williamsburg in 1800.
Massachusetts (1925):
These. Latin-American Grand Lodges are constantly accused of
being political. Those which we have investigated are no more po·
litical than our own Masonic. bodies before and during the American Revolution. The principles of liberty, equality, and fraternity
were taught in our Lodge rooms and then the brethren as citizens,
though not as Masons, put these principles into practical effect in
their civil lives. Paul Revere did not make his famous ride as a
Master Mason, but as a citizen. General Warren did not fight at
Bunker Hill as a Mason, but as a patriot. Washington did not lead
the soldiers of the Revolution as a Mason, but as an officer duly
authorized by organized government. Yet the principles which actuated their public lives were taught in their Masonic Lodge rooms.

Michigan (1924):
Ancientness is not necessarily a sign of greatness. The py;amids
of Egypt are worth less than the modern school house. Things of
value are slow coming. They travel over roads that are long and
travel slowly. There is no instantaneous greatness, perfection is the
last to come.
The flag that floats over the nation and that adorns our lodge
rooms has in it every bit of emblem that was ever unfurled in
the name of liberty. It has taken the tears of Israel, the conq~sts
of Alexander, the victory of Marathon, the campaigns of Caesar,
the ashes of Savanarola, the exile of Dante, the blood of William
the Silent, the daring of Martin Luther, the Magna Charla, the
will of Cromwell, the slaughter of the Huguenots, the landing of
the Pilgrim Fathers on Plymouth Rock, the career of Napoleon, the
valor of \Vashington, the chivalry of Jefferson, and the martyrdom of Lincoln, Garfield and McKinley to make its field so blue, its
bars so red and its stars so bright.
Missouri (1924):
At the end of that struggle (the American War of Independence) when Masonic Lodges here turned away and constituted
themselves independent of the Parent Grand Lodge, the Grand
Lodge of Pennsylvania communicated to the Grand Lodge of England an expression of the wish that the friendly fraternal relations
which had existed between the English and American Freemasons
would continue; and though England at that moment was smarting,
as any proud nation would have done, under defeat, hy her own
children, the Grand Lodge of England responded at once with a
communication which the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania values
among its records, a communication which thoroughly and heartily
reciprocated the good wishes of the Brethren in Pennsylvania, and
gave from the Grand Lodge of England, to American Freemasons
then, and for all time, fraternal good wishes.

Scotland (1924):
A matter of ancient history has come to light. It appears that
in 1872 the Earl of Dalhousie was presented with a bust of himself subscribed for by members of Grand Lodge and other craftsmen, and that after paying expenses the promoters of the Fund
had £ 150 left over. Upon the Earl being consulted as to the disposal of this sum he directed that it should he placed in the hands
of a Committee to form a special charity to he known as "The Dalhousie Annuity"; the annual proceeds to he paid to the aged wife
or widow of a Scottish Freemason. The application of the interest
seems to have been lost sight of, or at all events no action was
taken, and at the present day the original £ 150 has increased to
£648, so it was decided to get to work forthwith and spend the interest earnings.

and important item on page 125:
"The Pennsylvania Gazette, No. 480, February 15 to 21, 1737-8,

Freemasonry had been introduced as early as 1731 or 2, by Brother
Thomas Whitmarsh, a partner of Franklin and fellow member of
St. John's Lodge, who had gone to Charleston to set up a press and
establish a branch printing office."

Virginia (1925):
California-As Washington and most of his Generals, several of
the signers, Thomas Jefferson and Patrick Henry were all Virginians, it is up to this writer to set him straight. Contrary to his
bold statement· the fact remains that Jefferson was not a Mason nor
was Patrick Henry. It cannot be shown that all the signers of the
Declaration of Independence except four were Masons, nor that
Masonic pins were worn in Paul Revere's day and time. It is true
that the country was organized chiefly by Masons and along Masonic lines, but while nearly all Washington's Generals were Masons, Charles Lee was the exception, and not Benedict Arnold who,
unfortunately. was, till expelled.
I have on my desk a pamphlet published by the Smithsonian
Institution relating in detail the discovery in North Carolina of a
buried Lodge some six feet by nine with all the characteristics
of a Lodge including the skeletons of the Stationed officers with the
gavels, stone pedestals, and a stone altar. Each of these were in
their proper places with nothing in the north. The article is elaborate and the conclusion was irresistible to the investigator that it
was a Masonic Lodge of great antiquity and that it proved that
the Indians had Masonry prior to the settlement of the land by
white men. This conclusion is not mine. I think that members of
Sir Walter Raleigh's lost Colony of Roanoke Island, whose bodies
were never found, were prisoners of the Indians and left this as the
best possible notification to future generations of the fact, because
those of those generations would know that it was necessarily the
work of Englishmen and hence of members of that lost Colony.
This goes to show, if my reasoning is correct, that there was Masonry in that lost Colony in what was then Virginia. The document is copied verbatim in the work I am slowly doing on a history .of Masonry in Virginia.

HOMES
These Institutions already in existence are and will remain
monuments to the Fraternity. It will always be a debatable question
as to whether this is the cheapest and the best form of handling this
activity.
Some Grand Lodges who have Homes question whether greater
efficiency could not be had and at less expense through a system
other than an institution. Having once started, however, they must
continue.
Georgia (1925):
In all of its undertakings the Masonic Home is the most
prized and deeply loved feature of our institution. We know the
history of its progress, but there should be laid upon the heart and
conscience of every Georgia Mason its hopes and its needs. We are
the big brothers of those who are following on, and their future and
their success depend upon us. This Committee points with pride to
the successful administration of the Home's affairs during the past
year. In the development of the institution an interesting feature has
arisen. Following a careful inquiry it has developed that there are
instances where orphan children can be kept in the homes of their
mothers provided an appropriation be made for their maintenance.
In a number of cases the expense would be less than the cost
of the care of the child at the Home. Under our present law, the
Board of Trustees of the Masonic Home is not authorized to make
such appropriations, and your committee recommends that the
Board of Trustees of the Masonic Home be clothed with this authority.
This statement would seem to bear out the idea that an institution is not always the best solution for all cases of needed relief
and assistance. The inmates of the Masonic Home number 154 boys
and girls, and two old ladies.

Maine (1925):
Is Masonry in Maine doing the amount of benevolent work
which it should do? Many states are maintaining Masonic homes,
hospitals, orphan asylums and schools. New York with approximately 300,000 members spends annually for charitable purposes
more than $350,000. Illinois with its 270,000 members spends $130,000
per year in maintaining its Masonic homes, besides doing other
charitable work. Pennsylvania with about 200,000 Masons maintain~
several homes and hospitals including one which accommodates
over 700 guests and is the largest Masonic home in the world. It
has more than $2,000.,000 devoted to benevolent purposes. To accomplish these results every initiate in Pennsylvania has been required to contribute $20.00 for charity in addition to the regular
fees for the degrees. Last year this amount was raised to $40.00
to be paid by each initiate. Compare this contribution with the
minimum fee of $30.00 charged by most of our Lodges in Maine
where oftentimes the entire amount is spent for running expenses
of the Lodge before the end of the year, leaving nothing for
charity. Ohio with 187,000 members already has a home for over
200 guests and is building a hospital to cost $700,000. Indiana with
120,000 Masons spent last year nearly $100,000 in running its home
where over 300 guests are cared for. Georgia with 67,000 Masons
spends over $40,000 per year for charity. Alabama with 50,000 members cares for its adult dependents and orphans at an annual expense of $65,000. Connecticut with 41,000 members spent in 1923
over $100,000 in charitable work. New Jersey with 78,000 cares for
its dependents at an annual expense of over $65,000 and also pro-

86

vides adequate hospital facilities for the sick. Kentucky with 72,000
Masons spends $75,000 per year for its orphan children and is raising a fund of $1,000,000 to provide a home and hospital. Massachusetts has recently voted an annual assessment of $2.00 per year,
for each member, for charitable purposes. These instances show that
Masonry in Maine is not doing as much charitable work as other
jurisdictions.

Pennsylvania (1925):
Grand Lodge (Minnesota) is performing a fine work of Masonic philanthropy at Rochester, Minn., where the noted Mayo
hospitals are located. It has a representative there who calls upon
and, when necessary, gives aid and relief to Masons and their kin
who are there for treatment. In 1924 he made 6,601 such calls; he

arrangements for caring for the bodies, routing and shipment, and
often attending to railway tickets and sleeper reservations for
friends. As we understand the statement, for this service $3,149.83
was disbursed during the year. This is a fine demonstration of practical Masonry.

and it proves also by comparison, if in no other way, that the claim
sometimes made that there is no need for an old folks home in Virginia is entirely unwarranted by the facts in the case.

INSURANCE
It seems impossible to make a law drastic enough to prevent
Insurance Companies or others from advertising and soliciting business "for Masons only." Masons patronizing them naturally expect
preferred treatment. When not given it, of course, results in dissatisfaction and criticism.
Perhaps the only logical treatment is to educate the Fraternity
generally to the idea that all business is subject to the same general
rules; and that when patronizing concerns operated "for Masons
only" they must expect only such treatment as they would receive
from any other Corporation.
From some of the things that thrive on this basis we must conclude that "Barnum was right."
Arizona ( 1925) :
The Grand Master: Last August I received a communication
from one of our lodges stating that a certain well known member
of that lodge had died, but that the Masonic insurance company in
which he held a policy of life insurance was acting queer in what
looked like an effort to avoid payment of the claim.
Having known the deceased brother very well indeed and having visited in his home, I immediately took the matter up with
the said company as Grand Master and called for a full explanation and statement of its side of the story. Sometime later I received
a letter to the effect that the company had decided to pay the
claim, which I understand was done.
The lesson for the Craft to draw from this is that the general
prejudice of Masons everywhere against the use of the word "Masonic" in any business connection is neither unreasonable nor wholly
unfounded in past experience.

right to furnish a member of such Lodge with a list of its members
for the purpose of soliciting insurance. Your committee heartily
endorse this decision of the Grand Master and hope that any similar
attempt on the part of any Mason in this jurisdiction to commercialize Freemasonry will be stifled at its inception.

Pennsylvania (1925):
The Grand Master: Recently there came to my notice certain
activities on the part of Masons holding agencies for some foreign
insurance corporations which confine their insurance privileges to
Masons only. These activities are so marked in certain sections of
our Jurisdiction that I fear very few of the newly made Masons
escape their solicitation.
While I have no desire to find fault with the character of the
insurance offered, nor question the benefits to be derived therefrom, nevertheless, I do feel that at least in some cases the methods
employed to sell policies are undignified and unworthy on the part
of any member who values the good name of the Fraternity.
It is not a difficult matter to presume on the Masonic relationship especially when dealing with the newly initiate. Indeed so
thoroughly do some of these agents prosecute their work that they
do not wait until the petitioner has been approved but enroll him
as a policy holder at once, with the assurance that. in the event his
petition for initiation and membership is not approved, his money
paid for the insuranec policy will be refunded.
It would be illuminating to know by what method any insurance
agent is given the names of prospective members of our Fraternity,
and I regret that this whole subject came to light so very recently
as to preclude the possibility of a searching investigation being
made.
However, I deem it of sufficient importance to throw out a
note of warning to all offenders by saying that any improper use
of the Masonic relationship, in my judgment constitutes a :Masonic
offense and while we do not have jurisdiction over corporations encouraging such sharp practices, we do have jurisdiction over those
who represent them, and I trust the District Deputy Grand Masters
will see to it that Lodges are duly informed as to their rights, as
well as their duty, and govern themselves accordingly.

INVESTIGATION COMMITTEES
If we. were to select the most important Committee in the
Lodge organization we would unquestionably choose the Investigation Committee. Upon the results of their labors depend the success
and prosperity of the Lodge. Too often the view is taken that if
nothing can be found against an applicant he should be admitted.
Every inquiry should be directed to ascertain whether or not the
petitioner will be of aid, strength and stability to the Institution.
Upon the Committee rests the proposition as to whether their
Lodge will contain "Members" or "Masons." This is an age in which
the door should always be open to the reception of the worthy and
well qualified, but closed against the self-seeking, curious or ambitious.
Kansas (1926) :
The increasing number of trials suggests that the neglect upon
the part of investigating committees may be working a serious injury to the institution of Masonry. So many men are knocking at
the door of Masonry that it behooves every lodge to exercise the
utmost caution in admitting new members, and this can only be accomplished through efficient service on the part of investigating
committees. Members of this most important committee should first
make careful investigation as to jurisdiction, and to do this they
must know the law. They should make it their business to know
from personal observation whether the candidate is physically qualified. They should then make diligent inquiry as to his character
and habits and should satisfy themselves as to his fitness for :Masonic honors. If the petitioner has resided but a short time within
the jurisdiction of the lodge, then the inquiry should extend to the
several places of his former residence.
Montana (1924):
Once more have we traveled over thQ Masonic quarries and
viewed the labors of the craft. What impressed us most is the fact

that most of the jurisdictions are seeking to inquire more intimately

showing that he was made a Mason in that large city where he
spent a few months. If the petition had demanded fuller details of
residence and an inquiry at the place where he resided in Montana,
Masonry would have no cause to blush in shame at the travesty of
this man being made a Mason. Expulsion for misrepresentation will
not wholly cure the malady.

LEGISLATION
The original idea was that governments were established to
protect the rights of the individual from invasion by others. In the
present day we have departed from that and started upon a course
of regulating the individual by law.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Some one estimated that in the last five years 62,000 laws were
passed; 65,000 decisions were made to interpret them. Over 630
volumes of law reports have been published during the same period
to set forth these decisions. Perhaps the pendulum may swing back.
It is impossible to get away from the fact that there is too much
"Thou shalt not."
Former Vice President Marshall gave a solution when he said
he would repeal all laws of conduct and re-enact the Ten Commandments, the Golden Rule, the Declaration of Independence, the
Constitution of the United States, and enforce them.

a long while that Congress was turning out too many laws and the
48 Sovereign States so called were doing the same thing. By reading some of the Grand Lodge reports throughout the 48 Grand
Jurisdictions, I note the craze for legislation. Legislation is the
panacea for all our ills. If a law is placed upon the statute books
in a State, there are some Masons who think it should be enacted
immediately into Masonic law. Now the position I take is one that
every Mason is amenable to the laws of the State and Country, and
there is no necessity for the fraternity to re-enact statute law into
the Masonic law. If we do so towards one law, it will mean the
enactment of the entire statutes of the State. I think it is sufficient
that when a man is made a Mason he assumes an obligation to .be
true and loyal to the laws of the country in which he lives. I think
that in itself is quite sufficient.

Montana (1925):
Past Grand Master Day writes a long letter to the Grand Lodge
(Montana), in which he says that Masonic Grand Bodies are attacked by "an excessive desire to legislate," and he adds that "Masonry does not depend upon legislation for existence." He adds:
"If Masonic bodies can not exist without the regulation of the
minutest details, not only of their own procedure, but also of the
life and conduct of the individual members and those who would
seek to unite with the fraternity, then the process of decay of the
fraternity has already commenced. We are usurping the functions
of the Master, whose duty it is to set the craft to work and give
them good and wholesome instructions for their labors."
Masonic Grand Bodies have found themselves affected by the
same malady or disease which has attacked all public organizations,
namely, an excessive desire to legislate. When an assumed evil is
called to attention, the desire seems to be almost overpowering to
deal with it by legislation, regardless of what the results of such
legislation might be.
But it is time to remind our brethren that Masonry does not
depend upon legislation for its existence. If Masonic bodies can not
exist without the regulation of the minutest details, not only of their
own procedure, but also of the life and conduct of the individual
members and those who would seek to unite with the fraternity,
then the process of decay of the fraternity has already commenced.

Virginia (1926):
Grand Master Price's address was quoted with judgment, making one natural mistake. Grand Master Price was not "bound by
the constitution," Brother Ponton, for we never had any such imitation of the system of civil government of these United States, individually and collectively. We have "The constitutions of Masonry"
only, as our fixed and binding law. We have a Digest of our Statute
Laws which we can amend, alter, or repeal at will. We hold to the
prerogative of the Grand Master to temporarily set aside any of
those laws when he thinks it best for the good of the Craft In
recess he is the Grand Lodge. This has always been our law and
ours is the senior of all the Grand Lodges as now organized, dating
from 1778.
LIBRARIES
Those jurisdictions that have provided traveling libraries have
supplied a long-felt want, and the demand for such a service continues to increase. With the advance in science, this means of
information may in time become obsolete, but there is no better
way of furnishing a Masonic education to a member located in
outlying districts than through this plan.
The Grand Lodge libraries of Iowa, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and the Supreme Council of the Southern Jurisdiction
A. & A. S. R. are examples of what time, patience, and perseverance
may accomplish.

Canada (19~5):
The office of Master of a Lodge is one of the greatest importance
and requires of the incumbent vastly more than the ability to learn the
ritual and confer the degrees.
The welfare of the Lodge is in his keeping and its success or failure
is in proportion to the wisdom and discretion with which he manages its
affairs. A knowledge of Masonic Law as practiced in our jurisdiction
is essential. No one should accept the office of Master of a Masonic
Lodge unless he has a fairly good knowledge of Masonic Law and
parliamentary procedure, and is determined by study and research to be
in reality what he is in name, Master of his Lodge. The means are
within the reach of all; all that is required is energy and application.
The Wardens, who may be required in the absence of the Master to
succeed to his duties, should feel that their responsibility in this matter
is as great as the Masters. In a great measure, it is the fault of the
Lodge and its members, if the government is faulty. No one should be
elected to the East who has not shown that he possesses the necessary
qualifications for that important position.
A poor Warden or Senior Deacon will never make a good Master.
A good Warden or Senior Deacon may not have the necessary qualifications for a good Master. For this reason, the system of regular
promotion, regardless of qualifications, should be at least modified,
remembering that merit is the just title to our privileges. I know of
cases where a year's apprenticeship in the kitchen is necessary to gain
the coveted office of Junior Steward.
Manitoba (1924):
The success of the Lodge depends, in the last analysis, on the zeal
and efficiency of the Secretary, and we can always justify extended
reference to his duties. We do not propose to elaborate our views here,
but we beg to express the hope that serious attention will be given to the
the desirability of training Lodge Secretaries in their work. For our
own part, we would lay down the dictum that a Past Master is the best
type of individual to be chosen as a Secretary. He has a fairly good
conception of the work of the Lodge, and a more or less. intimate
acquaintance with its members. He is, presumably, qualified to initiate
policies and practices for the advantage and progress of the Lodge. It
may, likewise, be assumed that he is dependable, enthusiastic and mindful
of his obligation to the Craft as a whole. With a fair amount of instruction in the keeping of books, he could be expected to render satisfactory
service as long as he cared to hold the position. It would not be
advisable to enact constitutional provision, making it obligatory for a

REPORT ON CORRESPONDE.c\fCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Lodge to appoint a Past Master as its Secretary, but an understanding
to this effect would go a long way towards improving the administration
of affairs in the constituent Lodges.

Nevada (1924):
Next year they are to act upon the proposition to make Secretaries
of Lodges, who have served for five years, permanent members of the
Grand Lodge, with a vote. We have not encountered anything that will,
in our opinion, work for the greater interest and efficiency than this.
The Secretary of a Lodge is a tremendously important factor in Masonic
life. The thing that will make his service more intense and energetic
will work for the greater good of all. This proposition ought to work
out that way.
Utah (1926):
The Grand Master: The suggestion has been made a number of
times in the past few years that it would be well to have at least one
of the Stewards a Past Master so that the neophyte at our door might
be assured such a reception as would leave with him pleasant memories
of the minutes devoted to preparation for our initiatory ceremonies. I
am in hearty accord with this suggestion and hope that some of our
Lodges will try the plan and see whether it is as good in practice as it
seems to be in theory.
In this connection may I also say that it seems to me that the
brotherly custom that prevails in many if not all of our Lodges of
advancing a brother once appointed to the line as Junior Steward, each
year during good behavior and without the scrutiny of his qualifications
as they would have were he not in line, is all wrong. The elective
officers of a Lodge, as well as the appointive ones, should be chosen for
their qualifications successfully to govern the Lodge and to perform their
respective functions in the Lodge and should not be advanced except for
merit.
I observe from the Lodge returns that in at least one case a very
young Mason has been elected Secretary of his Lodge. The Secretary
of a Lodge might be likened to the hub of a wheel. If he is the right
kind of man he is the center of Lodge activities and is usually retained
in office as long as he is willing to keep the job. The Secretary can
be and nearly always is the Master's most trusted and valued lieutenant.
There may have been particular reasons for the choice in this case but
it seems to me that Lodges ought to exercise great care in the selection
of a Secretary and that generally speaking he ought to be a seasoned
member of the Craft.

vVe are all agreed upon the question of the kind of Institution
to which we are privileged to belong. Let us endeavor to keep it so
by not allowing it to be used for the protection of those who do
wrong or promote the welfare of one who is not entitled to it. Freemasonry is performing a great service in welding men together and
teaching them ideals of a great common Brotherhood, and if we by
our efforts can strengthen these bonds we will have fulfilled that
duty which is required of us. While we continue to do this there
is no power on earth that can undermine our Fraternity. It is only
when we are inclined to deviate from this path of righteousness that
we are in danger of weakening an Institution founded on the purest
principles of piety and virtue.

Missouri (1925):
What do we care about the antiquity of our Fraternity? \Vhat
does it matter whether our ancestors did or did not participate in
the building of King Solomon's Temple? Neither pedigree nor ancestry can make any institutioi'.i or individual great. Not what Freemasonry was yesterday, or a thousand years ago, but what it is to·
day and what it shall be tomorrow, these are the all important questions to the good Freemason and the true man everywhere.
We should elect to our Fraternity only those men who are good
and true, and then the symbolic story of the ritual in the various degrees should be given to the candidates in a sincere and earnest
manner by only those sincere and earnest Freemasons who exemplify
out of the lodge, in their daily lives, at home and in business, the
sublime lessons and truths which are intended to be taught the candidate. Unless we stand before the candidate as clean and true men,
the language of the ritual will be as sounding brass and tinkling
cymbals, falling on deaf ears because the candidate, knowing us,
will likewise know that the ceremony is mere hollow mockery. We
cannot honestly ask the candidate to wear his apron spotless unless
we keep our own aprons clean from the stain of sin in this life.
Freemasonry is not a political organization, but through the influence of its moral teachings on the mind of the individual it should
exert a powerful and wholesome influence on the politics of the land
and likewise should become a beautiful handmaiden to the church,

Every Freemason should be a builder and each one must build his
own building, not a building of bricks of clay, bound together by
common mortar, but a temple built within the heart of the builder
with bricks of virtue, cemented by righteous thoughts and deeds,
where the God of Love may dwell in peace.

New Zealand (1924):
Individual judgment is never perfeet. It is ever prone to look
upon the apparent and to overlook the actual-and so Freemasonry
is judged as I have remarked by individual failures which are apparent, but the great silent and unseen work of the Craft is overlooked.
Time is the only impartial judge, and it is. judging Freemasonry
kindly.
During the last two centuries many once great institutions have
been swept away by an ever-advancing wave of public opinion. They
have outgrown their usefulness, the world no longer had time for
them, and they died and are forgotten.
Oklahoma (1925):
If the Masonic Order is to take and maintain that leading and
commanding position which is its inherent right, if we are to
constitute it that living, breathing, vital and vitalizing force of
which it consisted in the early days of our republic, it is necessary for us to look to our acts; it is required that our activities
shall not consist solely and simply of conferring esoteric work
upon candidates and members, but we must reach out with the
tentacles of our acts and the fingers of our performances and touch
the lives of our brothers and all those needing the help and assistance that our fraternity can give.
The social call has been substituted for visits and for companionship. Conversation is a lost art. Entertainment and music have
been professionalized, and are furnished almost solely by hired performers. Even home music has been professionalized until the untrained members of the family are expected to remain discreetly
silent.
Nursing the sick and administering charity are being transferred to the paid nurse, the salaried official, the organized and
officered institutions. The home is asking the school to take its
job off its hands. In short, the tendency of the times which transfers every service to the community or to the paid employee has
invaded the Lodge and left the average Mason with nothing to do
in Masonry except to sit by and witness the conferring of an
occasional degree.

Utah (1926):
Too long, Brother, Masons have been taught, in effect, that
conferring degrees and attending banquets about represent the limits
of Masonry. The habits and sentiments of generations are not to be
changed over-night. Further, our Fraternity has received too many
members who are unable to see over, or around, or beyond the
lapel pin they wear-the beginning and the end of Masonry for
many are to be found in that alone.

PAST MASTERS
The conferring of the Past Master's Degree, either under the
express provision of a Grand Lodge law or as a supplemental ceremony is educational. If it does nothing else it serves to give the
Master-elect some additional historical information that he would
not otherwise receive.
If during his term of office a Master has lived up to his responsibilities, he will continue his interest. Past Masters by reason of
lack of opportunity too often must be satisfied with honor only.
In other cases, their ambition satisfied, they sink to the level of
non-serving, dues-paying members.
Alberta (1925):
The Grand :-.faster: A brother who had received the Past :-.faster's
degree in a Royal Arch Chapter and who was denied the right of heing
present while the installed Master's degree was being conferred upon
the W. M. elect, appealed to the Grand Master for his ruling thereon.
Ans. A Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Alherta
can recognize only those degrees which have been conferred by Lodges
under this jurisdiction or as is expressly provided for hy our constitution, by Lodges under some other Grand Jurisdiction recognized hy this
Grand Jurisdiction. In no case will this Grand Jurisdiction admit to
participation in its degrees a person who has received such degrees in
a Royal Arch Chapter or in any other body conferring other than
the first three degrees of Masonry. There arc other reasons which
cannot he fully explained, inherent in the degree of Installed Master,
which would not permit of a brother being present who was not either
a Past Master or one duly elected to that office. I therefore ruled that
the brother was not entitled to sit in Lodge while the lustalled Master's
degree was being conferred.

New York (1925):
Tbis committee's report is interesting in that it prescribes a form

North Carolina (1926):
Florida is one of the states in which the Past Master's Degree is
controlled by the Grand Lodge, wherefore we find a report that same has
been conferred on almost all installed Masters of the year. We note
that in Florida, as in North Carolina, all officers of the Grand Lodge
advance. While neither of these Grand Lodges has suffered from it
within this writer's own experience, we are nevertheless opposed to the
plan ; for it virtually means that every Grand Master appoints a successor, and the "election" of officers is reduced to the status of a farce.

will serve some useful purpose. Personally we should be reluctant to
add any degree, or near degree, or anything that might be construed or

has a place.
Virginia (1926):
The Grand Lodge at its last Grand Annual Communication adopted
a recommendation of the Grand Master that no brother can be installed
'ls Master of a Lodge until he shall have received the degree of Past

* * *
We are sometimes puzzled to know why some other young Grand
Lodges as well as Alberta, which Grand Lodge is not alone in that
particular, hold the view of the P. M. degree. In Virginia it was, like
the Royal Arch, conferred in Lodges. In 1808 the Grand Chapter was
established with the consent of the Grand Lodge, to have exclusive jurisdiction of all of the Chapter degrees except that one over which it was
agreed that jurisdiction was to be concurrent. Tbe result was that
Chapters omit it as regards those who have had it in Lodge and Lodges
do the same as to those who have had it in Chapters. Any Chapter
Mason having had the same degree is eligible to sit in any Lodge of Past
Masters and they often confer it for Lodges in the Chapter by request.
How it ever, anywhere, became two separate degrees is hard to account
for. Every Warden must have it to qualify him for presiding and it is
held to be a prerequisite for the R. A. Why the latter is lost in the
mists of time. Tradition is that it was once given only to Past Masters
as a sort of reward for a year of service already rendered, hence the
title is now an absurdity. It should be called the Present Master's
degree and should be abolished in the Chapter because it is nothing more
than a subterfuge at best.
POLITICS
Masonry as an organization has no part in partisan politics.
This, however, does not mean that a Masonic Lodge should not
be an Open Forum for the discussion of matters of public interest.
If a Lodge, as part of its work can bring home to its members the
responsibility that rests upon them through their right of franchise
and the necessities for active participation as individuals in the affairs
of their Nation, their State and their Community, a lasting good
may be accomplished.
The tendency of the present time is to shirk this responsibility-the great open spaces, business affairs, social duties and in
some cases down-right laziness or indifference make more of an
appeal to the average voter on election day than the polling place
with a ballot box.

The excerpt under Vermont gives figures that support this
statement.
President James Madison said: "A popular government without
popular information or the means of acquiring it is but a prologue
to a farce or tragedy, or perhaps both. Knowledge will, forever,
govern ignorance; and a people who mean to be their own governors must arm themselves with the power that knowledge brings."
Colorado (1925):
The Grand Lodge of Colorado is the supreme Masonic authority of
this state. It publishes no magazines and endorses none. It resents the
brazen claims of certain publications that they are Freemasonry's representatives. The Grand Lodge of Colorado speaks only through its
constituted authorities, and it has no representatives at Washington or
elsewhere, except those duly appointed to represent it at other Grand
Lodges.
Furthermore, The Book of Constitutions of the Grand Lodge of
Colorado provides : A Lodge as such shall not present a petition to the
civil authorities, or take part in municipal, state, or national affairs.
This Grand Lodge will not assume to regulate the action of any one
as a private citizen; but its laws prohibit Masons, in any Masonic capacity,
from presenting petitions to the civil authorities. All Lodges and all members of Lodges will therefore take due notice and govern themselves
accordingly.
Iowa (1926):
We do not believe that Masonry as an institution should ever be
mixed up in matters of politics and state-craft, but there are many other
organizations in which Masons, recognizing their common ideals of better
government and real happiness for humanity, can combine in united
efforts for the common good. And it is along these lines that we believe
the teachings of the craft are destined to make themselves most vitally
felt.
New Jersey (1925):
One of our Lodges, in its official publication, urged that the members participate. actively in a partisan political primary, and give their
support to certain members of the Lodge.
Upon having the matter brought to my attention, I sent for those
who were responsible for the notice and, being unable to obtain a satisfactory explanation, I caused the Lodge to be summoned in emergent
communication. As no member of the Lodge attempted to repudiate the

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

111

notice, the offense thus became chargeable to the entire membership and
was a Lodge offense. However, as the brother directly responsible
apologized for his act, I felt that censure was a sufficient punishment
and I accordingly adopted that course. 'Ibis matter might well have
been omitted from any mention but for the fact that one of the Past
Masters of the Lodge asserted there is no express prohibition of political
activity in our written law. From time immemorial it has been our
proud boast that no subject of race, creed or partisan politics is or may
be permitted to enter our tiled doors ; that around our altar all good
men may gather in harmony and that brother may meet brother without
fear of partisan disputes and controversy. The discussion of religious and
partisan questions in our Lodges is unmasonic and prohibited.

Indiana (1925):
The Grand Master : I recommend that it be the will and direction
of this Grand Lodge at this present meeting, especially, that the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee of three to submit to the
Congress of the United States, the proposition, and urge the passage of

South Carolina (1925):
The Grand Master: Only one incident of general interest threatened
to disturb the tranquility of the Craft. This was the publication, bf a campaign manager, of a letter from our Grand Secretary, giving the principal
dates and affiliations in the Masonic history of a candidate for public
office. This letter was copied-head, salutation, body, and signatureto show that it was official, though no attempt was made to make a
facsimile. It was sent out as campaign material without the authority
of any Grand Lodge officer. Both the campaign manager and his
principal are Masons in good standing in our Jurisdiction. The inquiry
and the Grand Secretary's letter in reply were and are perfectly proper;
the use made of the Grand Secretary's letter was highly improper. A
number of the brethren all over the state were justly incensed-some
thinking the Grand Secretary was attempting to aid a political aspirant,
some thinking he had been duped by the campaign manager.
The
letter was mailed out one night. I heard of it the next morning, and
immediately took such steps as occurred to me to stop it. The Grand
Secretary was in Portland, Maine, at the time, attending the Triennial
of another Masonic Body. The candidate was defeated at the polls a
