day or two later, and I believe this letter contributed in no small
measure to that defeat.
I bring this matter to your attention in order to impress the fact
that we, as Masons, do not capitalize our connection with the Order
for social, financial, or political ends, and whoever attempts to thus
prostitute his Masonry inevitably meets disaster. This discloses a characteristic case of an attempt at the prostitution of :Vfasonry to political
purposes, with the usual result.
Texas (1925):
The Grand Master: I have been forced to defend the purposes of
this Grand Lodge on many occasions when I would be confronted with
the question, "Do you not believe that it is time for the Masonic Fraternity to actively engage in politics?" I regret to say that, in my opinion,
there is a growing tendency on the part of some members of our Fraternity to have Masonic Lodges participate actively in politics and
unless this tendency is checked, Masonry will pay a greater price for
such activity than it has, and is paying, for permitting outside matters
to become injected into its internal affairs contrary to the declared
purposes of this Grand Lodge. The brethren who have talked to me
appear to be honest in their views but, in my judgment, are misled as
to Masonic ideals and teachings.
If Masons, as an organization, can urge the passage of the SterlingReed bill, why should they not have the right as Masons to use their
influence for the Maternity bill, or any other legislative measure pending
in Congress or the Legislature? Strange. such a difference there should
be, 'twixt tweedledum and tweedledee.
Masonry as an organization cannot afford to use its influence for
or against legislation of any kind or character. The individual Mason
is free to favor or oppose any proposed legislation in Congress or in
the legislature of his state, without dictation or restraint from the
Grand Lodge. When Masonry, as an organization, engages in partisan
politics it is on a toboggan slide to a condition of chaos, just as we
find in Mexico.

Vermont (1926):
Brother Theron (South Dakota) believes it is not only the right,
but the duty, of every Mason to exercise his right of suffrage in the
election of civil officers, and he issued the following circular letter to

As an organization, we have nothing to do with party politics, yet
we are pledged to do our best for this America in which we live and
from which we receive uncounted blessings.

Do you know that :
In 1920 twenty-seven million voters stayed away from the polls?
As a result twenty-six million voters-a minority-elected a
President.
In North Dakota we learn 87,054 voters failed to perform their
solemn obligation?
In South Dakota, 1920, number votes cast 182,237 and that
there were 139,646 slackers?
This year steps are being taken all over the land to get out a
vote that will represent 100 per cent of the voting public?
Business organizations, Boy Scout troops, clubs and societies
are sending forth urgent appeals to the voters to see to it that
this indifference be done away with.
Give serious thought to the following figures: In 1896, 80 per cent
of the eligible voters of the country went to the polls and voted. In
1900, 73 per cent cast their ballot. In 1908, 66 per cent. In 1912, 62 per
cent. In 1920, less than 50 per cent of those eligible to vote went to
the polls.
Therefore, your Grand Master urgently requests that the Masons of
this jurisdiction do their utmost to secure a 100 per cent vote and further
directs that this communication be read in open Lodge and that copies
be sent to all the members of your Lodge resident of this state.
Vote November 4th. Vote as you please, but vote.
We agree with him that the average citizen does not take an active
interest in the election of public officers as he should do, and the result
in many instances is inefficiency and corruption in public office. We
believe with Brother Theron, that it is the solemn duty of every Mason
to take an active interest in the selection of public officers, not as
Democrats or Republicans, but as law-abiding citizens.

Wisconsin (1925):
We think of nothing so new or novel as to require especial notice,
unless it be the growing tendency of several Grand Lodges to act upon
matters purely political in their nature, generally concerning school
affairs. They have probably done this unwittingly without considering
that they were by so doing violating the time-honored traditions of the
Craft. Usually such measures have been recommended for favorable
legislative action as the result of sentiment and on the spur of the
moment without serious discussion or consideration of the various
features in the matter. The tendency is a dangerous one and should be
avoided. We refuse to recognize foreign Grand Lodges that permit
the discussion of political questions in their Lodges ; why trespass in
this behalf ourselves?

PROHIBITION
The effects of the 18th Amendment and the Volstead Act in
the Masonic World as well as in every-day life continually receives
attention. They are the law of the land and a Mason through his
obligations and teachings is bound to obey them. The charge that
. the Master Mason should obey the moral and civil law cannot be too
strongly impressed. Generally we believe it would have a better
effect if this great basic principle was brought home to our membership. Masonry demands obedience to law and should require it
generally rather than legislation on specific matters.
Arkansas (1925):
Grand Lodge adopted the report of the Jurisprudence Committee,
making it obligatory on the Junior \Varden, when notified that a member
had been convicted in any court of competent jurisdiction of violating
the prohibition laws, either national or state, to procure a certified copy
of such conviction and present it at first meeting of the Lodge, and
thereupon it shall be the duty of the Lodge, after due trial, to expel or
indefinitely suspend such member, and the certified copy shall be conclusive evidence of the violation of the law.
I believe that we are coming into a better attitude toward the 18th
Amendment. The drinking among our young people, which a year or
two ago flourished so widely, has begun to wane-the thrill of forbidden fruit has died away with the first unpleasant taste and our
young people's admiration for clean, wholesome bodies as well as alert,
active minds has saved them. Only the lounge lizard persists in carrying
his hip flask, and maybe that is Nature's way of altowing him to work
his own destruction, with the least lost motion for the rest of us.

the Grand Lodge of Kentucky; and any Kentucky Lodgt;! knowingly
electing such a person shall forfeit its charter.

· any Mason to sell, buy, transport, or be in any way connected with
or interested in, the sale, purchase or transportation of intoxicating
liquors, and if any Mason shall be guilty of so doing, it shall be the
duty of the Master of the Lodge in whose jurisdiction the offense may
occur, to order charges to be preferred against the offender, and a trial
proceed thereon as in other cases. If any Master shall refuse to perform
his duty under this section, or if any Lodge shall fail to do its duty upon
proper charges preferred, the Grand Master shall suspend the Master or
arrest the Charter of said Lodge, as his judgment may deem best, and
report his action to the next Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge.

PUBLICITY
The attention given in the public pres's to the doings of the
Masonic Fraternity in a large number of cases produces results
that are far from satisfactory. Too often the information is incorrect
or garbled. It is only the unusual that appeals in this age of
rapidity. If the following thought could be practiced it would have
a beneficial effect:
"Lamps do not talk, they shine. A light house sounds no drum,
it beats no gong, and yet over the water its friendly light is seen
by the mariner."
England (1926):
There is only one point in the report to which attention need
be called. That is the concluding paragraph of the effective portion,
which deals with the unauthorized publication of matters affecting the
secrets and inner proceedings of the Craft. Some mischief already has
been caused-and there have received in the past few hours a letter testifying to that mischief-by the circulation of an entire misconception and
misconstruction of what the Board proposes in this paragraph. As will
be seen by any who carefully read it, what is aimed at is the publication
of anything purporting or affecting to give particulars of the secrets
and inner proceedings of the Craft; and every Freemason is fully

118

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

aware of what that sentence means, as showing that what we are
striking at is the increasing number of books, pamphlets, and other
publications which affect to reveal the hidden secrets of Freemasonry.
The Board is determined, as far as its powers allow, to prevent trouble
within the ranks of Masonry, either through renegade Masons or through
reckless Masons; and we would not permit that trouble to be committed
for the sake of either notoriety or personal gain. We, therefore, give
full warning through this Grand Lodge that, while we are not witchfinding or heresy-hunting in any sense, we will endeavor to keep a v.ery
strict watch on the increasing laxity of some of our Brethren, who, in
their anxiety to earn either popularity or some more material substance,
circulate that which is secret, and should be secret, to Members of the
Craft alone. And in that we are certain we shall have the hearty support
of every good Mason.

We have found newspaper reporters and editors who seem to look

Manitoba (1925):
Within the past few years there are many signs which point to an
increasing desire on the part of many Lodges to secure a cheap publicity
by having inserted in newspapers lists of officers elected or write-ups of
social happenings. Individuals break into print with matter which had
better be left unsaid. Freemasonry was never intended to be a popular
institution in the common meaning of that word, but in response to the
clamor of some brother, "What is Freemasonry doing?" we find publicity courted, not shunned, for fear our time-honored fraternity will not
receive due credit or the public forget our existence.
Constantly we hear the cry that this order and that order are doing
something we never attempted, and that we must mend our ways and
become up-to-date, or in otherwise-advertise. Can we not in some way
bring our brethren to realize that the purpose of Freemasonry is to teach
the individual to do these things, and that being accomplished Masonry
has attained its objective. Must we forsooth join in parades and publish
our doings in order to let the world know where we stand. Brethren,
the world does know where we stand, and that almost every movement
for the betterment of each community, no matter under what name
organized, is headed and fostered by Masons. That in short is all
the public need to know and all they should know.

119

Every brother upon his initiation is supposed to have read to him
that clause in our Lodge by-laws which forbids the imparting to the
profane of any information concerning what takes place in the Lodge,
but it would appear as though to many this article has become a dead
letter.
Legislation will not cure all our ills and no great harm has been
done so far, but this is a liberty which may develop into license, and we
would strongly urge that no information or matter for newspaper publication touching Freemasonry or concerning our Lodge or Grand Lodge
activities be given out by any member until the same has been approved
by our Grand Master or Grand Secretary.
North Carolina (1926):
We notice the difference between the British attitude toward Masonic
publicity and the American conception of it. But we, in America, do not
object to having many things about Masonry appear in the secular papers.
Not only is this difference found, but we, in America, are "button
Masons" and "watch charm Masons," the exceptions being in the minority.
In these countries, on the contrary, such jewelry is not worn in public.
In some of them its use in public is prohibited by Masonic law. One can
see at a glance that there is a different conception in the minds of many,
of what Masonry is. Moreover, the fellow who would join so that he
may parade his Masonry, would be eliminated in these countries. Here
the condition of Masonry is improved. Altogether the attitude of these
people, which makes public parade of Masonry impossible, is worth considering. We remember that one American Grand Master ruled that it
was improper to put Masonic emblems on the radiator of an automobile,
but he did not, of course, object to the use of the same on the front of
your coat. We told the Review-reading public that we didn't see the
difference, and the Reviewer in the jurisdiction in which came this
decision tried to explain this difference, but he made a dismal failure
of the attempt.

South Australia (1925):
The Grand Master: It has seemed to me that reports of Lodge
meetings and gatherings immediately connected with Lodge meetings
appear with greater frequency in the non-Masonic press than they did.
This, in my view, is wholly undesirable. There is, when reports are
supplied to what in this connection I may term the profane press, a
very grave risk that matters may be communicated which, for a Mason
to communicate, would be a Masonic offense. I trust that W. M.'s
will do what they can to discourage such reports. It is not in this
Jurisdiction alone that attention has been called to this tendency. In
1918 the Board of General Purposes of the Grand Lodge of England
expressed its grave disapprobation of it. A communication which may
with propriety be made to a Masonic journal may yet be wholly
inappropriate for the public press, cause misunderstanding, and injure
the Craft.

Masonic Journal.
RELIGION
Brother Edgar A. Guest has very aptly expressed the thought
in the following entitled "Religion":
"When the talk turns on religion I have notions of my ownI have my versions of the Bible and the things I think alone,
And I've found them satisfying, found them comforting to me;
But I'll never lose my temper if you chance to disagree,
For religion, as I view it, is a pathway to a goal,
And is something to be settled between each man and his soul.
Now, I'm not a Roman Catholic, but I wouldn't go so far
As to fling away the friendship of the folks I know who are.
I have lived and neighbored with them, come to love them through
and through.
I've respect and admiration for the kindly things they do;
And I've come to the conclusion, though the bigots think it odd,
That it makes no difference to me how a good man worships God.
I know Methodists and Baptists, Lutherans, Scientists and Jews,
Whose friendship is a treasure which I shouldn't want to lose.
And l honor and respect them for I wouldn't dare condemn
The form of prayer and worship which is comforting to them.
So when bigots talk religion, I just settle back and see
The helpful, loyal friends that every church has given me."

121

Attempting to compel other persons to believe and live as we do
is a mistake. Perhaps no virtue is so needed in the world or less
common than toleration. Theoretically most of us desire to be big
and tolerant but in reality the accident of birth and early training
are a factor that works against any man in reaching the ideal.
Delaware (1924):
Attending divine services in a denominational church is not Masonic
labor, and it is therefore improper to open a Lodge for that purpose, to
wear the regalia of the Lodge or to take its paraphernalia. This, however, does not prevent individual Masons from attending such services
in a body.
Idaho (1925):
Masonry begins and ends in prayer. A Mason's Hrst act within
the Lodge-room as an Entered Apprentice, like his last act in the Sublime
Degree of Master Mason, is to kneel in prayer. And so, on through all
the degrees of Masonry, and in the closing Masonic obsequies, when our
lifeless forms are laid beneath the silent clods of the valley, prayer is
a constant, integral part of our ceremonies. In this, Masonic brethren,
The
whether Christian, Hebrew, Mohammedan, or Brahmin, join.
ancient fire-worshipping Aryan in his Himalayas; Zarathustra on the
plains of Persia; Moses at the Burning Bush; the Egyptian monarch
erecting his pyramid-tomb ; Solomon, King of Israel, dedicating his
incomparable Temple; our medieval Knight Templar brethren in
twentieth-century worshipper, whether in mosque, pagoda, synagogue, or
Christian church, have had one Holy Doctrine-one aspiration-one
prayer-and have lifted up their God-illuminated souls to their one
Beneficent and Eternal Creator-Father, who is not their magnificent
cathedrals of "frozen music in stone," and the only, the Supreme, the
All-Knowing, the All-Present, the All-Powerful, the Infinite, but who
is as welt the All-Loving, the Tender, Heavenly Father, "closer (to us)
than breathing, and nearer than hands and feet."

Manitoba (1925):
Believing that many of our Lodges consider it is necessary to secure
a Dispensation in order to attend Divine Worship as a body, I would
emphasize the fact that no Dispensation is required. Our Constitution
prescribes that a Dispensation is necessary only when they desire to form
a public procession and wear Masonic clothing. Knowing that many of
our Lodges are cross-sections of sectarianism, all worshipping the Living
God, but preferring their own form, and believing that the desire to
wear regalia at such functions is due to an inherent desire to advertise,
which is not compatible with the teachings or practices of Freemasonry,
and holding strongly to the belief that the family group is the ideal
unit in attending any religious service, 1 would recommend that Grand
Lodge recognize only two occasions as fitting for the display of Masonic
clothing in public, namely: Masonic funerals and the laying of corner
stones, when the same are duly laid by the Grand Lodge or under its
authority.

Attend church, if you wish to do so, as individuals, not as
Masons. Form no procession; wear no regalia; observe due decorum;
do not seek to attract attention ; don't advertise.

Alberta (1925):
The Grand Master: It has been drawn to my attention on several
occasions that books designated as copies of the "Work" are offered for
sale in book stores and are being purchased by any who may desire "
them. Those who are guilty of commercializing Masonry in this way
are contemptible Masons and are not worthy of membership in the Order.
There is not a member, no matter how uninformed he may be, who can
plead ignorance of what is right in dealing with this question. It is
the duty of every brother into whose possession any such book may
come, to immediately hand the same to the W. M. of his Lodge who in
turn should forward it to the Grand Secretary.

New Jersey (1925):
The Grand Master:
Several requests having been received for
permission to wear costumes in degree work, I referred the matter to
the Committee on Ritual. That committee has submitted to me the following opinion, which I approve:
"Your committee are of the opinion that the wearing of costumes
adds neither to the dignity nor impressiveness ol our ceremonies and
we feel that some costumes might even have the opposite effect. We,
therefore, are of the opinion that it is not desirable that costumes be
worn in our Lodges, but that the brethren should wear the generally
accepted style of clothing and should be properly clothed with an apron
and with head uncovered."
It is not intended to prohibit the use of costumes in lodge work,
but rather to discourage the general adoption of costumes.

Quebec (1925):
The Grand Master: The temptation in Masonry is to over-stress the
form. There are brethren who wear regalia and exhibit the ornaments
who are void of the spirit of Masonry. There are excessive ritualists
who will split hairs over a word or accent while all the while they are
wholly unmindful of the spirit enshrined in the form. Cases have been
known where "good men and true" have been barred from a lodge because of some trifling difference in a password or grip. This is surely
to caricature Masonry. Have we not all known brethren who were
moved by the highest and fullest spirit of Masonry and yet were profoundly unlettered in the use of forms? I want to urge, with what
force I may. have, the paramount importance of the spirit of Masonry
while at the same time giving to form its proper value.
West Australia:
The Grand Master: It has been reported to me that in some Lodges
a popular form of entertainment at the festive boa.rd is for a brother to
deliver some parody on certain parts of· the ritual, most frequently the
investiture of a Steward. I have seen a few of these, and, while they
may afford amusement to some brethren, I cannot too strongly condemn
the practice as being un-Masonic and calculated to bring about a lack
of reverence for our dignified and beautiful ritual and its ceremonies.
I need say no more but would ask the brethren to peruse our Ancient
Charge No. 6, Section 2, which was designed to regulate the conduct of
Freemasons at the festive board. It enjoins the brethren "to enjoy
themselves in innocent mirth
not doing or saying anything
offensive . . . not to do anything that would blast our harmony and
defeat our laudable purpose."
We have done everything in our power to discourage the wearing
of regalia where non-Masons are present, and our attitude has been
generally supported by the other Grand Lodges of Australia. We can
never understand the mentality of the Mason who desires to wear his
regalia in public.
TEMPLES
"Our ancient Brethren assembled on the highest hills and in
the lowest vales," but time has changed this. The ideal Masonic

128

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Temple we believe should be a Home not only for the Lodge proper
but also for its social and fraternal activities. Often the building
and maintenance of a Temple is the chief objective of a Lodge.
In the pursuit of the necessary material thing to carry on such
a project the real work that the Lodge should do is lost or overlooked.
Delaware (1924):
The suggestion has been urged that the different branches of Masonry should build separate Temples, independent of each other. To my
mind anything which brings Masons into closer fellowship and understanding is a distinct advantage to our Order and to its membership.
And likewise, anything which separates us or divides us into cliques, ~s
a corresponding source of regret. A building housing all of our Masomc
activities would bring us closer together, would be more imposing than
two or more smaller structures, and would be more economical in construction and maintenance. These are objects so eminently desirable that
the plan for one central comprehensive Temple should not be abandoned,
except for the most urgent reason.
England (1925):
The most notable event in England is the completion of a fund of
more than £850,000, for the erection of a great Masonic Temple in London which is to be a center for the activities of the Grand Lodge of
England and a memorial to the English Masons who fell in the Great
\Var. This great fund has been raised by voluntary contribution without
calling upon the funds of Grand Lodge for assistance, and without
interfering in any way with the very generous contributions which our
English brethren make to Masonic charities.
Georgia (1925):
The Grand Master: Many of our subordinate Lodges have by-laws
prohibiting smoking in their Lodge room. Some observe such a rule
without a law prohibiting it; but many have neither such a law or
observe such a rule. The result is that often the room is filled with
tobacco smoke and at times officers have taken part in the work of
degrees and the ceremonies puffing cigars or cigarettes.
Such practice is not in keeping with the sacred ceremonies of our
Order, is not in place in the precincts of our halls dedicated to Freemasonry, virtue and benevolence, and not in accord with the dignity and
sacredness of the exalted and sublime ceremonies of the fraternity. I
can see no more reason for a man smoking in our Lodge room than I
can in our churches. The practice seems to me to be as much out

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

129

of place in one as the other. In addition, there are many to whom the
odor of tobacco fumes it not only unpleasant, but sickening, in a close
room, and when permitted and allowed, it prevents these brethren from
attending. I have had brethren tell they could not attend Lodge meetings for this reason.
Therefore, I recommend the enactment of a law prohibiting the
smoking of tobacco in our Lodge rooms. All of our Lodges have anterooms, where it could be indulged in; but within the sacred precincts of
the Lodge itself, let it be prohibited.

All social rooms should be dark on nights when Lodge is in session,
and it is the duty of the Worshipful Master to see that this is done, and
to do any and all other things that are for the best interest of the Order
and the Lodge over which he presides. A member who says if he cannot
play cards in the social room he does not care to attend Lodge, is surely
lacking in Masonic spirit. If card playing is higher or more important
to him than Masonry, it surely can make but little difference to Masonry
whether he is there or not. Masonry is higher than card playing, and a
Mason should attend Lodge for what he may do for Masonry, and what
it, in return, may do for him.
Iowa (1926):
Brother Hamrick (Georgia) reports that while eight lodges had
their buildings burned during the year, only two of the eight carried
any insurance. In this day and age it ought to be a Masonic offense for
a lodge to fail to carry fire insurance.
Maine (1925):
The Grand Master answered the question, "Can a Lodge allow a
Brother to use its hall for a marriage service?" by deciding that it
should not allow its hall for such service, that "Masonic halls are dedicated to Masonic purposes and the marriage ceremony could hardly be
construed as Masonic."

South Carolina (1925):
The Grand Master: I consistently refused to approve the circula·
tion of begging letters. Quite a number of these came to me from
outside the State, and two or three from our own members. In two
cases, Lodges asked aid in rebuilding on account of fire. They carried
no insurance because the rate was too high. My position was that it
was a matter of cold-blooded business. The Lodge deliberately decided
to carry its own risk, and, therefore, when a loss occurred, it was not
fair to distribute this loss over the entire Jurisdictfon.
Pennsylvania (1924):
It was decided that the term "Masonic Temple" could only be applied
to a building absolutely restricted to Masonic purposes, and that where
the building was to be used for commercial purposes as well, there would
be no objection to calling the building a "Masonic Hall."
Pennsylvania (1925):
Another incident arose in Grand Lodge (Indiana) which evoked
general debate and a "show down'' by a standing vote. It was a proposed
amendment to the law to prohibit the use of Lodge rooms "for any purpose whatever except for legitimate Masonic purposes, under penalty of
the forfeiture of its charter!' The record does not disclose the particular reasons for this proposed new regulation and policy of Grand
Lodge, nor the opinions advanced pro and con; but apparently there was
some excitement over it. The Committee on Jurisprudence reported
against the adoption of the amendment to the law; but a majority of
the members of Grand Lodge thought otherwise and it became part of
the law. Just what organization or object it was aimed at can be only
a matter of conjecture to an outsider.

Indiana (1925):
In reply to the Research Society's query whether a Grand Lodge
should regulate the time between the raising and the petition for Royal
Arch or Lodge of Perfection the Grand Master says: I answered that
the Grand Lodge of Indiana has taken no action on this subject. I cannot see how a Grand Lodge could pass a law preventing a Master Mason
from doing anything as long as he conducted himself as a man and a
Mason. I think a Grand Lodge would have as much right to say that
a newly made Master Mason could not join a church for one year after
he was rais~, as to say he could not petition for membership in the
Royal Arch or Scottish Rite Bodies. I cannot see how a Grand Lodge
can assume control of a Master Mason, except as to his general behavior.
Iowa (1926):
Under the head of Recommendations Brother McCroskey (Washington, 1925) reports that a year ago the Grand Lodge had added to
the form of the petition for the degrees the following : Do you promise
on your honor that, until you have been a Master Mason for a period of
one year and have creditably passed an examination of proficiency as a
Master Mason, you will not petition for or accept membership in any
other organization which has membership in a Masonic Lodge as a
prerequisite?
He now recommends that this action of the Grand Lodge be rescinded
giving as his first reason : Because it is too drastic. The amendmen~
was really intended for the so-called higher degrees, but as it is worded
it also includes the Eastern Star, Masonic Clubs, College Masonic Fraternities, et al.
·
We still think that this law is not too drastic and is just as it
should be.
Brother McCroskey's next reason for recommending this rescission
is put by him in the following words: I do not believe that> you can
legislate a man into being a good Mason. If it is in him to be a good
Mason, he will be one regardless of how soon he takes the so-called
higher degrees ; if it is not in him to be a good Mason, then all such
legislation cannot change him.
Again we do not agree with him, for we never did have any use for
either the doctrine of fore-ordination or of predestination, and think it

New Mexico (1925):
Tf the donation by the Masonic Service Association to the American
School in Japan had been applied toward the founding of beds for the
caring for afflicted members and restoring them to health, would it not
have accomplished greater good to humanity? For, by placing these
tubercular brethren in a sanatorium where the proper treatment would
be given, they would have not only returned them to their families and
thus added to the nation's wealth, but also removed them from contact
with innocent children of such families and prevented the children from
contracting the disease at the most susceptible age of from birth to about
fifteen. It is almost a certainty that a child living in a home with an
active tubercular will contract the disease; so, by placing such afflicted
Masons in sanatoria and hospitals for proper care, such a menace will
be at least in part removed. If the money appropriated for the rebuilding of a school in Japan had been used to provide beds for tubercular
Masons, thus enabling them to return to health and care for themselves
and families, besides adding to the national wealth-would it not have
been better, although not with such a grandstand effect?
This has been the third year of organized activity by this Grand
Lodge in the development of what is generally known as the Fort Bayard
undertaking of the Grand Lodge of New Mexico. In many respects it
has been the most successful year of all. . . . Accounts are carefully
audited; records of all financial transactions are properly kept; the details of relief work are watched in a thoughtful and intelligent manner;
and the ideal of making the Sojourners' Club at Fort Bayard an agency

for practical relief, a home for those away from horn:, a~d a ~enter for
needed social and recreational activities, has been mamtamed m a most
commendable manner.
North Carolina (1925):
New Mexico earnestly desires the Service Association to take on
the business of establishing tuberculosis sanitaria. It is disappointed in
the Southern Jurisdiction of the Scottish Rite, because that bo~y has
taken no action. It feels that the money which was given at the time of
the Japanese disaster, for the rebuilding of the America~ Sch~ol, oug~t
to have been kept in America and used for tuberculosis relief. It is
disappointed that the Service Association has apparently "side-stepped"
the problem. We sympathize with New Mexico in her problem. She
sees these thousands of tuberculars go to her salubrious climate, and
feels that nothing big should be undertaken henceforth until t~is herculean task of the tuberculosis patients be handled. The Committee goes
into the matter of the relation of tuberculosis and crippled children; we
are caused to suspect that this is an indirect suggestion that the Shriners'
Hospital program would better have been a tuberculosis progra~. It is
significant that the most of the centers t~ which tuberc~lars go m great
numbers abound with those of similar views. The residents there feel
the matter acutely, and for good reason. It does seem as if we might
do something with this task.

Texas (1925):
This institution is a tubercular welfare organization located at the
United States Hospital No. 93 near Kerrville, and is the property of this
Grand Lodge, conducted through this committee. The work of this club
was supported through voluntary donations during the first half of the
year. I ts responsibilities increased, and the field of service became so
great that, in the opinion of your committee, endorsed by the Grand
Master and the Junior Grand Warden, it became necessary to employ
a full time welfare worker. Freemasonry is called upon for various
kinds of service at this institution, our work starts with a new patient
when he comes to the hospital. Our Masonic brethren are given attention first and then we direct our attention to other patients regardless
of fraternal or religious affiliation. Our Charity Fund has been used
by the Mason and the non-Mason; we have supplied the comforts of life,
have assisted the patient individually and have now begun a broader
service to all members of the Masonic Fraternity living in that particular
section. There have been 79 Master Masons from our Grand Jurisdiction in Kerr County during the past year, 68 of whom are yet there;
and a large number from foreign jurisdictions are there for their health.
"FOUND IN THE QUARRIES"
The following excerpts from the various Proceedings reviewed
give the constructive work that Masonry has accomplished and is
now carrying out in their Jurisdictions. They are concrete examples
of Service to which we may "point with pride!'
British Columbia (1925):
We confess that the idea of a mechanical prayer-maker has not occurred to us, although a progressive Brother did once suggest to us that
it would be a happy idea to have the lectures of the degrees recited by a
phonograph; and there is this to say in favor of the suggestion-whether
as applied to prayers or lectures-that one can stop a phonograph.
Delaware (1925):
The Masonic Field Day, held in June, 1925, appears not to have
proved a success. Only a small number took part. The total receipts
of the day were $30.93, while the expenditures amounted to $228.11. The
deficit was taken care of by a fund provided by Grand Lodge for the
purpose.
Idaho (1925):
The attempt to acquire the famous "old Masonic oak tree" at
Brazoria, Texas, from the feminine owner was not successful. On the

in Sullivan.

Indiana (1925):
Grand Master Dinwiddie made an investigation of the Sojourners'
Club at Ft. Bayard, New Mexico. He decided from his investigation
that the Club was doing good work, and he therefore sent $500 to the
Club.
* * *
One of the Lodges attempted to sell a one-half interest in its Temple
to the Order of the Eastern Star. The Lodge was properly informed
by the Grand Master that such a procedure would be contrary to Masonic
law, and not only contrary to Masonic law, but an attempt to defraud
the Grand Lodge out of what might become its rights.

* * *

A certain Masonic Temple was permitted to be used by the Grotto
for initiating its candidates, and the Grand Master informed the l:°dges
owning the Temple that such use of their Temple was un-Masomc and
must be stopped.
* * *
A candidate for Judge of the Circuit Court in his campaign advertised his :).fasonic relations to influence Masons to vote for him.. The
Grand Master advised his Lodge that his method was un-Masomc and
ordered the Lodge to direct him to discontinue such publication or have
charges preferred against him.
Kansas (1925):
Although it should be unnecessary it is again urged that the remair:ing Lodges send their charters to the Grand Secretary. for safe deposit
in our fire-proof building. The Grand Lodge furmshes a ~roperly
framed and certified copy without charge, except where restoration also
is necessary. Let all representatives note this and handle at the first

Kentucky (1924):
An astounding situation was reported in one of the Lodges. A
member had killed a .brother Mason; had been tried and convicted in
the Civil Court and sentenced to 10 years in prison. The Lodge continued him a member in good standing, and were being criticized for
not giving him a Masonic trial. The Grand :\faster advised (should
have ordered), a trial which was held and the accused found "not
guilty."
Louisiana (1925):
The Grand Master recommended that each constituent Lodge of
Louisiana purchase the Little Masonic Library from the Masonic Service
Association, which sells for only $5. The writer has these books in his
library and he is convinced that they are worth many times the price.
Every Lodge should have a set of these books and the brethren encouraged to read them.
Maine (1925):
Some ten years ago, Brother George A. Carpenter of Freedom
Lodge, No. 42, presented to his Lodge, Masonic memorial flags with
which to decorate the graves of its deceased members on Memorial Day.
Since then the practice has been continued. The flags are white, with the
square and compasses and letter "G" in blue in the center, and the words
"In Memoriam" across the bottom. Each year a committee is appointed
by the Lodge to see that the flags are properly placed and no brother
forgotten.
Michigan (1925):
During the past year the presiding officers of the Grand Lodge,
Grand Chapter, R. A. M., Grand Council, R. & S. M., Grand Commandery, K. T., and the Council of Deliberation, A. A S. R., of the State of
Michigan, have perfected an organization named the Masonic Grand
Council of Michigan for the purpose of promoting closer co-operation
and co-ordination of interests in all Masonic bodies.

* * *

The Grand Master commends the Craftsmen's Club at the University
of Michigan, which is doing good and commendable work in conferring
the degrees in Masonry, not only for the Lodges in Ann Arbor, but in
going about the State and making visits to other Lodges. Like his predecessor, he recommended that the sum of $500 be contributed to this
Club to assist in carrying on its work. The Committee on Finance
approved the recommendation and it was adopted by Grand Lodge.

North Carolina (1925):
The Grand Master held that a man whose grandmother is a ncgro
is ineligible to Masonic degrees ; that a man must be able to read and
write in order to petition for Masonic degrees ; that no Master Mason

The incoming Grand Master was authorized and directed to appoint

Grand Lodge endorsed the project of erecting a Masonic Building

The Masonic Home is operating a print shop, equipped largely

monthly paper, The Messenger, edited and controlled by the officers of
the Grand Lodge. A noteworthy project, and it should be generously
supported.

The names of the distinguished dead of other Grand Jurisdictions
were called. As this was being done, a white' flower was placed upon
the altar for each, in their memory, by the Senior Deacon. It is wholly
unlike procedure elsewhere, but as a ceremonial it has a very sweet appeal.

To increase Lodge attendance three prizes were offered. The Lodge

you think of the Rotary Clubs it is a poor showing.

Philippine Islands (1926):
The Shrine Ceremonial : Your committee regrets that it ~as to deal
with this subject. We had thought until recently that the action of th.e
dge in 1924 requesting the Imperial Potentate of the Mystic

two years ago, and, according to our information, has issued a dispensation for a Shrine ceremonial to take place in Manila in February, 1926.
The fraternal request of our Grand S·ecretary that such dispensation be

been acknowledged by the Imperial Potentate of the Mystic Shrine.
"Self-preservation is the first law of nature." This Grand Lodge
has no power to prohibit the members of Afifi Temple holding a ceremonial in Manila. It is not our desire to interfere with those Masons
who are already Shriners in the enjoyment of their privileges as such,
but this Grand Lodge has the right and power to protect the membership
of its Subordinate Lodges against the discordant influence of the Shrine
ceremonials as conducted by visiting Shriners by prohibiting the members of its subordinate lodges to take the work of the Mystic Shrine in
the proposed ceremonial.
We therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution:
Resolved, That this Grand Lodge does hereby prohibit all members
of the Subordinate Lodges under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of
the Philippine Islands from taking the Shrine degrees during the proposed Shrine ceremonial in Manila in February, 1926.
Any violation of this resolution shall be a Masonic offense.

* * *

The use of the word "Profane": \Ve find that this word is often
used by Masonic writers in referring to persons who are not Masons,
and its use is justified by well known writers, such as Albert G. :Vfackey,
yet we are of the opinion that its use should be avoided, because nonMasons rightly claim that the term sounds disrespectful, and, generally
speaking, those so classed do not like to be called profane.
Therefore, we recommend the adoption of the following resolution:
Resolved, That the use of the word "profane," when reference is
made to persons not Masons, be avoided whenever possible by the use
of some other word or expression in its stead, such as "uninitiated" and
"non-:Vfason."

Utah (1925):
The decision of the United States Circuit Court of Appeals in the

of the United States District Court in sentencing these two men, convicted of using the United States mails to defraud, to the U. S. Prison
at Fort Leavenworth, where they are both now serving their sentences.
This ends the last chapter in this remarkable Masonic fraud, which had
his headquarter~ in our jurisdiction.

Victoria (1925):
In the great struggles of the world today the United States of
America is certainly bearing the brunt of the battle on many fronts, and
the greater the struggle the more clearly is seen the fundamental unity
of ideals and objectives of the English-speaking peoples. These lines
are penned during the visit of the American Fleet to Australia, which
again is significant.

West Australia (1924):
The Grand Master: I have been asked if it is essential that waitresses should retire from the Festive Board after the Toast List has been
commenced. The question in this instance more particularly refers to
the wives and relatives of members who frequently, in country Lodges,
prepare the Installation Banquet. I think the circular issued by the
Board of General Purposes in 1918 will be an answer to that question.
It is as follows: It has been reported to the Board of General Purposes
that on several recent occasions non-Masons have been present at the
Festive Boards of Lodges for the purpose of contributing to the harmony
of the evening. The Board is of the opinion, that this practice is highly
improper, and should be discontinued. Masters of Lodges are, therefore,
advised that the presence of non-Masons at the Festive Board, after the
Toast List has been commenced, is prohibited.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

This procedure is universal among the Grand Lodges within the
British Empire, and who shall say that there is no wisdom in it?

APPENDIX
AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are
generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly
speaking, they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish Rite, for the one commonly called York is peculiar in its organized proceedings only to the United States.
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.
The Symbolic degrees are conferred in a lodge and are the Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They
are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction
is by symbols.
The Capitular degrees arc conferred in a Royal Arch Chapter
and are the Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent
Master and the Royal Arch. The supplemental and honorary degrees of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of High Priests
upon those who have been regularly elected to preside over a
Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. They arc called Capitular because
they are conferred in a Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning "done
in a Chapter."
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the
Royal Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called Cryptic because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees 'arc conferred in a Commandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight Templar
comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take the temple
at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the 33rd,
inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States (which
includes all territory south of the Ohio River and west of the Mississippi River) the organization of the different bodies, and the degrees conferred by them are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 ° to 14 °, inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix, 15° to 18°; Council of Kadosh, 19° to
30°; Consistory, 31° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.
In the Northern Jurisdiction (which includes all States north
of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River); the degrees

RULES FOR MASONIC DATES
Ancient Craft Masons-Add 4000 years to the common era.
Thus: 1923 and 4000-5923.
Scottish Rite-Add 3760 to the common era. Thus: 191!3 and
3760-5683. After September add another year.
Royal Arch-Add 530 years to the vulgar era. Thus: 1923 and
530-2453.
Royal and Seleet Masters--Add 1000 to the common time. Thus:
1923 an.d 1000~2923.
Knights Templar-From the Christian era take 1118. Thus: 1118
from 1923-805.
Order of High Priesthood-To the Christian era add 1913, the
year of blessing. Thus: 1923 and 1913-3836.

George Louis Jones

GEORGE LOUIS JONES
Crand Master
!c)26-1927

The sixtieth gentleman to occupy the exalted station of Grand
Master of ),/[asons in the jurisdiction of California, has endeared himself
to the members of our fraternity and to his legion of friends outside the
mystic tie, by his unfailing courtesy to every human being with whom
he has come in contact, by his sterling integrity, his industry, and
conscientious devotion to the manifold duties which have been imposed
upon him.
George Louis Jones comes from hardy and good \Velsh stock. He
was born at Truckee, California, May 11, 1873, of William C. and Annie
M. Jones. The father was a prominent physician and surgeon who
practiced his profession in Nevada county for nearly thirty-five years,
known and loved by all the people in that county, and indeed by nearly
all the people of the mountain counties. Father Jones was a member
of Madison Lodge, No. 23, at Grass Valley.
The retiring Grand Master received his education in the public
schools of Grass Valley and the lJniversity of California, from which
institution he was graduated in 1895. The following two years were
spent at the Hastings College of the Law, and from which he graduated as
a lawyer in 1897. Jn 1902 Brother Jones was elected District Attorney
of Nevada county, and re-elected in 1906. J\t the general election of
1908 he was elevated to the position of Judge of the Superior Court
of California for Nevada county, and was twice re-elected. He resigned
his office of Judge in January, 1926, and became the President of the
Nevada County Bank, which important and responsible office he now
holds.
George L. Jones received his Masonic degrees in Madison Lodge,
No. 23, Grass Valley, as follows: First degree January 15, second
degree February 11, third degree March 26, 1901, and retains his membership in that Lodge. He was exalted to the degree of Royal Arch
in Grass Valley Chapter No. 18, R. /\. M., in June, 1904; is a member
of Nevada Commandcry No. 6, Nevada City, having been knighted
August 19, 1904.
In Grand Lodge Brother Jones has for years been active as a
member of the Committee mi Grievances, and in 1923 was elected Junior
Grand Warden; Senior Grand Warden in 1924, Deputy Grand Master
in 1925, and Grand Master at the annual communication in 1926.
Past Grand Master Jones is blessed with a wife (nee Helen Crocker
Mott) who is indeed a hclpmcct and counscller, and the home is further
made happy by the presence of two charming daughters, Helen F. and
Nancy M.
It is impossible in this too short sketch to recount the many virtues
of our brother, but it may be encompassed in the brief statement that
in him we have the embodiment of all that goes to make up a good
man, a good citizen, a good husband and a good father.

MESSAGE OF THE GRAND MASTER
The Grand Master then read his Annual Message, which
was by the Deputy Grand Master referred to the following
committee for segregation and distribution: Olin L. Derry,
Thomas J. Fraser, William L. Hovis.
Brethren of the Gran<i Lodye:

In accordance with the provisions of the Constitution under which
we work, it becomes my duty to render to you a report of my activities
as Grand Master, and to make such recommendations as my judgment
may dictate.
During the year just concluding, I have constantly experienced that
great joy which comes from associating with those splendid men
throughout the State, who are engaged in the work of this Fraternity;
but, in the attempted performance of my duties, I have realized, with
great regret, that limitations both of time and ability would not permit
me to do many things which the position demands of one who has been
selected to fill it. Though many miles were traveled, many hours spent
and much thought given in the effort to comply with the obligation I took
when I assumed the duties of Grand Master, yet I realize that much has
been left undone that should have been done.
It has not been, however, a mere sense of duty that has prompted
the effort to live up t0 the terms of my obligation, but there has also
existed ai keen desire on my part to be of real service to the Fraternity,
to guide it along proper lines, to keep it from taking a single backward
step, to maintain the high standards of the past, and I can only hope that
that effort has not been in vain.
Meeting Place of Grand Lodge.
The remarkable growth of Masonry in this jurisdiction in the years
just past has been reflected in the increased attendance at each succeeding
Annual Communication until we find that the Commandery room in our
Masonic Temple is inadequate to properly accommodate those Masons
who are members of Grand Lodge and who desire to attend. A realization of the discomfort caused the brethren by the crowded conditions of
several sessions impelled me to approve of and direct the convening ·of
Grand Lodge in the Scottish Rite Temple, in which I feel certain· 110
cause for complaint, as to either room or air, will be furnished.
The directors of this building are entitled to our hearty thanks for
the very generous and fraternal manner in which our requests for rooms
have been met. While many of us will greatly miss the surroundings
in which we have gathered for so many years past, yet I trust that the
thought of increased comfort to the greater number will tend to reconcile
ils to the change which has been made.
At our last Annual Communication a resolution was adopted directing
the appointment of a committee "to survey the entire situation with refer-

ence to the facilities for the meeting of Grand Lodge in its Annual Communications and to report thereon not later than the next Annual

be given earnest and careful consideration.

But when a Lodge confers, say over two hundred degrees in one year,

Lodges Constituted.
Immediately following the adjournment of the last Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, I proceeded to constitute the twenty-two new
Lodges which had been granted charters, and I completed this work well
within the sixty days allowed by the Constitution. In the performance of
this duty, valuable assistance was rendered to me by the Grand Lecturer,
Brother Thomas J. Baker, who accompanied me on each occasion when
this ceremony· took place.

380

General Condition.
It is a matter of unlimited satisfaction to he able to report that the
general condition of the Craft in this jurisdiction continues good. Peace
and harmony have marked the activities of the year, and from the report
of the Grand Secretary, you will note the increase in membership and in
new Lodges. The remarkable growth of Masonry of late years means
that the Fraternity is far from the point of stagnation, hut what its ultimate effect will be, it is yet too early to determine. If we could be but
convinced that we have been making Masons in heart as well as in name,
then we could rightfully boast of our augmented rolls of membership and
feel that the influx has been for the strengthening and upbuilding of our
Institution. May such prove to be the case and may each novitiate
demonstrate, by his every act, that he has become a better man, appreciative in every way, of his duties and his obligation as a Mason. I would
quote the words of that splendid man and Mason, Past Grand Master
David J. Reese, when he said: "If we can raise but one brother who is
worthy and well qualified, a credit to the Fraternity and an honor to the
Craft, we have accomplished more for humanity than rubber stamping a
hundred and making them Masons in name only."
The old admonition to seek quality, rather than quantity, should he
carefully heeded in these days of our Masonic prosperity, for the admission of unworthy material will weaken the whole structure and tend to
produce difficulties and dissensions which thought and care could have
avoided.
A consideration of the degree work done by the Lodges during the
past year has caused me to feel that the "degree-mill" has in some locali~
ties been working overtime and that a grave injustice is, perhaps, resulting
to both the Fraternity and the new member. It has been well said by our
Grand Secretary that "it is apparent that some of our Lodges have lost
sight of the genius of Masonry and the reason for their existence, which
is to unite and bring to their service a world-wide fraternity of free men,
whose mission it is to make men friends, to refine and exalt their lives,
to uphold every noble and redeeming ideal of humanity, 'teaching the
Fatherhood of God, the brotherhood of man, the moral law, the Golden
Rule, and the hope of a life everlasting.' They are bound by every impli~
cation of honor to adopt their novitiates as part of the Lodge family, to
assist them in a friendly way to enlarge their field of usefulness to their
fellows, to help them in the cultivation of friendships among the brethren.

Flag Day
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes, following the sub.nission by Junior Past Grand :Master Boynton, of a suggestion that the
fraternity should celebrate the lSOth anniversary of the official recognition
uf the Flag of the United States, recommended at the last Grand Lodge
that "the Grand Master in his judgment make such arrangements and
give such directions as may seem to him best for the holding of such
celebration." This recommendation was adopted, and pursuant thereto,
I later directed the issuance of a proclamation in which I called on the
Lodges to observe, in fitting manner, this particular anniversary. While
a very satisfactory response to the proclamation was made throughout the
jurisdiction, yet there was one observance of the day which stands out
pre-eminent and is worthy of special notice.
In San Diego, it was suggested that the Lodges of the county raise a
fund with which to erect a substantial base and flag pole in Balboa Park
in the city of San Diego. With that enthusiasm which is ever present
among the Masons of that county, the project was carried through, and,
realizing the character and magnitude of the movement, I consented to
convene Grand Lodge at San Diego on Flag Day and perform a ceremony
of dedication of the base and pole, which ceremony was prepared by our
Grand Secretary. On June 14, in company with our Grand Lecturer,
Thomas J. Baker, Grand Orator, Fletcher A. Cutler, and Brother ·warren
Libbey, I went to San Diego, opened Grand Lodge and, in the presence
of an audience composed of several thousand people, formally dedicated
the base and pole. On the completion of the ceremony, the Flag of our
Country was hoisted by Brother J. H. Pendleton, and, as it was flung to
the breeze, I gloried in the fact that here beneath its folds were men
who as citizens and as Masons were giving expression to their love and
devotion to those glorious principles for which it stands.
In the evening at the High School Auditorium another interesting
program was presented to a large audience, and here our Grand Orator
made one of the best addresses it has ever been my privilege to hear. It
proved a fitting conclusion to a splendid day and on all sides words of
praise for his inspiring talk were uttered.

The brethren of San Diego county are certainly entitled to the congratulations of this Grand Lodge for this glorious demonstration of
their loyalty and patriotism as Masons, and the committee headed by
Brother David W. Schick should be given hearty commendation for the
very able manner in which it planned and conducted the important undertaking.

Masonic Homes
The affairs of the Homes at Decoto and Covina continue under the
able ·direction of those Trustees who have been accorded the highest
praise for their devotion to and interest in the great humanitarian work
which is. being performed by our Fraternity. To have served with these
brethren has been a pleasure and a delight; to have been associated with
them in the direction and management of these two havens of rest and
refuge has been a source of satisfaction which has meant much to me.
At Decoto, Brother Frank B. Hartman, the Superintendent, and his
assistant, Mrs. Minnie Richardson, are exhibiting, as they always have
done, those remarkable traits of character which have endeared them to
all with whom they come in contact in the performance of the many
exacting duties imposed upon them. With unfailing cheerfulness, great
tact and undiminished energy, they unceasingly strive to bring cheer and
happiness into the lives of all the family.
At Covina, a change in the superintendency has taken place since our
last Annual Communication. Mrs. Maude E. Miller, who for several
years has lavished love and affection upon one hundred and more boys
and girls at the Home, decided, at the urgent pleading of a brother of
this Order, to limit her attention to one individual, and, as a result, she
tendered her resignation, and became Mrs. Mervyn J. Newburg. Her
years of service at the Home had shown her to be a woman of great
ability, one of splendid qualities-both of mind and heart, and she has
left the service carrying with her the good wishes of those who have
been associated with ber in the life at the Home.
As her successor, the Board selected Brother John M. Downen, and
those of us who have had an opportunity of meeting and observing him
are of the opinion that the selection was indeed a happy one. He came
not untrained in the work of such a position, and he quickly convinced
us that he was a sympathetic student of childhood-one who possesses
both administrative ability and a knowledge of child-life which has gained
for him not only our confidence and respect, but as well the confidence
and respect of our children in the Home.
The members of the Board are giving the closest attention and consideration to the many important problems which arise in connection with
Homes, such as these, and particularly are they anxious to give to our
children not only food, clothing and shelter, but also that essential training
which will tend to fit them to become self-supporting and self-respecting
men and women.

George Washington Memorial
During the year the necessity of determining whether I should visit
the Hawaiian Jslands arose, for it has become the custom of Grand
Masters of this Jurisdiction, if time permitted, to journey across the
Pacific and pay a fraternal visit to the Lodges of the Islands. While
there, every rnurtesy has bc''l shown the visiting officers, every kind
deed that hospitality and fraternal love could impi1e, has been performed,
and each Grand Master who has had the good io1 tune to be the guest of
those big-hearted, generous brethren, has returned to his home, unable to
fittingly express his feeling of gratitude to those who had left nothing
undone to make his sojoi:rn with them the outstanding event of his official
year. He brought back with him, not only impressions of what true hospitality really means, but <1lso a knowledge of a strong, active Masonry
existing in that far-off section of our Jurisdiction, which gladdened his
heart and prompted words of praise for our Island brethren. There naturally existed a desire on my part to likewise visit the Islands, but there
has come to my mind the advisability of a trip to Alexandria, Virginia,
for the purpose of inspecting the work that has been accomplished in the
erection of the George \Vashi11gto11 Masonic Memorial. Feeling that I
could not give the time to take both trips, I finally concluded that t!ie
journey to the Memorial should be given preference, and word of my
conclusion to the brethren across the water was reluctantly sent-reluctantly because there was being surrendered an opportunity of visiting
those delightful spots uilder conditions which would not for me exist
again.
The visit to Alexandria was made, and accompanied by Brother J.
Claude Keiper, Past Grand Master of the District of Columbia and Secretary-Treasurer of the Memorial Association, and by Brother Percy Crawford of the building company, an examination of the great structure in
course of erection was made, and, after that view of the work and an
explanation given me of the plans for the completed building, I do not
hesitate to say that the temple will be one of the wonder buildings of the
world, which will attract tbe attention, not only of Masons, but of .all
persons whose eyes shall behold its beauties and its magnificence.
My brethren, seventeen years have now elapsed since the representatives of eighteen Grand Lodges met in th Masonic Temple at Alexandria
and there took the first steps in a movement which gave life to the George

Washington National Memorial Association. In 1908, Brother Oscar
Lawler, a Past Grand Master of this Jurisdiction, in urging the con'struction of a proper building within which would be placed the pricele~s

"Whereas, Alexandria, Virginia, was the home town of George

that a nation might call him father; and

and urge upon them their hearty co-operation and assistance."
On February 22, 1911, pursuant to a resolution adopted at the 1910
meeting, representatives of twenty-seven jurisdictions gathered at Alexandria, and "The George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association" was formally organized. Later the Association was incorporated
under the laws of Virginia. Today, the active members of the Association
are the forty-nine Grand Jurisdictions of the nation. The plan was early
adopted to secure the sum of One Dollar from each Master Mason in the
United States, and to the appeal which was made for funds, varying
responses have been made. Many States have exceeded their quotas,
others have completed or nearly completed theirs, while a number have
fallen far short in the amounts contributed. Thus New Hampshire has
met the demand made of it by almost doubling its quota, while other
Jurisdictions have exceeded theirs and, in addition twenty States
have contributed over one-half of their assignments. California is
given credit for $23,009.00, or about eighteen per cent, and on the list
of contributing jurisdictions, we are sixth from the bottom.
The present plans call for the expenditure of $4,000,000 for the entire cost of the temple, while a sum of $1,000,000 should be raised as an
endowment fund, and up to February 22, 1927, the sum of $2,331,593.90

had been collected. It is thus evident that if this splendid project is tu be
brought to an early completion that those Jurisdictions which have been

splendid personality."

Public Schools Week
To act as chairman of the Public Schools Week Committee I
"drafted" Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams, and the wisd,om
of the choice cannot be questioned. He it was who conceived the idea
of setting aside a week, during which, "in every Lodge in this Jurisdiction some phase of the questions affecting the Public Schools be brought
to the attention of the members present"-and it must be a matter of
great satisfaction to him to realize how, from year to year, the report
of meetings held in compliance with the proclamations issued by each
succeeding Grand Master show a growing interest in this important
movement. With this increased interest existing, it may be truly said
that the observance of the week by the Fraternity this year was in the
main, notably successful and attracted the attention of larger nu~bers of
citizens in the different communities than ever before. This is a work
which .calls for intelligent and enthusiastic leadership in each Lodge, and
the existence of such leadership has been generally reflected in the success of the meeting. \Vith it, large attendance and great interest have, as
a rule, resulted; without it, then sparsely attended gatherings have characterized the observance.
The movement is one which should have the hearty support of every
Mason, for here is given us the opportunity of demonstrating the sincerity of our professions of unceasing interest in the welfare of our
public schools.

By the provisions of Section 57 of the Constitution, each Inspector
is required to attend the Lodge of Instruction held by the Grand Lecturer
immediately before each Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge,
and he is aliowed transportation in the same manner as is allowed the
officers or representatives of the Lodges. That the Inspectors should be
made a more liberal allowance is evident to me, particularly in view of the
fact that the same brethren hold these positions, not for one year only,
but as a rule for successive years. The amounts paid those who come
from a distance will not compensate them for the expenditure required,
and they should not be required session after session to pay the difference
from their own funds. These brethren are doing a great service for
Masonry, but they should not be asked to serve at such cost to themselves.
I, therefore, trust favorable action will be taken to correct this condition.

At this conference there was organized the Masonic Blood Reliel
Board, composed of the Grand Masters and other Grand Officers of
Mississippi, Louisiana and Arkansas, and of representatives of the Masonic Service Association, which board was formed to direct all operations and receive and disburse all contributions in the work of Masonic
relief and rehabilitation in the entire flood area.
Appreciating the fact that an appalling toli of life and property had
been taken by the most destructive flood in the history of the world and
that prompt and generous aid should be extended to our stricken brethren
an appeal was made to the various Lodges in the Jurisdiction for a con~
tribution for this worthy cause, and for other possible emergency calls
equivalent to at least. ten cents a member, and the response to this cali
amounted to nearly $17,000.
The flood waters continued to spread and each day brought news of
the awful conditions resulting from the unprecedented and increasing
floods. Food, clothing and shelter for those who had been compelled
to leave their homes were imperative.
It was estimated that over 10,000 Masons were affected in the flood
area and that a fund of $500,000 would be required to provide the necessary assistance. Word to this effect reaching us, another appeal was
made to our Lodges, to which a similar generous response was made. The
total sum contributed as a result of these two appeals was $32,431.38, but
the contemplated amount of $510,000.00 having been raised by the Board
of Control of the Relief Fund p:ior to the receipt by the Grand Secretary
of a large portion of the respm ses to t>Ur second call, we held for further disposition the sum of $10,• 31.38. Our total contribution, therefore,
to the Relief Fund was $22,000, md I submit for your determination the
disposition of the moneys receiv d over and above those transmitted.

Emergency Relief
Florida.
In his message to Grand Lodge, M. W. Grand Master Albert E.
Boynton reported that on receipt of information of the results of the
hurricane on the West Coast of Florida, he had authorized Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Florida to draw on us for $2,500, and,
though the authorization had later been renewed to the M. W. Grand
Master, Cary B. Fish, of Florida, no draft had been received against our
funds, and it was concluded that the situation had been handled by the
brethren of Florida, without assistance. Our offer was, however, permitted to stand, and I now desire to report that the need of aid from the
brethren in general having become evident, a draft for the amount tendered was gladly honored, and we were thus given an opportunity to join
in helping those of our unfortunate brethren who had been made the
victims of this disaster.
Mississippi.
When, at the commencement of the great Mississippi flood, an appeal
for funds was made by the American Red Cross, I directed that the sum
of $500.00 be contributed to assist in the relief work which it was undertaking. The disaster daily increasing in magnitude, it became evident
that greater assistance would be required, and 011 receipt of word that a
conference of Grand Masters of the afflicted States was being held in
New Orleans, the sum of $1,000.00 was immediately forwarded. In
acknowledging the receipt of the telegram announcing this contribution,
M. W. James H. Johnson, Grand Master of Mississippi, said: "I want
to express to you, on behalf of all present in this conference, our thanks
and appreciation for your prompt and generous response to our call.
The Grand Masters of the suffering States, acting together, realize, as
you cannot realize at a distance, the tremendous scope of this disaster,
and the great neetl for every available dollar for Masonic relief and
rehabilitation." ·

Interpretation of Section 82a
At its last Annual Communication, Grand Lodge adopted section 82a,
of the Constitution, relative to concurrent jurisdiction of Lodges, it being
therein provided that "a petition for the degrees of Masonry may be presented by any person otherwise qualified to receive the degrees, if such
person shall reside within ten miles of the Lodge room of the Lodge to
which such petition is addressed." After adjournment, numerous inquiries were received by me concerning the effect of this new section, and
I deemed it advisable to present to the Lodges an interpretation of its
provisions. Securing the views of several brethren who had been instrumental in preparing the amendment, and cndca voring to construe it in
such manner as would avoid confusion and unnecessary labor, I held as
follows:
"That the purpose of the amendment was not to enlarge the jurisdiction of Lodges in every respect, but solely in regard to the reception

of petitions for degrees, and its provisions should be limited to that
matter alone.
"Lodges still retain what may be termed their normal Jurisdictions,
as defined in Sections 82 and 95 of the Constitution. If a petitioner for
degrees resides within the normal Jurisdiction of a Lodge, then notice
of the petition need not l?e given except to the Lodge or Lodges entitled
to notice prior to the enactment of the amendment. If, however, a person
residing within the normal Jurisdiction of a Lodge applies to a Lodge
without that Jurisdiction and within ten miles of his residence, then
notice of the petition should be given to the Lodge within whose normal
Jurisdiction the petitioner resides. If petitioner resides within the corporate limits of a city having two or more Lodges and makes application
to a Lodge without such city, then notice should be given to each of the
Lodges in the city.
"As an instance: If a petition should be received say by a Lodge
in the city of Piedmont from one who resides in the city of Berkeley,
all the Lodges in Berkeley should be advised as required by the last
clause of Section 82."

or with difficulty or by the aid of an artificially substituted hand or leg
and must be able to honestly acquire the means of sustenance notwithstanding his deformity."-Wyoming.
