Physical Qualifications
At the Annual Communication of 1925, the Committee on Jurisprudence was "directed to submit at the next Annual Communication some
provision of law which will relieve the Grand Master of the burden of
defining to Masters of Lodges who are physically fit for the degrees of
Masonry." This direction was evidently overlooked by the committee
at our 1926 Communication, with the result that a number of queries
were sent me during the past year concerning the propriety of receiving
petitions from men who had been unfortunate enough to have lost both
legs, or one leg, or one arm. While I appreciate the fact that the matter
of determining the qualification of such applicants rests with the Master
of the Lodge to which the application is presented, yet I have advised
that I would consider them as unable to conform substantially t() what
the several degrees required. It may be that, in view of the action taken
by Grand Lodge in the past, this advice was incorrect, and, if so, the
error is easily corrected. However, I am firmly of the opinion that the
policy of Grand Lodge on this important matter should be definitely
stated, so that uniformity of action may prevail throughout the Jurisdiction. Without discussing the abstract question involved, I present for
consideration the opposite rules followed in two Jurisdictions of this
country, the adoption of one of which would tend to clarify the situation
in our own Jurisdiction:
"No man who is unable to perform every part of the work in the
three degrees of symbolic Masonry, without artificial aid, is eligible to
receive those degrees."-Rhode Island.

393

Use of Lodge Funds
It might be well at this• time to again call the attention of the
brethren to the limitation which has been placed on the right of a Lodge
to contribute to movements which may be most laudable, but which are
not Masonic. It is a well-settled rule that the funds of a Lodge cannot be
used to assist in any activity which is not recognized as a Masonic one.
Thus our Lodges are not authorized to make donations to even so worthy
an organization as the Red Cross, though that same limitation does not
apply to the Grand Lodge. It will, of course, be understood that there
is nothing to preclude the collection of funds from the members of the
Lodge for the assistance of a movement with which the Lodge has
properly allied itself, and in this way those brethren desiring to contribute
may do so from their own pockets and not out of funds collected for
other purposes.

Anniversary of Initiation of George Washington
On November 4, 1752, George Washington was made an Entered
Apprentice Mason, and it has been suggested that the 175th anniversary of
that event should be properly observed by the Craft. When we consider
the part played by this great man in the history of our Nation and in
the life of Masonry in this country, and when we view the imperishable
glory that his membership has reflected upon our Fraternity, the propriety
of the suggestion is apparent, and I submit it to you with the recommendation that due observance of the anniversary by the Lodges be
requested.

Decisions
While a number of questions were asked me, yet they concerned
matters which called merely for references to the Constitution and not
for decisions. I, however, report the following :
1. In acting upon a petition for restoration of a brother who had
been suspended for non-payment of dues and who had neglected for the
period of more than two years to pay the same, it was moved and carried
by unanimous vote that "the Secretary be instructed to cast the ballot
for the Lodge," I held that the ballot on such a petition should be secret
(Sec. 473, Decisions), and that the method followed was therefore
improper.
2. I held that a brother who had received the degree of Master
Mason in April last, was prohibited, by the "six months rule" from

394

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

making application for membership in the Eastern Star until the expiration of six months from the date of raising.
3. I held that it was not proper for a Lodge, in purchasing a
present for its retiring Master, to substitute a watch or other gift for a
Past Master's jewel, which latter article is distinctly specified by our
Constitution.
4. I held that if a brother who had been declared suspended for nonpayment of dues, paid to his Lodge within two years after such suspension an amount sufficient to cover his arrearage and accrued dues,
as required by Section 118 of the Constitution, then he is entitled to a
receipt even though he may be under suspicion of being an unworthy
person and one against whom charges might be preferred.
5. In view of the action of Grand Lodge at the last Annual Communication in repealing Regulation 410, I held that. the preferring of
charges of un-Masonic conduct against a brother by the Junior Warden
at the direction of the Master, no longer disqualifies the Lodge from
proceeding with the trial of the case, but that a Past Master should be
designated by the Grand Master to preside at such trial.
6. I held that the creation of a "Centennial fund," all of which fund
is to be used solely for a Centennial celebration twenty-five years hence,
and to which there should be annually appropriated from the "Social
Funds" of the Lodge, not less than the sum of $200.00, is objectionable.
It provides for a segregation of the funds of the Lodge not contemplated
by the Constitution and attempts to improperly bind the future membership
of the Lodge.
Grand Master Burke interpreted Section 89 as amended in 1921, in
the following manner: "As the law now stands, twenty per cent of the
total revenues of the Lodge constitutes a fund exempt from the inhibition
of Section 88 insofar as expenditures for purposes specified in Section B9
are concerned, and available for such purposes at any time, regardless of
the year within which it was received, but not prior to January 1, 1920."
In recommending the approval of this ruling, the Committee on Jurisprudence commented as follows : "Prior to the amendment of 129, only income for the preceding year was available ·for those purposes" (referring
to expenditures for the purposes of refreshments and the promotion of
fraternal intercourse), "and any unexpended portion reverted to the. general funds of the Lodge. The purpose of the amendment was to re·
move the restriction so that a permanent refreshment fund might he
established to be expended at such times as the best interests of the Lodge
required."
The question under consideration by the Grand Master and the Committee on Jurisprudence was the right of a Lodge to expend, after the
expiration of a current year, any unused portion of the twenty per cent

GRAND LODGE 01" CALIFORNIA

395

of the income for that year, and I am satisfied that there was no intention
to hold that an actual separate fund might be established to be expended
solely for the purposes of refreshment and fraternal intercourse. Conditions might arise which would make necessary the use of such funds for
charitable purposes and no restriction should be placed upon the funds of
the Lodge which might preclude it from meeting those demands.
While there may be other objections raised, I felt satisfied that those
referred to were, in themselves, sufficient to justify me in holding that
the creation of the fund as proposed should not be approved.
Politics
It having been reported to me that a meeting had been called at a
certain Masonic hall for the purpose of organizing a club of Masons to
participate in the political situation of the city, I communicated with
the Grand Secretary and requested him to notify the brother arranging
the meeting that such a movement would not be tolerated. In notifying
the brother, the Grand Secretary very pertinently said:
"It goes without saying that Masons as loyal citizens should take an
active and intelligent interest in the political and all civic affairs of the
communities in which they live. They should give careful consideration
to the fitness of candidates for public office, and as was so well stated
by Grand Master Boyton in his message to Grand Lodge last October,
'this consideration should go to the individual worth and ability of aspirants for public favor.' But as Masons, acting as a' body or as a part of
the great body of Masons, we have no concern with anything but the
cultivation of brotherly love, the relief of those in distress, the search
for truth, and to teach men to so live and act that the world will be
better and the people happier for the benign influence of our venerable
and honorable Institution.
"The Old Charges of 1722 wisely laid down. the proposition that we
'are resolved against all politics, as what never yet conduced to the
welfare of the Lodge, nor ever will,' are good law today, and the Grand
Lodge of California has repeatedly affirmed that proposition and in strong
terms decreed against any participation of Masons as Masons in the
political affairs otf the country or any subdivision thereof.
"You will please advise your brethren if so be they do meet for the
purpose of forming a political club, that such formation will be looked
upon as a plain violation of Masonic usage and custom, and if any brother
should persist in any such effort, he will be subject to stern discipline."
We were informed that the proposed meeting was not held in the
Masonic hall, and we are of the opinion that if any such activity continues, it is doing so under the cover of secrecy.
The injection of politics into the Fraternity must be condemned in
strongest terms. The brother, who in his desire to advance the interests

396

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of some particular candidate for public office issues a letter signed by the
writer as a Mason; the Masonic publication which in its pages indorses a
candidate for election; or the brother who would induce his brethren
to join a political club composed solely of Masons, is doing that which
tends to bring the Fraternity into the political arena and which has
ever been condemned. Masonry seeks the preferment of no man in office. It does urge upon its membership the duty of exercising the privi~ges of citizenship intelligently, leaving it entirely to the individual to
determine how or for whom he shall cast his ballot. Great care must be
taken not to involve the Fraternity in political activities, lest it be said that
Masonry has fallen from its high plane to do that which tradition and
good judgment have demanded it should avoid. To elect some particular
candidate or to defeat another one, calls for no Masonic action, and he
who would have it otherwise counsels a change in our policy which
can result only in grave injury to the Fraternity.

the worth and usefulness of our brotherhood is to deepen its understanding
of its own system, to educate its members in the deeper meaning and true
purpose of its rites and its philosophy. Were this achieved, our Institution would then become in proportion to that achievement, a spiritual
force-greater than can ever be so long as it continues content with a
formal, word-perfect perpetuation of its rites. It is from a lack ol
instruction, rather than of a desire to learn the meaning of Masonry,
that the Craft suffers today."
I believe that the large majority of the Craft desire to learn more
of Masonry, and, so believing, I feel that no effort should be spared
to satisfy that desire. I, therefore, recommend that the Committee on
Masonic Education be continued and that the Lodges be urged to comply
with the suggestions of the committee and adopt the program proposed by it.
Approval of Building Projects

District Deputy Grand Masters
At our last Annual Communication, the matter of creation and appointment of Deputy Grand Lecturers and District Deputy Grand
Masters was ordered referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence and
Policy and General Purposes, with the direction that they report thereon
at this Communication, and I assume that a report on this important
matter will be forthcoming. That the plan is both desirable and practicable has been shown in its presentation to Grand Lodge on several
different occasions, and I therefore trust that favorable action may be
taken thereon, not only for the benefit of the fraternity, but also for the
relief of the Grand Master.

The advisability of compelling Lodges, desiring to consb uct temples,
to first secure the approval of some authority designated by Grand
Lodge has been prestmted by other Grand Masters, but favorable consideration of the idea has not been given. The good name of the Fraternity is involved in the trying efforts of many Lodges to overcome the
difficulties of building projects which have been entered into with enthusiasm but without proper advice or reflection. Many Lodges are struggling today to lift the burdens of unwise undertakings, burdens which
could have been avoided had calm reflection been substituted for local
fervor. I earnestly recommend that legislation be enacted requiring the
submission to and approval by a committee of Grand Lodge of all building propositions desired to be undertaken by Lodges in this jurisdiction.

Masonic Education
The Committee on Masonic Education will report to you on its
activities during the year in carrying out the program previously adopted
by it. It was not contemplated when the work of this committee was
initiated that the educational program would be accepted by the Craft in
general in the course of a year or so, but it was the belief that it would
take several years to bring about the desired co-operation of the Lodges,
and it is the opinion of the committee that this co-operation is increasing
to a noticeable extent.
The importance of this movement cannot be doubted. The need of
greater knowledge on the part of Masons and particularly of the newlymade Mason, of the history, the symbols, the teachings of Masonry, of
its aims and objects, is imperative, and, in Masonic education may be
found a force to effectually combat those influences which are today
. threatening to make of Masonry a jazz-loving, Sunday-picnicking society. It has been well said that "wJ-..at seems now needed to intensify

Entertainments
I have constantly during the year urged upon the bretnren the necessity of not permitting the presentation by Lodges of programs which
would tend in the slightest degree to bring reproach upon the Institution,
and I have without hesitation condemned the character of entertainment
which is too frequently given in gatherings made up of Masons. I cannot
but feel that the high standards of Masonry are being lowered when
groups, composed of Masons and meeting at weekly luncheons, will permit
the form of entertainment which is heralded through the columns of the
newspapers or by circulars, and then presented under circumstances which
nullify any contention that such numbers are but artistic efforts. There is
grave danger that unless checked, the bad example set will be followed
by Lodges, and I therefore recommend that an expression of disapproval
of these questionable entertainments be given by this Grand Lodge, with
the warning that unless discontinued, further action will be taken against
those responsible therefor.

Proceedings Against Masons C~nvicted of Crime
I would call to your attention those provisions of Section 192 of the
Constitution which read as follows: "In the event of a final judgment of
conviction against a l'vfason in the State or Federal Courts of a crime
involving moral turpitude, it shall be the duty of the Junior Warden of
any Lodge having jurisdiction of such Mason to prefer charges against
the Mason so convicted on account of the matters involved in said conviction; provided, that such charges have not already been preferred,
and to press to conclusion a trial on account thereof." It is accordingly
the imperative duty of the Junior Warden of the Lodge having jurisdiction of such a Mason to bring him to trial to the end that if the conviction
in the court was justified, "the criminal should find no abiding place in
Freemasonry." Grand Lodge has spoken in no uncertain terms in regard
to this matter, and there should be no hesitancy whatsoever in proceeding
in accordance with its dictates.
Visitations and Receptions
It is with deep regret that I cannot report a visit to every Masonic
district. It had been my desire to go into each district, but conditions
arose which compelled me to forego the fulfillment of that hope. In every
visit I succeeded in making, such a cordial reception was given me, such
hospitality was shown,' such evidence of Masonic devotion and enthusiasm was displayed, that I am prouder than ever of California Masonry.
It may have its faults here and there, but, in the main, it is sound and
glorious, and justifies the confidence that you and I have in it. I will
not attempt to relate to you in detail the visits I have made, but reference
to several meetings and receptions may not be amiss. The receptions
tendered me by Madison Lodge and by Nevada Lodge were affairs that
pleased me greatly; the reception to Mrs. Jones and me by the Masonic
organizations at the University of California was a most delightful occasion to us, while the never-to-be-forgotten hours spent in Los Angeles
as the guests of the Lodges of that city and vicinity impressed us with
the hospitality and strength of Masonry in that section. Nothing was
left undone to make our stay a memorable one in every way. The reception given by the Masonic Lodges of San Francisco at the Civic Auditorium stands out as a notable event of the year-one that gave great
pleasure to those who had . the good fortune to attend.
A district meeting held at Camptonville with Gravel Range Lodge
No. 59 acting as host; the meeting of Pacific Lodge No. 136, when M. W.
Grand Master Henderson of Nevada and. members of Reno Lodge No. 13
were present as the guests of Pacific Lodge, and at which meeting the
third degree of Masonry was conferred by Reno Lodge upon its own
candidate; the meeting of Fidelity Lodge No. 120, when the third degree
was conferred by members of the Pacific Fleet; the "beef-steak" dinner

Conclusion
In a very few days my work as Grand Master will De concluded
and the gavel will be handed to one who will perform the important duties
of the office in a manner that will reflect great honor both upon him and
upon the Fraternity. I cannot look back over the year's task with the
thought that I have done all things wisely and well, or that I have accomplished even but little for the welfare of the Fraternity, but there has
been an effort on my part to impress on the membership "the dignity and
high importance of Masonry," that Masonry stands committed to the
enforcement of and obedience to the law, that it stands for the tolerance,
and for charity, both of purse and mind. The temple of Masonry has
been building for centuries; it is a splendid structure which has attracted the attention of men in every walk of life, and they have eager!)
sought to enter its enclosures and participate in its mission.
That temple has withstood the savage attacks which envy, malice
and intolerance have made upon it for ages past, and we know today that
no outward power can destroy it. But what of the attacks by those
who are within the sacred precincts? The assaults of enemies may leave
no marks upon the edifice, but the mud cast upon it by thoughtless, heedless
brethren m;i.y produce stains which only time can eradicate.
This, then, has been my admonition to the brethren-to so act,
wherever you may be, that no discredit shall be brought upon the Fraternity, and, my brethren, if as the years go by your minds should revert
for even a moment to him who now addresses you, think of him as one
who valued your friendship, appreciated your favors and who admonished you to Keep Masonry clean.

Nevada City, April 3, 1927.
Brethren of the Jurisdiction:
On June 14, 1777, the Congress (as it then existed) of the United
States, meeting in Independence Hall in the City of Philadelphia, adopted
the following resolution:
Resolved, That the flag of the thirteen United States be
thirteen stripes, alternate red and white; that the union be thirteen stars, white in a blue field, representing a new constellation."
We as Masons are proud of the part that Masonry has played in the
creation and perpetuation of this Government, and we at all times pay
reverence to the flag of our country, the glorious symbol of the splendid
principles for which this Nation stands.
"There is something in the flag,
And the little burnished eagle
That is more than emblematic :
It is glorious, it is regal."
In accordance with the recommendation of the Grand Lodge, I do
hereby urge that in each Lodge, in the month of June, such celebration be
held as shall mark suitable observance of the one hundred and fiftieth
anniversary of the official recognition of the flag of our Nation, and that
all Masons be invited to join therein.
I particularly suggest that each Mason in the Jurisdiction, on the
14th of June next, renew his allegiance to our country in the following
pledge:
I pledge allegiance to the flag of the United States and to
the Republic for which it stands; one Nation indivisible, with
liberty and justice for all.
Fraternally yours,

San Francisco, California, December 31, 1926.
Pursuant to the recommendation of Grand Lodge, October, 1926,
the Committee on Masonic Education has prepared the following statement, a copy of which is required to be given, by the Master, to each
candidate at the time he receives the first degree:
To the Initiate:
There may be some who might approach you with business
propositions, saying to you, now that you have become a member
of the Fraternity you should extend your business favors to
• members of the Craft or particularly to some organizations who
state that they confine their activities exclusively to members of
the Masonic Fraternity. Examples of such approaches are solicitors who may endeavor to sell you insurance in associations
advertised as insuring Masons only; the subscription to magazines devoted largely to Masonry; the purchase of books on
Masonic subjects which, it may be suggested, will tell you all
about the Institution.
Let us urge upon you to refrain from committing yourself
until you have taken up the matter with the Master of your
Lodge or some older Mason who will be able to advise you. Indeed, if you view such solicitations in the same light as you
would before you became a member-that is, on the merits of the
proposition presented to you-you will be doing the fair thing to
the solicitor and yourself. There may be some who might presume' on your zeal as a new member to take advantage thereof,
and while we do not advise against extending favors, we likewise
do not suggest that you make purchase or subscription merely because you have become a member of the Fraternity.
Please deliver a copy of this circular to each candidate at the time he
receives his first degree.

PROCLAMATION
E10HTH ANNUAL OnsERVANCE PUBLIC ScHOOLS WEEK

To the Masters, Wardens and Brethren of the
Secc'eral Lodqes in this f11risdictinn:
The challenge of childhood is eternal; and the Nation is ever confronted with the demand that every child shall be assured his rightful
heritage of an education appropriate to, and commensurate with, the demands of the age in which he lives. We have sought to answer that
challenge by the creation of a purely American institution-the Public
School; and of all our American institutions this is the most useful and
the most deserving of public support.
As is true of every human institution, it is of course far from perfect; and there has never been a time when it has not been subject to
cntlc1sm. Jn so far as that criticism is intelligent and constructive it is
to be welcomed, and should be encouraged; but in so far as it is
destructive and designedly hostile it is to be deplored, and should be
vigorously combated by every friend of our public school system. To
combat that destructive criticism, to bring about desired improvement,
and to preserve that faith and conlidence in the Institution on which its
perpetuity and usefulness depend, there must be close contact between
the public and its schools, together with free and open discussion of all
questions involved. That is the aim and purpose of Public Schools
Week.
Now, therefore, J, George L. Jones, Grand Master of Masons in
California, do proclaim the week commencing Monday, April 25th, 1927,
as "Public Schools \IV eek"; and I do now request and direct that during
that week there be held in every community in California in which there
exists a Masonic Lodge at least one public meeting (and more, if practicable) for the Eighth Annual Observance of Public Schools Week
by the Masonic Lodges in this Jurisdiction.
It is likewise my request and direction that wherever practicable
the meetings be held in the auditoriums of public schools; and that all
local organizations interested in civic work be urged to co-operate with
the idea and purpose of making these meetings public in every sense of
the word.
I do furthermore request and direct that no "work" be done by any
Lodge on a night on which any meeting for the observance of Public
Schools Week is held in the town or city in which the Lodge is locate<;!.
Dated at San Francisco this 1st day of February, 1927.
GEORGE L. JoNES, Grand Master.

To the Brethren of the Jurisdiction:
Advices from the Grand Masters. of the Jurisdictions affected by
the floods in the Mississippi river and tributaries, indicate that the losses
in life alld property are so great that ordinary relief measures will not
be adequate to the task of feeding and clothing the sufferers and carry
on the necessary work of rehabilitation in the stricken territory.
With grateful remembrance of the prompt and generous aid extended
to California at the time of our urgent needs in April, 1906, we now have
an opportunity not only to do our duty as Masons, but in a measure to
repay those who assisted us.
It is a trite saying but nevertheless pertinent, that "he gives twice
who gives quickly," and the Grand Master fraternally requests that each
Lodge of the Jurisdiction promptly contribute a sum equal to ten cents
a member ior this worthy cause, and for other possible emergency calls.
Checks may be sent to the Grand Secretary, and due credit will be
given to all contributors.
GEORGE

Attest:
]OHN WnrcHER,

Grand Secretary.

L. ]ONES, Grand Master.

GRAND WDGE, FREE AND ACCEPTED MASONS
OF CALIFORNIA
GEORGE L. JoNES, Gratid Master
Nevada City, June 8, 1927.
To all Masters, Wardens, Brethren and Lodges in the Jurisdiction:
Again a call comes from our brethren in the Mississippi flood district
for further help, and again we ask for contributions. The response to
our circular appeal of April 28th was prompt, and some Lodges contributed more than the ten cents per member requested. The total amount
received by our Grand Secretary to date is $16,902.69 and the total moneys
received by the Joint Committee at New Orleans from all sources is
$226,402.07. A half million dollars or more wilt be needed. Our quota .
should be at least $30,000.00.
·
The Grand Masters of Mississippi, Louisiana and Arkansas report
that more than 600,000 people have been made homeless by the flood, of
whom 500,000 are dependent for their daily bread upon the thoughtful
generosity of people outside of the flood area. In the Louisiana flooded
area there are 5300 distressed Masons and their families; in the devastated district of Mississippi there are 4200 Masons and their families,
without homes or food except through relief committees; and in Arkansas,
the area and loss are double that of Mississippi.
These afflicted brethren and their families must not only be supplied
with daily food, but property damage must be considered. After the
flood waters shall have dispersed the world will speedily forget the distresses of those brethren, their wives and little ones, whereas the real
work of practical relief will then have only begun, for the rehabilitation
of those whose crops are lost, homes destroyed, and for the care of the
sick.
California Lodges have contributed liberally to the Masonic relief
fund, and individual members have done their duty through contributions
to the Red Cross-but we have not done enough. It is our earnest desire that a further contribution b,e made to our Grand Lodge Emergency
Relief Fund by all Lodges and brethren, to the end that our brethren
in the flood area may know for a surety that California Masons will
never fail of their full duty. We hope to receive, including the previous
contribution, not less than 25 cents a member.
With every good wish, and in the full belief that you will promptly
respond to this appeal, I am
Sincerely and fraternally yours,
Attest:
GEORGE L. JoNES, Grand Master.
JonN WHICHER, Grand Secretary.
Please make checks payable to Relief Fund, and mail them to the
Grand Secretary, Masonic Temple, San Francisco.

Membership

members, and lodges under dispensation 644 members, an apparent gross

of 6897.

Degrees by Courtesy
The usual and I regret to report not always reasonable requests
to have degrees conferred upon residents of California for Lodges
of other jurisdictions, have been received, and in most cases approved. Some requests, however, have not been approved, notably
when it has appeared that the candidate received the first degree
many years ago. In such cases we have replied to the requesting
jurisdiction that we believed the interests of Masonry would be
best subserved by the granting of a dimit or waiver of jurisdiction,
and permitting the candidate to lawfully petition for the remaining
degree or degrees at the place of his home, and thereby give him an
opportunity to actively participate in the affairs of the Lodge. I

GRAND LODGE OF CALII<'ORNIA

409

respectfully renew the suggestion I made last year, that we adopt
the policy of refusing to confer degrees by courtesy upon men who
actually hold legal residence within our jurisdiction, except when
proper reasons may be shown why the candidate should remain a
member of the requesting Lodge. Under our present policy we
merely add names to the rosters of outside Lodges, with no resulting addition to the moral or material strength of Masonry.
Our Lodges have conferred 337 degrees for other jurisdictions,
and have requested like favors to the number of 66 degrees.
Hand Book for Secretaries
At the annual communication of Grand Lodge in 1865 the
the following resolution was adopted;
"That the Grand Secretary be instructed to prepare and publish
a form for the proper keeping of Lodge records."
The Grand Secretary, Alexander G. Abell, thereupon prepared
and presented to Grand Lodge in October, 1866, a form bearing
the title "Record Book of Example Lodge," which was approved
with the following comment by the Committee on Jurisprudence:
"That it will not only subserve the primary object had in view when
it was proposed,-that of instructing new Lodges in the proper
method of recording their transactions-but will be an excellent
guide even to the older ones, as showing a concise and uniform yet
distinct and expressive manner of noting the manifold transactions
of a Masonic Lodge."
The work has been revised from time to time to meet the
changes in our laws, and I now request that it be revised to date
and reprinted in pamphlet form, and one copy sent gratis to the
Secretary of each Lodge in the jurisdiction.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Report of Experts
September 17, 1927.

•••••••wWH•

~·-~

Finance Committee, Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In accordance with your authorization we have made an
examination of the financial records of the Grand Lodge, F. &.
A. M., of California, during the fiscal year ended July 31, 1927,
and present herewith the following exhibits:
1. Exhibit A-Grand Secretary's report of cash receipts and
disbursements for the fiscal year, General Fund.

2.

Exhibit B-Cash receipts-Masonic homes.

3.

Exhibit C-Emergency Relief Fund.

4. Exhibit D-Grand Treasurer's report of cash receipts and
disbursements for the fiscal year, and schedule of assets as at
July 31, 1927.
5.

Exhibit E-Endowment Fund.

We certify that, in our opinion, the finances of the Grand
Lodge have been properly accounted for during the fiscal year
ended July 31, 1927, and that the attached statements are correct.
Respectfully submitted,

Unfinished Business
RUCKSTELL

The recommendation of the Committee on Pay of Members
that Section 6 of the Constitution be amended by striking out the
words "An unlimited first-class railroad fare." This was referred
to the Committee on Jurisprudence and Finance. (1926, p. 212.)
A proposed amendment to Section 70 of the Constitution, presented by the Masters' and Wardens' Association of Los Angeles,
providing that Inspectors shall be allowed payment for necessary
expenses in attending Grand Lodge. Laid over for consideration
at this annual communication. (1926, p. 217.)
That portion of the Grand Master's Message (1926, pp. 35-38).
relating to the appointment of Deputy Grand Lecturers and District
Deputy Grand Masters. Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence
and Policy and General Purposes, to report 1927. (1926, p. 218.)

& LAND,

Certified Public Accountants.

By FLOYD T. WEBB.

To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee to which was referred the consideration and distribution of the Address of the Most Worshipful Grand Master, and
the Report of the Very \Vorshipful Grand Secretary, begs leave to
report as follows :
In touching slightly upon those portions of the report of the Grand
Master that need not be referred to committee, as it is necessary to do,
we do not wish to be misunderstood. Every portion is worthy of careful
study and each member of the fraternity who wishes to comprehend the
nature and importance of the work in which our fraternity is engaged,
should make the acquaintance of this document in mass and master it in
detail.
While we regret to learn that the Grand Master feels that the
"degree mill" has, in some ·localities, been working overtime, we are
gratified to know that the general condition of the craft in this jurisdiction
continues good.
A different report of the condition of the Masonic Homes was not
to have been expected. Those two institutions, monuments to the love
and generosity of the membership in this jurisdiction, are indeed the
pride of true Masons.
\Ve regret that the Grand Master did not have the good fortune to
be the guest of the brethren of the Hawaiian Islands, and we are confident that those brethren sustained a deep loss by being deprived of
the inspiration that his presence would have provided. But we are convinced that since he was unable to give the time to take both trips, his
decision to visit Alexandria, Virginia, there to inspect the George Washington Memorial, instead of going to Hawaii, was a wise one.
Your committee heartily approves and commends that portion of
the Grand Master's report appearing under the head of Politics. Care
must be taken to keep Masonic activities within proper Masonic bounds.

438

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

A man's political views are not the concern of Masonry so long as his
conduct is just and honorable.
Under the heading of Proceedings Against Masons Convicted of
Crimes, the Grand Master calls attention to Section 192 of our Con·
stitution. It is of the utmost importance that the rolls of our Lodges
should not be disgraced by having upon them the names of those convicted of offenses involving moral turpitude. The Grand Master's
comments upon this subject will be unanimously approved.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the M:.rv:.Grand Lodge of C~lifomia:
It is with much honor and pleasure that I herewith present to you
my twenti.eth annual report, giving an account of my stewardship during
'.he. y~ar. Just close:!. At the outset l will say that the Lodges of the
JUrtsdiction are all m a healthy condition and prospering. Some of them
possibly arc not doing as much degree work as they did a few years
ago, but this has given them more time for educational and social affairs
:md more devotion to the welfare of their members. This has great!;
rncrcased the attendance at the meetings, both stated and special.
Lodges should be particularly card ul in the selection of material
for officers, and choose only those who will make Masters. It should
be very. definitely understood that Lodges arc not created for the purpose
of passmg Masters through the chairs and making Past Masters. Unless
a prospective Master has shown some executive as well as ritualistic
aptitude for the work and has already given some evidence of the zeal
necessary for the performance of the duties in a manner that will be
creditable to the Craft, his Lodge and himself, there can be no justification for his preferment. There are many essential factors in the work
o.f th: ~faster of a Loc.!ge. He should be competent to do the necessary
ntuahstic work and give evidence of his competency by the frequent
performance of it. He should realize that the honor, reputation and
usefulness of the Lodge are in his hands, and be prepared to study the
problems that arise, so that he can, by exercising his talents, plan and
direct the activities in a way that will make for real progress. This
unfortunately is not always the case. It would appear that some Masters
are n?t aware of the requirements of the office, and consequently do
not give the thought necessary to a proper appreciation of its respon-

440

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

sibilities and to a performance of the duties that are essential to success.
The authority of a Worshipful Master is absolute, and he should not
hesitate to exercise it within reasonable limits. The ritual itself is but
a means to the end, but not the end. \Ve must obtain ritualistic interpretation as well as ritualistic instruction. We must learn the true
significance of the Masonic ritual in its relation to business life, to home
life, to everyday intercourse, and to social obligations. Thus only will
the ritual prove its worth, for it is first know your ritual and then to
know what it means.
I have visited all the one hundred and four districts in the State,
and held Lodges of Instruction, both day and night sessions in each,
and in some districts more than once. In many individual Lodges, as
well as individual instruction has been given to many of the brethren,
with most satisfactory results, all anxious to perfect themselves in the
ritual. I have received reports from all the Inspectors, and they report
the Lodges over which they preside to be in good condition, financially
and otherwise. Peace and harmony prevails throughout the jurisdiction.
All the Lodges seem to be carrying on the business and work in good
style.
My sincere thanks are tendered to the Inspectors for the courtesies
and help that was always gladly given. Much credit is due the Inspectors
for their untiring efforts, and I know that the Grand Lodge appreciates
the good work they are doing.
On Thursday evening, October 13th, the Inspectors will exemplify
the third degree in the Scottish Rite Lodge room. The brethren may
expect to see a most creditable degree conferred. Presidio Lodge, No.
354, will furnish the candidate and preside over the meeting on that
occasion.
There have been 12 new Lodges formed this year. Most of them are
in the southern part of the State.
I have accompanied the M:.w:.Grand Master on many of his visits,
and ceremonies where he has performed installations, corner-stones and
dedications. All these meetings were well attended and the brethren
greatly appreciated these visits, as evidenced by the enthusiastic receptions
given the Grand Master.
In one of the old reports I found a beautiful and simple Masonic
lesson that is worth quoting: "Little acts of kindness, every day, should
be our aim. It's not the big duties that we are expected to perform, but
the every-day little courtesies and kindnesses that take so little time
and require so little energy. At home, in business, in the Lodge. They
give a savor sweet and lasting to all we do, and create perfect con- ·
tentment in our own bosoms. The balmy odor of sweet flowers is not
more pleasing. Practice little acts of kindness and your symbolic wages
will soon grow larger."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
WEEK ON EIGHTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE
SAN FRANCISCO, October 11, 1927.
To the M.".W.".Grand Lodye of California:

In compliance with the request of the M.".W." .Grand Master this
report is presented in this form, and distributed to those in attendance
at this Communication, not merely to advise Grand Lodge of the result
of the Eighth Annual Observance of Public Schools Week, but as well
and more particularly for another reason :
The observance this year was a stupendous success. Never before
was there so much public interest manifested; and not even last year
did we receive anything approaching the amount of publicity that was
given us this year by both the metropolitan, and what is generally termed
the "country" press. In far more instances than ever before the auditorium in which the meeting was held proved inadequate for the attendance. Nevertheless we still have with us some who insist that in their
own particular communities there are certain local conditions that preclude a successful observance of Public Schools Week. It is
hoped that a detailed report of what was accomplished this year in
localities where it was believed similar conditions existed will convince
everyone that there is no city, town nor hamlet in the state of California
in which a successful observance cannot be held. It is also believed that
a knowledge of some of the methods that were adopted to awaken public
interest will be of material assistance to those who are willing to devote
to the movement in which we are engaged the effort its importance certainly warrants. It is therefore suggested that after being read by the
Masters who receive it, this report be by them transmitted to their successors or to the chairmen of the committees that will make the arrangements for the observance next year.
Lest it may be assumed that your committee is unduly optimistic in
its estimate of the success achieved this year and that "the wish is
father to the thought," we quote from an editorial that appeared in a
widely circulated and influential Masonic publication.
"For the eighth time Public Schools Week was observed in April
throughout California. In crowded city and lonely hamlet; from the
Sierras. to the sea, enthusiastic meetings were held. From scores of
platforms respected educators and prominent public men told of the
organization and scope of our great educational system. One fact be-

443

comes increasingly evident as the years pass-the heightening interest of
the general public in this observance. For the first few celebrations the
attendance was restricted almost wholly to members of the Fraternity
and their families. Little by little public interest grew. The people as a
whole discovered that the organizers of the week had no axes to grind,
no ulterior motives to be served. As a result they showed their approval
in the most practical way-by attending the meetings. Irrespective of
color or creed, Public Schools Week appeals irresistibly to every citizen.
The more thoroughly people understand the organization of the schools,
the methods of teaching, the whys and wherefores of curricula, the benefits of vocational education, the development of modern ideas in mental
training and the many seeming complexities that have developed during
the past generation, the more emphatically will the public schools be
endorsed."
This is what might be termed a "bird's-eye view" of the situation.
The opinion expressed by the writer of that editorial was probably
based on newspaper reports, and comment in the periodicals that came
to his desk. It is, however, more than confirmed by the reports made
to the Grand Master setting out in detail the information sought in the
questionnaire issued by him. Indeed it is only with the knowledge gained
from these reports, and by comparing them with the reports from the
same lodges in previous years, that the real success of the observance
can be gauged.
There were fewer instances this year in which only one meeting had
been held in a community sufficiently large to support three or more
lodges; and the same trend is to be noted in the fact that there were
several individual lodges that sponsored more than one meeting. A notable
instance was that of a little lodge under dispensation that held three
successful meetings during the week in the school district in which it is
located.
As was the fact last year, it has been practically impossible to determine whether the most successful observances were in the larger centers
of population or in the small communities. In each of the largest cities
of the state wonderfully successful meetings were held; but no more so,
from any point of view, than many in some of the smaller cities and
in various towns throughout the state.
In proportion to the population the attendance this year, as heretofore, was better in the smaller communities everywhere than it was
in the large cities. Indeed there were several lodges that reported attendance varying from forty per cent to eighty per cent of their entire population. It was in the smaller communities, too, with few exceptions, that
the interest was more nearly universal. This was, of course, to be
expected. In the report of the Sixth Annual Observance we pointed out

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

444

445

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

that there were two reasons for this: The first and generally accepted
one, that in the smaller communities there are fewer attractions and
distractions ; and the second, that not only is the population in the small
communities, generally speaking, homogeneous with a strong civic pride,
but the people are closer to the institutions they maintain and naturally
evince a greater interest therein.
The only Masters to whom failures can be justly attributed are the
few, the very few we are glad to say, who for one reason or another
made no effort to comply with the request of the Grand Master for the
observance of Public Schools Week. This does not mean, of course,
that there were no meetings at which the attendance was disappointing;
because there were several Masters who reported that although the
attendance far exceeded that of previous years it was neverthless not
commensurate with the effort involved. This, however, was to be
expected. There probably will never come a time when the people everywhere, on all occasions, will co-operate as they should in the effort made
by public spirited citizens who are willing to devote their time, talent
and enthusiasm to the cau:se of public education. In this connection
we cannot forbear here repeating, because it cannot be too often reiterated, what we said in our report last year with respect to attendance.
"It is, of course, desired that all our meetings shall be well attended;
hut if that desire were everywhere achieved it would he extraordinary.
The fact of the matter is that we are prone to expect too much. Those
arranging the meetings work hard and earnestly and, not unnaturally,
are disappointed, and perhaps discouraged, if their efforts do not result
in attracting the attendance for which they hoped. They lose sight
of the fact that they are contending with a condition that in itself
militates against the probability of a large attendance. Indeed, paradoxi·
cal as it may seem, there would be no need for holding meetings if they
were as well attended as they should he. The lack of attendance of which
we complain is due primarily to the apathy that brought about the condi·
tions that gave birth to the idea of Public Schools Week; and it is to
overcome and dispel that apathy that these meetings are being held."
That that apathy is being gradually dispelled is evident from the fact
that in nearly every report received this year comment is made on the
increase in attendance over previous years ; and where complaint is made
of a poor attendance it appears that the lack of public interest might
be reasonably attributed to the fact that the suggestions made by our
committee, and that were based upon experience extending over several
years, were either completely ignored or only half-heartedly complied with.
For instance, one of the suggestions particularly stressed was that the
observance should be made a community affair, and not a Masonic event;
and that in making arrangements for their meetings, the Masters of our

Lodges should endeavor to secure the active co-operation of not only the
school people, but also of the Parent-Teacher Associations and the
Service Clubs. Now where complaint was made of a lack of public interest it usually appeared that this had not been done; and where the
report showed that no assistance was received from any organization it
also showed, in the majority of cases, that it had not been asked. In
other instances, the only effort apparently made was to notify the organizations referred to that a meeting would be held to which they were
invited, and of which it was hoped they would give notice to their members. This, of course, is not sufficient ; and perhaps it will be well, even
though it may seem a digression, to here devote a few moments' consideration to this particular matter.
Every individual is, of course, more interested in a movement in
which he has a part than he is in one in which he is merely an onlooker.
This is likewise true of organizations. To secure from the service clubs,
the school people and the Parent-Teacher Associations the sort of cooperation we desire, they should be given a part in the undertaking. It
must be their meeting as well as ours. Indeed, if the observance is to
be made a community affair and not a Masonic event, as is our desire, it
is not merely advisable, but eminently proper that these organizations
should be represented on the committee of arrangements. Where this
was done there was no complaint of poor attendance or lack of public
interest ; and our extraordinary success was due to the fact that this
year this seems to have been the rule rather than the exception.
The failure to arouse public interest in any community is not accounted
for merely by saying (we are now quoting literally from a report):
"It is impossible to get the people of this community interested in anything of this sort." We cannot believe that there is any community in
the State of California in which people are not interested in their school
system, and would not willingly and gladly support any movement for
its benefit if they thoroughly understood it. The Master making the
report to which we have just referred would probably not have had
occasion to make that complaint if he had done what was done by another
Master who reported a particularly successful meeting. The latter per·
sonally addressed two Parent-Teacher Associations and twenty-six
classes of school children ; and personally interviewed the principals of
the schools, and met and talked with every teacher explaining to them
the object of the meeting and inviting their co-operation. By similar
methods he aroused the interest of the members of other fraternal organizations in his community and secured their support. The attendance at
his meeting exceeded his expectations. Although the auditorium in
which the meeting was held seats six hundred, he reports that he was
counting on only about four hundred people; but that by actual count
there were more than eight hundred in attendance. Not only was every

446

PUOCFiEDlNGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

seat filled, but all the standing room was taken and there were many who
were unable to gain admission. Incidentally, by the way, and of extreme
significance, it appears from a letter accompanying his report that he
started his preliminary work in February immediately upon receipt of
the first letter sent to the Masters of the various lodges.

consent of the school authorities and by them made a part of the school
work. Announcement of the result was made on the night of the meeting
and the prizes there awarded. Such was the co-operation received from
the school people in some communities that instead of holding the regular
afternoon session, the pupils were dismissed at noon and assembled in
their classes in the evening, in order that people who could not, or would
not, make their visits during the day, might gain a personal knowledge of
the actual work being done in the schools.

In the instance to which reference has just been made, practically
all the work was apparently done by the Master. In view of the splendid
success that attended his effort, we are not disposed, of course, to
question the wisdom of his action. It is our belief, however, that, generally speaking, the arrangements should be made by a committee suffi·
ciently large to be divided into sub-committees with specific duties ; and
that the committee representing the Lodge should not be changed each
year, but should consist of members who have gained experience
through service in former years. The ideal committee would seem to be
one composed of representatives of the various organizations to which
we have referred and of the various bodies of Masonry in the com·
munity, with a general chairman possessing executive ability, and whose
position in the community is such as will convey the impression that the
observance of Public Schools ·week is a civic event demanding the support of every good citizen.
"What can be accomplished through wisely conceived and carefully
executed arrangements will be made evident by the reference we purpose
herein later making to certain specific instances. In passing, however, and
concluding this digression, it may be said that irrespective of the methods adopted in making the arrangements, wherever the observance was
a community affair, and the program was furnished by the pupils of the
schools, it was an unqualified success. This was particularly evident
where there were provided special features that would inevitably arouse
the interest of those in the community to whom the meeting alone might
not be especially attractive.
The instances this year in which special features were provided, and
the meeting itself was but an incident of the observance, were far more
numerous than ever before; and it has been extremely gratifying to your
committee to note the initiative displayed in this direction. There were
many reports showing that visits to the schools and a display of school
work had constituted a part of the observance. In more than one it
appeared that prizes had been offered to stimulate interest among the
school children and their parents; in some cases the prize was given
to the class attracting the largest number of visitors; and in others to
individual pupils in competitions of various sorts. These included essays
having subjects peculiarly appropriate to Public Schools Week, and in
some cases specifically pointing out the purpose thereof as well as explaining its origin and development. This was, of course, done with the

447

It has been the rule of your committee in making its report, to mention no Lodge by name, either in praise or criticism; because obviously
we could not name every Lodge that had held a successful observance;
and we believed no good purpose would be served by calling attention
to the few that had failed. This year, as we have already said, the only
Masters who could be justly criticized were those who made no attempt
whatever to hold an observance; and it is hoped that their failures will
be redeemed by their successors in office. To name every Lodge entitled
to great credit would be almost like calling the roll of the Lodges in this
jurisdiction.
It has been particularly pleasing to your committee to note the large
number of meetings at which the chairman evidently had been selected
without regard to his fraternal affiliations and solely because of his
prominence in the civic life of the community. There could be nothing
better calculated to characterize the gathering as an essentially public
affair. In some instances it was the Mayor of the city, or corresponding
official in smaller communities ; and in others, the President of the
Chamber of Commerce, the Chairman of the School Trustees or Board
of Education, or the County or City Superintendent of Schools; and not
infrequently, the presiding officer of the largest of the service clubs.
As in the past, the principal speakers included the most prominent
educators in the state, many with national reputations. We are obviously
precluded from naming all of them; and we ·therefore forbear making
special mention of any except Bro. William John Cooper, our State
Superintendent of Public Instruction. Indeed reference is made to him
only because of the fact that his itinerary during the observance .indicates the cheerfulness and willingness with which these men sacrifice
their personal comfort and convenience to contribute to the success of our
observance. Superintendent Cooper spoke in San Francisco on Monday
night, leaving after the meeting for Fresno where he spoke on Tuesday
night; he again made a night trip from Fresno to Riverside County to
speak there on Wednesday night; from there he went to Ontario to
address a meeting on Thursday night; and on Friday night spoke at a
meeting in San Diego.
Heretofore the support we have always received from the leading
school men in the state has been the only answer that we were able

448

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

to make to the question as to whether or not Public Schools Week was
really worth the effort entailed; because it is one of those things that
cannot be definitely evaluated, but must be "sensed." It seemed to us
however that the question was conclusively answered in the affirmative
by the fact that we were receiving the active and enthusiastic co-operation of those who because of their intimate connection with our Public
Schools were best qualified to form an opinion as to the value of our
annual observance. Obviously they would not be so willing, indeed eager,
to forward our effort if they had any doubt of its worth. This year,
however, we are able to cite a definite tangible result that is attributed
to the work we have done.
It may be perhaps remembered by some that in the report of the
observance held a few years ago we referred to a small Lodge that had
arranged a meeting at which practically the entire population was present.
This year the ~faster reports that, in spite of cold, bad weather, with the
roads wet and slippery, there were included in the audience five persons
who had traveled one hundred miles, one fifty miles and four twenty-one
miles solely to attend the meeting. It is not, however, to the attendance
at that meeting to which we desire to call particular attention; but to the
fact that the interest that of course accounted for it is attributed to the
annual observance of Public Schools Week. More than this, that interest
has produced a definite, concrete result. In this little mountain town
with a total population of less than 300 people there has been established
a branch of a union high school. There was recently sent to the chairman
of your committee a program of the commencement exercises held in
June; and in an accompanying letter the Master wrote: "It seems like a
fairy tale to say that this little town is having commencement exercises
and giving forth real diplomas ; but we are, and you may be sure that it
is a great satisfaction to us to know that we have really been a benefit
to this cause. We are sending you this program to let your committee
know what has resulted in great part from our efforts ; because the interest was really started by your committee and the beginning of Public
Schools Week."

.
We think we speak not only for our committee, but as well for every
Mason cognizant of the situation, when we say we believe that this
alone is worth all the time and effort that has been devoted to the
observance of Public Schools 'Week.
Although as we have said it was in the smaller communities that the
interest was more nearly universal, it was not only there that a widespread public interest was manifested this year. There were two citiesone with a population of approximately 40,000, and the other with a
population of nearly 150,000, in which this feature of the observance
was particularly noteworthy. It was the more remarkable because in each

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

449

of these cities the excuse for failures in the past was that the people
were not interested. Here we have another paradox. A successful observance could not be held because the people were not interested; but it was
the interest of the people that made the observance this year such a
wonderful success. Of course the truth of the matter is that the people
were interested here as they are everywhere; but that the right sort of
appeal to that interest had not been theretofore made.
The somewhat extended reference we make to these two observances
is with the purpose of showing that nowhere, in town or city, are there
any conditions that preclude success; and that it is simply a question of
determining upon the proper course of procedure. In this connection we
hope no one will fail to note that although there was a wide difference in
the methods adopted in the two instances we are now considering, both
were successful. Furthermore, although the public interest was widespread
in both places, it was manifested in different ways. This was of course
due to the difference in the nature of the appeal. In one, an extraordinarily large attendance was attracted to the place where the single meeting
was held and where the work of the schools was being exhibited; and in
the other, although there were three public meetings held, all well attended, the best work, we think was done in focusing the attention of the
whole community on the public schools throughout the entire week. As
to which was the better method we do not pretend to say. There is no
method that could be devised that would suit the varying conditions of
the different communities. Indeed it is probably not so much a question
of the method, as it is of the intelligence, industry and enthusiasm with
which it is pursued. Of what was done in each of these instances, it may
be said that no more intelligent and enthusiastic effort was ever made
anywhere since the institution of Public Schools Week.
There were two conditions common to both cities. In both the
observances in the past had been failures; and in each it was apparently
believed that the failure was due to conditions that could not be overcome.
Two years ago, in the first city to which reference is made, the brethren
had become so disheartened by their failures in the past that they were
disinclined to make any further attempt. There were, however a few
men with vision who persisted ; and although the meeting that ~as held
that year could not be said to have been a very great success, it was so
much better than those that had been held in preceding years that they
entered into the observance last year with a far different spirit. The
result of that meeting was so encouraging that they became satisfied
that notwithstanding the conditions that confronted them a really successful meeting could be held if they went about it in the right way.
This year the first thing on which they determined was that it should
be a strictly community affair and not a Masonic event; and although the

arrangements were handled by a committe appointed by the Masters and
\Vardens Association it appears from the report of the observance. that,
"In the preliminary publicity the only reference to the Fraternity was

and Wardens Association; but it, too, was made a community affair
through the co-operation of the churches, service clubs, women's clubs,
Parent-Teachers Associations and the school authorities. The reports of

it would appear to be well deserved. He is one of the most prominent
citizens of the community, possessed of great executive ability, with vision
to discern the importance of the movement, and apparently motivated by
an enthusiasm that must have been infectious.

450

As a part of the publicity arranged by the committ~e charged with
that duty quarter cards were placed in the show windows of approximately two hundred stores. Invitations were prepared and distributed
by the Boy Scouts to every home, and special "write ups" were prepared
for the newspapers. Carefully selected members of the Craft made ·
announcements of Public Schools Week at the services held in every
church on the preceding Sunday. The Superintendent of Schools prepared
and distributed to each teacher a sufficient supply of invitations for each
pupil with the request that they be taken home and given to the parents.
The invitation was over his own signature and was accompanied by a
mimeographed program.
Every effort was made to have it distinctly understood that the
observance was a purely civic event. The Mayor of the city presided as
Chairman of the meeting; and although the auditorium seats approximately 2200 people not only was every seat occupied, with standing room
at a premium, but by actual count 947 were turned away. It was estimated
that the attendance at the meeting was not less than 2500.
Moreover "in connection with the meeting there was held in the
gymnasium an exhibition of school work taking in all the classes from
the kindergarten to the senior class in the high school. This exhibit was
arranged in order by classes from the lowest to the highest grades and
included specimens of penmanship, art work, wood craft, shop work,
laboratory demonstrations, cooking classes, dressmaking and millinery.
This exhibit was open all day to the public; and one of the teachers in
attendance estimated that at least 1000 people had attended during the
day and more than twice that number, exclusive of those attending the
meeting in the auditorium, visited it during the evening. It would thus
appear that the observance had attracted a total attendance of more than
5000 people during the day and evening. The exhibit was thronged until
nearly midnight, and proved so popular that by special request it was kept
open on Monday of the following week."
In the other city (a very much larger one it will be remembered)
the arrangements for the observance were likewise made by the Masters

There were three public meetings, each in the auditorium of a high
school, and all well attended. This, however, was the least of what was
done. The work that was being accomplished in their public schools was
brought immediately to the attention of all the representative business
men and women of the community through programs that were presented
by students before practically every service club and women's organization
in the city. The reports show that in addition to the three evening meetings
there were thirteen of these "luncheon meetings" held.
The newspapers were exceedingly generous in the amount of space
that was devoted to the observance. In the preliminary publicity the
proclamation of the Grand Master was published in full; and during the
week not only did the news columns carry complete accounts of all the
meetings with reports of the addresses that were made, but there were
also editorials commenting with great favor on the work that was being
done. In addition to the newspaper publicity, the week's activities were
broadcast three times daily during the period from April 24th to April
30th.
If it be true, as was said in a proclamation issued by one of our
Grand Masters, that the real purpose of the celebration of any anniyersary is to direct the attention of all the people to the same thing at
the same time, there would seem to be no question of the success of the
observance to which we are referring; because during that entire week
the attention of all the people must have been directed to their public
schools. It was indeed just what it was termed in one of the newspaper
reports-"an unprecedented success;" and it gives splendid promise for
the future.
We feel that we cannot conclude our reference to these particular
observances without calling attention to the reports thereof that were
received by this Committee. They were both extremely comprehensive
and models as to form. Not only was there detailed information of the
work done by the Committee, but attached to the report neatly pasted on
sheets of paper of uniform size there were copies of all notices, announcements, invitations and programs and newspaper clippings all carefully
indexed. Reports in similar form were received from several other
Lodges; and in every instance the observance had been a notable success.
Mention is made of this because it is in our opinion extremely significant.

It indicates the probability that the attention and care with which the
report was prepared had been given to every detail of the arrangements;
and that this was responsible for the resulting success.
In both the cities last referred to it was the apparent apathy of the
people that constituted the "peculiar conditions." There was another city,
however, a very much smaller one it is true, where what was complained
of was not merely apathy, but actual opposition on the part of certain
people constituting a large proportion of the population. The Masons
there believed that they could not hold a successful public meeting and
requested permission of the Grand Master to hold a closed meeting in
their Lodge room. This request the Grand Master felt compelled to
refuse because it would not be carrying out the purpose of Public Schools
Week. It was pointed out to them that what was desired was a community meeting to which there could be no objection on the part of anyone.
A conference was arranged with a representative of our Committee, and ·
the entire situation was thoroughly discussed. Although the brethren were
somewhat dubious as to the result, they finally decided to make an effort
to hold a public meeting. A committee was appointed with the President
of the Chamber of Commerce as its chairman; and he suggested a program that gave promise of the success that was achieved.
The time set fo.r our observance happened to be also "Better Homes
Week", and the Committee very wisely, and properly, too, availed themselves of the opportunity for a joint observance. We say "properly"
because, as was pointed out by the Superintendent of Schools, "Every
thoughtful citizen will agree that our schools, churches and homes are so
closely connected in the service of the growing youth of America that it
would be almost impossible to celebrate one of these agencies of citizenship without doing honor to the efforts of the other two."
As one of the means adopted to awaken public interest, the Lodge
offered a cup as a prize to be given the school having the greatest number
of visitors in proportion to the enrollment. This cup was publicly displayed during the week and was awarded at the meeting. In announcing
the winner, the City Superintendent of Schools made the statement that
more interest in the public schools was shown during that one week
than had been thereto! ore manifested in the entire history of the city;
and that including the pupils, twenty-five per cent of the entire population
had been inside the schools within the past four and one-half days. In
concluding his report the Master of the Lodge said, "Our Public Schools
Week was a success far beyond our fondest hopes."
vVe have commented on the extraordinary amount of publicity that
was given us this year. There was one instance in which it was not
favorable; and the burden of the complaint was that the California
Masons were endeavoring to make the public schools their own peculiar

GRAND I,ODG.l<J OF CALIFORNIA

453

charge and were attempting to dictate the policies of public institutions.
The reasoning was not very logical ; because the Editor stated that the
people for whom he was presumably speaking "were quite prepared to
grant their Masonic fellow citizens every right to talk themselves blue in
the face on the subject of public school educational needs within the
privacy of their Lodge rooms." Now if we were doing that, there might
be some suspicion as to our motive. What we are really attempting to do,
however, is to make the public schools not the peculiar charge of the
Masonic Fraternity, but of all the people; and the public community
meeting is the most conclusive answer that could be made to the complaint
brought against us. We trust that notwithstanding his views, or perhaps
because of them, the writer of that editorial attended some of these
meetings. He would have been particularly interested, we think, in a
meeting held (quoting from the report) "Under the joint sponsorship of
the clubs, the fraternal orders, the clergy, both Protestant and Catholic,
the industries of the district, and a number of representative citizens,"
and where, "The platform guests included a minister, a priest, a bank
officer, the President of the Business Men's Association, a representative
from the three major industries of the district, a representative from
the Odd Fellows, the K. of P., the Woodmen and the Eastern Star."
That meeting, by the way, was held in a district in which the
observance extended over the entire week. The meetings were held on
Monday night. The addresses made outlined the object of Public Schools
Week and described what was being done by the schools in the district.
The parents and citizens generally were invited to visit the schools
during the week and attention was called to special events. These special
events consisted of a demonstration by the Sewing class on Tuesday,
open house and the serving of light refreshments by the Domestic
Science class on Wednesday, an exhibit of the work of the Manual
Training class on Thursday, and a Kindergarten exhibit on Friday,
especially arranged for parents who had children ready to start. Saturday
was boys' day and was given over to athletic events with a baseball game
between two schools.
There was one other observance to which we feel we must make
especial reference not merely to show .what can be accomplished by
persistent effort, but because it also furnishes evidence of the importance
of our Public Schools Week in the opinions of educators of national,
and international, prominence; and of their willingness to avail themselves of an opportunity that was presented to extend material aid and
assistance. In this instance a recital of the circumstances necessarily
involves the name of the Lodge.

With that idea in mind the Committee communicated with those in
charge of the program for the Conference; but to their dismay they
were informed that it would be impossible for them to secure Dr. Tigert
because all his time would be occupied with the official program and no
provision had been therein made for a visit to the island of Kauai. This
was a "facer." The Committee, however, was evidently composed of men
who not only knew what they wanted, but who were determined to leave
no effort untried to secure it. They immediately sought the co-operation
of the Educational Committee of the Chamber of Commerce, the Americanization Committee of the American Legion and the Kauai Educational
Association. In addition to this the Deputy Instructor of Public Instruction in Honolulu who happens to be a member of Kauai Lodge was urged
to make every effort to induce Dr. Tigert to make such changes in his
program as would enable him to take part in the observance at Kauai.
'When the situation was explained to Dr. Tigert, and he was fully
advised of the purpose of Public Schools Week, he promptly accepted
the invitation extended him, although it necessitated the cancellation of
three important engagements he had made in Honolulu. The troubles of
the committee, however, were not yet over. It was found that there was
no boat leaving for Kauai. This obstacle was overcome with the co-operation received from Governor Farrington through whom there was provided a warship on which Dr. Tigert was conveyed to Kauai. With him
there went Dr. W. H. Smith, Commissioner of Education of Australia,
and Dr. George E. Raiguel, Assistant to Secretary Work and one of the
delegates to the Educational Conference, escorted by Deputy Superintendent Long.
Addresses were made by all the visitors ; and in addition there were
various exhibits of high school students, of the Domestic Science and
Manual Training classes, and of the General and Commercial course.
The music was furnished by the Kauai Community Orchestra and a
women's community chorus. The Master reports, "We could not have
had a better meeting, and it was a grand success."
This with the other observances to which special reference has been
herein made should certainly convince everyone whose mind is open to
conviction that success or failure is largely a question of the work that
is done, and of the spirit in which it is undertaken. They are but a few
of the scores that might be cited.
This report would be incomplete without mention of the wholehearted co-operation that was received from all the co-ordinate bodies of
Masonry; and also, with one exception, from every allied organization

Public Schools Week is now a firmly established activity of Grand
Lodge. If there was ever any doubt of its success, that time has p~ssed.
Each year it is becoming better understood that the observance although
instituted and fostered by Grand Lodge is not a Masonic event, bttt a
community affair; and with a growing realization of this fact there
will come a corresponding increase in the support received from the
public at large as well as from the Craft.
It has meant, and of course will continue to mean, the expenditure of
considerable effort, and the incurring of trouble and bother. There are,
however, few things in this world really worth while that do not involve
some trouble and effort. The Master who is content to merely "get by,"
and who lacks the vision a leader should have, will naturally not welcome
our annual observance with very great enthusiasm; nor will the one who
believes that his full duty is performed in raising candidates and entertaining his members with whist parties and vaudeville shows. Fortunately,
however, these constitute a very small minority. The overwhelming
majority are earnest and sincere in their desire to be of real service to
their Lodges, and to have their Lodges serve the communities in which
they are located. They recognize the fact that the annual observance of
Public Schools \Veek furnishes them the best opportunity of the year;
and they eagerly avail themselves of it.
