MEETING PLACE FOR GRAND LODGE
To the M:.W:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee appointed for the purpose of surveying the situation
with reference to the facilities for the meeting of Grand Lodge in its
· annual communications, reports as follows :
Your committee has conferred and met with the Board of Directors
of the Masonic Temple Association of San Francisco, and has with all
the means in its power surveyed the general situation and condition of
our imposing Temple, has carefully studied the building plans thereof,
and procured the advice of competent architects and engineers with
reference thereto.
It is obvious to all that under present arrangements there is not any
place in the Masonic Temple adequate to comfortably or properly
accommodate the members of Grand Lodge. This present meeting place,
chosen under direction of the Grand Master, emphasizes that fact and
gives impetus to the necessity for some action to be taken for future
housing. The demands for a suitable meeting place will no doubt increase
with each succeeding communication, and any plans which are adopted
should look. well into the future.
Your committee finds that considerable expense must be incurred
to make such changes in the present Temple as will prepare it to meet
the demands of the Grand Lodge communications. Extensive structural
changes are necessary, and the details of these can be determined only
upon a more thorough survey by architects and engineers employed for
the purpose. Careful planning must be had, and we feel that a committee
should be appointed at this communication further to survey the entire
situation and to make definite report at the next session of Grand Lodge.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved, That the committee be continued, with two additional
members (making five), to be appointed by the Grand Master, to report
at the next annual communication plans for providing in the Masonic
Temple at San Francisco a suitable and adequate meeting place for
Grand Lodge; and be it further
Resolzoed, That the committee be and if is hereby authorized to
expend such money as may be necessary for this purpose, under the
direction and with the approval of the M:.W:.Grand Master.
0RRJN S. HENDERSON,
ARTHUR JOEL,

M. J. NEWBURG,

Report was adopted.

W. D. RICHARDS,
R. E. ALLAN.

DAVID WOLF.

The report was adopted, except that part relating to the
probable expenditure of funds, which was referred to the
Committees on Policy and General Purposes and Finance.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON REPORT OF
GRAND LECTURER
To the Jf:.W:.Grand Lodge of Califoniia:
Your committee to whom has been referred for consideration the
report of the Very \Vorshipful Grand Lecturer respectfully submits the
following:
\Ve congratulate the Grand Lecturer on his twentieth annual report.
Jt clearly indicates that time has not lessened his efforts in caring for
the ritualistic welfare of the Craft, yet it is significant to note that on
this his twentieth anniversary as our Grand Lecturer, he has sounded a
warning that we may well heed, to-wit:
"The ritual itself is but a means to the end, but not the end. \Ve
must obtain ritualistic interpretation as well as ritualistic instruction."
His report of the decline in the amount of degree work is, we believe,
something to rejoice over rather than to view with alarm, for it ap~ears
that it is resulting in greatly increased attendance at Lodge meetmgs,
and it is hoped that the opportunity thus afforded the members to become
better acquainted will result in impressing upon them that Masonry is
not a workshop, but an Institution for the practical application of our
avowed virtues of brotherly love, belief and truth.
His suggestions in relation to the selection of officers is most timely
and important, and we commend to all Masters and prospective Masters
a careful study thereof, with the firm belief that a compliance therewi~
will be greatly beneficial to Masonry in general and the Lodges m
particular.
Finally, your committee expresses its appreciation to the Grand
Lecturer for the service he has rendered, and we are sure the era ft of
this Grand jurisdiction will long cherish his unfailing kindness and
courtesy and his devotion to duty and service.
DWIGHT

vV. STEPHENSON,

A. L. WELLS,
FRED G. MANARY.

GEORGE WASHINGTON NATIONAL MEMORIAL
Past Grand Master Boynton presented the following:
Resolved, That a per capita tax of 20 cents per year for a period
of four years be and is hereby levied upon the membership of this Grand
jurisdiction as a contribution to the George Washington National
Memorial Association, the same to be payable with other Grand Lodge
dues.

Referred to the Committees on Policy and General Purposes and Finance.

ORDER OF DE MOLA Y

tion; that Lodges may not lawfully contribute to or sponsor Chapters
of De Molay, but that individual Masons may and should encourage this
worthy organization for boys.

The Deputy Grand Master assumed the chair and the
Grand Master presented the following:

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes .

.\t the Annual Communication in 1922 Grand Lodge adopted a
resolution approving the ideals, aims and purposes of the Order of
De Molay, and requesting the members of the fraternity to lend their
moral and personal support to the Order.
In 1924 a resolution was presented in which reference was made
to the resolution adopted in 1922, and setting forth that under said
resolution twenty-four Lodges had sponsored Chapters of the Order,
the resolution concluding as follows: "Now, therefore, be it resolved
that the sponsoring of said Chapters already established or that may
hereafter be requested shall be deemed to be within the terms as said
resolution of 1922 and the legislative powers of the Lodge as set forth
in Section 77 of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of California."
This resolution was referred to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes.

The Committee reported that Grand Lodge should do no more than
had been done two years before; that "to legislate to the extent of directly
permitting the subordinate Lodges throughout the jurisdiction to sponsor
Chapters by Lodges such action would have the effect of committing
the Grand Lodge to a policy that it has never departed from. . . . .
That it is a matter which must rest with the individual members of the
craft." The Committee recommended that the resolution be not adopted
and Grand Lodge accepted this recommendation.
The Annual Message of Grand Master Crites referred to the matter
of sponsoring Chapters, stating that he had ruled that a Lodge did not
have authority to so sponsor, and when his attention had been called to
a case where a Chapter was being sponsored by a Lodge he had requested
the Inspector of the District to arrange for the Lodge to withdraw its
sponsorship. The Committee on Jurisprudence reported that "Upon the
question of subordinate Lodges sponsoring Chapters of the Order of the
De Malay it is unnecessary to add to the expressions of the Grand Master
in his Message."
I respectfully request that the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes present a report at this communication reaffirming and clarifying our policy with relation to the Order of De Molay, so that all may
know that the Order of De Molay is not a part of the Masonic Institu-

The Grand Master resumed the chair, and at 11 :45 o'clock
?rand Lodg~ was called off until 9 :30 o'clock Thursday morning, to permit the representatives and their families to visit the
Masonic Home at Decoto.

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred trial record
No. 548 from Maricopa Lodge, No. 434, beg leave to report as follows:
In this case the charge was preferred by the Junior \Varden of the
Lodge, by direction of the Master, and the trial was presided over by
the same Master who had ordered the charges to be preferred. Decision
No. 5 of M.".vV.".Grand Master Jones, interpreting Sec. 189 of the
Constitution as amended in 1926, holds that while charges when preferred by the Junior Warden by direction of the Master may be tried in
the same Lodge in which they are preferred, yet the Master who directed
the charges to be preferred cannot preside at such trial. The record shows
in this case that the Master presiding at the trial was the same Master
who ordered the Junior Warden to prefer the charges.
\Ve, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resofoed, That the judgment of the Trial Commission herein be, and
the same is hereby reversed, and the case remanded for a new trial.

Adopted.

your Committee the judgment of .the trial Lodge should be reversed

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

When we contemplate the long list of those who have served their
Lodges as Masters and who have passed away during the last year, we
are reminded of the outstanding activities of men in their several communities who have rendered a distinct contribution to the uplifting of
humanity irt good citizenship, friendly devotion and helpfulness to those
in need or distress. They leave behind them the fragrant memory of
the many virtues that adorned their lives. We feel compassion for their
loved ones and we regret the breaking of the golden link in the chain
of their fellowship. But may we not forget that this breaking is but
temporary and that in some future time that golden chain will be
reforged in a glorious common bond for all eternity.
"'What is it which alleviates and sanctifies toil, which renders men
strong, wise, patient, just, at once humble and aspiring, but the perpetual
vision of a better world, whose light shines through the darkness of
the present life?"
We, too, will join the departed brethren in "the glory of going on
and yet to be," and will experience that supreme consolation of the soul
vouchsafed unto us by the Great Architect of the Universe. In the
meantime, as the tide of human life sweeps onward, let us strive with
renewed ambition to accomplish the purpose of our brotherhood-service
to our fellowmen.
JOHN

D. SHENK,

A. PLUMB,
\V ALTER L. BERGER,
Committee.

PROPOSED STATUE TO GEORGE WASHINGTON
To the M:.w:.Graiid Lodge of California:
Whereas, Pursuant to a proclamation of the President of the United
States, the Governors of the forty-eight States of our Union have adopted
legislation authorizing the appointment of committees for the purpose
of commemorating the bi-centenary of the birth of our illustrious
brother, General George \Vashington, the Father of his Country; and
Whereas, Worshipful Brother George \Vashington has always been
regarded as our most illustrious American Mason, and the mention of
his name causes feelings of pride in the minds of all true Masons; and
Whereas, It is a regrettable fact that the great State of California
is the one State in the Union which has not commemorated the memory
of the illustrious Father of Our Country in the form of a statue, monument, or memorial in any public place in our State, and believing that it
is fitting and proper that some suitable memorial be erected in his
memory, be it
Resolved.• That the Grand Master be authorized and requested to
appoint a suitable committee to consider the best method of perpetuating
the memo~y of our illustrious brother and that said committee carefully
canvass the situation and report at the next Annual Communication of
this Grand Lodge.
HARRY L. Tooo.

Adopted.

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON POLICY AND
GENERAL PURPOSES
To the l\'1:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
With respect to the several matters referred to it, your Committee
on Policy and General Purposes respectfully reports as follows :

District Deputy Grand Masters and Deputy Grand Lecturers
I. At the Annual Communication of 1926 your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes recommended that consideration of the
matter of appointment of Deputy Grand Lecturers and District Deputy
Grand Masters be postponed until this Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge, which recommendation was adopted. The subject matter has
now been under consideration for another year, and your committee
has not altered its opinion and adheres to the recommendation made by
it to Grand Lodge at the Annual Communication of 1925. At that time
we reported to you that, in the opinion of your committee, the Inspectors
provided by our laws are performing, under the supervision of the Grand
Lecturer and subject to the orders of the Grand Master, an important
work in a splendid manner, and that it appeared to the committee that
no persuasive reason existed for curtailing the duties of the Inspectors
or for establishing a new group of Grand Lodge offices.
At the Annual Communication of 1922 your committee recommended
that the policy creating District Deputy Grand Masters and Deputy
Grand Lecturers be not adopted, and Grand Lodge rescinded its action,
taken in 1920, to adopt the policy of creating District Deputy Grand
Masters and Deputy Grand Lecturers.
\Ve are of the opinion that the most plausible argument in favor of
creating the new officers is to relieve the Grand Master of some of his
burdens. Because of the territorial extent of this Grand jurisdiction,
the large number of subordinate Lodges and the manifold activities of
the craft, the duties of the Grand Master are most onerous. He should
be in a position to delegate many visitorial, ceremonial and social duties
to others. By reason of the zeal and activities of our Grand Master, a
practice has grown up through the years of demanding of the Grand
Master that he personally perform many functions that overtax his time
and strength. This practice has operated to relegate the Deputy Grand
Master, and the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens to positions of comparative inactivity. This is wrong. These officers are distinguished
members of the craft, are held in high favor by their brethren, will each
in his turn become Grand Master, and should have an active participation
in the official work of Grand Lodge, not only at the Annual Communication but throughout the year. By availing himself of the services

of his fellow Grand officers, the Grand Master will find the relief that
some expected would be afforded by District Deputy Grand Masters. We
are also of opinion that the necessary expenses of these Grand officers,
incurred in the performance of duties assigned to them by the Grand
Master, should be provided for and paid by Grand Lodge.
Your Committee therefore recommends
(a) That the offices of District Grand Masters and Deputy Grand
Lecturers be not created.
(b) That Section 70 of the Constitution be so amended as to
provide for the payment by Grand Lodge of expenses of the Grand
Master, Deputy Grand Master, Senior Grand \Varden and Junior Grand

Degrees by Courtesy
7. The Grand Secretary presents the oft-recurring and troublesome
subject of degrees by courtesy. Your committee for several years has
been inclined to temporize with the problem, hoping for an improvement
in the situation and desiring to continue every possible courtesy to the
Lodges of other jurisdictions. Our hopes for improvement have not
been realized, and we fear that our efforts to be kind have not served
the best interests of Masonry.. It is a fact that in many instances requests
to have degrees conferred upon residents of California for Lodges of
other jurisdictions have been unreasonable.
At the last annual communication your committee asked that this
subject be postponed until the present communication in order to permit
a further study. Your committee feels that there is a definite inconsistency in expecting the Lodges of this jurisdiction to devote so much
time and effort in the conferring of degrees on men who thus become
members of a Lodge in a State in which they no longer reside. The
Grand Secretary rightly contends that those who make their homes here
and earnestly desire to become Master Masons should secure <limits or
waivers of jurisdiction from the old home Lodges and in due time regularly petition a Lodge near their new home for the remaining degrees.
That is the reasonable and practical thing to do, and it would be no
breach of courtesy for us to insist upon such a course.

Adopted.

Building Projects
11. Your committee is in entire accord with the Grand Master on
the subject of approval by or for Grand Lodge of all projects to erect
Masonic temples. He wisely states that the good name of the fraternity
is involved in the trying efforts of many Lodges to overcome the
difficulties of building projects which have been entered into with more
enthusiasm than good judgment, with more local fervor than calm
reflection. An ill advised temple project weakens a Lodge, diminishes
its usefulness, discourages its members, invites laxity in order to raise
money and reflects adversely against Masonry. It certainly is a better
plan to approach Grand Lodge regarding temple finances prior to the
assumption of a burden of debt rather than 'afterward.
This is a
delicate as well as a difficult subject, because Grand Lodge should not
unduly interfere with the !audible and zealous efforts of the memb10rs
of a Lodge to secure for themselves an adequate and suitable home.
Nor should Grand Lodge concern itself in the matter except to advise,

580

PROCEEDINGS OF THF
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

assist and protect the Lodge. It is the belief of your committee that
Lodges in this jurisdiction contemplating the erection of temples would
gladly welcome the advice and assistance of an experienced and impartial
committee representing this Grand Lodge. If the funds of the subordinate
Lodge are to be invested or hazarded, as the case may be, in a temple
project, certainly this Grand Lodge is an interested party and should
be consulted before the investment is made.
Your committee respectfully recommends
(a) That a committee consisting of the Grand Treasurer, the
Chairman of the Finance Committee, and a brother designated by the
Grand Master, be appointed a committee on Masonic building projects;
(b) That before a Lodge shall invest any of its funds in a Masonic
building project, there shall be submitted to said committee a full and
complete statement of the proposed plan of financing, the character and
cost of the proposed building, the extent of the participation of the Lodge
therein, and such other pertinent facts as shall be required by said committee, and there shall be secured from said committee, or a majority
of the members thereof, a written approval of such building project;
(c) That the Committee on Jurisprudence prepare and submit to
Grand Lodge appropriate legislation to carry these recommendations into
effect.

Payment of Expenses of Inspectors
12. The Masters' and Wardens' Association of Los Angeles
proposes that Section 56 of the Constitution be amended to provide for
the payment by Grand Lodge of the expenses of an Inspector incurred
in performing the duties of visitation, etc., instead of requiring such
payment of the Lodge. It has been called to our attention that the
proposal is made because of an unusual situation in the cases of two
out of one hundred and five Inspectors.
In each of these cases the Inspector has a Lodge situated at a great
distance from his home, entailing a considerable expense for visitations,
which neither the Lodge nor the Inspector can reasonably be expected
to bear. Upon a suggestion being made to the Grand Master of the
circumstances of these cases, he undoubtedly will cause the Lodges in
question to be reimbursed by Grand Lodge for the unusual outlay. We
see no good reason for the proposed change in the law, and recommend
that the proposal be not adopted.

Report adopted.

Grand Lodge of Vienna
19. The petition of the Grand Lodge of Vienna asking for recognition was received in 1926 and consideration was postponed for purposes
of investigation until this Annual Communication.
VVe find the Grand Lodge of Vienna to be a regular Masonic
power, representing a substantial unity of Freemasonry in Austria, and
to be sovereign and independent in its authority and jurisdiction. The
Constitution and ritual are fundamentally based on the Ancient Charges
and Landmarks of Freemasonry. A belief in the Supreme Architect of
the Universe is required, the Bible is present on the altar, the three lesser
lights shine in the Lodges, the columns and ashlars are in evidence, the

583

division of Masonry into three degrees is observed, and the temple legend
is the basis of the ritual. Candidates for the degrees must be men above
the age of twenty-four years; the second degree is not conferred until
at least one year after initiation and the third degree not until two
years after initiation. Secrecy is required, and discussions of religion
and politics are excluded from the work.
Freemasonry in Austria has experienced many difficulties. The
first Lodge was organized in 1742, but the stern repressive measures
of Maria Theresa extinguished the Institution in her realm. Her son,
Francis Joseph II, was sympathetic and interested, and under his rule
Freemasonry had a brief period of security, which was soon destroyed
by political and military opposition. The Grand Lodge of Austria founded
in 1784 was dissolved by the government during the reign of Francis I,
and the Institution was interdicted until the close of the \N'orld War.
Since 1871 Austrian Lodges have existed in secret, but held their
meetings on the soil of Hungary near the Austrian frontier. These
Lodges enjoyed the protection of the Grand Lodge of Hungary. In
1914 there were fourteen such Lodges in existence. While initiations
and other Masonic work was done in Hungary, each Lodge had in
Austria a fraternal society of profane name for social, charitable and
cultural purposes. The first Austrian orphanage was founded by one
of these Lodges, and special benevolences were undertaken and carried
on by several of them.
In 1918 the fourteen Lodges above referred to, finding the age old
conditions in Austria to be ameliorated and altered by the breaking up
of the Empire, assembled to found the Grand Lodge of Vienna, to which
the Grand Lodge of Hungary issued a charter in January, 1919. The
new Grand Lodge has solidified Masonry in Austria and has attracted
to its membership many persons prominent in the social, political and
intellectual life of the country.
Grand Lodge now has jurisdiction over twenty-three Lodges, with
a membership of about sixteen hundred Masons. Brother Wollenberg,
Junior Grand vVarden, visited the offices of the Vienna Grand Lodge
during the spring of the present year and was received with charming
fraternal courtesy and hospitality.
This Grand Lodge enjoys fraternal relations with many of the
American Grand Lodges, and your committee is satisfied that it conforms
to all the requirements of our law on the subject of recognition, and
therefore recommend fraternal recog-nition of the "Grossloge von vVien"
of which Dr. Richard Schlesinger is Grand Master and Dr. vVladimir
Misar is Grand Secretary.

Adopted.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The National Grand Lodge of Egypt
20. Your committee has carefully considered the petition of the
National Grand Lodge of Egypt for recognition, and respectfully reports
as follows:
The National Grand Lodge of Egypt was organized about 1866 and
now has seventy Lodges and approximately seven thousand members.
Forty-five Lodges work in the Arabic language, fourteen in Greek and
four in English. The charities are represented by a General Fund of
Benevolence; a fund for aged invalid Masons; a widows' and orphans'
fund, and a special fund for the education of children of Freemasons.
Two orphanages are maintained in Cairo.
The work is divided into three degrees, a belief in God is required,
the Holy Bible is on the altar, with the other Great Lights, the Lodge
rooms are furnished with columns, ashlars and other equipment according
to the ideals of American Freemasonry, and the ritualism and practice
is based upon the fundamentals of the Ancient Landmarks and Charges.
Candidates must be men twenty-one years old or upwards. At least six
months must elapse between the conferring of degrees upon a candidate.
Your committee is satisfied that this Grand Lodge conforms to our
requirements for recognition, is recognized by England, Ireland, Scotland,
and forty-two other Grand jurisdictions, and therefore recommends
fraternal recognition of the National Grand Lodge of Egypt, of which
Prince Mohamed Ali is Grand Master and Abdel Meguid Younis is
Grand Secretary.

Your Committee on Jurisprudence has considered the decisions

Decisions of GTand Master
In Decision 1, (p. 15 of his Message) he correctly ruled that in
acting upon a petition for restoration of a brother who had been
suspended for non-payme11t of dues and who had neglected for a period
of more than two years to pay the same, a secret ballot on the part of
the members present is essential. and that it is improper to have the
Secretary on motion cast the ballot for the Lodge. (Sec. 119, Constitution, and Sec. 473, Decisions.) We recommend that the decision
be approved.

Adopted.
In Decision 2 he correctly decided that a Master Mason cannot
make application for membership in the Eastern Star within six months
after receiving the degree of Master Mason, without violating the
promise made by him in his application for the degree of Masonry to
the effect that he would not within such time petition for or receive any
degree or be initiated in any body, order, or organization, the prerequisite
of membership wherein is that a person be a Master Mason. (Sec. 245,
Constitution.)
We recommend that the decision be approved.

In Decision No. 3, the Grand Master correctly held that a Lodge
could not, in view of our written law, use its funds in the purchase of
any present for the retiring Master other than a Past Master's jewel.
The Constitution (Sections 88 and 89) is explicit as to the purposes
for which Lodge funds may and may not be used, and expressly limits
the power of the Lodge in the matter of a present to its retiring Master
in the way stated by the Grand Master.
We recommend that the decision be approved.

Adopted.
In Decision 4, the Grand Master correctly holds that a Mason
suspended simply for non-payment of dues may, within two years from
the date of his suspension, restore himself to full membership by complying with the provisions of Section 118 of the Constitution, entirely

regardless of considerations of his fitness to be a member. If guilty
of any Masonic offense he can be proceeded against only in the usual
way, namely, by charges preferred therefor.

In Decision 5, the Grand ~faster correctly held that the effect of
the repeal at the last Annual Communication of Regulation 410 was to
remove the disqualification of a Lodge to proceed with a trial of a
brother charged with un-Masonic conduct when charges were preferred
by the Junior \Varden under direction of the Master. The Master,
however, by reason of giving such direction, is disqualified from presiding at the trial, and any Past Master of this jurisdiction may be
designated by the Grand Master to act in the place of the Master.
(Section 200, Constitution.)
\Ve recommend that the decision be approved.

Adopted.
Decision 6: The Grand Master correctly held that it was improper
for a Lodge to provide for an annual appropriation from its social
fund of not less than two hundred dollars for twenty-five years, for
the purpose of creating a fund to be known as the Centennial Fund, to
be used for a centennial celebration twenty-five years hence, because
providing for a segregation of the funds of the Lodge not contemplated
by the Constitution and attempting to improperly bind the future membership of the Lodge. As was held in the previous ruling of this body,
quoted in the decision, the purpose of the 1921 amendment of Section
89 was to provide for a permanent refreshment fund "to be expended
at such times as the best interests of the Lodge required," and a Lodge
has no right to so tie up any portion of this fund that it may not be
expended by it at any time for such purpose (consistent with our laws)
as it may in its wisdom deem proper. It has been held that a Lodge
may not by resolution allocate a fixed portion of its revenue to a
particular purpose. (See 180a, Decisions and Regulations.) While we
think it is the established law that the amendment of 1921 of Section 89
did contemplate a separate permanent refreshment fund, we are likewise
satisfied that it was never intended that such fund should not be available at any time for expenditures for any purpose (consistent with our
law) that the Lodge deemed proper. This we think is the full effect
of the decision of the Grand Master.
We recommend that the decision be approved.

Adopted.

Physical Qualifications
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, referring to the portion of the
Grand Master's address relative to physical qualifications of applicants
for the degrees, feel that it is impracticable to attempt to define by our
law with any greater particularity than is already contained in Section
94 of our Constitution, what physical defects make an applicant in·
eligible, and believe that, subject to such general provisions, the matter
should be left to the subordinate Lodge to which the application is made.
The law, as now written. is simple and concise. The applicant must
have no defect that renders him "incapable of learning the art" and
he must be "physically able to conform substantially to what the several
degrees require of him." These are the only prohibitions prescribed by
our law, and these prohibitions are addressed to the Lodge. A Lodge
necessarily shall have a wide discretion in determining whether a candidate, all things considered, substantially measures up to this standard,
and to attempt to define with any greater particularity what defects
must exclude would result in technical rules that would embarrass rather
than assist, and flood the Grand Master with requests for rulings on
the question of eligibility of applicants. We frankly confess our inability
to prepare a provision "which will relieve the Grand Master of the burden
of defining to Masters of Lodges who are physically fit for the degrees
of ~fasonry."

The report was adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the M: .W: .Grand Lodye of California:
Your Committee on Charters has had under consideration the
petitions for charters of certain Lodges hereinafter named, for the
formation and opening of which dispensations were issued within the
past Masonic year.
In the report of this committee at the last Annual Communciation
there was enumerated the respective yearly gains in the number of
applicant Lodges during several preceding years. It was then found
that we had had an average of 27 new Lodges yearly, for five years,
on all of which the Committee on Charters had given approval and made
recommendatory reports to the Grand Lodge.
Some of our leading brethren have frankly stated that they think
we are starting too many Lodges. They called attention to the greatly
increased inflow of candidates and of Lodges that followed for several
years after the close of the great \Vorld \Var. They were alarmed
that from the adventitious prosperity then generally created, men of
lesser standards of worth had been enabled to pay the fees for the
degrees, resulting in a reversal, as they thought, of our fundamental aim
that quality was to be preferred over quantity.
It was inevitable that within ten years after the close of that great
struggle, and the violent economic upheaval that was incident to it,
there should be a sane settling and adjustment of financial standards;
and the present "return to normalcy" pleases Masons who had the view
that there were too many Lodges and perhaps too many members who
were not Masons at heart.
It is true that the Institution is not helped if in a rush of prosperity
many men who otherwise would not regard themselves as eligible, under
the urge of a greater temporary earning power, should in great numbers
stampede the doors of our Masonic Lodges. A reasonable prosperity
in any institution is always admirable, but Masonry is not organized
to be popularized as an institution.
Masonry never advertises for members; it even discourages the
acts of any of its own unthinking brethren when their over-laudatory
sentiments cause them to err in actions inducing outsiders to become
Masons. Any solicitation is altogether unmasonic. No man is ever
invited to become a Mason. He must himself ask to share in our great
privileges, and he must do this asking of his own free will and accord.
Other leading brethren argue for many new Lodges. They call
attentio11 to the great quantity of ritualistic work as disclosed by some
Lodges being obliged to confer more than one hundred and fifty different
degrees in one Masonic year. There are some Lodges that have facilities

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

591

for, and without departure from our ideals, may welcome that amount of
degree work. But if there were a greater number of Lodges, they say
that this burden would be reduced with corresponding benefit to all
the Lodges.
Observation discloses that in many instances the larger part of the
dispensation petitioners who start a new Lodge, are '.'.fasons from some
other grand jurisdiction. The starting of the new Lodges stimulates the
interest of such brethren; they are given some activity they did not
formerly enjoy; their former apathy is killed; and both they and
California Masonry are aided by the rekindling of their enthusiasm.
A Masonic Lodge is always a strong factor in encouraging moral
growth and civic development. Accordingly, it is your committee's
conviction that in every new community in our rapidly-growing State,
when once well established and circumstances permit, the local brethren
should see the necessity, and be enthusiastic with the need of starting
a movement for an application for a dispensation, so that nearly as
early in time as those other great moral agencies, the public school and
the church, there may be established also therein, a Masonic Lodge. In
the larger cities the need seems at present to be fairly well supplied.
The labors of the committee have been less this year than before,
so far as tl'te number of new Lodges is concerned. Only thirteen are
working under dispensation, .but there is no cause for alarm. There
is actually no less progress than before, for the net gain in members
(two more than last year) is 6897.
Two of the thirteen lodges do not now petition for a charter.
They will continue to work under dispensation and their cases will be
considered at the next Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge.
This was voluntary on their part, but the committee commends such a
course in all cases where the dispensation is issued only a limited time
before Grand Lodge convenes.
A dispensation
a right that otherwise would not exist. It is
of course not final, and the new lodge is under probation. The law
requires the Committee on Charters, when a petition for a charter is filed,
to make an examination of the "work and proceedings" of the new Lodge
(Sec. 75, Constitution). If it has been organized too recently to make
a favorable showing that it is actually a going concern (disregarding
here any question of proficiency of its Master and Wardens and the
care and accuracy of its Secretary, these being very important, of
course), or too recently to show that it is doing good Masonic work
in the reasonable quantity and with the harmony expected at its origin,
then .such Lodge should patiently remain under dispensation for another
Masonic year, even though our law does not define any definite period
of such probation.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In the other eleven cases, the committee is convinced of the high
standing of the representatives of the new Lodges and was pleased with
the prompt avouchment of the respective Inspectors that these lodges
were indeed worthy; had no debts; and had been conducted in due
Masonic manner. The dispensations, by-laws and books of record were
found to meet the requirements of the Constitution. Where minor
errors occurred showing a failure to comply with some of the provisions, on our request the corrections were legally and properly made
with cheerful compliance before the report of this committee was
formulated.
We are glad to welcome these eleven new lodges, having charter
members from California 67, and from outside jurisdictions 194; with
the 212 Master Masons they raised and the 173 affiliates; a total of
644 added to our rolls by their permanent accession to our great Masonic
family; and we recommend that charters be issued with the following

George Washington Memorial
Your committee has had under consideration that part of the Grand
Master's Address, having reference to his visit to Washington and his
investigation of the George Washington National Memorial now being
constructed by the Masons of the nation, together with his recommendations that tlie craft in California assume their share of the financing
of the enterprise.
The recommendations of the Gr<1nd Master are in accord with the
conclusions of the three previous Grand Masters; and also are in accord
with the previous recommendations of this Finance Committee.
It seems to your present committee that some plan should be adopted
by this Grand Lodge that will ultimately result in the payment by this
jurisdiction of its full share of this enterprise and also that whatever
plan of financing be adopted, that it should fall equally on all members
of the craft.
It also appears to your committee to be undesirable to attempt to
raise the funds by a drive among the membership, but that rather the
per capita assessment of the Lodges be raised by a proper resolution to
cover the amount required.
It also appears that California has so far paid approximately 20
per cent of its assessment, and as the entire amount should be paid not
later than January 1, 1932, it would mean there still remains about four
years to raise the remaining 80 per cent.
Your committee therefore recommends that the per capita tax on the
Lodges be increased 20 cents per member yearly for the coming four
years, ::Ind that when the amounts are paid in to the Grand Secretary,
that he be authorized to remit yearly the amount collected to the proper
authorities of the Memorial Association.

Alexandria Lodge, No. 531
Your committee has had under consideration the request of
Alexandria Lodge, No. 531, for $50.00 per month to assist it in caring
for a brother suffering from tuberculosis and who is being cared for
at an expense of $150.00 per month. The Lodge has shown by its financial statement that it can and will assist with $25.00 per month; a brother
of the afflicted promises $75.00 per month; and the Lodge requests this
Grand Lodge to pay the other $50.00. We commend Alexandria Lodge
for trying to give this brother the best medical care possible, but we
doubt theii; good judgment in taking him out of the San Francisco
hospital, which is free, and removing him to a sanatorium at an expense
of $150.00 per month, not having the requisite finances to do this. It
would be a dangerous precedent if this Grand Lodge would assume
matters of this kind, and there is no limit of cases which could not
be referred to it. We therefore recommend that this application be denied.

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
On motion, yesterday's reference of the Report of the
Board of Control to the incoming Grand Master was rescinded
and the Report adopted with the exception of recommendation
No. 8, requiring Lodges having concurrent jurisdiction to
become members of Iloards of Relief. The full Report is as
follows:
To the l>f: .W: .Grand Lodge of California:
Pursuant to the provisions of the legislation enacted by Grand Lodge
at the annual communication of 1926, and in accordance therewith, the
M:.W:.Grand Master appointed a Board of Control whose duties, as
prescribed in said legislation, included the control and supervision of
the activities of Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus now existing
or hereafter to be created under the authority of the Grand Lodge.
The members of the Board of Control received their commissions
in April, and as soon as possible thereafter held preliminary meetings
in San Francisco and in Los Angeles to organize and to outline the work
for the year.
Following the directions of Section 3 of the Act, the Board of
Control proceeded to have made a survey of all Boards of Relief and
Employment Bureaus, and to that end secured the services, at agreed
compensations, of Thomas & Moore, certified public accountants of
Los Angeles, and of Benjamin F. Garrett, certified public accountant
of San Francisco. To Thomas & Moore was assigned the audit and
survey of the Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus at Los Angeles,
San Diego, Long Beach, Pasadena and Bakersfield. To Benjamin F.
Garrett was assigned the audit and survey of the Boards of Relief and
Employment Bureaus of San Francisco, Oakland, San Jose, Sacramento,
Richmond and Fresno.
The reports of the public accountants covering in detail the financial
accounts, the operations and procedure of the respective Boards of
Relief and Employment Bureaus, were received in July. In addition
to the services of these certified public accountants, the Board of Control
secured, through the generous cooperation of the Hon. Walter G.
Mathewson, Commissioner of Labor of California, the services of Dr.
Louis Bloch, statistician and employment expert, who made a careful
and detailed survey of the Employment Bureau at Los Angeles. The
valuable services of Dr. Bloch were furnished without expense to this
Board of Control or of Grand Lodge.

San Francisco
All San Francisco Lodges contribute to the support of the Board,
having paid a per capita assessment of 25 cents for the year 1927 and
35 cents for the year 1926.
Two representatives from each lodge comprise the Board, which
holds meetings twice each month.
The paid employes are the Secretary, who received $300.00 salary
and $50.00 automobile allowance monthly, and the bookkeeper, who
received $150.00 ·monthly. Both devote their entire time to the business
of the Board. The Treasurer receives no compensation.

The amount of relief work handled by this Board is the largest,
with one exception, of any of the Boards now in existence, and its
records and methods are superior to all others. A good record of the
cases handled is maintained.

It is noted that with the single exception of Honolulu the Board
of Relief of San Francisco operates at a lower cost for overl;ead expense
and, on the other hand, disburses a larger percentage of its funds than
any other Board of Relief.

Arrangements have been made with undertakers whereby funerals
are provided at an expense of not more than $100.00 each, including the
cost of the grave. Also the services of physicians are secured gratis
for applicants who are unable to pay. Reduced rates are obtained at
several hospitals.
.

Oakland
This Board is supported by most of the Lodges of Oakland and
Berkeley. Alameda and Piedmont Lodges do not contribute. Three
Berkeley Lodges do not contribute, and several of the newer Lodges in
Oakland have not yet commenced contributing.

No automobile is provided by the Board.
Contributing lodges pay a per capita of four cents per month.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Masters and VV'ardens of the contributing Lodges constitute the
Board, which meets once a month.
The paid employes of the Board are the Secretary-Treasurer, who
receives $150.00 per month, and the Assistant Secretary, who is paid
$80.00 per month. Both are on a full-time basis. The Board provides
an automobile for the Secretary-Treasurer and defrays the expense of
operating it. We have the distinct impression that he does not find a
great deal of need for an automobile in transacting the business of
the Board. It appears that the Secretary himself does not drive the
car, but has a member of his family drive for him, and we therefore
recommend the elimination of this expense item.
Funerals are costing the Board $120.00 each at the present time,
exclusive of grave plots, which are being donated by Mountain View
cemetery.
In 1921-1922, funerals were obtained for $100.00 each; they later
rose to $140.00 each, and are now costing $120.00 each. The Assistant
Secretary is of the opinion that they could now be obtained for $100.00
if the matter were taken up properly with Oakland undertakers. The
experience of the San Francisco Board of Relief makes this appear
probable. The donation of grave plots by the cemetery is likely to be
withdrawn soon, as the space provided at no cost is nearly filled.
No definite arrangements have been made with physicians or hospitals
for free or part-free service. There are, however, two or three
physicians, members of the fraternity, who will serve when asked.

Sacramento
All Lodges contribute a per capita of three cents per month. Masters
and \Vardens of all the Lodges constitute the Board, which meets once
a month.
The Secretary serves for $30.00 per month and keeps the records
of the Board in his downtown business office. There is no automobile
expense for the Secretary.
An Employment Bureau is not operated, the Board of Relief doing
what it can in employment matters.
Funerals cost $100.00, plus $50.00 for burial plot and grave.
Grand Lodge carries fidelity insurance of $500.00 each on the
Secretary and Treasurer.

Your Board of Control believes that an expenditure of 21.1 per
cent of the total disbursement for relief, with an overhead of 68.9
per cent, does not justify the existence and operation of a Board of
Relief. Your Board, however, is not willing to recommend that this
Board be abolished, at least not for the present, and not until due time
has been allowed for the Fresno Board to correct this unequal and
impossible situation.

!!er Capita Assessnient: This is based upon the rate of 10 cents

Funerals: Originally funerals of Master Masons belonging to
Lodges outside of Los Angeles were conducted by the various Lodges in
·rotation, This duty gradually became a heavy burden on the Lodges,

608

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

I

funeral~/

as is evident from the fact that during the year 1925-26, 206
were conducted, and during the eleven months under review the numbet
was 199. Consequently it was determined by the members of the Board
of Relief as representatives of the local Lodges, that all funerals should
be conducted by the Board of Relief and that the Board should provide
Masons to attend such funerals. Previously, members of Lodges summoned to attend funerals had been privileged to furnish substitutes, or to
subscribe $1.00 for this purpose. By placing the conduct of funerals in
charge of the Board of Relief, all expense in connection therewith was
spread over the entire Masonic membership through the per capita
assessment. The Board furnishes fifteen members for each funeral
and allows them each the nominal fee of $1.00 for attendance. We
consider this a reasonable arrangement.

The report of the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles shows
certain items set forth as relief expenses not appearing in other reports.
The report, as submitted, gives a total of $35,541.71 as expenditure for
relief, and $14,951.94 as expenditures for operation or overhead, making a
total of $50,493.65. Calculating upon this basis, it appears that about
71 per cent was expended for relief and 29 per cent for overhead. But
included as reli'ef disbursements, there appear $1,500 loaned to the
Employment Bureau, $1,000.00 contributed to the Employment Bureau,
and $2,000.00 expended for a sea wall for the Masonic Home at Balboa.
These three items are of a different class of relief expenditures than
those of other Boards, and if they are eliminated and the calculation of
percentages made upon the same basis as a!l other Boards of Relief, it
will appear that about 66% per cent was expended for relief and 33¥.i
per cent for overhead.
The expenditure of the three sums referred to are not being criticised,
but it is just and fair to show percentages of overhead upon the same
basis 0£ calculation as is shown by the reports of other similar agencies.
\Ve also deem it proper to call attention to the method of conducting
funerals in Los Angeles, as it differs from the method adopted in other
places. The number of Board of Relief funerals in that city would seem
to Justify the custom, as they average about four such funerals each week,
or about 200 in a year. One set of officers officiates at all funerals,
and those who attend are paid a nominal sum for so doing. In this way,
it is claimed, a fair attendance is assured and proficient officers bring
favorable comment upon our services. Thus, the sum of $3,112.00 shown
by the report to have been paid for conducting funerals, is accounted

(Proceedings, 1926, pages 258,

"In the 1918 Proceedings, page 207, the Los Angeles Board
of Relief reported as fo!lows :
"'The Masonic fraternity of Los Angeles has had no satisfactory place for the burial of its dead until this year, when
arrangements were made with the Fo~es~ L_awn Memo.rial P~rk
to set aside a beautiful tract of land w1th111 its boundaries, wh1cp
will receive perpetual care and be for~ver kept_ greei;. This
tract of land is known as the Masomc Plot, m which only
Masons or members of their families will be interred. The ~ost
of these interments is considerably lower than can be obtamed
for a like situation in other cemeteries.'
"At the time these arrangements were made with the Forest
Lawn Memorial Park, a contract was entered into by the Masonic
Boo.rd of Relief of Los Angeles, to purchase 1000 graves, at
$19.00· each, paying therefor an installment of $1,900.00 annually.
Annual appropriations have been made by this Grand Lodge, 1918
to 1925, inclusive (eight years), or a total of $15,200.00.
"The Los Angeles Board of Relief has now come forward
and offered to pay the remaining two installments out of its
trust funds, thereby relieving the Grand Lodge from any further
appropriations on this account.
"In the 1922 Proceedings, page 276, your committee made
the following recommendation, which was adopted :
"'That the Board of Relief of Los Angeles keep a separate
account of all moneys received on account of the sale of said
graves· that all moneys so received be repaid to this Grand
Lodge by said Board; and that the Grand Secretary be annually
apprised of these facts and figures, so that proper record may
be kept.'
"We recommend that these instructions be strictly
adhered to."
Your Board of Control .reiterates this recommendation and here
indicates its purpose, if this recommendation be given approval, to have
a survey and audit made during the coming year to ascertain the exact
status of this matter.

of Relief to s~bmit to the Finance Committee of Grand Lodge their
re~uests for ren~bursements for financial relief distributed from their
relief funds durmg the year. Section 5 of the Board of Control Act
made a change in this procedure. Said section provides:
"Sec. 5. All applications from Boards of Relief or Employment
Bureaus or Lodges for funds for reimbursement shall be made to the
Boa~d of Control at least thirty days prior to each annual communication
of ?rand Lodge. '!'he Board shall make thorough investigation of the
ments of :uch applications and report its findings and recommendations
to the C~a1rman of the Finance Committee of Grand Lodge on or before
the openmg day of each annual communication.''

has forwarded to this Board the requests for reimbursement of the
s~veral. Boards .of Relief and the same have been given careful cons1deratwn and mvestigation, and the findings and recommendations of

From the survey of the Boards of Relief, a study of the official
reports of said Boards and the reports of the certified public accountants,
your Board of Control makes the following recommendations:
(I) Under the present procedure there is no uniformity in the
period covered by the reports of Boards of Relief. It is therefore
recommended that all Boards of Relief be required to report for the
same period and that this period coincide with the period in which
Lodges report to Grand Lodge, namely, for the year ending July 31st.
It is further recommended that reports of Boards of Relief must be
filed with the Board of Control on or before August 25th of each year.

It is further recommended that Boards of Relief be required to
submit at the close of each year ending July 31st and before August 25th,
uniform financial and statistical reports, and also requests for reimbursement on uniform blanks, which must be secured from the Grand Secretary. (Forms for said blanks are submitted herewith and are made a
part of this report.)
(2) Inasmuch as there is no uniformity in the forms of records
used by the .respective Boards of Relief, it is recommended that uniform
records for cash transactions be adopted showing segregations as follows :

Receipts
Relief Fund
Grand Lodge of California
Other Lodges in California
Other Lodges in United States
Lodges in Foreign jurisdictions

Individuals (if needed)

(3) It is recommended that each Board of Relief keep a ledger
record of each case of relief, with a card record for indexing and cross
reference. This record to contain a complete financial account with
the case and with the Lodge.
(4) It is recommended .that at the close of each year the Board
of Control be authorized to cause an audit and survey to be made of
each Board of Relief, and that the officer, who has charge of the boo~s
of said Board, be required to have his books in readiness for such audit
between July 31st and August 25th of each year.
It is further recommended that the expense of such audit be charged
to the respective Boards of Relief.
(5) It is recommended that a uniform code of By-Laws for Boards
of Relief be drafted and that the Board of Control be authorized to
draft such uniform code for such Boards, subject to the approval of the
Grand Master and Grand Lodge.
( 6) It is recommended that all Boards of Relief be required to
carry fidelity insurance and that said insurance be arranged for and
carried through Grand Lodge.
(7) It is recommended that all Boards of Relief be required to
carry Employers' Compensation Insurance in accordance with law.
(8) It is recommended that when Boards of Relief shall be
organized, or where Boards of Relief are already organized, all Lodges
holding concurrent jurisdiction be required to hold membership in such
Boards of Relief and contribute their per capita share of expense of
said Boards of Relief; provided that Lodges adjacent to said concurrent
jurisdictions may upon application unite with said Boards of Relief.
(Not adopted.)
(9) It is recommended that all Boards of Relief be placed upon
a business basis, and that the salaries of the officers of such Boards be
regulated according to the services performed.
"It is recommended that the Board of Control be empowered to
formulate a plan similar to that now in operation by the Masonic Relief
Association of the United States which will provide a central clearing
house of all relief cases and which will furnish to all Boards of Relief

of this jurisdiction a record of all applications for relief and relieI
applications granted, particularly of applicants ,who have imposed upon
or attempted to impose upon the Boards of Relief.

Comments
From the reports made by the accountants who surveyed and audited
the affairs and the accounts of the respective Boards' of Relief, we believe
that their financial records are being handled in good faith.
The
records of cash receipts and expenditures are reviewed by members of
the Boards from time to time. The Boards of Relief of San Francisco
and Los Angeles cause their financial accounts to be examined by a
public accountant annually.
Your Board of Control is satisfied that the Boards of Relief
through their Secretaries are giving their best efforts to the relief of
worthy needy Masons and relatives of Masons who are entitled to such
relief. California Masonic Lodges are peculiarly subject to calls for
relief and assistance, inasmuch as very many peopie, Masons and others,
eome to this State. Among these there are many Masons, hundreds
perhaps, who as time goes on find themselves in want and must appeal
to our Masonic Lodges for relief. And prompted by the true spirit
of brotherhood, characteristic of this State, where men are men and
Masons are Masons, relief is promptly extended. And while the Lodge
to which the needy brother belongs is directly responsible, our relief
is extended first and reimbursement is asked afterward. Many sister
jurisdictions of the United States seem to make no provision for the
relief of their needy and unfortunate brethren. With Lodge dues at
a ridiculously low figure, they can provide no funds for relief nor to
reimburse the Lodges of California which have granted such relief.
In our review of the requests for reimbursements from other jurisdictions
we find scores of cases where the Lodges in the sister jurisdiction have
rejected and denied the request for one flimsy excuse or another, and
in most cases have absolutely ignored and failed to reply to the request.
A case in point is that of our Athens Lodge, No. 228, at Davis, California,
which rendered aid and assistance to a needy brother in good standing
of Clebourne Lodge, .No. 115, of Texas, during his illness, and after
his death conducted his funeral and buried him at the expense of Athens
Lodge. The actual expense incurred amounted to $257.35. Upon being
notified of this expense, Clebourne Lodge refused to pay the claim,
but very magnanimously allowed the sum of $5.00 for flowers at the
funeral.
Another instance is that of our Oakland Board of Relief, which
incurred expense in caring for a stricken brother and his wife and
afterwards buried the brother. The Relief Association of Colorado
absolutely refused to reimburse the Oakland Board of Relief.

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Imposters and unqualified persons frequently attempt to impose
upon Lodges and Boards of Relief in California, and occasionally do
obtain funds from the Boards, but vigilant Secretaries are doing their
best to guard against these fraudulent efforts.
Your Board of Control believes that the lack of uniformity in the
procedure of Boards of Relief is due entirely to lack of regulatory
measures by Grand Lodge. It believes that the Boards of Relief and
the respective Secretaries are acting earnestly, consistently and conscientiously to administer relief to the sick and needy and unfortunate.
While procedure and methods may be standardized and regulated, charity
and relief cannot be. The cost of relief work in this jurisdiction is
very large indeed, but there is no criticism that the expenditures for
relief are not justified and worthy. \Ve desire to compliment the Boards
of Relief in general, but particularly do we commend the Boards of
Relief of San Francisco and Honolulu for the thoroughness of their
administration, as well as the economy of their service.
Your Board of Control is not fully satisfied as to the efficiency,
usefulness and necessity of the Boards of Relief at Fresno, Richmond,
Bakersfield and Pasadena. Fresno and Long Beach Boards of Relief
are without question out of line so far as the amount of relief extended
compares with the expense of overhead. It is within the province of
the Board of Control to recommend to the Grand Master that when
Boards of Relief are not functioning to the satisfaction of Grand Lodge,
that said Boards be abolished; but before making any such recommendations it is the desire of this Board of Control that every
opportunity be given to these respective Boards to adjust and reorganize
their business affairs, and every assistance and cooperation will be given
by the Board of Control to said Boards of Relief to accomplish this
purpose.

Employment Bureaus
There is an ever-increasing need for more cooperation on the part
of the Masters of industry who are members of the craft, and there
must, in many cases, be a charitable attitude on th~ part of the employer
for those brethren who are not physically able to measure up to their
ideas of the standard to be attained. Masons who are in charge of
employment and who are not willing to give preference to their Masonic
Brethren ought to be willing to give them an equal opportunity to apply
for positions, and should make use of the Masonic Employment Bureaus
and advise the Secretaries to send applicants for an interview.
In aid of the foregoing, we believe that there should be in each
Lodge one or more of the Brethren who would be willing to give a little
time for the benefit of our less fortunate brothers in becoming acquainted

Survey of Los Angeles Employment Bureau
In addition to the audit of the Employment Bureaus, it was deemed
advisable to make a physical survey of said Employment Bureaus to
determine the methods, effectiveness and the results of the operation of
the respective Employment Bureaus, and to that end the Board of Control
secured the services of Dr. Louis Bloch, employment expei:t and statistician of the State Department of Labor. His valuable services were
given to the Board of Control without expense to Grand Lodge.

I.

Joint Quarters
The Masonic Free Employment Bureau of Los Angeles is operated
in the same rooms as the Masonic Board of Relief. The entrance to the
Employment Bureau and to the Board of Relief is the same. In the
entrance corridor there is a switchboard attended by an "Information"
girl, who directs applicants either to the Employment Bureau or to the
Board of Relief, depending upon where the applicant desires to go.
We are of the opinion that the information girl and the switchboard
are of no value whatever to the Employment Bureau, and while the
switchboard may be useful in the operation of the Employment Bureau
and the Board of Relief in the same quarters, we feel certain that the
switchboard would be entirely unnecessary if the Board of Relief and
the Employment Bureau were operated in separate offices.
In allocating the cost of operating the Employment Bureau half of
the salary of the information girl operating the switchboard is' charged
to the Employment Bureau and the other half to the Board of Relief
i. e., the Employment Bureau is charged with $600.00 a year for the serv~
ices of the information girl at the switchboard.
We feel that it is detrimental to the interests of the proper
operation of the Employment Bureau to be located in the same offices
with th~ Board of Relief. While we realize that the two agencies can be
of service to each other, we nevertheless feel that the connection between
them should not be so close as it is at present. ·fhe Employment Bureau
should be operated on a businesslike basis, without any tinge of charity
attached to it. As it is, one cannot avoid the impression that the applicants for employment at the Bureau are men and women on the border
line of poverty, ready to apply for relief in the event of failure to secure
employment. We do not know to what extent unsuccessful applicants for
employment apply for relief, neither do we know how many persons
applying for relief are referred to the Employment Bureau; but we feel
certain that the operation of the two agencies in the same offices is an
influence detrimental to both of these agencies.

should be expected to patronize its Employment Bureau only if and when
the Employment Bureau can render efficient service. The Bureau should
have an adequate record showing how the employers patronizing the
Bureau are served. At present there is no such record whatever. We will
take up the matter of record keeping under the following heads:
(1) Applicants.
(2) Positions secured.
(3) Orders for help.
(1) Applfrants. Applications for work are received from males and
females. 'vVe are told that about forty per cent of the applicants are
females, but we have not checked this point. According to the report of
the Masonic Board of Relief and Employment Bureau for the period
from September 1, 1926, to August 31, 1927, the Employment Bureau
received 4,906 applications for jobs during the twelve months ended
August 31, 1927. There are approximately 308 working days a year,
which means that about sixteen applications a day are received in the
Employment Bureau. This should enable the present personnel of the
Bureau to handle the volume of business efficiently and to give good
service to both the employer and the applicant.
We are informed that of the 4,906 applications, about 90 per cent are
new applications, whereas 10 per cent represent renewals. No record has
been kept of renewals; so that no one can tell with certainty whether the
4,906 applications are from different persons.
The present system of filing applications does not enable one to tell
whether a certain individual has applied for a job once or more. For
instance, if you desire to ascertain whether John Doe has ever before
applied for a job at the Masonic Bureau, it would be impossible to tell,
as the records are kept at the present time, unless he applied for the job
recently. The applications are filed according to position applied for, and
are taken out of the files every three to four months. After they are taken
out of the files they are put away alphabtically and kept for two years,
and are then destroyed. When an applicant is sent to a job, his name is
entered in the Day Book showing where he was sent; for instance,
"Thomas Jones sent to the M. & F. Manufacturing Company," etc.
Entries are made in the Day Book every day showing the applicants sent
to positions. If, therefore, one wishes to know whether a certain applicant was sent to a position, jt is necessary to look through the Day Books
to find the man's or woman's name and the jobs to which they were sent.
There is no index to the books, and if the applicant was sent out sometime ago it is necessary to look through many books to find out where
and when he was placed.
The applicant's application card is simply marked "vVrkg," meaning
working; but the application card does not show whether he is working
through the efforts of the Employment Bureau or whether he got the job
himself:
The records of the Bureau should be able to show at a glance when
and where the applicant was sent to work and how many times he was
placed by the Employment Bureau. It is important for an efficient Employment Bureau to know whether a man can hold his job and how often
a man applies to the Bureau for a job. An adequate record of the number
of times the man has been placed by the Bureau is essential to the proper
handling of applicants.
(2) Positions Secured. The report of the Employment Bureau for
the year ended August 31, 1927, referred to above, shows that the Bureau
secured 2,982 positions in addition to 3,068 temporary positions lasting

628

.from one day to one week, making a total of 6,050 positions. (These
positions do not include temporary jobs given to persons attending
funerals.) \Ve do not hesitate to state that this number of positions is
.an overstatement of fact. \Vhen an applicant is referred to a job, the
Employment Bureau takes it for granted that the employer hired the
applicant unless the B11reau knows definitely that the applicant was not
hired. Even if an applicant is referred to a position which he refuses to
accept, it is considered a "position secured" on the theory that the Bureau
offered a job to the applicant. It is. of course, fallacious to assume that
'a position was filled because the applicant did not return, or the employer
did not call again. The Bureau can afford to take the time to ascertain
whether the applicant received the position to which he was referred and
to be able to tell definitely how m:J.ny persons were actually hired by the
employers. This inform:1tion is important not only from the standpoint
of accurate record keeping, but is also significant because it gives the
manager the necessary knowledge to gauge the effectiveness of his office.
( 3) Orders for H clp. Adequate records are not kept of orders for
help received from employers patronizing the Masonic Free Employment
Bureau. It is impossible to tell to what extent orders are received from
the same employers. In other words, the Employment Bureau does not
keep a record of its patrons. Mr. Purdy knows, "in his head," who are
the employers frequently applying for help, but there is no systematic
record kept of the patrons of the Bureau. \Ve think that this is a serious
mistake. It is impossible to conduct the business of the office efficiently
and intelligently without being able to tell whether the Bureau can
sustain the continued interest of employers in its service. The manager
of the Employment Bureau should be able to tell the "mortality rate" of
firms patronizing his Bureau. If a firm has been patronizing his Bureau,
let us say, for the period of a year, and then ceased to patronize it, that
fact is worth knowing.
The manager spends most of his time out in the field trying to get
jobs for applicants, but he does not keep an adequate record showing the
success of his interviews with employers. This failure to keep a systematic
tab on patrons of the Bureau is a grievous mistake and does not speak
well for the manner in which the Employment Bureau is operated.
If the Employment Bureau is able to fill an order by sending some
one to the job, the nature of the order as well as the name of the applicant is entered in a Day Book, but if the job is not filled, then the order
of the employer, which is first entered upon a loose slip of paper, is
thrown into the waste basket and no record at all is kept of that order.
This, of course, makes it impossible to judge the efficiency of the Bureau
from the standpoint of service to the employer. It is impossible to tell
how many men and women employers call for, and how many of these
jobs were filled.
When an employer calls up the Employment Bureau for a· worker
which the Bureau is unable to supply within the time required by the
employer, the order is not taken at all and the employer is told that the
Bureau cannot fill the order. In our opinion, this is a poor practice. If
an employer is told that his order cannot be filled, he will go to some
other employment agency where he will get his order filled; if he is told
that again, he is likely never to come back to the Bureau for help. It
would be far better for the Bureau to take the order and endeavor to fill
it through some other agency, such as the State Free Employment Bureau.
For example, let us assume that the employer wants a plumber to be sent
to him within an hour or two. If the Bureau is at present unable to fill

VI.

At the present time, it seems, the Masonic Employment Bureau has
no supervision other than that of the managers of the Bureau. In other
words, the managers supervise themselves. They have been associated
with it for nearly two decades. It would be most desirable if the Board
of Relief or some other agency were actively to supervise the operation
of the Bureau. It would be better still if some one person were charged
with the responsibility of taking an active interest in the Bureau and
watching its activities. The manager of the Bureau should be held responsible for the manner in which the service is operated and for its
growing usefulness to the community. He should make comparative
reports of progress. The reports should be made in a prescribed way
calculated to yield essential facts necessary to give an executive an adequate idea of the work and accomplishments of the Bureau.

OLIN

Summary of Recommendations

In the preceding paragraphs we have outlined certain recommendations for the improvement of the service of the Masonic Free Employment Bureau. These recommendations are:
1. That the Employment Bureau be moved to separate quarters,
apart from the offices of the Board of Relief, either in the same building,
or in another building.
2. That the name of the Bureau be changed to the Masonic Employment Service, thereby laying emphasis on Service rather than on Free.
3. That the services of the switchboard operator and information
girl be dispensed with, as not needed by the Employment Bureau.
4. That the manager of the Bureau take full and complete responsibility for the operation of the Bureau. There is no need for two managers in this office.
5. That an adequate and intelligent record-keeping system be instituted. Among other essential information, the records of the Employment Bureau should readily yield the following facts:
(a) How many times the same applicant applies for a position.
(b) When and where the applicant was placed.
(c) The difference between the number of persons referred to positions and the number actually placed.
(d) Positions lasting seven days or less, one month or less, and one
month and over.
(e) Number of persons wanted by employers and number of persons sent to employers, and number actually placed.
( £) Kinds of jobs offered by employers and kinds of jobs filled.
(g) The number, location and names of firms patronizing the Bureau,
and the turnover of such firms.
6. The Employment Bureau should be operated as though it were
run for profit, and the manager of the Bureau should be fully informed
of the costs of operating the Bureau. While it ought to be the object of
the Bureau to keep down the cost per placement and the total cost of
operating the Bureau, stress should be laid upon increased service both
to the employer and the applicant for employment. The number of do!-

Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
CORRESPONDENCE.
October, 1927
By JESSE M. WHITED

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
I herewith submit my Seventh Report as Chairman of the Com·
mittee on Correspondence. The views expressed under the various
subjects, as heretofore, are the individual ideas of the Chairman.
The topics embodied in the Report are those that present questions which have generally brought forth expressions of o.pinion or
action in the various Jurisdictions. There are others which might well
and properly be included, but lack of space prevents. Some of the
most important may be briefly outlined in the following paragraphs:
BIBLES: The practice of presenting Bibles to candidates haa
met with approval in a number of Jurisdictions, in some cases being
required by regulation. Whether it will have any particular eft'ect is a
question upon which there may be a dift'erence of opinion. If some
plan could be formulated that would induce a study of the Volume
of the Sacred Law the purpose might be obtained.
HIGHER DEGREES: We have always inclined to the belief
that the Masonic organization bears a close resemblance to our Public School system, and the "Higher Degrees" should bear the same
relations to the Blue Lodge that the University bears to the Common
School. The wish to join such organizations too often is from motives
other than a sincere desire for knowledge, both Masonic and otherwise.
HOMES: Whether Relief through the Home system, which
considered in its final analysis, is not making the Fraternity more
and more of a beneficiary society in the minds of the general public
and its members is a debatable question. We have never heard of a
Grand Lodge erecting a Masonic Home and afterwards abandoning
it, or failing to maintain it. Those who have not yet adopted s11Ch a
plan believe there is a closer touch and responsibility in disbursing

THE NATIONAL MASONIC TUBERCULOSIS SANATORIUM: Some twenty-six Grand Lodges and the General Grand
Chapter of the Eastern Star have appcinted members on the Board
of Governors. The matter is still in formative condition. The report
of the Secretary of the Association shows receipts of $12,956.62;
expenditures $10,029.12, balance on hand $2,927.50. Most of the funds
were spent for publicity purposes. The refusal of a number of Jurisdictions to become associated with the proposition is based upon the
following objections: (a) The large amount of money necessary to
perfect the plans, the bulk of which must come from Jurisdictions
now taking care of their own cases; (b) The Association being a
separate corporation might impose legal and financial obligations
upon a Member of the Association, which would prove dangerous;
(c) The advice of recognized hospitals and associations dealing with
tubercular cases is that generally it is better to treat patients in the
locality wherein they reside rather than concentrate them in any
particular section of the United States.
The Grand Master of Alabama expresses in the following words
an opinion that is worthy of serious consideration:
"It seel)ls to be the habit of Grand Masters to place their fingers
on the public pulse and then inform the Craft of the worst symptom
they think they can find. If I had to venture an opinion as to the
most discouraging one I find, it would not be the increase in murders, highway robberies, bootlegging, or crime in general. It would
be the disposition so prevalent and conspicuous everywhere to do
the least and poorest work for the most pay. The prevailing watchword is 'Get by.' Interest in an employer's business or pride in the
quality of one's own work is with a very large and increasing percentage of the people wholly lacking. The idea is to do just enough to
keep from getting fired. There is constantly increasing clamor for
shorter hours and fewer days work, not in order to give more time for
self-improvement but more time for idleness and joy-riding, and other
frivolities, not to say in many instances for dissipation and vice. The
experiences of mankind have crystallized into two aphorisms which
condemn utterly this indolent and shirking spirit. They are 'Idleness
is the devil's workshop' and 'There is no excellence without great
labor.' The man or nation that falls into idleness is going to fall
behind in the race of progress.
This slovenly, lazy, frivolous, or indifferent spirit just described
gets no encouragement from Masonry. Most of its symbols are implements of labor; its very name is a synonym of labor. It says
much for the beauty and dignity as well as utility of labor, but
nowhere has a word of approval for idleness or for a disposition to
slight one's work."
