ADVERTISING
We believe it was Barnum who said that "there was one bom
every minute." The average member of the Fraternity has faith in
our Institution; tell him that a thing is Masonic and in a large number of instances the statement is accepted as absolute truth. Rules,
regulations and edicts seem powerless to prevent designing persom
from "grafting" upon the Fraternity. Experience is an expensive
teacher and more so when a person purchases it at the cost of an
ideal. Pe!;haps experience plus education may in time assist in curbing this evil.
In a large number of cases it is due to the man who joined the
Fraternity to· see how much he could gain from a personal and com·
mercial standpoint. An endeavor to secure political, commercial or
social preference by reason of membership in. a Fraternity should
place the persons employing such a method outside the pale of Masonic respectability, if not subject him to regulation.
Alabama (1926):
(Gratid Master) : Brethren sometimes (no doubt unthoughtedly)
embarrass 'officials of Grand Lodge or of other Masonic bodies by
using the Masonic title of such officials in political or business advertising. This should never be done; no use of the fact that one is a
Mason or that he holds office in any Masonic body should ever be
made or referred to in any way that might generate a suspicion that
one's Masonic character or his official prominence as a Mason was
being used for either political or business purposes.
England (1926):
The Board of General Purposes deprecates "the exhibition in
public of Masonic certificates often shown on business premises for
what can be considered only trade purposes; and it urges brethren
generally to take every means to stop the use in connection with the
Craft with advertisement or appeal in any form which is for private
advertisement * * * ."
Ireland (1926):
(Grand Master) : Members of the Craft are strictly forbidden
to use the fact of their membership as a means of promoting business or of securing private advantage. They are forbidden to use
any of the emblems of Freemasonry on a sign or in any other way
on business premises, business correspondence paper, or in comaection with any business advertisement. ~ Masonic Certificate must
not be displayed or allowed to be displayed on business premises.
Any breach of this ruling will be considered as un-masonic conduct.

Not believing in Masonic advertising the Grand Master (Manitoba) asks that it be enacted that there are only two occasions when

Virginia:
(Grand Master): I regret having to repeat the warning uttered
before regarding Insurance Companies for Masons Only, and
wish to call the attention of the Craft to the fact that such
organizations are in no way identified with, nor have the endorsement of this Grand Lodge. The insurance may he as sound as
any, I cannot say that it is not, but do not get the idea that it
has any connection whatever with Masonry.
The Grand Lodge of Virginia does not endorse business
ventures of any character, nor does it lend its name or influence
to any commercial business of any kind. Section 139 of the
Methodical .Digest forbids this, and it is a violation of this section,
in my opinion, for a company of Masons to use the name Masonic
in connection with any business enterprise conducted solely for
pecuniary gain.
I fear some of the representatives of these companies in their
enthusiasm promote their own interests at the expense of Masonry,
and I feel that action should be taken to prevent or check as
far as possible, these tendencies to modernize or commercialize
Masonry.

ATTENDANCE
The great desire of the present day is amusement and until a
Lodge furnishes something more attractive to the average member
than the movie, the radio and automobile and other forms of enjoyment, the lack of attendance at meeting will continue. We cannot

help but think that too much importance is now being given to the
matter of ritual and the Lodge has ceased to be a place where a
brother can find recreation, companionship and enlightenment
To~ often meetings are not called on time, the evening is devoted
only to routine and ritual, with vacant seats resulting. An organization, to continue, must live in the present and not in the past. Those
that walk with their heads in the clouds also stub their toes. The
abridgment of the Ritual, less degree work and a smaller membership
in Lodges so the members could become acquainted, would assist in
solving this question.

New Zealand (1926):
(Grand Master): It appears that considerable difficulty is
found in keeping up the interest and activity of some of our

10

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

younger brethren, and this, when viewed in conjunction with what
I have just said, gives cause for serious thought. Many young
Masons, I am told, drop away, finding, as they say, monotony, and
even boredom. You may, perhaps, think that I overstate the case;
yet I am assured that many earnest and promising young Masons
find themselves disappointed in their aspirations and become slack
in their attendance.
I have no hesitation in saying that the fault must lie in our
system. We must somehow have failed to impress on our brethren
the fundamental object of Freemasonry, which I take to be the
moulding of characters, which will, by the force of their example
and their influence, spread a light in the world and draw mankind
closer together. We may have become too stereotyped in our
Lodge working, have devoted too much time to ceremonial, have
paid too much attention to the outside of the cup and platter, and
forgotten that it is to the heart that we must make our appeal. It
may be that in our lectures, papers, and addresses we have become
too abstruse and idealistic, and have neglected to point out the
practical application of our ideals. We have, perhaps, not spent
enough effort in teaching our brethren that while it is to the Lodge
that we come for inspiration, yet the real interest and use of our
Craft lies outside the Lodge, in our everyday life, in the happiness
that it brings us, and in the happiness that we can impart to
others; in the personal influence which we are enabled to wield
over our fellow men.
We who are older men, we on whom is laid the responsibility
of guiding and teaching our younger brethren, must be careful lest
in becoming absorbed ourselves in the beauty of our ritual, in the
fascination of the working of degrees and of research work, in
the interest which our position in the Craft gives us, we forget
the yearning of younger miflds to be something more than spectators and listeners. We must ever remember to lead them on to
the underlying meaning of what they see and hear, and to show
them that all is designed to teach how all day and every day in
their workaday lives we can be active Freemasons by ennobling
ourselves and helping and elevating others.

CLUBS
Any Club whether using the word "Masonic" or emblems designating it as such acting contrary to Masonic ideals is a menace. When
conducted along proper lines they should have encouragement and
support, for they are of great advantage, not only to the member
of a Jurisdiction, but also to unaffiliated brethren. We cannot subscribe to the idea that membership in a Masonic Club produces nonattendance at Lodge meetings or support of its work and activities.
In numerous cases the result has been exactly opposite and beneficial
to Masonry in general. When a Lodge provides a method for social
intercourse and hospitality the Club perhaps will go out of existence.
Where a Club or any other organization of a like character with
Masonry as a prerequisite follows practises not in keeping with the
ideals of the Fraternity there should be discipline of individuals
through their Blue Lodges, rather than by legislation to penalize all
for the acts of the unwise or unthinking.
Colorado (1926):
(Grand Master) : I feel that I would be false to my duty as Grand
Master, did I not call the attention of the Craft to the alarming·
growth of Masonic Clubs in our midst. It seems to be all the
rage, especially in the large populated centers, to organize clubs,
some of them with grotesque names, limiting their membership
to Masons only. These clubs are being organized, no doubt, with
good intent, but in most cases are making violent departures from
Masonic standards and usages for their amusement and pleasure,

Louisiana (1926):
(Grand Master): During the year the Masonic Drug Club of New
Orleans was organized. This matter was called to my attention
by one who thought that it was commercializing Freemasonry.
Upon investigation, I found that it was holding under the National
League of Masonic Clubs, that it was organized for social purposes
only and that there was no commercial element in it. I therefore
consider it in the same class with a Square and Compass Club,
the Salesman's Square and the Masonic Club of New Orleans, all
of which have received our approval.

Nebraska (1926):
(Chairman Corresponde11ce Committee) : Masonic clubs, in some

New York (1927):
(Grand Master) : The situation on . clubs remains practically unchanged and the warning issued by my predecessor was timely and
good. The social features of Freemasonry are an essential part of
the Masonic life and have long been recognized as such. Good
Masons }oined together in a club will not encroach upon the principles
of the Craft, since they know that the name Masonic belongs to the
Craft and to it alone. Moreover, their devotion to Masonry for its
own sake will move them to protect it at all times and prevent perversion, misunderstanding or misinterpretation of its laws, to which
we are all sworn to give obedience. Those of our membership who
would join other organizations called Masonic in order to gain the
right to do things un-Masonic are blind to the great Light and deaf
to the immutable principles so oft repeated. I admonish such that
Grand Lodge imposes the conditions of Lodge membership, and has
the inalienable right to enforce them.

I wish I could lay down a formula for clubs, or rather define
those which are good and those which are bad. 'Tis trite but trne,
that those whose activities help the Fraternity itself, its principles and
its work for mankind are good and should proceed with their work;
those that hinder, obstruct and even play false to the Fraternity
should be wiped out forever.

CO-ORDINATE BODIES
The co-ordinate Bodies appear generally to be functioning in
accordance with recognized Masonic standards and that they, perhaps, are not now "viewed with alarm" as in the past. They supply
a post-graduate course in Masonry to those who desire to take
advantage of it, and in many cases broaden the scope and meaning
of the Blue Ritual. We do not believe that, taken as a whole, they
have attempted to make Craft Masonry merely a recruiting ground,
and consider their own work as superior or greater thi\l.n that of the
Symbolic Lodge. There are, of course, exceptions.
The work of the Scottish Rite in Education, the Knights Templar
with their Educational Loan Fund, the Shrine with its Hospitals
for Crippled Children, the Eastern Star with their activities in the
various Homes now caring for convalescent and undernourished chil-

results .that are truly Masonic. The Mason who has the proper
viewpoint and realizes that his allegiance first, last and always in
things :Masonic is to the Grand Lodge of the Jurisdiction in which ~e
belongs. \There are always exceptions but these fortunately are m
the minority.

Massachusetts (1926):
(Grand Master) : The activities of external groupings of Masons, in
organizations which make membership in our Institution the basis of their
membership, have in recent years required, and have, in increasing
instances from year to year, been the subject of definitive action and
edicts by the Grand Masters and Grand Lodges of the several Grand
Jurisdictions of this country. On several occasions they have been
the subject of action in our own Jurisdiction.
This matter .is brought to attention at this time particularly
because of a further tendency which seems to he attaining some
vitality and which I believe to be due in no small measure to the
failure to understand and to appreciate the significance of the rules
of Masonic jurisprudence just quoted. I rdcr to an attitude which,

Masonry to keep such service headed in the right direction. It has
the power and can do it.

except upon the one subject of the Ku Klux Klan. Now we are not
of the membership of the Klan, but we are unwilling to say, as does
Brother Smort, that "a Mason cannot be a Mason and a member of
the Ku Klux Klan." This is a statement which no man may prove,
and as such ought never to be made. His explanation is, that
"Fraternity and Toleration" forbid that a man be a Mason, and at the
same time a "member of the Klan." Perhaps there are different
shades of opinion as to the meaning of Fraternity and Toleration, as
applied to the case of one who is a member of both bodies. Does
one necessarily surrender his right of free thought and action, solely
because he has become a member of either of these organizations?
And are there not instances bordering upon the lack of toleration,
upon certain printed Masonic records which some of us see occasionally, bearing not the slightest taint of the Klan?
As stated above, we don't belong to the Klan, don't have the
slightest desire to attempt to pin wings, or even bouquets, upon it;
but believe that Liberty, Equality, Fraternity, Toleration, Temperance, Consistency, should not be divorced.

CORRESPONDENCE COMMITTEE REPORTS
Perhaps the greatest work that any Committee on Education
could perform would be to evolve some plan whereby the Reports
of the Correspondents of the various Grand Lodges could be broadcasted to the members of their respective Jurisdictions. Touching
every phase of Masonry they reflect the opinions of men who have
given years of sacrifice and devoted service to the ideals and practical work of the Fraternity. While some Correspondents express
dogmatic ideas and are prone to judge others by standards applying
only to their own Jurisdictions, still these are exceptions. The
Reports of such men as Kies, Baird, Daniel, Block, Wilson, Ashley
A. Smith, McEwing, Gallagher, Cheney, Long, Allen, Humphrey,
Michie, Brockway, Harriman, Eggleston and Jenks, and a host of
others, deserve a better fate than to accumulate dust in a Grand
Lodge library.
Florida (1926):
(Chairman Correspondence Commitee): This report, as the writer
understands it, is mainly to acquaint the membership of the Craft in
Florida with the happenings in the Masonic world, and with the hope
that profit may come from the good examples presented and warnings
taken of the possible errors, confining this review largely to the
historical and to the jurisprudence, rather than to the literary gems
which so profusely abound.

New Zealand (1926):
(Board of General Pi,rposes): At the last Annual Communication
of Grand Lodge the following resolution was adopted: "That the
Board of General Purposes consider the question of including in the
Proceedings of Grand Lodge a review of the Proceedings of sister
Grand Lodges."
The Board has given very careful consideration to this questi?n,
a11d has come to the conclusion that the additional expenditure which
would be incurred would not be warranted at the present time. When
the discontinuance of the Summary of Foreign Correspondence was
decided upon in 1916, the Board reported that the saving would
amount to about £250, and at the present juncture, when the Lodges
are being earnestly appealed to to raise additional money on behalf of
our Annuity Fund, it does not appear an appropriate time to incur
additional expenditure upon what cannot be regarded as of great
utility. The Board therefore recommends that no action be taken
at present.

CRIMES
It is a matter of regret that part of the Proceedings of any Jurisdiction must deal with offenses against the laws of God and Man.
It is necessary however, that any organization must eliminate the
unworthy. To~ often there is a tendency to protect the individual
at the expense of the Fraternity. This may be due either to a spirit
of indifference or the "sob sister" attitude of the present time.
Unfortunately, the general public remember only the "horrible examples," forgetting the safe, sane and conservative citizens who make
up the body of Masonry.

Canada (1925):
(Grand Master): There is perhaps no more disturbing characteristic of the times in which we are passing than the evidences which
we constantly see of the prevalence of dishonesty in high places and
among those who are in positions of authority and trust, and I have
be.en greatly disappointed to find on the part of a number of our
Lodges a reluctance amounting almost to an unwillingness to deal
with those who have been accused and convicted of offences of a
serious and criminal nature. In one instance the unwillingness was
so pronounced that I finally took the case into my own hands and
suspended the offending Brother. The matter is too serious to b<'
passed over in silence. It is a very plausible argument for the Lodge
to say that the offending Brother is not a criminal at heart, that he
has simply made a mistake which will not be repeated, and that it is
not the part of Masonic charity to strike a man who is already down.
One can understand and appreciate the desire to assist one who has
fallen to rehabilitate himself; it is no more than our duty. But surely
the Lodge owes a duty to the Craft at large as well as to the offending
Brother. Masonry is not a thing of today only, or of this locality
alone. It is a great system and a world-wide organization. It is built
upon a foundation of mutual confidence and respect. Its usefulness,
its very existence depends upon the maintenance of a standard in
its membership, and upon the ability of a foreign Jurisdiction to receive
with confidence and safety those whom we permit to carry our credentials. And Canadian Masonry would soon forfeit the position it
now holds if, through a mistaken idea of our duties as Masons we

District of Columbia (1926):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Complaints of bootlegging and moonshining had been lodged against the officers in a
lodge by reputable members. (Query: \Vould those complaining
brethren be apt to make an equal exertion to bring an offending
relative to court for being drunk, or would they conceal that offender?)
Masonry borrows trouble whenever it steps outside its landmarks, as
it did in prohibition.
England (1926):
(Board of General Purposes): When the Licensing Act of 1902
was being passed through Parliament, an undertaking was given to
the then Home Secretary by the Grand Registrar (the late V.-.\V."
Brother John Strachan, K. C.) that the Masonic authorities would
condemn the practice of consuming any intoxicating liquor in Lodge,
or. on premises directly associated with a Lodge, in connection with
the ceremony of Installation. This undertaking was carried out in
instructions issued from Freemasons' Hall, with a direction for them
to be read at the next meeting of each Lodge; and the course thus
taken was approved by Grand Lodge on 3rd December, 1902. A
highly undesirable practice was thus for a time ended; but the Board
has had its attention drawn of late to a certain, though happily small,
amount of revival. It, therefore, re-affirms the course taken in 1902;
once more condemns the practice alluded to; and enjoins that neither
directly nor by any colourable evasion shall it be indulged in at any
period <luring the meeting of a Lodge when engaged in the Ceremony
of Installation. The Board expresses the wisj;t that the Master of.
every Lodge, in accordance with the hope endorsed by Grand Lodge
on 4th March, 1925. will cause this announcement-as the others now
made, all of them binding on each member of the Craft-to be by
him communicated at the next regular meeting.

DEMOLAY
The Order of DeMolay continues to receive the attention of
the Masonic world. Statistics for its year ending September 30,
1927, are not yet available, still the advance sheets show that there
has been a material gain, not only in the number of Chapters, but
in the membership itself.
The tendency to consider the Order of DeMolay as a Junior
Masonic organization or a Masonic Kindergarten or Preparatory
School is gradually dying out. Much has been written regarding
the DeMolay from the standpoint of the Mason.
That the reader may have the view of a DeMolay we quote
an article written by a member of the Order of DeMolay of Sunnyside Chapter of Portland, Oregon. While the article refers to the
Order of DeMolay, we believe that in the first paragraph he has
unconsciously set forth the "Spirit or Soul of Masonry."
"It's fine to meet a fellow Mason, isn't it? It's fine to go up
to a Mason knowing you're approaching a friend. It's splendid to

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

know here is one you can trust, and to think of the thousands of
men with whom you have something in common, with whom you
can meet on common ground. It's fine to think of the many Lodges
where you can find such fellowship-a fellowship nourished by the
teachings of a Master.
"It isn't difficult to imagine that a DeMolay, too, might appreciate such advantages, that he would appreciate meeting as a friend
one who would be a stranger if both hadn't seen that Ceremonial
of Honor, Clean Living, Reverence and Patriotism-The DeMolay
Initiation. Have you seen it? Maybe, too, he feels pride in his
organization of more than 150,000. Maybe he, too, is glad for
gathering places where he can meet the right sort of fellows, in
the right way, and under proper conditions. Maybe he, too, can be
influenced by this fellowship based on ideals of Virtue, Chivalry and
Manliness. But must you take my word that these are the ideals
of DeMolay, or are you close enough to know that such ideals
dominate the Order?
"Here we find a DeMolay illness with a possible Masonic cure.
Is Masonry close enough to The Order of DeMolay? Has Masonry
done enough in formulating plans for the Order, sponsoring its
rituals, and then saying, 'There you are. Go to it!' No, that isn't
enough. And why? Well, all boys aren't DeMolays, but all DeMolays
are boys. DeMolay boys must be taught by their elders those things
necessary to a useful life and to furtherance of Masonic teachings
if Society is to progress-just as the savage youth had to be taught
what to eat and wear in order to live. We aren't born with knowledge of life. We have to be taught that. Young fellows are
gathered here in DeMolay. What sort of knowledge are you going
to communicate to us, and who is going to teach it? True, the
purposes of The Order are pretty well defined by ritual and we
put on our own work. But, after all, human nature hasn't changed
much. Just as the savage youth needed someone with prestige to
point out just how he was being helped, showing him the finer
points of life, and helping him with the advice of experience, so
DeMolays need men to help them over the doubtful points, showing
by example the results of these ideals, showing by personal interest
that the work really is worth while. Masons are the men who have
this prestige among DeMolays. Nowhere, Masons, will you find
stronger support or more ardent champions.
"But what is the attitude of many Masons toward DeMolay?
Let me give an example. On the train returning from school, I met
a Mason, and soon he was telling me of the good teachings of
Masonry. In the course of the conversation I mentioned that I
was a DeMolay. He said, 'Yeh?' sort of dazed-like. 'Is your father

a Mason?' Never a word of encouragement for, or interest in The
Order-only visible indifference. I had just completed a history
course at school which included the reason for the origin of a
certain Order, high in Masonry. As I looked at this Mason's
emblem, I couldn't help thinking here was a Knight of The Temple
who wasn't seeking to guide pilgrims. This was not an exceptional
occurrence. It has happened many times, and with members of
different degrees of Masonry. Can a DeMolay be blamed for
wondering if the work of his Order is worth while when those
who have delved deeper into life present such indifference toward it?
"As I have said, Masons have the prestige to quiet such wondering. You have the prestige to firmly establish our belief in our
work. You are a potential energy which can guide the natural
instincts and the knowledge of an army of American youths along
lines conducive to the program and betterment of society. And
isn't work for the betterment of society a Masonic ideal-and duty?
Surely, from being Masons, you best of all can understand what
DeMolay may accomplish among its members. I can promise you,
and a talk with a DeMolay will convince you, that you have the
power to make DeMolay accomplish its objectives. And it need
not require .unreasonable effort or time; just attendance at meetings,
support of activities, not only in money but in person, a bit of
advice, and a lot of interest."

Illinois (1925):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : There are divergent, even
diametrically opposite views expressed by Grand Masters regarding the
Order of De Molay. Very likely the extremists on both sides of the
question are both not quite right. How far Lodges of Masons should take
part in organizing and sponsoring these chapters is the main point of
controversy. All agree that the chapters are valuable aids to the boys
interested. It would seem that with proper limitations Masons and
Masonic Lodges might properly and safely lend substantial as well as
moral support to these chapters. The question is, what are the proper
limitations? Time will surely clarify this problem.
Montana (1926):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : The Chairman of the
Correspondence Committee of Manitoba disagrees with the writer, who
suggested that the "Order of De Molay has passed inspection and is permitted to be sponsored by Masonry," by saying that "as far as Craft
Masonry is concerned no permission to sponsor has been given"; perhaps
not in Manitoba, but certainly in a large portion of the United States
Jurisdictions; there is "no such thing" as Craft Masonry granting anything; we must judge action of each separate Jurisdiction, and if we are

is an example; there is no set alike recognized by all Jurisdictions; what

Masonic bodies in the United States and is accorded a certain status.

if you feel it is that, to do anything and everything possible to shield our
boys and girls. It is my predi<;:tion that many of the great Masons of
the future will come from the boys who began their Lodge training in the
De Molay Chapters under the sheltering wing of Masonic Lodges.

DUAL MEMBERSHIP
We believe that the advantages of dual membership more than
counterbalance the objections. The argument that such a system
is in violation of one of the Landmarks has no historical basis.
The Mother Grand Lodge (England) has found it to work satisfa~­
torily, and in Massachusetts, the home of the first Grand Lodge m
the United States, it has been successful. The fact that New York
and some of the other older states have swung into line may aid
in having it favorably considered in other Jurisdictions.
California contains a large number of unaffiliated Masons, many
of whom hesitate to take their dimits from their "Mother Lod~e:•
more from sentiment than otherwise. If they could have the pr1v1lege of being other than mere visiting brothers to Lodges in our
Jurisdiction it should work for the benefit of the locality and the
Lodge wherein they reside.
Alabama (1926):
(Grand Master) : A brother holding membership in two .lodg~s in
Virginia obtained a dimit from one of them and present~d 1t ~1th a
petition for affiliation to an Alabama Lodge and was admitted st1U retaining his membership in the other Virginia lodge. Held,
1. Dual membersl;ip being permissible under the Masonic law of
many Grand Jurisdictions, including Virginia, there is nothing inherently wrong or un-Masonic in it.
Our edict No. 262 says that "a person can be a member of only one
Masonic Lodge." I construe this to mean only one Masonic Lodge in
Alabama. It is my opinion that this edict was adopted by our Grand
Lodge for administrative reasons only in order to avoid the difficulty, if
not impossibility, of maintaining accurate records of the number of
Masons in a Grand Jurisdiction where dual membership is allowed.

33

There is no way to terminate the brother's membership in his Alabama Lodge e.xcept to prefer charges against him and expel him. Surely
it cannot be a Masonic offense in Alabama for a brother to do in Virginia
a thing that is Masonically lawful there and which is not violative of
fundamental Masonic principles anywhere. Besides, an expulsion here,
if legal, would result in depriving him of the rights and privileges of
Masonry everywhere. The absurd consequence would be to deprive
him of Masonic standing in Virginia, as well as Alabama, for a thing
perfectly legal in Virginia. Such a doctrine would be violative of that
comity which should prevail among sister jurisdictions.
My decision is that the membership of the brother in both his
Alabama .and Virginia lodges is legal.
New York (1927):
(Grand M ~ter) : It is my purpose to call your attention only to
one or two outstanding features which the question presents.
First, single or exclusive membership is largely an American custom
and is not therefore a Landmark of the Craft. Some American Jurisdictions have used a plural system for many years, apparently with
good results: To adopt plural membership, therefore, would not be an
innovation in the body of Masonry.
Second, brethren coming from other Jurisdictions who may desire
membership in one of our Lodges must first make sure that their possible
affiliation with us will not be in violation of the laws of their home
Jurisdiction.
Third, he who would join Lodges other than his Mother Lodge, must
present his petition, which shall be the official form used by the Grand
Lodge of the State of New York, pass the ballot, and qualify in every
respect under the by-laws of the Lodge he would join and the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of the State of New York.
Fourth, after being duly elected, he would have the same rights and
privileges as any other member of the Lodge with which he becomes
connected.
The question may be argued both affirmatively and negatively, but
after all is said and done, the positive arguments seem to preponderate,
whereas the negative arguments are more or less technical and easily
overcome.

other jurisdictions.
Historically, the ban on plural membership is comparatively modern,
and orgi'nally members of the Fraternity were free to ally themselves
with any group of Masons at will. From time to time since membership has been limited by law to one Lodge, certain jurisdictions have
experimented with plural meml'crship and abandoned it. In 1876 South
Carolina abandoned it: in 1869 Texas abandoned it, because of the
alleged difficulty resulting from the collection of dues, and in 1888
Maryland investigated the subject and decided against it chiefly on the
basis of the objection to a member being the Master of more than one
Lodge at the same time, and the great power or influence that he might
exercise thereby due to his "greater wealth," which would enable him
to pay dues in more than one Lodge and the inability of his Brethren
to do likewise.
For many years plural membership has prevailed in England. According to M.' .w: .Melvin M. Johnson, Past Grand Master of Massachusetts, no prohibition against plural membership exists outside of
the United States, save by the Grand Lodges of Prince Edward Island
and New Brunswick; and it is permitted by Delaware, Massachusetts,
Rhode Island, Tennessee, Virginia and Wyoming.
The advantages of plural membership in our opinion exceed the disadvantages.
Many are the cases of Masons who, moving from their old home and
the neighborhood of their Lodge to a location, distant frequently, in
another State and Masonic jurisdiction, and desirous naturally of Masonic intercourse, discover a group in the neighborhood in which they
have established themselves with which they delight to foregather, but
find, as is natural and manly, embarrassment by reason of the fact that
they have no status, are merely guests and hesitate to wear out their welcome. \Vhether Masonic hospitality is all-extensive as distinguished from
normal human relations may be debatable, but we doubt it. We see no
reason why the Masonic relation should so transform the human creature
as to make him an unending and great welcomer of the visitor who pays
nothing, who bears no burdens, who takes no part in activities, who
has no status. And it seems self-evident that the lack of opportunity tc
bear burdens, assume responsibilities, to render service, and to take
active part in Masonic life inevitably sooner or later saps and kills
Masonic vitality. Indeed, we consider it axiomatic that upon activity,
responsibility, right and duty to perform service depend Masonic life,

ss grows m some measure from this cause.

revenue of Grand Lodge which is seriously necessary. The ordinary

Grand Lodge shall be amplified from such a source.
Rhode Island (1926):
(Jurisprudence Committee) : (Report adopted.) The proposed
amendment to Article VII, Section 16, is in no sense a change in the
meaning or intent of the section as at present worded. It has always
been understood by the Committee, and the language of the section
clearly justified the interpretation, that the privilege of dual membership under this section is one enjoyed only by Rhode Island Masons
in Rhode Island Lodges.
This Committee has for some time felt that the section should be redrawn, and to this end has given careful study to the entire question of
dual membership.
It has seemed to the Committee that. Grand Lodge is unduly restrictive
and perhaps selfish in confining the right of dual membership to its own
members and to its own l,odges. There are many estimable brethren,
members of Lodges in this Jurisdiction who, having removed from the
Jurisdiction, are desirous of becoming affiliated with Lodges located near
their homes. And there are many estimable brethren, members of Lodges
in other Jurisdictions, who have taken up their abode in our midst and
who are desirous of affiliating with our Lodges. It is most natural that
these brethren should be unwilling to sever their connections with the
Lodge in which they received the degree. It is equally natural that these
brethren should be diffident about seeking or accepting the hospitality of
Lodges to which they are denied the opportunity to contribute through
the usual channels.
It is, in our opinion, the part of wisdom and good judgment to permit
our members to continue and to increase their Masonic activity and
interest by 'affiliation with other Masonic Lodges, and it is altogether
unreasonable to require them to <limit before so doing from Lodges to
which they are bound by very strong sentimental ties.
Comparatively few men will avail themselves of the privilege of dual
membership under our present regulation. At least two, and possibly

REPORT GN C0RREi3PONDENCE

37

three new Lodges have, however, been made possible because of the
privilege so granted, And it is fair to presume that still greater benefits
will result from an extension of the privilege.
The Committee believes that it has further justification for its attitude
in the fact that there appears to be a growing tendency in America1;
jurisdictions to permit affiliation without insisting upon a dimit as a
prerequisite thereto.
We therefore present the following amendment and recommend its
adoption:
SECTION 16. No subordinate Lodge shall admit to membership
a brother made in any other Lodge, or confer the first degree
upon any person, except upon a clear ballot therefor at a regular
Communication. No subordinate Lodge shall permit a brother
admitted to membership to qualify himself as such until he shall
have presented a dimit from the Lodge of which he was a member or a certificate showing his good standing in the Lodge of
which he is a member, nor permit such a brother, if a member
of more than one Lodge, to qualify himself as such until he shall
have pr.esented either a demit or a certificate showing his good
standing in each Lodge of which he was or is a member. Involuntary loss of membership in any Lodge shall constitute loss of
membership in all Lodges.
Massachusetts (1926):

(Jurisprudence Committee) : If a brother who is a member of two
or more Lodges desires to withdraw from membership in one or some
b~t not i~ ~II of them, ~e is, of course, entitled so to withdraw provided he is 111 good standmg at the time of his withdrawal· and a certificate of his withdrawal from membership should be gi~en him. A
<limit is not an appropriate certificate in such cases. A certificate of
clearance is being prepared and when completed will be furnished to
all the Lodges to be issued to a brother who withdraws from membership in a Lodge when he is at the time in good standing in one or
more other Lodges.
. When a brother who is a member of another Grand Jurisdiction
which does not permit dual membership, applies to a Lodge in this
Jurisdiction for affiliation, our procedure heretofore has been such that
the applicant is informed of the law of the Grand Lodge to which
~e owes allegi~ce, with the result that, generally speaking, the applicatt~n has been withdrawn; and, if not, so far as I can discover, it has been
re1ected. I fear, however that our practice has been misunderstood and
that some feeling or opinion has existed that we ought not to entertain jurisdiction over a petition for affiliation from a brother from

38

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

another Grand Jurisdiction which does not permit dual membership. I
regret that any misunderstanding has existed, and am of opinion that
our practice ought to be such as to avoid any ground to feel that we
are unwilling to accord full recognition to the laws of Grand Lodges
with which we are on terms of fraternal intercourse.
The question is not one of the advisability or inadvisability of permitting dual or plural membership. Massachusetts has its law and its
practice which permit such membership, and feels that it has worked well
and is an advisable practice. But we freely recognize the undoubted
right of each Grand Jurisdiction to decide this question for itself and
we also recognize that full faith and credit .ought to be given in each
Grand Jurisdiction to the laws and decisions of other Grand Lodges,
acting within their territorial jurisdictions; indeed we require our
brethren to obey the law of any recognized Grand Lodge within which
they may reside and accord full credit to proceedings for discipline had
in other Jurisdictions against members of Massachusetts Lodges offending against the Constitutions or laws of such Grand Lodges.
If application for affiliation is made by a member of another Grand
Jurisdiction, communication should be had with the Grand Secretary.
If it is discovered upon inquiry, which will in all cases be made, that the
Jurisdiction of the applicant's membership does not permit dual membership, the petition for affiliation should be dismissed, and order will
issue to that effect.

Vermont ( 1927) :
(Jurisprudence Committee): The following amendment to the bylaws was proposed at the last session, to-wit:
"Re Dual or Plural Membership.
"Resolved, That Article 24 of the by-laws be amended by changing
the last sentence so as to read : 'Every Mason should belong to a
regular Lodge ; but a brother cannot be a member of more than one
Lodge in this Jurisdiction at the same time'."

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

39

This amendment in ef feet provides that a Mason may be a member
of a Lodge in this Jurisdiction and without a dimit or other transfer,
may also become a member of a Lodge in another Jurisdiction, while
retaining his membership in this. In effect this provides for daal
membership. The question of dual membership is an old one, permitted in some Jurisdictions and has been much discussed in this. Our
Grand Lodge has thus far refused to re1:ognize such dual membership,
and your Committee finds no sufficient grounds for changing that rule
or practice at this time. In our opinion dual membership would cause
more confusion and trouble than its advantage would warrant. We do
not think that a Mason should be permitted to double or increase his
right to charity or other Masonic privileges by joining different Lodges.
We see no more reason why a Mason should be permitted to be a
member of a Lodge in different Jurisdictions any more than he should
be permitted to be a member of different Lodges in this Jurisdiction. The
co_nfusion which would arise in case of Masonic offense, whereby he
nught be expelled in one Jurisdiction and stilt retain his membership
as a Mason in another, and all the confusion which would follow from
dual membership, we think, render it inadvisable that we should adopt
such pract!ce. We, therefore, recommend that the amendment be not
adopted.
DUES
Dues in many Lodges, perhaps not only this Jurisdiction but in
other States are too low, taking into consideration the increased cost
of ~ng. Membership in the Masonic Fraternity may properly be
comndered a luxury. Those who desire to avail themselves of it
shou~d. ~e .Perfectly willing to pay for it. Some one has suggested
that 1nitiat1on fees should be set aside as a reserve fund for benevolent purposes and the dues used for the maintenance and operation
of the Lodge itself. This plan might work to advantage.
Membership reports for the last year show a large number of
suspensions for non-payment of dues. The cause for this may be
on account of financial reasons, but perhaps it is more properly due
to the acceptance in the first instance of petitioners whose curiosity
has been satisfied, indifference, or failure to find that which they
sought. Perhaps a large number in the first class were not financially able to pay for it and the condition has continued.

In Maryland, there is no living Past Grand Master. Brother
Shyrock served as Grand :\1 aster for something like a quarter of a
century, and his successor, Warren S. Seipp, is likely to do the same.
This Brother Seipp is a most useful and valuable Mason. He gives us
most valuable thoughts sometimes. For instance, here is his epigram
as to uncollected dues:
There is no reason in my mind why a man should be over
two years in arrears. One year is a bill, two years is a burden,
and over two years, practically impossible. If he can pay and
won't pay, the law is dear. If he is unable to pay, charity is
recommended.
This is not far from correct. We believe that one of the greatest
problems before us in the Lodges at present, is the salvage of membership material which is almost if not entirely lost, and about to be
dropped by the non-payment of dues route. This is partly due to conditions after the big growth, and partly to the increases in dues which
are almost universal; and further, to the increasing demands on a
Mason's time for other matters, which serve to take his attention and
interest away from his Lodge.

Philippine Islands (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): There is an increasing
loss of membership in many Grand Jurisdictions through suspensions
for N. P. D. This is partly the result of the great influx of members
a few years ago when many unsuitable men were taken into the Fraternity. In some cases Masonry is regarded as a luxury, and, when
"hard times" come, the money for the payment of dues is lacking.
Those who have a real interest in the Fraternity will not remain suspended, but will eventually pay up and seek reinstatement. The unfit
should be kept out, if possible.

Wisconsin (1927):

that part of their new Masonic Home set apart for hospital purposes.

the storage shelves being kept at all times filled with choice homemade jellies, preserves and other dainties that would appeal to the
appetite of a sick person. The Eastern Star does not claim to be
Masonic and only asks the Masonic brethren to permit them to help
in the care of the needy and unfortunate. There is no standard by
which this kind of unselfish support and assistance can be measured.
And yet some Grand Lodges look with suspicion and distrust upon the
Eastern Star! We wonder if there is really any reason except that of
ignorance of its purposes and aims?

EDUCATION-MASONIC
The question of Masonic Education is present in all Jurisdictions. There is no doubt but there is a need for active and constructive work along this line. In some instances the Committees have
been disheartened by the lack of interest taken in their program.
There are two factors that cause this; first, has it been found what
is education along Masonic lines? and, second, will the average
Mason be interested in any program that has so far been given
them or that may hereafter be determined upon? It must be broad
· enough to include things particularly Masonic, but also in its relation to the ever-present questions of religion, political government,
economics, philanthropy, etc. This necessarily requires the expenditure of a large amount of money, voluntary service and leaders with
a vision. Too often after the first excitement the interest of the
Fraternity in general ceases. Time and growth gives strength to
all things and this may be the solution. The section of the report
of the Committee on Masonic Education of Wisconsin quoted under
this section expresses, we believe, the condition that generally prevails.
District of Columbia (1926):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : The report on educational
service to the Grand Lodge of Arizona is an admirable essay, full of
wisdom and fact, but it assumes, like the others on the subject, that
the brethren want to be educated. Seriously, we find very little in the

*

*

*

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): We beg leave to invite
attention to the prevailing subjects in the reviews. In almost every
report we find some action on Education. Nearly all, or probably all
of the writers of the correspondence reports know that it is difficult
to induce Masons to read and keep up with education. The esoteric
and monitorial lectures of the three symbolic degrees are so full and
complete that there is little left to be learned, and if we essay to
improve or amplify them we will find it as futile as an effort to improve
on the great paintings of the old masters. The members of the Lodges
know this and balk at so much oratory. Let us not dissemble, nor
cloak this, but try to find where we may educate.
It is within our grasp. We can find apt, eager pupils in the Sunday
Schools and in the graded public schools. The Jesuits find their pupils
in the parochial schools. Why not take their cue?
Ask a parochial school boy who was Benedict Arnold and he will
tell you lie was a traitor, a Freemason, a Protestant. He will tell you
the same of Aaron Burr; and of Captain Kidd, the pirate, and of
John Brown, of Ossawatamie, who precipitated the Civil War. But ask
a Sunday School boy who was Torquemado, or what of the Spanish
Inquisition, or the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew, or who were the
Albigenses, the Waldenses, the Lollards, or John Wycliffe, John Huss,
Savonarola, Martin Luther, Hugh Latimer, Giordano Bruno, or Lorenzo
Dow, and you will find he knows but little about these. The child's
mind is plastic. He retains what he learns. The writer believes we
could do more good by sending lecturers into the Sunday Schools and
graded public schools than into the Lodges.

The corollary consideration was the ~fasonic instruction, education,

North Dakota (1926):
(Committee on Masonic Service and Education): We again direct
the attention of lodge officers to the unquestioned importance of efficiency in Lodge organization and administration. Efficiency may be an
overworked word, just as service sometimes appears to be, but no other
word will do. We must have efficiency everywhere in this 20th century.
It is just as important in a "'.\fasonic Lodge as in a bank, a factory, or a
Rotary Club. \Vhy? Because we cannot command the unflagging
interest and the enthusiastic support of our membership unless that
membership feels that we have an objective in our Lodge and are making some progress toward it.
What must be the objectives of the successful Lodge?
(1) It must provide good, accurate and effective ritualistic work.
The impressive conferring of our degrees is essential.

47

(2) It must provide for the proper financing of all Lodge
activities, the planning and preparation of a balanced budget for a Lodge
is now imperative.
(3) It will take heed to the needs of Masonic Relief for the distressed worthy brother. The efficient Lodge will have a Relief Fund.
( 4) It must include a more definite and far-reaching program of
Masonic Education.
(5) It will take cognizance of the need of an adequate plan for
the social life of the Lodge.
(6) It will include a definite contribution to the life of the community through Masonic Service.
There may be other things which might be included but these we
feel are important. If we admit the value and importance of the above
then the whole question resolves itself into the attainment of the same.
How? By proper organization and effective administration. This means
that Lodge officers must take their election and appointment more
seriously. The mere holding of an office no longer can be tolerated;
too much is at stake. It should be incumbent upon every Master just
as soon as he is installed, to call his officers together, select the various
committees· and survey with care the Lodge situation, then formulate a
comprehensive plan including the several objectives of a Lodge and then
keep everlastingly working the plan. The Master must be efficient and
then demand efficiency all down the line. The time has gone by when
careless and haphazard methods will do. We earnestly solicit the consideration of these suggestions to the end that the same efficiency may
exist in a Masonic lodge as exists in any other worth while organization.

Virginia (1925):
(Grand Master) : Masonic education consists of at least four distinct branches, ritualistic, philosophic, symbolic and historic. All these
are of deep interest and l may say in a sense essential for an intelligent understanding of the principles of our Fraternity, but a thorough
knowledge of the ritual is a primal factor and of the first order of
importance. No Lodge can attain or hope to attain an air of dignity
without proficiency in the work of the ritual. This is, indeed, as
essential as a code of members of the legal profession or as tools of
the builders' trade to the practical mechanic. It is, therefore, an
imperative necessity that every officer of the Lodge should be thoroughly
equipped from this particular standpoint to perform the duties which
may without a moment's notice, devolve upon or be assigned to him.
Wisconsin (1926):
(Committee on Masonic Education): Modern Masonry is so occupied with initiating, passing, and raising of candidates-with mere
ritualism-that it has overlooked the more important and higher duty
of making real Masons. The novitiate is hurried through the degrees,
and turned out into the world, as a nominal Mason, with but a hazy
understanding of what it is all about, with no adequate knowledge of
Masonry, with little appreciation of his responsibility to the Fraternity
or to society at large. Barely does a candidate acquire any real understanding of Masonic truth while receiving the degrees. To continue
making Masons without giving them an intelligent knowledge of what
Masonry is, or what their responsibilities are, is little short of stupid.

It is a trite saying that "The Youth of Today is the Trustee of
Posterity." The interest of the Fraternity, both individually and
collectively, in the Public Schools is increasing and consistent and
steady work in this field of activity is one that cannot help but remedy
existing conditions. Some one has said that "when you open a school
you close a jail" and another "that the finest penal institution is but
a monument to misguided youth." Translating these into dollars
and cents, will perhaps appeal more to the average citizen than
slogans. The Superintendent of Public Instruction of California

EMBLEMS
The wearing of emblems, like anything else, can be and is, in
a nwnber of cases, carried to extremes. The member displaying the
lar'gest amount of Masonic jewelry is too often a Mason in name
only. Perhaps the English custom against advertising one's con-

nection with the Craft has advantages that are self-evident to one
who gives this matter serious consideration. They are commonly used
for making "a touch."
In the olden days the wearing of Ma.sonic regalia when appearing in public as a body was common. It still prevails in some Jurisdictions, both in and outside of the United States. Even where it
does, however, the tendency is to limit it as much as possible.

North Carolina (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): On page 137 of the pro'
ceedings of the Grand Lodge of England, we find the following as a
part of some amendments to law:
No Masonic jewel, medal, device, or emblem shall be worn
in the Grand Lodge or any subordinate lodge unless it appertains to or is consistent with those degrees which are recognised
and acknowledged by the Grand Lodge as part of pure and Antient Masonry, and has been approved by the Grand Master.
The language of this is not very specific. vVe do not know offhand. what "device" would be described as "consistent with" degrees
which are "recognized and acknowledged by" the Grand Lodge as "part
of pure and Antient Masonry." On its face, this looks like a prohibition of the use of such as we know as Shrine and Grotto jewelry in
all Lodge rooms. vVe know that English Masons do not use Masonic
jewelry outside of Lodge rooms at all. Therefore, this means that if
you belong to the Shrine, and are in England, you co~ld with propriety
use the Shrine Emblem, but none other, on the street ; but if you attended a Lodge, you would have to take it off and put on the emblem of
Symbolic Masonry.
Seriously, we cannot pick quarrels with either our own way of doing
these things, or that of our English brethren. Their taste tells them
not to wear any such jewelry, and they don't; not in England, or in
Australia, or in other parts of the Empire, though the custom is not so
rigid in parts of Canada. In America, it is customary, in so far as one's
sense of good taste suggests, to use lapel and watch chain jewelry.
Some of this is in exceedingly poor taste; some is big enough to flag
a freight-train; some Masons wear as much as the available spaces will
permit ; it is told on some that they are so proud of their honors that
they wear the jeweled emblems on their nightshirts (we have actually
seen this done by college frat men); but for the life of us, we cannot
see anything out of good taste in wearing attractive and tasteful jewelry
on street clothes. This is not worn with any attempt to commercialize
Masonry, not one time in a thousand where we have observed it; but
because, as the membership is an ornament to the man's life, so is the
jewelry to his habit. We know that the public wearing of emblematic
jewelry is fraught with some dangers to the fraternity, such as its use
by impostors, and its use by lawful members in compromising situations.
We have seen Masonic jewelry on the lapels and watch chains of men
in beastly intoxication; and the sight did not inspire us with added
respect for the Order.
Altogether, we are glad that less of such jewelry is being used.

FUNERALS
We hold to the idea that the Masonic funeral should be a
private rather than a public function. We do not go so far
as to say that the average Masonic funeral service produces a poor
impression upon the public, but in a large number of cases it does.
The ritual is given in a slipshod manner, there is lack of uniformity
in dress, a small attendance and generally the entire standard is
low.
If Lodge Officers could be brought to realize their shortcomings
and be persuaded to delegate the services to Past Masters or members who are particularly fitted to give a sympathetic and dignified
rendition of the Ritual, it would be a great improvement.
As long as it is a duty which we must perform, it should be
conducted in such a manner as will produce a deep and lasting im·
pression.
Kansas (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A member of their (Arizona) Grand Lodge known as w: .Brother Rev. J. Rockwood Jenkins, sub~
mitted a resolution to the effect that the present funeral service had
become "increasingly unsatisfactory"; that it was too long and contained many expressions not consistent with the .deeper principles of
Masonry and the truth of immortality and that it does not fulfill its
purpose in bringing consolation to the bereaved; also, that lodges are
even compelled to cut portions of the service and make changes in the

brother goes further and suggests that there was no necessity of regularly
opening and closing a Lodge of Master Masons to perform this service and after all this, he recommends that a committee be appointed to
revise the funeral service and report at the next Annual Communication.
To our absolute astonishment we find that the recommendation was
adopted and he was made chairman of such committee.

Utah (1926):

a suggestion might not be amiss. The brethren also ought to be

GENERAL GRAND LODGE
The possibility that there will be a General Grand Lodge is too
remote to receive serious consideration. The doctrine of "State
Rights" would prevent it. Such a thing might have been poasible
after the Revolution, but there the effort to form one came to nothing.
Even the suggestion that George Washington be made the first
General Gt-and Master was not sufficient to crystallize the idea.

the Grand Master has great hopes that much good may come from such a
council. We have grave doubts that the council will ultimately prove
advantageous and we. shall await with much interest further reports
from Michigan showing how the Grand Council really functions and in
what way it contributes to the we! fare of Masonry in the state. We
shall be glad to be convinced.
Iowa (1926):
(Grand Master) : My brethren, let me say that I am convinced that
no greater calamity could befall our Fraternity in the United States
than would result from the establishment of a General Grand Lodge.
The several Grand Lodges of the United States are now bound to·
gether by our ancient laws, customs, and landmarks. The most pleasant
relations exist among them. It is realized by the leaders of Masonry
that a general organization endowed with any power at all would inevitably lead to discord and strife and contention and dissatisfaction
and confusion. In fowa there are 86,000 Masons, 550 Lodges. Do we
need some super-organization to lead our footsteps aright, to dictate to us
the wording of our ritual, to force upon us laws and customs unfitted to
our experiences ?

Pennsylvania (1926):
(Grand Master) : Among the medals in Philadelphia Masonic
Museum is a George Washington General Grand Master Medal, presented by Mr. Zephaniah Wetzel through R. W. Past Grand Master,
Brother Samuel M. Goodyear. 1t was found among the debris of an
old house that was undergoing demolition. It is a good specimen of a
rare Masonic medal.
"This medal was struck at a time when there was a movement on
foot to establish a General Grand Lodge of Masons for the United
States, with Brother George Washington as the first General Grand
Master. It is not known when and where the medal was struck, but
in all probability it was done at the first United States Mint, established in Philadelphia in 1792. The metal is brass, and the obverse
shows the same pattern of bust as that of the Washington Cent of
1791. Not many were struck, and a specimen in fine condition is a
great rarity."
The Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania first suggested the General Grand
Lodge with Washington as General Grand Master, and although favorably considered by a number of other Jurisdictions, Washington declined
the honor which it was proposed to bestow upon him, so that while the
medal in commemoration of the event was struck, no General Grand
Lodge was instituted and Washington never was a General Grand
Master.
South Carolina (1926):
(Grand Master): We are indebted to our friend, J. Claude Keiper,
Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia, for
the original notice and resolution, copies of which are shown on the
inserts.
These documents are more than a hundred years old and prove that
. the idea of a General Grand Lodge is not a new one.
Experience has proven that our brethren legislated wisely at that
time.. I agree with the opinion then expressed that there is no necessity for a General Grand Lodge, although I am heartily in favor of a
common meeting place for the interchange of views as afforded the
Grand Lodges through the Masonic Service Association.
I am fully satisfied that our brethren may rest content that a
General Grand Lodge will not be established.

REPORT:
That they have seriously reflected on the important subject committed to their investigation ; that they have also derived much satisfactory information from the luminous and minute details of the various arguments which naturaHy suggest themselves from a careful
examination of the proposed establishment, contained in the reports of
many of the Committees of the Grand Lodges of other States : That
your Committee are sensibly impressed with the conviction that the
establishment of a Grand Lodge in each State, under whose jurisdiction, superintending care, and vigilance, the several subordinate Lodges
are placed and fostered, is amply sufficient for all the valuable and
interesting purposes of the Masonic Order. That as it does not appear
to your Committee any necessity exists for the establishment proposed,
in order to promote or advance the interests of the Craft; so, also,
would they deprecate even the possibility, if not the probability, of its
producing in any degree, however remote, the least injury to Masonry
generally, by its diversion of the parental vigilance of the State Grand
Lodges, towards the focus of the General Grand Lodge; by the impeding multiplication of its duties and concerns; by its alienation by distance, from the local concerns and character of the several si,bordinate
Lodges as well as the Grand Lodges themselves of the respective
States ; by its breaking in upon the funds of the several State Grand
Lodges, which could be applied so much more cheerfully to the endearing claims of charity; or in any other view, creating difficulty or disadvantage, to the present felicitous situation of the Masonic Order.
Your Committee, therefore, beg leave to recommend the following
resolutions:
Resolved, That the establishment of a General Grand Lodge of the
United States, and the calling of a Masonic Convention for the purpose of instituting and organizing the same, as proposed, is, in the
opinion of this Grand Lodge, unnecessary and unadvisable.
Resolved, That the Corresponding Grand Secretary be requested
to transmit copies of the foregoing Report and Resolution, to the
respective Grand Lodges throughout the United States, and a copy of

Wisconsin (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : The documents produced
by the Grand Master of South Carolina are more than one hundred
years old and prove that the idea of a General Grand Lodge is not a
new one. The incident mentioned is but one of no less than twelV'e
attempts that have been made from time to time to institute a General
Grand Lodge for the United States. Periodically some well meaning
brother (with more zeal than knowledge) is seized with a burning
desire to have such a central governing body. But when we consider
the different desires and ideals of the inhabitants of the different
states, the impracticability of having the supervision of the Lodges so
far removed from the governing body, and endeavor to figure out just
what sovereign powers the different Grand Lodges will surrender to
such a Genefal Grand Lodge, it is found that no agreement can be
had. For over seventy-five years no attempt in that line has been made
and no one acquainted with the situation seriously proposes such action
at the present time.

59

Those interested in this project still have faith that the lllatter
will be cacried to a successful conclusion. Raising the approximate
balance of two million dollars to finally complete it, and then a
million and a half endowment fund for its upkeep, is a task that will
require some work.
How much better would it have been if the money ahiea.dy sub·
scribed and to be raised could have been used to establish a National
University, along the lines outlined by Washington himself. The
problem might have been easier and it would have been a practical
Memorial.
We do object, however, to branding California and other Jw:itt·
dictions, who never formally agreed to the plan as "slacken.'' because
they have not contributed the dollar per member, as agreed UpOn lty
those who launched the project.

New Jersey (1926):
Brother Louis A. Watres, Past Grand Master of Pennsylvania and
President of the Washington Memorial Association, was introduced to
the Grand Lodge of New Jersey and said in part :
Now, let me point out to you a factor and feature of this movement which is worthwhile. When this movement was first begun it
was thought they would build a hundred thousand dollar monument to
the memory of Washington the Mason-a hundred thousand dollars, the
main purpose of which was to build a fire-proof building to house the
relics of Washington. When they got down to "brass tacks" and began
to see the importance of it, they said. "Why, that won't do," there are
a mi:llion five hundred thousand Masons in the United States to build
a monument to Washington, the Mason, for a hundred thousand do1·
lars t "It won't do." Forthwith they resolved to make it not less
than five hundred thousand, with an endowment fund of two hundred
and fifty thousand dollars, and as they progressed and as its significa11ee
presented· itself, they said that wouldn't do. "We will have to ha~

plans bigger than that." And they made plans for seven hundred and
fifty thousand dollars, because there were a million and a half Masons and
fifty cents a Mason would pay for it. It went along and in 1921 one
of our brothers from North Dakota moved that we have plans for a
building costing a million dollars. You see how it climbed and pretty
soon, as its far reach appeared they said, "No, we want a better building than a million dollars will produce," and they then made it a million
four hundred thousand, and after a while, a million eight hundred
thousand, and then, two million two hundred thousand. Why? Why,
because they had developed the great significance and the far reach of
this mighty movement, and as they saw that we were building a building
there which was to last for all time and that should carry the message

may look upon us as an ancient race, they said, "Why, two million· two

the same dollar per capita, and the Masons grew from a million and a

New York (1927):
(Grand Master): What is to be the ultimate cost of the Memorial?
I know that many of you have been asking that question. In order
to make sure what our Jurisdiction's pro rata financial obligation will
be I addressed a letter to President Louis A. W atres. In a reply
dated April 4th he said :
"The estimate of the architect for the completed building was
$3,200,000. These figures have been submitted and have been approved
The furnishing and equipment is put down at $800,000, which will
make a total of $4,000,000 (for building and grounds). As to the
equipment I am not prepared to express an opinion other than to say
that we must confine it to that figure. This of course would include
elevators, steam heat, electric lighting, power plants, etc. As to the
Endowment Fund, it is about like this : The estimate furnished by
experts as to the upkeep and maintenance amount to $40,000 a year.
We have felt and now feel that there should be an Endowment Fund of $1,500,000."
Adding the figures furnished by President Watres, we reach a
grand total of $5,500,000. It is indeed a "grand total," one worthy of
the Craft in this nation with its more than 16,000 Lodges and its
3,500,000 members. To carry our own just share, my brethren, we
must take up the working tools with increased vigor and prosecute
our task with untiring loyalty. Let us hereby dedicate ourselves to
that task now in order to make this the est year so far!

It seems that one hundred thousand dollars 1s being expended to
house these relics and that the balance of five million, four hunded
thousand dollars is being expended to represent the soul of Freemasonry and for a "Mecca." We will not say that the soul of Freemasonry is not worth the sum being expended, for we think otherwise,
but we do maintain that it could have been "expressed" for a much
smaller sum, and we could very well have got along without a
"Mecca." We want no Mecca and Freemasonry has had its soul
very well represented for a long time without any such expensive
memorial.
The entire cost originally was only to be one hundred thousand
dollars, while now it is thought that four million dollars will be
inadequate for its completion and that an additional endowment fund
of one and one-half million dollars must be provided for its upkeep.
_"Great oaks from little acorns grow." Who would have thought that
this little germ would have attained such gigantic proportions within
ten years?

GRAND LODGE
This is a day of big business and as a Grand Master of Oregon
once stated, the meeting of the Grand Lodge was an annual stockholders meeting and the members were but proxies for the stockholders of the corporation. The English custom of conducting routine
business through the Board of General Purposes and making its
Grand Lodge Communications a ratification of its actions with the
social and fraternal idea predominating has its advantages.

Georgia (1926):
(Grand };faster) : The charter of our Grand Lodge merely incorporates this body under the name and style of "The Grand Lodge of

North Carolina (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): It is interesting to note
the differences which prevail among the several Grand JurisdiCtions
about matters of various kinds. We know of one Grand Lodge in the
United States, whose official home was to be built, and the cornerstone thereof was laid with accompaniment of brass bands, Templar
escort, orator, etc., on a Sunday afternoon. That would not be permitted in the most of the other states. Another Grand Lodge does
not sanction the custom of Lodges of going to some church in town,
to hear there a sermon to the Masons, while the greater number of
them. approve it in some form or another. One Grand Lodge will not
permit a dollar of Lodge funds to be used for any purpose which is
not strictly Masonic; while we know of some good Lodges which provided funds to aid in the matter of the Confederate Memorial on
Stone Mountain. One will not permit Lodges to have any relation
whatever with the DeMolay Order, while others lend tacit approval, or
more; Some by edict prohibit their membership from being attached to
certam. other organizations which are in no wise related to Masonry,
as for mstance the Klan while others forego this opportunity. of giving
su~h free advertising to these organizations, and are none the worse for
this treatment of the "problem."
These remarks are occasioned by an act of the Grand Master of
the Grand Lodge of ·Saskatchewan, wherein he, on seeing that a certain
Lodge was about to debate in regular communication "the advisability
of opening an Eastern Star Lodge," had the Lodge instructed "that such
a question was not Masonic business and should not be brought before
the Lodge as such." And it is this same Grand Master who when the
mo?1ent for the closing of his annual address to Grand Lodge has
arrived, deems to be Masonic business appropriate for discussion in his
only. strictly formal Masonic message to the Craft, the subject of the
relatwn of employer and employee.

It may be unfortunate that in practically all of the Jurisdictions
the Grand Master serves for but a year. About the time that he has
gained the experience that makes him valuable he must relinquish
the reins of power.
Where the Grand Master serves two terms, his second year is
usually productive of greater good for the Fraternity by reason of
his first year's experience. Grand Masters generally regret that
through lack of time they have not been able to carry to a successful termination some of their ideals. Undoubtedly the petty duties
of the office and the details of administration. taken in connection
with the private affairs of the Grand Master himself, must cause him
to breathe a sigh of relief when his term is ended.
Kansas (1927):

attendance at the dedication of a Shriner's hospital. May we venture to

have been practiced for several hundred years. One might· ask whether
the participants are really Masons first or Shriners first. A proper respect for Ancient Craft Masonry would have prompted the p()wers that
be in the Shrine to have invited the Grand Lodge of Quebec to have
performed this ceremony.

The Duke of Connaught was elected Grand Master and proclaimed
as follows:
Be it known, that the Most High, Most Mighty, and Most Illustrious
Prince, Arthur William Patrick Albert, Duke of Connaught and Strathearn, Earl of Sussex, Knight of the Most Noble Order of the Garter,
Knight of the Most Ancient and Most Noble Order of the Thistle,
Knight of the Most Illustrious Order of St. Patrick, Great Master and
First and Principal Knight Grand Cross of the Most Honourable Order
of the Bath, Knight Grand Commander of the Most Exalted Order of
the Star of India, Knight Grand Cross of the Most Distinguished Order
of St. Michael and St. George, Knight Grand Commander of the Most
Eminent Order of the Indian Empire, Knight Grand Cross of the Royal
Victorian Order, Knight Grand Cross of the Most Excellent Order of
the British Empire, one of His Majesty's Most Honorable Privy Council,

Worshipful Grand Master of the United Fraternity of Ancient, Free and
Accepted Masons of England for the ensuing year, whom may the
Great Architect of the Universe long preserve.
Iowa (1926):
(Grand Master) : Here is something worthy of consideration. Often
Grand Masters complain because they are asked for opinions or advice
or decisions when the matters could have been handled by the Masters
making use of the Code. Says Grand Master Wellington: "I am of the
opinion that Worshipful Masters should be encouraged to consult the
Grand Master about all important matters both of law and policy.
It is much easier * * * to direct them aright in the first place than to
extricate their affairs after errors have been made."
Texas (1926):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Without the thought of
criticism of any specific item here, we feel impelled to give expression
to our own conviction that no surer means for the cheapening, if not the
absolute destruction, of a man's respect for the value of our Institution
could be employed than to thus reverse the order and have him feel that
he rather than Masonry is the bestower of honor. Of course, there are
cases of extreme emergency, but let all.men know of a truth that while
Masonry has existed without him or them during the years of majority,
they have lived under her very shadow, he or they in turn must not come
at a late hour expecting her to meet him bowing and scraping as though
to meet a dignitary long longed for. The higher the rank and standing,
the greater his disgust and our humiliation.

Utah (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): We regret it always when
a Grand Master enters the "confessional," as it were, with reference to
his own short comings, and in general terms proclaims to the world his
failure to measure up to the responsibilities of the station he occupies.
'Whatever the motive, such a course seems to reflect not only upon the
Grand Master, but also upon the Craft of the Jurisdiction who elected
him to the high station he occupies. No good end is served, and if all
be true that is said, under such circumstances-what, of it? It does not
concern the world at large, the brethren will cover all with a mantle of
charity because of their affection for their 'leader. In his first brief paragraph the Grand Master refers to "my weakness," and "my feeble way"
and "my limited ability."

Western Australia (1926):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : We have frequently questioned the wisdom of Grand Lodges changing the Grand Master yearly,
and of electing at the close of their Annual Communication a Grand
Master who does not meet Grand Lodge until he is going out of office.
It appears to us that in such cases, the Grand Master cannot exert the
same personal influence on the Craft as coould be done by a brother holding that office for a term of years, who would meet Grand Lodge on a
number of occasions and have a personal acquaintance with all his officers and a great many of the brethren. Something of this kind must
have been running through the mind of M. W. Bro. Strain (Kansas)
when he made use of the following remark :"Our Grand Master is installed in the closing hours, with no opportunity to speak to his field men of his plans to carry on, and goes out to
a leadership, the demands of which, if conscientiously construed,, are
almost beyond the possibility of any business man's life."
Wisconsin ( 1926) :
(Chairman Correspondence Committee); In Wisconsin it is customary for each Grand Master upon retiring from office to present his
portrait to the Grand Lodge. Most, but not all, of our Past Grand Masters have done so.

Instead of reporting decisions made by him, the Grand Master
(Georgia) simply announced that he had submitted to the chairman on

What is a reviewer to do if the rulings of the head of the Craft are reported in this fashion? It cuts out one of the most fertile fields for
criticism and comment.

The Alabama Grand Master's account of his official visitations is
one of the best we have ever found in Grand Masters' addresses· it
reads:'

"It has been my pleasure to visit a great many of our subordinate
Lodges, both by invitation and voluntarily, and at all times and in every
instance was received in the most cordial manner."
This tells all that is necessary to know, with commendable brevity.
Why extend it and particularize as to the Lodge and the date of the visit,
the work that was put on, with compliments as to its rendition and the
banquet served, etc., etc. Yet we have found Grand Masters in their
addresses giving page after page of such stuff, to the delight of the
printer.
GRAND MASTERS' CONFERENCE
The report of the Representative of the Grand Lodge of Arizona
at the last Grand Masters' Conference, held in Chicago in 1926, outlines some of the practical good that can be done through such meetings. If these Conferences could be extended to include not only
the Grand M_asters, but also Deputy Grand Masters, Grand Secretaries, Grand Treasurers, Educational Dir~ctors and perhaps the
Chairmen of Correspondence Committees, it .. would help produce
uniformity in matters that are often a source of annoyance and
cause differences between various Jurisdictions.
