The Deputy Grand Master of \Vest Australia was present as a
guest, being in the United States on his way to visit England. A
pleasing gentlemen, who said they have similar problems on the other
side of the globe.
The conference was presided over by Most Worshipful Brother
David D. King, Grand Master of Illinois, who extended the invitation
on behalf of his state, as did his predecessor in 1925. Brother C. C.
Hunt, the able and affable Grand Secretary of Iowa, was Secretary.
The meeting was held in the Hotel LaSalle and an excellent program of Grand Lodge problems was followed during the day, being
interrupted only by luncheon served in an adjoining room.
It is well that Grand Lodge officials meet for discussion. It is
just as necessary as that Masons should get together. This is especially
applicable to the junior officers.
The General Grand Lodge ghost could hardly be distinguished in
the <listance, though Grand Lodge officials must admit that among the
rank and file of the fraternity there is the eternal question of why
not a General Grand Lodge. It should never be and never will, but
the average brother can hardly understand why other organizations
function so · well nationally-including some Masonic bodies. The
Masonic Service Association is the happy medium between the two
positions.
Transfer of membership opened the program. Some recognized the
certificate plan as we do in Arizona between our own Lodges, but most
Grand Jurisdictions insist on an absolute <limit. This discussion resulted
in the only report of a committee and recommendation of the Grand
Masters, the purport of which was to suggest to the Jurisdictions that
insist on a <limit to give serious consideration to recognizing a certificate
from other Grand Jurisdictions so the Mason transferring membership
will not lose his standing in the event of rejection.
Dual membership has strong advocates in Massachusetts, Rhode
Island and Virginia, who follow England, where one Mason was a Past
Master of 23 Lodges. Others mostly frown upon the idea, assigning
reliable statistics being not available and penal jurisdiction as the
major objections. The most interesting side-light was that Manitoba
seemed to be turning from dual membership to single, as prevails in
most of the states.
Uniform receipt for dues, which is really very close to Arizona's.
is used in most Jurisdictions, but some good brothers wanted a different colored card each year like various national bodies use. Thought
seemed to be those who do not use uniform receipt for dues should get
in line with a majority of the Jurisdictions that do.

Collateral Groups of Masons and Their Activities. A great subject in this day of over organizations, but it was not discussed at any
great length. A few Lodges in the East had been raising funds by
gambling. County clubs as offshoots of Lodges, etc., were mentioned.
Many Jurisdictions prohibit the use of the word Masonic as in \:Visconsin and Arizona. In Michigan and Utah Organizations must submit
propositions of this nature to the Grand ~faster for approval. In
Nebraska the petitioner pledges himself not to join any organization
basing its membership on Masons, unless first recognized by that
Grand Lodge. Michigan has an edict preventing organizations using
as emblems the square and compass and letter G.
The next conference of Grand Masters will take place in Washington, D. C.. with some sessions within the George \Vashington
National Memorial itself in Virginia, in February, 1927, just prior or
subsequent to the meeting of the George 'Washington National Masonic
Memorial Association. Washington, D. C., was advocated as the
proper place to meet annually, but the thought seemed to crystallize on
other cities as well, especially more central locations to serve the
Mississippi Valley and Western States. From the inspiration the writer
feels he received from the only meeting of this nature he ever attended
and the consequent furtherance of his usefulness to this Grand Lodge,
even in any minor capacity, in the future, he most strongly urges the
representation of Arizona at the two sessions in Washington in
February.
Legal tangles galore of Masonic Jurisprudence arose in disrnssing:
"Conditions Relative to Applications from Persons Rejected, Suspended,
Expelled, etc." and "Uniformity of Legislation Relative to Applications
from Expelled Members." For instance, what is the Masonic standing
of a Mason expelled in one Grand Jurisdiction who years later petitions
a Lodge in another Grand Jurisdiction, stating the circumstances of
expulsion, is accepted and received the three deg·rees all over again?
That is, what is his particular status in Jurisdiction No. 1, which is in
fraternal relations with Jurisdiction No. 2. Echo seems to answer.
Such a case did occur, and quite similar ones have. As a collateral
discussion the matter of jurisdiction over rejected and expelled material
brought out the fact that but few Jurisdictions follow similar ideas. A
committee is to go into the subject with a view of first obtaining all
available information and making some recommendations as to uniformity for the Grand Lodges to consider.
The last subject was "Attitude Toward Institutional Activities.
Should Grand Lodges paricipate in Institutional Activities not controlled by Grand Lodge or support relief programs except those controlled and directed by Grand Lodges?" I suspect this was partially

aimed at the National Masonic Tuberculosis Sanitoria Association organiz:ed by the Grand Lodge of New Mexico. Some eastern Grand
Masters believe their Jurisdictions can not legally contribute to any
cause however worthy unless it is under the immediate control of its
own or a sister Grand Jurisdiction. Further, some think there are

Thus the session ended with the best of fraternal feeling of good
will among the leaders of the Craft.
Wisconsin (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master
(Utah, 1926) received an invitation to attend a conference of· Grand
Masters at Chicago, which he was unable to accept. He states, "I
feel that great good may be accomplished by such conferences and
sincerely hope that they may become an annual event, as they seem
to promise much good for the Craft." Well, the conference has been
held, but we have failed to learn of any good that was accomplished.
Why anyone should desire to make such useless gatherings an annual
affair we are at a loss to understand. No doubt a good time is enjoyed by all who attend, but that is all that can be said. They are
dangerous to the Craft, in that they carry with them the desire to
set up and establish a National Grand Lodge, which would mean that
each Grand Lodge would be compelled to surrender a portion of its
sovereign powers and prerogatives. Many such conferences have been
held in the past, but the results have always been unnoticeable.

HISTORY
Masonry is rich in historical events, not only in connection
with the Institution itself, but also in the formation of the United
States. Those Jurisdictions who have in their organization Grand
Historian or Historical Committee that function are performing a
real and valuable service. While Masonry is often given credit for
results that are not properly due to its labors as an organization,
still it is "interesting, even if not true."
Someone has said· that the hieroglyphical emblem "The Book
of Constitutions guarded by the Tyler's Sword," was conceived in
the thought of in "The Constitution of the United States, guarded by
the sword of Masonry."

District of Columbia (1926):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : The report of the Grand
Historian (Georgia) is a gem of education for the lay brethren. The
Church of Rome keeps its priesthood as well as the lay member on
feather edge all the time on church history, and in time they are saturated with it, while we have not given proper attention to this until
recently. Any parochial school boy can tell the names of bad Masons,
as Aaron Burr, Benedict Arnold, Robert Kidd et al., but our own
school boys know not of Guy Faux, Ravaillac, Torquemada, nor do
they know that the Pope blessed the poniards used in the massacre of
40,000 Protestants on the anniversary of St. Bartholomew. The history
of Freemasonl'y is almost without a blemish; the history of the Church
of Rome is a record of crime. At one time the Papacy was so low
that it was sold at auction; at another time three Popes claimed the
tiara, and one Pope was deposed for incest with his mother. Then
where is the Apostolic succession to link?

England (1927):
The original Grand Lodge of England was formed in 1717 by four
Lodges, of which three remain to the present time, viz., the Lodge of
Antiquity, No. 2, the Royal Somerset House and Inverness Lodge, No.
4, and the Fortitude and Old Cumberland Lodge, No. 12. The Committee has gratefully accepted the offer of these three old Lodges
to present the foundation stone for the new Central Home, thereby
forming a unique link beween the original Grand Lodge and the great
undertaking of the present.
Pennsylvania (1926):
Columbia Lodge No. 91, Philadelphia, held an extra meeting,
September 7, 1926, in Independence Hall, Philadelphia, in commemoration of the 125th anniversary of its Constitution, it being established
that the Lodge was constituted in that historic building.
On June 2, 1926 the Sojourners Club an organization whose
membership is composed of commissioned officers of the United States
Army, Navy and Marine Service who are Master Masons, erected a
tablet on the building now occupying the site of the Old Tun Tavern
in Water Street. This ancient hostelry was famous not only as the
meeting place of the first Grand Lodge in America, but also as the
place where the first Company of United States Marines was organ·
ized in 1786 by Captain Robert Mullin. The tablet is of bronze and
measures thirty-two inches by twenty-two inches and in addition to a
representation of the Old Tavern as it has come down to us by tradition and other appropriate Symbols it contains the following inscription:

On May ·31st, 1926, the opening day of the Sesqui-Centennial, the
Masonic Temple was thrown open to visitors. During the morning
and afternoon there were 6010 persons who visited the Library and
Museum. In the evening from 7 to 10 o'clock the number who passed
through was 6049. Long before the doors were thrown open the lines
formed outside and extended from the entrance throughout the building
without any mishap.
The total attendance during the week was 22,876.
Tennessee (1927):
The Historical Committee is collecting much valuable information.
Journeys were made to neighboring Jurisdictions. Tn the minutes of an
old Lodge reference was found to a Lodge of unknown origin known· as
North Fork Lodge No. 20. The committee believes that this old Lodge
may have been acting on a Revolutionary military warrant, or permit.
"Nay, more, it is logically conjectural that Brother Andrew Jackson, then but little past twenty-one, may have received the degrees in
this veteran Lodge, during the summer of 1788, while sojourning at
Jonesboro; where he was thrown into close contact with Brother John
Sevier, so recently governor of the Lost State of Franklin, and then
serving as clerk of the \Vashington county court; also with Brother
John Anderson and other craftsmen of those early days."

• • •

A very able and interesting address was delivered before Grand
Lodge of Tennessee by Brother Rev. Joseph Fort Newton. From his
address, we quote this interesting incident in this distinguished Mason's
life:
"Perhaps you will let me give you a brief sketch of a personal
background, which will explain why I am here, why I belong to any
Masonic Lodge, and why I have been trying to do something for
Masonry. During the war between the States a young Texas soldier
went into the army of the South. He was just a lad and he was
afraid that the war would be over before he got there, and after
he got there he was afraid it never would be over. He was made a
Mason, and was later made a prisoner, and escorted up the Mississippi
River to Rock Island. The Northern climate was very severe 011
Southern prisoners. This young man fell dangerously ill. He made
himself known as a :\fason to an officer of the prisoner, and that

officer was a real Master Mason. He took that young man to his
home and nursed him back to life. He loaned him money when the
war was over, and gave him a little pearl handle pistol to protect
himself ill the unsafe condition of his country.
That young man came back home and was made the Master of
his Lodge, and that young Southern soldier was my father. I. heard
that history as far back as I can remember, and you can readily see
that that made a very deep impression upon my heart."
Texas (1926):
A number of Masons applied to J. H. Holland, Grand Master
of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana, for a Dispensation, and Holland
Lodge U. D. was instituted and opened at Brazoria, on December 27th,
1835, but its existence was short, for in March, 1836, Brazoria was
abandoned, and the records, books and jewels, and everything belonging
to the Lodge were utterly destroyed by a detachment of the Mexican
army, under General Urrea. In the meantime, a charter had been
granted to them by the Grand Lodge of Louisiana, which was brought
to Texas by Brother John M. Allen, who delivered it and the ,other
papers to -Anson Jones, Worshipful Master of said Lodge, and our
first Most \Vorshipful Grand :Master. on the prairie near the battle
ground of San Jacinto, who carried it in his saddle-bags through the
battle of San Jacinto. This Lodge was not reopened at Brazoria, but
was opened at Houston in October, 1837, and is now known as Holland
Lodge No. 1, in this Grand Jurisdiction. It is interesting to know
that many of our pioneer brothers, and the charter under which they
were to work, participated in the battle that freed our land from
Mexican rule, and that General Sam Houston, who commanded the
Texas army, was afterward elected president of the convention that
organized the Grand Lodge of Texas.

Utah (1926):
(Chairman C orrespondencc Committee) : Brethren who assume the
role of teachers, in addresses and orations, continue to give currency to
utterly absurd, fantastic and unsupported theories concerning the beginnings of Craft history. And this is done, usually, without so much as
a suggestion of any qualification. This is inexcusable. We profess to
be seekers after Truth. Yet we propagate, or permit and applaud the
propagation of absolutely false and wholly misleading accounts of our
origin.
Why should any man, if in his right mind, assert that Masonry had
a beginning "coeval with the dawn of creation"? that it existed "before
the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy"?
Or why declare that it has teen fou1:d that Masonry was practiced in

rected by the Spirit of Revelation." He tells us that Satan made Cam a
"Master Mahan" so that he might slay his brother Abel and escape thr
consequences of his crime. (Gen. 5 :15-16, 35-37.)
But why disseminate such unmitigated nonsense ? There is ~o much
in our history, and symbolism, and philosophy, and rituals, that 1s beautiful, and sane, and elevating, that could be presented, why should we
have our intelligence insulted and our eyes filled with dust from the
stirring of such worthless rubbish!
If these irresponsible excursions into the "land of nowhere" concerned, or affected, only those who undertake them, the situation would
be different. But such is not the case. Often the atrocious caricatures
of Craft history referred to above, come from men who have been honored by the Fraternity, and who, presumably, are men of sound se~se
and wisdom, and who have given time to study, and research, and meditation, and hence their words carry weight with the inexperienced and
uninformed Mason. That is the pathetic, deplorable feature of the
situation.
Brethren of the Round Table, have we no responsibility in this
matter? \Vhy should we speak only "smooth things," and "prophesy
deceits" by our silence, when we meet with such burlesques of our
honorable Fraternity? Why not try the pillory, and make it so high
that Haman's "tree" would seem like a trellis for garden peas beside it?

Western Australia (1926):
Early Freemasonry in Ireland is shrouded in mystery, and how
long it existed before the Grand Lodge era no one knows, but ample
evidence is forthcoming to prove its great antiquity. An old brass
Square was discovered many years ago in. an ancient bridge in Limerick,
on which was inscribed a Masonic phrase, "I will strive to live with
love and care upon the level by the square," together with the date 1507.
There is a tablet on the walls of the Carrickfergus Church annm1nci11g
that the work was begun in 1614 by Thomas Paps, Freemason. There
are tombstones in Antrim erected to the memory of Freemasons and
dated as far back as 1626. Trinity College, Dublin, possesses two manuscripts, one dated 16i8, making it clear that the Fraternity was then
known to the College Students; the other, dated 1711, purports to be
a Masonic ritual and is said to be the earliest known of its kind.

brother on account of his action in this respect.

Manitoba (1926):
LEGISLATION
In Masonry, as in governmental affairs, the practise of enacting
a law to remedy conditions rather than appealing to common sense,
still continues. It is said that a Prime Minister of England when
urged to introduce a law under such circumstances made the very
sane reply: "Why pass a law? Let it try and work out its own
remedy."
Masons are enjoined to obey the moral and civil law and
any infraction of them is necessarily a Masonic offense. Duplication
by the Grand Lodge of existing laws is, we believe, a waste of
time. As has been aptly stated, "Within the confines of the Lodge
rooms we are Masons, outside we should be citizens only. If in
the outside sphere we live up to our Masonic teachings it will not
be necessary to do any broadcasting."

(Grand Master) : I trust you will exercise sparingly the function of
legislation. The present generation has a witless urge to make laws as
though a volume of printed matter, however bulky, could alter either
human nature or economic law. That the Craft is not free from this
mania to legislate is sufficiently apparent in the constant alteration in
the by-laws of Lodges submitted for approval.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The question is still before us: Can we find any subject on which this world-wide institution

of democracy'has been a Masonic Lodge, in the first two centuries of otir
organization. It has injured our feelings to watch the beginnings of a
slow, but sure, process of curtailment.

South Carolina (1926):
(Grand Master) : An effort is still being made to use Masonry to
support political ends, such as the creation of a new cabinet position
and the formation of a Federal Department of Education; but I am glad
to say it seems to be without effect in this jurisdiction. It is unfortunate
for any man to appeal to :Masons as such to endeavor to influence legislation, and it is sheer impertinence for anyone to urge legislation as
the representative of .'.\fasons, for no officer and even no Grand Lodge
can speak politically for any individual Mason. This is a fundamental
of Masonry and should not be ignored or forgotten.

LODGE OFFICERS
The worth of a Lodge, of course, depends upon the efficiency
not only of the Worshipful l'daster but every officer, both elective
and appointive. Whether it works for the good of a Lodge to continue brethren in an unbroken line from Steward to Worshipful
l'daster is a question. It often results in .a mere ritualist becoming
the l'daster. If the appointing power could be brought to realize
that in selecting the lower officers they are in reality choosing
future Worshipful Masters, they might be more mindful of their
responsibility.

Nevada (1926):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The doctrine in Masonry
is. against resignations during the term of office. An office may be
vacated by death or removal from the jurisdiction, but not by resignation. Brother Mackey firmly asserted that he could not see how resignations could be permitted if the ceremony of installation is properly
performed. Like everything else Masonic, however, in these days it is
growing to be another matter open to regulation in each jurisdiction. It
may be a prevailing custom that resignations of installed officers is unMasonic, but we have run across no ancient regulation or usage of general application to that effect. It seems that if there is no rule against it,
and the general requirements of the Craft have been complied with, that
no un-Masonic thing has been .done. If so, why a dispensation? Dispensations are useful only to set aside laws or to do things you have no right
to do otherwise.

Utah (1926):
(Grand ltfaster) : The suggestion has been made a number of times

In this connection may I say that it seems to me that the brotherly
custom that prevails in many if not all of our Lodges of advancing a
brother once appointed to the line as Junior Steward, each year during
good behavior and without the scrutiny of his qualifications as they would
have were he not in line, is all wrong. The elective officers of a Lodge,
as well as the appointive ones, should be chosen for their qualifications
successfully to govern the Lodge and to perform their respective functions in the Lodge.

MEMBERSHIP
The acquisition of members, whether due to the war or other
reasons, seems to have reached the peak. The gains during the
past year show a decline. As Grand Secretary Wilson of Nebraska
states, "This is the first time during the past 26 years that any
Jurisdiction in the United States has shown a net loss in membership. Three Jurisdictions have that distinction." Various causes
may have produced this result. In Masonry, as in a number of
other Fraternal organizations, other interests and other activities
have undoubtedly attracted the attention of those who otherwise
might have become members.

Wisconsin (1926):
(Grand Master) : We are not ambitious for an increasing number
of candidates for degrees. We are not zealous for the increasing size of
the fraternity, but we are extremely zealous for the increasing power;
influence and service of the fraternity.
You could walk into my delightful little city of Waukesha this afternoon and ask the first twenty citizens you meet to name for you twenty
outstanding citizens of our town. An overwhelming majority of the nien
named .would be members of the Masonic fraternity and probably active
members in one or more of the Masonic bodies. You can ask the same
twenty men or any other twenty men you meet to name the most important
community and service agencies in the city and I doubt seriously whether
one man out of the twenty will name the Masonic Lodge as being among
the agencies working for community uplift and community good. This
ought not to be. There are increasing numbers of the men who are
members ·of our Masonic fraternity throughout the state that are
constantly seeking membership in other clubs and organizations in order
that they may find a worthy channel through which to express their
community interests and their community service. It is a growing and
increasing conviction of mine that Masonry can better justify itself as
an organization for community inspiration, community uplift and community welfare than it can as a mere mill for the grinding of candidates
through the several degrees. Frankly, very frankly, you are familiar as
I am with Lodges of this Craft who initiate candidates through the
several degrees and wait longingly for months and even years, to greet
them again within the Lodge room. Why is this? There is a reason, and
that reason is to be found in no larger nor lesser fact than the failure to
provide for these men some friendly fellowship and some service
opportunity.

(Board of General Purposes): Controversy continues at intervals to

in some Lodges, purporting to be the opening in extenso of a Board of
Installed Masters, with signs and word,s peculiar thereto. When advice

in the precise terms adopted by his two immediate predecessors in office,

94

REPOHT ON CORHESPUNDENCE

V.'.W.'.Brother Col. Shadwell Clerke and R.'.\V.'.Brother Sir Edward
Letchworth, P.G.W., stating that this so-called ceremony is entirely
irregular, and was never recognized by Grand Lodge. It was adde~, in
this official document, that the ceremony formed no part of the ritual
authorized by the United Grand Lodge of England at the time of the
Union in 1813, or fourteen years later when the ceremony of installing
a Master was examined and considered by a Lodge or Board of Installed
Masters, warranted by the then M:.w:.Grand Master, H.R.H. the Duke
of Sussex, K. G., to examine and consider the ceremony in order to bring
about uniformity. The result of this examination and consideration
having been communicated to the Grand Master, the nature of the ceremony was approved by him, and afterwards imparted to Installed Masters
at meetings of that Lodge or Board until its warrant expired by effluxion
of time. Ever since that date, it has been made plain by successive Grand
Secretaries to all enquirers that no such Degree is known to, or recognized by, the United Grand Lodge of England as the Past Grand
Master's Degree, a Board of Installed Masters being defined as consisting
of three or more brethren who are either Masters or Past Masters of
Lodges.
As the question of the regularity of the prohibition of this ceremony,
which has never up to now been seriously challenged, has been again
brought forward, the Board desires to state that it is entirely in accord
with the policy in this regard pursued consistently for over a century,
and declares the practice of the ceremony in question to be irregular.

Western Australia (1926):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) ; Occasionally we read of
the degree of Past Master being conferred upon a M.M., and the question naturally arises "What is the status or right (if any) of such a
brother in relation to a Board of Installed M.asters ?" Grand Master
Reid (of Alberta) had to give a ruling in a case of this nature. Here is
the question submitted and the ruling given :"A brother who had received the Past Master's degree in a Royal
Arch Chapter and who was denied the right of being present while the
installed Master's degree was being conferred upon the W.)1. elect,
appealed to the Grand Master for his ruling thereon.

96

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

"Answer: A Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of
Alberta can recognize only those degrees which have been conferred by
Lodges under this jurisdiction or as is expressly provided for by our
constitution, by Lodges under some other Grand Jurisdiction recognized
by this Grand Jurisdiction. In no case will this Grand Jurisdiction admit
to participation in its degrees a person who has received such degrees in
a Royal Arch Chapter or in any other body conferring other than the
first three degrees of Masonry. There are other reasons which cannot
be fully explained, inherent in the degree of Installed Master, which
would not permit of a brother being present who was not either a Past
Master or one duly elected to that office. I, therefore, ruled that the
brother was not entitled to sit in Lodge while the Installed Master's
degree was being conferred."
This ruling was declared by the Committee on Grand Master's
Address as "sound and in accordance with our Constitution."

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Chairman of the

an.d said, "We have wondered just what induced them to pass the law.';

renounce Freemasonry and embrace her faith. Thereupon his portrait
:vas removed from the office of the Grand Secretary and the provision
1~ question was embo?ied in our Constitutien in order to make it impossible that the portrait of one who might prove unworthy should be
published, and there the regulation has stood ever since. We are not
defendihg the regulation, but simply accounting for it.

RELIGION
Masonry is not a Religion or a substitute therefor. Any attempt
to join the two will only be productive of trouble. We should have
no quarrel with the followers of any one of the 176 religions mentioned by Brother Baird of the District of Columbia. Man is by nature
intolerant or prejudiced when it comes to Creed. Masonry can perform no greater service than teaching its members to practice that
Virtue which is second to none, to-wit, TOLERATION.

Maine (1926):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): How bitter and decisive
bigotry can be in the hearts of otherwise good and noble men is seen
in the fact that a century and a half ago a little book appeared in England bearing the title. "An Old Fox Tarred and Feathered." It is interesting to read that the old fox was noble old John Wesley, and the man
who wrote the book was Toplady, the man who wrote:
"Rock of Ages, cleft for me,
Let me hide myself in thee."
Both men were followers and ministers of the gentle Galilean and
His Gospel, yet both carried their extreme sectarianism to the point of
bitterness and rancor against each other. It is safe to say that had both
men been touched by the genius of Freemasonry they could not have
carried such feelings and animosities against each other in their hearts.

*

*

There are, to be exact, 202 different denominational names; 202
different, often contradictory, versions of religion; we have been contentious, often it may be as bitter and bigoted as in the days of Wesley
and Toplady, about our special brand and trade-mark of it, while all the
time back of these 202 varieties and creedal labels there was only one
reli~ion, which sounds very much like what we as good and true Masons
are striving for, and which may be found in the Great Light of our
Fraternity in St. James 1 :27, "Pure religion undefiled before God
the Father is this-to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction,
and to keep himself unspotted from the world." That is the best definition of religion in the Bible, or out of, that we can find, and it rings true
to the teaching of every Masonic degree. A distinguished English playwright, George Bernard Shaw, who is also a prophet of our time, said
recently. "After all there is only one religion, though I know there are
more than a hundred versions of it." A good Craftsman, Lessing, said
more than a century ago, "Official, creedal and eccleciastical Christianity
has been on trial eighteen hundred years, the religion of Jesus has yet
to be tried."
Manitoba (1926):
(Grand Master): This is a quality of age. \Ve are apt to be narrow and intolerant in our younger years. Every institution is born in a
narrow bed-it is usually the expression of a single idea and that can
hardly avoid being bigoted. As time moves on we become mellowedour asperities are rubbed off-charity grows. Almost all societies are
exclusive in some one direction. Masonry stands as the very synonym
of tolerance. She has learned in her long passage down the years that

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

103

charity is the noblest virtue. If I were asked to name the most splendid
of the Masonic virtues I would unhesitatingly say tolerance. She knows
no racial barriers, she closes no doors against any human being on account
of his color, she raises no barrier of creed or class-kings and peasants,
rich and poor, Christian and Jew are found within her borders. There
is not a single criticism in all her ritual against any order, society, creed
or race. Her comer-stone is charity. She builds without walls or
boun,daries. Down the years she has travelled, passing through all
nations, and claiming the allegiance of all tongues and tribes. She seems
to me to offer a hope to the world today in its divided and antagonistic
state. Business is divisive, politics are separating, religion is sectarianMasonry alone offers a common ground for all the sons of men.

Georgia (1925):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Consequently there developed within the Fraternity a factor known as the "ritualist." He is not
to be confused with the advocate of efficient rendition of the degrees for
inspiring the candidate for the desire of knowledge.
A "ritualist" differs entirely from such a teacher. The "ritualist"
makes of the symbols a god : around rituali5m he has woven a religion
and science. In the Holy of Holies he has builded an altar of theatrical
drama and in his desire for ritualistic proficiency has overlooked the
ideal for which the symbol stands.
A skilled ritualist learns the secret work of Freemasonry until he
can say it backward, but he knows nothing of its application, even if he
be aware there is an application. Upon the other hand, the Intelligent
Craftsman can apply to life the lessons he learns from the symbols.
The danger that confronts our beloved Fraternity is an intensified
desire for outward pomp and pageantry and an increase in numbers. Too
much we are overlooking the need for inward progress in tone and
quality. We are µtore in danger from within than from without. The
alarm is being made upon the inner door.

A woman called us up the other day and wanted to know if we were a

any outsider, she wanted the name of both Master and Secretary. This
shows how utterly most, if not all, of us have become. She probably
knew that she could find out from someone anything she chose. This
should be a striking lesson to one and all of us. Which of us has not
thoughtlessly mentioned things said and done in Lodge? And yet we all
know that we should always be voluntarily deaf, dumb and blind as to
Lodge matters before any outsider, no matter whom.

Wisconsin (1927) :
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): This term, "profane," is
not used as a noun in the standard dictionaries, but is a term well understood by Freemasons. Mackey, in his Encyclopedia, says of it that it
"is compounded of the two Latin words, pro and fanum, and literally
means before or outside of the temple; hence a profane among the
ancients was one who was not allowed to enter the temple and behold the
mysteries." It seems to have quite respectable ancient authority to
authorize its use, as Mackey tells us in the celebrated hymn of Orpheus,
which it is said was sung at the Mysteries of Eleusis, this phrase is to be
met with: "I speak to those to whom it is lawful, but close the doors
against the profane." In the dialect of Freemasonry it has been adopted
as a technical term to signify merely that the person whom it is applied
to is not a Mason. We see no reason for avoiding its use.
SECRET ARIES
A large number of the Chairmen of Correspondence Committees also occupy the office of Grand Secretary. They speak
from experience when they say that the efficiency of a Lodge
depends upon the zeal and ability of this particular officer. A
Secretary not only performs his function in the Lodge but sometimes (?) "superintends it during the hours of refreshment."
Alabama (1926):
(Grand 1vfaster) : Much of the correspondence received by me during the year indicates that the only qualifications required by many lodges
to be possessed by those chosen as secretary of the Lodge are carelessness
and incompetency. The ignorance and unfitness of many of these socalled secretaries is truly astonishing. They can· neither write, spell,
punctuate, nor compose, and have not the slightest idea of form. llow
they can keep an intelligible minute or a correct record of collections
made and the dispostions of the funds or conduct the most meagre correspondence of the Lodge is a mystery to me. They may be and no doubt
are excellent men and Masons, but this, one of the most important offices
in a lodge, should not be committed into the hands of an incompetent
brother. I have no doubt the death of many a Lodge is traceable to an
incompetent and unsuitable secretary. Let me impress on the Lodges, if

Kansas (1927):
(Grand Secretary) : Your Grand Secretary noted with care the
various forms used by Lodges in paying their annual per capita tax and
out of the total payments 181 plainly indicated that the funds were neither
being kept nor dispensed according to law.
Each year the number of cases of misappropriation of Lodge funds
is increasing, which indicates that the law concerning the keeping and
dispensing of the moneys of Lodges is being violated.
While it is not expedient to list any number of the many forms
used in payment of Grand Lodge dues, yet as an illustration attention is
called to the following :
One remittance was issued by a Building and Loan Association;
another was in the form of a check signed by the Senior Warden ; a
number were checks issued by business firms; a large number of individual checks signed only by the brother having the account in the bank
in his own name ; other remittances were made over the signature of
the Secretary, indicating that he was in charge of the funds of the Lodge;
others were signed with the name of the Treasurer, by the Sceretary,
indicating that the Secretary could check out Lodge funds. This practice
is not confined to the small Lodges alone, but enters into the financial
affairs of the larger Lodges as well.
Manitoba (1926):
(Grand Master) : It has come to my notice that some Secretaries

such information. The fact of a brother's membership in a Masonic
Lodge is a sacred trust to be communicated by the Secretary only on
explicit instructions from the Worshipful Master, and for sufficient
cause. It is desirable that each Master should so instruct his Secretary.

Utah (1926):
(Grand Master): I observe from the Lodge returns that in at least
one case a very young Mason has been elected Secretary of his Lodge.
The Secretary of a Lodge might be likened to the hub of a wheel. If
he is the right kind of man he is the center of Lodge activities and is
usually retained in office as long as he is willing to keep the job. The
Secretary can be and nearly always is the Master's most trusted and
valued lieutenant. There may have been particular reasons for the
choice in this case, but it seems to me that Lodges ought to exercise great
care in the selection of a Secretary and that generally speaking he ought
to be a seasoned member of the Craft.

TEMPLES
Building Masonic Temples must be governed by the same rules
that apply to any other business proposition. Too often the building
of a Temple and the financial operation thereafter ends in disaster.
Questionable methods are sometimes adopted for the purpose of
raising funds. After the enthusiasm and interest in the beginning
of the project .have evaporated the burden rests heavy upon a few.
It would be a wise provision, and in many cases would save endless
trouble, if before a Lodge erected a building the entire project
should be passed upon by disinterested parties, created and authorized
to deal with such a question. This might be either the Grand Master
himself or a Grand Lodge Committee created for that purpose.
Georgia (1926):
(Grand. Master) : A Masonic hall may be rented to the Knights of
the Ku Klux Klan for their regular meetings, the closing paragraph of
Section 275 of the Masonic Manual and Code reading as follows: "A
Lodge shall not ·rent its Masonic hall for other than Masonic purposes
except for benevolent, charitable or other secret organizations, nor shall
it be used for dancing." The Klan being both a secret and a charitable
organization, therefore comes under the exceptions specified as being
eligible to meet in the Masonic hall.
Indiana (1926):
(Grand Master) : While it is important that the members of a
Lodge in session should by all means attend the meetings of the Lodge
rather than engage in social entertainments, I do not know of any good
reason why the social quarters of the building should be kept dark in
order to induce or force the members of the Lodge in session to attend
their Lodge. I assume that you have some sort of Masonic work in
your building most of the time, and to compel the social room to be
kept dark when any one of the Lodges is in session would, in practice,
mean that your social rooms would be dark most of the time, if not all

It has been my idea that a Masonic Temple, especially such as

where a Mason can be assured of an "open house" any week day night.

Kansas (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : During the year eight of
their Lodges (Georgia) were burned and of this number but three had
any insurance. The question might consistently be raised whether Grand
Lodges should not compel all Lodges to carry sufficient insurance to

(Grand Master): There comes a time in the life of every ambitious
man when he outgrows his habitation and reaches out for better and
larger accommodations; so it has been with many of our Lodges over the
State; magnificent temples, beautifully furnished and splendidly equipped,
have gratified this laudable ambition, but in too many instances the
"pay as you go" plan has been relegated to the background and Lodges
have become so involved in debt that it is proving not only burdensome
to the members but detrimental to the Lodge as well.
We point with pride to our beautiful edifices, but this erection of
costly temples should not be undertaken until a substantial sum has been
accumulated for their building and equipment.
Perhaps the most serious trouble, arising in our Lodges the past
year or two, is the result of improper and inadequate plans for financing
their undertakings and in addition to the architect's plans being passed
upon, I believe the manner of financing new temples should be under the
observation and with the approval of the Grand Master.
Unsatisfactory results have followed the issuance of life memberships in return for funds advanced to finance building projects.
At least the certificate plan should be adopted rather than the blanket
mortgage plan, for by the former plan all feel a personal interest in the
undertaking and consider their stock as an investment for their own
personal good and for the good of the Fraternity in their locality.

New Hampshire (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): He (Chairman Correspondence Committee, 1926) invokes the Spirit of Masonry to keep out
of Masonic halls anything and everything that is not Masonic. Bless you.
that old spirit has deceased. A new spirit has taken its place. There is
to be no resurrection of the old. The new has come to stay, until it, in
the interpretation of our life and efforts, shall in turn pass on it. We
cannot avoid progress, we cannot stifle our visions, if we are to have
any excuse for our organic life. We have not changed-we are merely
giving better expression to our desires and to our hopes. We are whiteheaded, getting down the hill, but these things do not disturb us. Rather
do they tend to make us feel that this thing we call Freemasonry shall
never die.

North Carolina (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Grand Master Davenport
alluded to certain irregularities and unfortunate matters, along with others
more in happy vein. Among the former is a discussion of the experiences
which have been observed in various places with the financing and erection of Masonic Temples. In this connection it is well to remember the
wise observation of our distinguished friend and brother, Benjamin

for an impecunious person to be honest as for an empty sack to stand

better that it were not thus to become a burden in this manner to its
owners. It is an honor to own a handsome Temple; but that honor is
changed to disgrace, if it has to be paid for through the income from
questionable tenants, and questionable uses.

THIRD DEGREE LECTURE
Some of the Jurisdictions requiring an examination in the
lecture of the Master Mason's Degree a prerequisite to membership
have found that the theory does not always produce the desired
results. As we understand it, the true province of instruction along
this line is to enable a brother to satisfactorily establish the fact
that he is a Master Mason on visiting another Lodge. If this be
so, the questions and answers should be in such a form that learning
them would not involve a hardship, could be easily remembered, and
therefore would be of practical use. Too often Members refrain
from visiting other Lodges or Jurisdictions because of a fear that
they cannot satisfactorily answer a set of routine questions.
North Carolina (1927):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Speaking further of
Masonic Education, we note that North Dakota has beome awakened to
the fact that learning by rote the lecture of the Master Mason's degree

115

* * *

If the great aim of Masonry were rote-memory work, we should
look well upon that requirement to learn the catechism of the third degree
in six months. But if we were going to judge between rote-memory work
and some good Masonic reading, as to which was more important to the
newly-raised Mason, we should without hesitation take the latter. Therefore, we promise the Masonic woorld that if we should be Grand Master
we should recommend that every Master Mason be required to read ten
good Masonic books out of a multiple list which we should offer, within
the space of a year or two, and certify that he had read them carefully.

Oregon (1927):
(Grand Master) : Probably no sections of the Code are causing more
confusion in this Jurisdiction than Sections 203 and 218. Under an interpretation of these sections no brother is entitled to a certificate of membership, nor is he entitled to sign the by-laws of his Lodge until after he
has passed satisfactorily an examination iii the lecture of the Third
Degree. These sections which raise the question, "When is a man a
Mason?" are not popular with the Craft, and in the opinion of many
are in direct conflict with the fourteenth landmark. The provisions of
these sections may be beautiful in theory but in practice they are a
nuisance and should be amended in conformity with the true spirit of
Masonry.

Wisconsin (1927) :
(Chairman C01·respondeiice Committee) : The Grand Master of
North Dakota ( 1926) recommended the repeal of the regulation requiring
all Master Masons to pass a satisfactory examination upon the lecture
of the Master Mason's Degree. The regulation not only barred them
from voting, holding office in the Lodge or demitting therefrom, but they
were not entitled to a receipt for current year's dues paid until such
examination had been pa5sed. After investigating the working of this
legislation he said :
"The law apparently is incapable of enforcement, and with nearly a
thousand brethren raised in this Jurisdiction who are not yet entitled
to be considered as Master Masons, I would respectfully recommend that
the legislation be repealed. It is my humble opinion that Masonic education will do more toward making these brethren real Masons than drastic
legislation of this character will ever accomplish."
It is the old story of leading a horse to water but being unable to
make him drink when there. His recommendation was adopted.
VISITATION
The fundamental idea of Masonry is Brotherhood, and unless
this is put into practical operation, one of the beauties of Masonry
is lost. It has been truly said that "you can't hate a man that you
know," and "one of the tragedies of human existence is that men
are strangers."

Nevada (1926) :
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Visitations are a power for
good. Contact with different brethren adds a new force to Masonry,
blessing both visitor and the visited. The mind unbends agreeably when
among friends tried and true. New thoughts are engendered and enthusiasm is rekindled for what is good and great, all for the good of the
Craft. Visitations are like the little fountains that run down from the
hills. They refresh and stimulate a better growth for the good of all.
Rhode Island (1926):
(Grand Maste1·): Procedure for Examination and Introduction of
Visitors. The keynote of the procedure of examination is that it is a
conference of brethren, in which two groups, one of one member and
one of two, each satisfy each other of their mutual brotherhood. The
instant the examining committee is satisfied that the visitor is a regular
Mason, in good standing, courtesy, brotherly regard, and good manners
require that they should say so, and introduce him to the Master.
Charity of thought, toleration, kindness and courtesy are all Masonic
virtues, and there is no better place where they can be practised, than at
the door of your Masonic home, for the benefit of the stranger who would
refresh himself at your Altar.
The visitor having applied for examination, the Junior Warden
will appoint a committee of not less than two brethren, who will provide
themselves with the Holy Bible, Square, Compasses, and Apron and
proceed to the examining room with the visitor. They will request him
to sign his name, together with the name of his Lodge, on a card provided for that purpose, and then ask for his credentials for comparison,
first satisfying themselves that such credentials as he may present are
from a Lodge within a Grand Jurisdiction that is recognized by this Grand
Jurisdiction.
The committee, together with the visitor, shall then place their right
hand on the open Bible and repeat together the Tyler's Oath as follows:
I, ......................................................, do hereby and hereon, solemnly and
sincerely swear, that I have been duly initiated, passed and raised, to the
sublime degree of Master Mason, in a just and lawfully constituted Lodge
of such; that I do not now stand suspended or expelled, and know of
no reason why I should not hold Masonic communication with my brethren. So help me God.

dignity, will travel farther than sound with "jazz."

"BOUQUETS AND BRICKBATS"
The excerpts from the Repofts of the Committees on Correspondence of the respective Jurisdictions reviewed furnishes a mirror in
which we may see ourselves.
As in the past, the writer receives "the brickbats."
In this report we have given the author of the portions selected
from the various proceedings. This will fix the responsibility, and
we hope remove some criticism to the "topical form."
Our form of Report, of course, will always be criticised, but this
is a day of organization and condensation. The success of the
tabloid newspaper, magazine and "Cycs" demonstrates, we believe,
that the .average person wants facts, figures and opinions in the
most compact form possible. As a matter of fact the Correspondence
Report reaches only those who receive the advance copies at- the
session of the Grand Lodge, and the Correspondence Committees of
other Jurisdictions. If we had the. experience and the ability of
those who write reviews by Jurisdictions, we perh,aps would be
tempted to use that method.
·
Realizing our limitations in that respect we _have endeavored to
furnish what we believe is desired by the members of this Jurisdiction. There is also the hope that from a reference standpoint oui:
Reports might be worthy of preservation for future use.
The 76th Annual Communication, San Francisco, Oct. 15-16, 1925.
David J. Reese, Grand Master.

Even away back in the eastern section of America is felt the inspiration of our California brethren.

Those who know California Freemasonry, and particularly those

How well we remember our visit to England in 1919, when we met

Bi-Centenary of the Grand Lodge of Ireland, where he represented the
Grand Lodge of California.
A masterful address by Grand Orator Robert B. Gaylord on the
needs of the day presents striking paragraphs.
Worshipful James Lewis Matthews, who succeeded Brother Jesse M.
Whited last year, writes the reviews and steps aside for Brother Whited
to resume the work. The report of Brother Matthews is brief, and it
does not seem to occur to him that his California brethren may be interested in what the various reviewers think of California.

The address of Grand Master Reese proves conclusively that he
devoted much time and thought to the affairs of that Grand Lodge. It
is also one of the most comprehensive addresses it has been my good
fortune so far to review. \Vhile some of the matters discussed may be

new angles and in such a spirit of moderation and fair play that the
report makes good reading. The entire address is of such uniform
excellence that it is hard to decide what to quote and what to discard.
The Grand Secretary made two suggestions which are well worthy
of consideration by our Grand Lodge.
Pleasing reference was made to the celebration of the Bi-Centenary

Brother Jesse M. Whited, who wrote such outstanding reviews for
California (even if they were topical), apparently dropped out for a
year, as I note what is to me a new writer at the desk. The reports.
while condensed, are presented in a very readable form, evince a kindly

"FOUND IN THE QUARRIES"
One of the objections to a topical form of Correspondence
Report is the fact that the reader is unable to learn what has been
or is being done in other Jurisdictions. The selections given under
the various topics, we believe, represent the opinions of those
designated by their Grand Lodges to speak for their respective
Jurisdictions. -iJnder the above caption we have summarized the
activities of the various Grand Lodges. In compiling this data
we have made liberal use of the Report of Committee on Correspondence of the Grand Lodge of New York, particularly the work
of those Jurisdictions whose proceedings are in a foreign language.
We have also found therein information regarding other Jurisdictions
whose Reports were not received by us.
Alabama (1926):
The Grand Orient of France having taken under life protection "a
clandestine organization in Pennsylvania, claiming to be Masonic," th~
Grand Master recommended that "all fraternal relations between the
Grand Lodge of Alabama and the Grand Orient of France" be severed.
The recommendation was adopted.
The Grand Master ruled that "it is un-Masonic to mention in ad~
vertisements of political meetings that the speaker is a Mason or an official of Grand Lodge.
Edict No. 293 requires that a Mason in Alabama shall "believe in
God, the Creator and Governor of the Universe," and our Ritual says
that "no atheist can be made a Mason." Therefore, in Alabama, it is a
Masonic offense for a Mason to declare that he does not believe in Deity."
Two hundred and fifty dollars were appropriated for the International Ma$onic Asylum of Cuba toward the repair of the damage done
by a severe storm.
Co~ticut (1926) :

Grand Lodge voted to require the Lodges to pay $2.50 for each "taxable" member, $2.15 of this per capita to go to the Masonic Charity
Foundation and thirty-five cents to be appropriated for defraying the general expenses of Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master recommended also that the National Masonic
Tuberculosis Sanatoria Association, established by the Grand Lodge of
New Mexico, be indorsed and given support. Grand Lodge responded
by voting $500 toward the Emergency Relief Fund of that Association.

There was appointed also a special Committee on Education. Past

"Preparation," embodying helpful instruction for candidates who desire to
become Freemasons in fact as well as in name, was printed for distribution in order to start initiates right.
Among the corner-stone layings of the year was that of a new Children's Building of the Masonic and Eastern Star Home.
Fraternal relations were established with the Grand Lodge of Vienna.
The new Children's Building at the Masonic Eastern Star Home is
rapidly nearing completion. It will cost approximately $125,000.00, with
an additional cost of $10,000.00 for furniture. Fifty-two children are
taken care of in the Home.
The Grand Chaplain reports a continuance of the open-air afternoon
services from June 20th to October 17th on the spacious grounds of
Temple Heights, the new site for the projected Masonic Temple.
A resolution was adopted that no new Lodge shall be named "after
a living Mason nor for one who has not rendered conspicuous service to
a Grand Lodge or to one of its constituent Lodges."

Eight of the Lodges in the State lost their Temples by fire, and

The Lodges are warned by the Grand Master not to let their enthusiasm lead them into building enterprises which are likely to embarrass them financially for many years.

Cuba (1926) :

The Grand Lodge of Cuba publishes an official organ which is edited
by the Grand Secretary'. It was founded in 1881 and is an exceptionally
good Masonic periodical and important for noteworthy historical articles.
Every year, on December 5th, is held a Masonic Day. The chief
feature is a public meeting held in one of the theatres of the capital city
under the direction of the Grand Master. In the various Masonic districts similar public meetings are held at least four times a year, to let
the public judge the character of the men and to get reliable information
concerning the objects of the Craft.

In the Northern Jurisdiction (which includes all States North
of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River); the degrees
conferred are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 ° to 14 °, inclusive; Council
Princes of Jerusalem, 15° and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and 18°;
Consistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.

AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are
generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly
speaking, they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish Rite, for the one commonly called York is peculiar in its organized proceedings only to the United States.
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.
The Symbolic degrees are conferred in a lodge and are the Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They
are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction is
by symbols.
The Capitular degrees are conferred in a Royal Arch Chapter
and are the Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent
Master and the Royal Arch. The supplemental and honorary degrees of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of High Priests
upon those who have been regularly elected to preside over a
Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. They are called Capitular because
they are conferred in a Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning
"done in a Chapter."
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the
Royal Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called Cryptic because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight
Templar comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take
the temple at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the 33rd,
inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States (which
includes all territory south of the Ohio River and west of the Mississippi River) the organization of the different bodies, and the degrees
conferred by them are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 ° to 14 °, inclusive;
Chapter Rose Croix, 15° to 18°; Council of Kadosh, 19° to 30°;
Consistory, 31° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.

MASONIC CALENDAR
Ancient Craft Masons--Commence their era with the creation of
the world, calling it Anno Lucis (A. L.), "in the year of light."
Scottish Rite-Same as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish chronology is used. Anno Mundi (A. M.), "in the year of the world."
Royal Arch Masons-Date from the year the second temple was
commenl'.ed. by Zerubbabel, Anno Inventionis. (A. Inv.), "in the
year of discovery."
Royal and Select Master&--Date from the year in which the
Temple of Solomon was completed, Anno Depositionis (A. Dep.),
"in the year of the deposit."
Knight& Templar-Commence their era with the organization of
their order. Anno Ordinis (A. 0.), "in the year of the Order."
Order of High Priesthood-Dates from the year of the blessing
of Abraham by the High Priest Melchizedek, Anno Benedictionis
(A. B.), "in the year of the blessing."
RULES FOR MASONIC DATES
Ancient Craft Masons-Add 4000 years to the common era. Thus:
1923 and 4000-5923.
Scottish Rite-Add 3760 to the common era. Thus: 1923 and
3760-5683. After September add another year.
Royal Arch-Add 530 years to the vulgar era. Thus: 1923 and
530-2453.
Royal and Select Masters-Add 1000 to the common time. Thus:
1923 and 1000-2923.
Knights Templar-From the Christian era take 1118. Thus:
1118 from 1923-805.
Order of High Priesthood-To the Christian era add 1913, the
year of blessing. Thus: 1923 and 1913-3836.
